questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.e: (Repeat of Q67.) The intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage — the exception, C.

questions.q: Why is the outer layer of skin (epidermis) specifically keratinized, while the epithelium lining the esophagus — although also stratified squamous — is not?
o: The esophagus cannot regenerate, so keratin is unnecessary there
There is no functional reason; keratinization is random
Keratin only forms in tissues that lack a basement membrane

The epidermis needs a tough, water-resistant surface exposed to the external environment, while the esophagus needs a moist surface resistant to abrasion from swallowed food, without needing waterproofing
questions.e: Keratinization equips the epidermis with a tough, waterproof surface suited to protecting against the external environment, whereas the esophagus needs a moist, abrasion-resistant lining for swallowed food but does not require waterproofing, so it remains non-keratinized.

questions.q: True or False: Taking folic acid during pregnancy can help minimise the likelihood of cleft palate.
questions.e: True. The notes state that the likelihood of cleft palate is minimised by taking folic acid during pregnancy.

questions.q: A doctor opens the chest wall to access the heart for emergency surgery. This procedure is known as:
questions.e: A thoracotomy is a surgical incision through the chest wall — D. (-stomy = opening/drain; -scopy = scope; -centesis = needle aspiration.)

questions.q: Which best distinguishes the perichondrium (covering cartilage) from the periosteum (covering bone) in terms of a key functional similarity, despite covering different tissues?
o: Only the periosteum contains any cells at all
The perichondrium supplies blood vessels directly into the cartilage matrix, unlike the periosteum
Both serve as nutrient-supplying, protective outer membranes for their respective connective tissue, and both contain cells capable of contributing to growth or repair
They serve entirely unrelated functions with no meaningful similarity
questions.e: Despite covering different tissues, the perichondrium and periosteum share a key functional similarity: both act as protective, nutrient-supplying outer membranes containing cells (chondrogenic or osteogenic) capable of contributing to the growth or repair of the underlying tissue.

questions.q: Which muscle of the rotator cuff is described as the strongest?
questions.e: Among the rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus), the supraspinatus is described as the strongest.

questions.q: A small foramen at the base of the frontal crest, used for passage of vessels during development, is called the:
questions.e: The foramen caecum is located at the base of the frontal crest and is a small foramen for passage of vessels during embryonic development.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in all the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: Urothelium lines the renal pelvis, ureter, bladder and prostatic urethra. The membranous urethra is stratified/pseudostratified columnar — the exception.

questions.q: A man puts his foot on a table while standing to lace his shoe. At this point the hip would be in which position?
questions.e: Lifting the thigh up onto the table decreases the hip angle = flexion — B.

questions.q: In anatomical position, the scapula lies posterolateral to which ribs?
questions.e: The scapula is a large, flattened triangular bone that lies posterolateral to the 2nd through 7th ribs in the normal anatomical position.

questions.q: MULTIAXIAL JOINT
o: Universal movement is allowed in all axis
Rotation is allowed in all axis
An example is the shoulder joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Multiaxial (ball-and-socket) joints allow universal movement including rotation in all axes; the shoulder joint is a classic example.

questions.q: Which best captures why the thyroid gland, despite being made of epithelial tissue arranged in follicles, is classified functionally as endocrine rather than exocrine?
o: The thyroid actually has a duct that has simply never been observed
It secretes hormones directly into surrounding capillaries rather than through a duct system onto a surface
Endocrine glands must always be shaped like follicles
It has no epithelial cells at all
questions.e: Despite being epithelial in origin, the thyroid is functionally endocrine because its follicular cells secrete hormones directly into the surrounding rich capillary network rather than through a duct system to an epithelial surface — duct presence or absence is the defining functional criterion.

questions.q: How many cervical vertebrae are typically present in the body?
questions.e: There are 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7) in virtually all humans (and most mammals).

questions.q: True or False: The two parts of the ischiopubic rami typically fuse by the 9th year of life.
questions.e: The ischiopubic rami (the inferior ramus of the pubis and the ramus of the ischium) usually fuse together by around 9 years of age, earlier than the main triradiate fusion at the acetabulum.

questions.q: 'Nursemaid's elbow' refers to which condition?
o: Radial head subluxation pulled out of the annular ligament
questions.e: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) occurs when the radial head is traumatically pulled out of its normal position within the annular ligament, common in young children pulled by the arm.

questions.q: A weightlifter's shoulders visibly rise toward the ears when bracing under a heavy load. Which term describes this upward movement of the shoulder girdle?
questions.e: Elevation is the upward movement of a body part, such as the shoulders rising, and is the opposite of depression.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding the cells of connective tissue.
o: "Blast" cells are undifferentiated, actively dividing cells
Connective tissue does not contain cells
Chondroblasts are the main cell type of connective tissue proper
questions.e: "-blast" cells (fibroblasts, osteoblasts, chondroblasts) are immature, actively dividing matrix-producing cells — D. (Fibroblasts, not chondroblasts, dominate CT proper.)

questions.q: All the following are bilateral organs EXCEPT:
questions.e: Lungs, kidneys and testes are paired (bilateral). The paper's answer is the brain (a single midline organ) — A. Note: the spleen is also a single, unpaired organ, so this question is a bit ambiguous — but the exam key marks A.

questions.q: A patient experiences a sudden allergic reaction, with localized swelling and redness at the site of an insect sting. Which connective tissue cell type, releasing histamine and heparin from its granules, is most directly responsible for triggering this response?
questions.e: Mast cells release histamine and heparin from their granules during allergic and inflammatory responses, directly producing the swelling and redness characteristic of a localized allergic reaction.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly reflects the relative abundance of interneurons compared to sensory and motor neurons combined?
o: Interneurons are extremely rare, making up less than 1% of neurons
Interneurons do not actually exist as a distinct category
Sensory, motor, and interneurons exist in exactly equal numbers
Interneurons vastly outnumber sensory and motor neurons combined, comprising roughly 99.98% of all neurons in the body
questions.e: Interneurons, confined to the CNS and providing the integrative link between sensory and motor neurons, vastly outnumber the other two functional categories combined, comprising approximately 99.98% of all neurons in the body.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the femur?
o: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: The distal femur bears the condyles, adductor tubercle, intercondylar notch, and patellar surface. The gluteal tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest (C) belong to the proximal/shaft region, not the distal end.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the paranasal sinuses?
o: Paranasal sinuses enhance the resonance of the voice and lighten the skull.
Paranasal sinuses contain passages acting as one-way valves.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, frontal and lacrimal bones.
Paranasal sinuses open into the oral cavity.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, ethmoid, and lacrimal bones.
questions.e: The paranasal sinuses (in frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid, maxillary bones — not the lacrimal) reduce skull weight and add resonance to the voice.

questions.q: The pectoral girdle is composed of the
questions.e: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle consists of the clavicle and scapula; the humerus is part of the free upper limb, not the girdle.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining why hip disease can cause referred pain in the knee?
questions.e: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, which explains why hip joint disease sometimes presents with referred pain felt in the knee.

questions.q: A structure needs to allow substances to diffuse in from surrounding tissue while also providing a physical framework — but must NOT contain blood vessels of its own. Which of the following tissues satisfies this description?
questions.e: Cartilage uniquely fits this description among connective tissues generally, being avascular (no blood vessels of its own) yet still providing structural support, relying entirely on diffusion for nutrient exchange.

questions.q: True or False: In females, the sacrum and coccyx show greater curvature, arcing further into the pelvic outlet compared to males.
questions.e: It is the male sacrum and coccyx that arc more sharply into the pelvic outlet; the female sacrum and coccyx show LESS curvature, helping to enlarge the pelvic outlet for childbirth.

questions.q: Given that regenerating peripheral axons grow toward their distal targets at roughly 1.5 mm per day, approximately how long would you predict it might take an axon to regrow across a 3 cm gap, assuming ideal conditions (intact neurolemma, small gap)?
o: Regrowth speed is unrelated to distance
questions.e: At a rate of approximately 1.5 mm per day, regrowth across a 3 cm (30 mm) gap would be predicted to take roughly 20 days under otherwise ideal regenerative conditions.

questions.q: Rheumatism is best defined as:
o: A type of synovial fluid abnormality
A fracture of the epiphyseal plate
Any painful disorder of supporting structures not caused by infection or injury
questions.e: Rheumatism is defined as any painful disorder of the body's supporting structures that is NOT due to infection or injury.

questions.q: "Stove-in-chest" is another name for which condition?
questions.e: Flail chest, caused by multiple adjacent rib fractures in more than one place, is also called a stove-in-chest because the loose segment moves paradoxically with breathing.

questions.q: True or False: The lunate carpal bone is part of the distal row of carpal bones.
questions.e: The lunate belongs to the proximal row of carpal bones (scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform), not the distal row.

questions.q: How is hyaline cartilage DIFFERENT from elastic or fibrocartilage?
questions.e: In hyaline cartilage the type II collagen is masked by ground substance, so fibres aren't visible under the light microscope — C. Elastic and fibrocartilage show visible fibres.

questions.q: A fibrous sheath that surrounds and protects individual fascicles of a muscle is called
questions.e: The perimysium wraps individual fascicles (bundles of muscle fibers); endomysium wraps individual fibers, epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

questions.q: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of which nerve and vessels?
questions.e: The supraorbital notch or foramen allows passage of the supraorbital nerve and accompanying vessels, supplying the forehead and scalp.

questions.q: Cranial nerves VII and VIII pass through which structure?
questions.e: The internal acoustic (auditory) meatus transmits cranial nerves VII (facial) and VIII (vestibulocochlear) into the petrous temporal bone.

questions.q: An area of the body exposed to the external environment would be composed of which tissue type?
questions.e: External surfaces are covered by epithelium — A.

questions.q: A cervical rib, an accessory rib arising from C7, is most strongly associated with which clinical condition?
questions.e: A cervical rib can compress the neurovascular bundle (brachial plexus and subclavian vessels) as they pass through the thoracic outlet, producing thoracic outlet syndrome. Flail chest results from multiple rib fractures, not an accessory rib.

questions.q: Most elbow dislocations occur in which direction, named by the position of the ulna and radius?
questions.e: Elbow dislocations are mostly posterior, and are named according to the position of the ulna and radius relative to the humerus, not the humerus itself.

questions.q: The bone(s) of the leg which bears no weight is/are
questions.e: The fibula bears essentially no body weight (its main roles are muscle attachment and ankle stability).

questions.q: Which characteristic of epithelial tissue would you expect in a duct subject to a high degree of pressure?
questions.e: High pressure/abrasion demands multiple protective layers → stratified layering — D.

questions.q: Joints are classified functionally according to which criterion?
o: The embryological origin of the bones
The amount of movement permitted at the joint
The number of bones meeting at the joint
The blood supply to the joint
questions.e: The functional classification of joints is based purely on the amount of movement allowed at the joint, giving the categories synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, and diarthrosis.

questions.q: A typical (thoracic-pattern) vertebra consists of a body and which other major component?
questions.e: A typical vertebra consists of a body and a vertebral (neural) arch, which together enclose the vertebral foramen housing the spinal cord.

questions.q: The elbow joint is composed of how many distinct articulations?
questions.e: The elbow joint comprises three distinct articulations: humero-ulnar, humeroradial, and superior radio-ulnar.

questions.q: A small foramen on the zygomatic bone, generally visible and used for passage of a sensory nerve, is the:
questions.e: The zygomaticofacial foramen is a small foramen typically visible on the anterior surface of the zygomatic bone.

questions.q: Muscle tone, important for maintaining posture, is best defined as:
o: Tension present in a relaxed muscle
The size of a muscle belly
questions.e: Muscle tone refers to the baseline tension present in a relaxed muscle, which is important for joint stability and posture.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the:
questions.e: The intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage, not elastic — the exception, C.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why cartilage, though technically part of the skeletal framework, is NOT typically visible on a standard X-ray the way bone is?
o: Cartilage is actually invisible to all forms of medical imaging
X-rays can only detect soft tissue, not hard tissue
Cartilage is less dense than bone and does not absorb X-rays as strongly, so it appears far less distinct on X-ray images
Cartilage contains no matrix at all
questions.e: X-ray contrast depends on tissue density — dense bone absorbs more radiation and appears clearly white, while less dense cartilage absorbs far less, making it much less distinct on a standard X-ray compared to bone.

questions.q: T1, an atypical thoracic vertebra, has costal facets on its body that are described as:
questions.e: T1 has circular upper costal facets on its body, along with smaller, semilunar inferior facets, distinguishing it from typical thoracic vertebrae.

questions.q: A researcher wants to identify the specific junction type responsible for mechanically binding epidermal cells together so the skin can resist friction and stretching without cells tearing apart. Which junction is most directly responsible?
questions.e: Desmosomes are spot-like junctions that mechanically anchor adjacent cells together, giving epithelium (such as the epidermis) resistance to mechanical stress like friction and stretching.

questions.q: Most synchondroses are permanent structures that persist throughout adult life.
questions.e: False. Most synchondroses are temporary structures that disappear during growth, such as the articulation between the diaphysis and epiphysis.

questions.q: Which best explains why bone tissue, despite being extremely hard, is not brittle and completely inflexible like a ceramic?
o: Bone contains organic collagen fibers alongside its mineral component, and this collagen provides some flexibility and tensile strength that pure mineral would lack
Bone's hardness comes entirely from water content
Bone is actually a type of cartilage with added calcium
Bone contains no minerals at all
questions.e: Bone's composite structure — mineral salts (hydroxyapatite) providing hardness, combined with organic type I collagen fibers providing some flexibility and tensile strength — is what prevents it from being as brittle as a purely mineral (ceramic-like) material would be.

questions.q: A characteristic feature of T9 is that it:
o: Has costal facets on transverse processes only
Has the largest body of all vertebrae
Fails to form joints with the 10th rib and lacks inferior demifacets
questions.e: T9 is atypical because it fails to form joints with the 10th rib and has no inferior demifacets on the body, unlike typical thoracic vertebrae.

questions.q: In standard anatomical position, which bone of the forearm lies laterally?
questions.e: In anatomical position (forearm supinated, palm facing forward), the radius lies lateral and the ulna lies medial.

questions.q: A motor neuron specifically innervates skeletal muscle under voluntary control, as opposed to smooth muscle or glands. Which functional subtype of motor neuron is this?
o: Sensory motor neuron (not a real category)
questions.e: A motor neuron innervating skeletal muscle specifically is classified as a somatic motor neuron, in contrast to visceral (autonomic) motor neurons, which innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

questions.q: Which cranial bones are described as paired, rather than single unpaired bones?
questions.e: Among the eight cranial bones, the temporal and parietal bones are paired, whereas the frontal, occipital, sphenoid, and ethmoid bones are each single (unpaired).

questions.q: The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperflexion of the hip joint.
questions.e: False. The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperextension of the hip joint when standing, not hyperflexion.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements about the mandibular and the mental foramina of the mandible.
o: The mandibular foramen is on the lateral surface of the ramus and is for injecting anaesthetic
The mandibular foramen is on the medial surface of the ramus
The mental foramen is on the anterior part of the mandibular body
The mental foramen is on the anterolateral side of the mandibular body and is for blood vessels and nerves to the lower lip
questions.e: A and D correctly describe the two foramina: the mandibular foramen is on the ramus's MEDIAL surface (entry point for the inferior alveolar nerve block), and the mental foramen is anterolaterally on the body, transmitting vessels/nerves to the lower lip.

questions.q: The functional unit of skeletal muscle is the:
questions.e: The sarcomere (Z-line to Z-line) is the contractile/functional unit — A.

questions.q: During a pudendal nerve block performed to relieve perineal pain in childbirth, the nerve wraps around which structure before giving its branches?
questions.e: The pudendal nerve curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament before dividing into its terminal branches, making this region the target for a pudendal nerve block.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type forms the myelin sheath and neurolemma around a single axon at a time, in contrast to its CNS counterpart, which can myelinate multiple axon segments simultaneously?
questions.e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath and neurolemma in the PNS, and each Schwann cell myelinates only a single axon segment — in contrast to oligodendrocytes in the CNS, which can myelinate segments of multiple different axons.

questions.q: Which movement pair correctly represents true opposites at the same joint action?
questions.e: Elevation (upward movement) and depression (downward movement) are true opposites of the same action category; the other listed pairs mix unrelated movement types rather than being direct opposites.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can result in avascular necrosis of the femoral head.
Reason (R): The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery that supplies part of the femoral head.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.e: Both statements are true, and the Reason directly explains the Assertion: damage to the artery enclosed within the ligamentum teres compromises blood supply to the femoral head, leading to avascular necrosis.

questions.q: A structural engineer studying biological materials notes that compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units, each centered on a canal carrying blood vessels. What is the name of this repeating structural unit?
questions.e: Compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units called osteons (Haversian systems), each built around a central canal that carries blood vessels supplying the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: Which statement correctly relates gross anatomy and histology as subdivisions of anatomical study?
o: Gross anatomy is a subdivision of histology
Histology can only be performed on living patients, never on preserved tissue
Histology and gross anatomy study entirely unrelated organisms
Gross anatomy studies structures visible without magnification; histology studies tissue at the microscopic level — they examine different scales of the same body
questions.e: Gross anatomy and histology examine the same body at different scales — gross anatomy at the level visible to the naked eye, and histology at the microscopic tissue level — making them complementary subdivisions of anatomical study.

questions.q: Which of the following structures serves as a "seat" of the endocrine system by supporting the pituitary gland?
o: Greater wings of the sphenoid bone
Lesser wings of the sphenoid bone
questions.e: The sella turcica, a saddle-shaped depression on the sphenoid bone, cradles and supports the pituitary gland.

questions.q: The oblique groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus, which transmits the radial nerve, is also called the:
questions.e: The radial groove (spiral groove) runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humeral shaft and houses the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.

questions.q: Which hormone produced by bone tissue helps regulate bone formation?
questions.e: Bones produce osteocalcin, which helps regulate bone formation. Insulin, cortisol, and prolactin are produced by other endocrine tissues and are not specific bone-derived regulators of ossification mentioned here.

questions.q: Which neck of the humerus joins the proximal end to the shaft, and is clinically significant because fractures here can injure the axillary nerve?
questions.e: The surgical neck joins the proximal end of the humerus to the shaft. It is clinically important because the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wrap around it closely and are vulnerable in fractures here.

questions.q: Body weight is transferred from the vertebral column to the femurs via which sequence of joints?
o: Directly from sacrum to femur with no joints
questions.e: Weight passes from the vertebral column through the sacroiliac joints to the hip bones, and then through the hip joints to the femurs.

questions.q: Which articulation of the elbow is classified as a hinge joint?
questions.e: The humero-ulnar articulation, between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna, is a hinge joint.

questions.q: The lacrimal bone can be identified within which structure when viewing the lateral aspect of the skull?
questions.e: The lacrimal bone, housing the lacrimal sac, can be identified within the orbit on the lateral aspect of the skull.

questions.q: A structure lies closer to the trunk than the elbow but farther from the trunk than the shoulder joint. Which single directional term best captures its position relative to the elbow?
questions.e: Being nearer the point of attachment to the trunk than the elbow is means it is proximal relative to the elbow — proximal/distal describe relative nearness to the trunk along a limb.

questions.q: Which bone contains diaphysis and epiphysis areas and is proportionally more compact than spongy bone?
questions.e: As a typical long bone, the humerus has a diaphysis (shaft, mostly compact bone) and epiphyses, and is proportionally more compact than spongy.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements concerning the radius:
o: The proximal end consists of a head, neck and tuberosity
The distal end is expanded and bears a pointed process known as the styloid process
It articulates with the carpus proximally and the ulna medially
It is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
questions.e: C and D correctly describe the radius. A is wrong (the ulna is longer), and B mixes up proximal/distal relations (the radius articulates with the carpus distally, not proximally).

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the ethmoid bone?
o: Styloid process, inferior nasal conchae, jugular foramen and carotid canal
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, hypoglossal canal and foramen ovale
Crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate and superior nasal conchae
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: The ethmoid bone bears the crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate, and superior/middle nasal conchae.

questions.q: Excretory glands are classified as "simple branched tubular and merocrine" by the:
o: Mechanism of secretion and shape of secretory units
Presence or absence of ducts and mechanism of secretion
Types of secretory products and mechanism of secretion
Shape of secretory units and types of ducts only
Nature of the ducts, shape of secretory unit and mechanism of secretion
questions.e: "Simple/branched" = nature of the duct; "tubular" = shape of the secretory unit; "merocrine" = mechanism of secretion. All three axes are used — E.

questions.q: If the distal fragment in a distal radius fracture is displaced anteriorly instead of posteriorly, the injury is termed:
questions.e: Anterior displacement of the distal fragment, opposite to the classic Colles' pattern, is termed a reverse Colles' fracture, also known as a Smith's fracture.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about epithelia?
o: Stratified epithelia are associated with filtration
Simple epithelia are commonly found in areas of high abrasion
Endothelium provides a slick surface lining all hollow cardiovascular organs
questions.e: Endothelium gives a smooth low-friction lining to the heart and vessels — C. (High abrasion needs stratified; filtration needs simple squamous.)

questions.q: Which best explains why blood, despite being fluid, is still classified as a connective tissue rather than forming its own separate category?
o: Blood contains no cells, matching the definition of connective tissue matrix alone
Blood follows the general connective tissue pattern of cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — in blood's case, the fluid matrix is plasma
Blood is actually classified as a type of epithelial tissue
Connective tissue must always be solid, so blood does not truly qualify
questions.e: Blood fits the defining connective tissue pattern — cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — even though its matrix (plasma) is fluid rather than solid or gel-like, which is why it is classified as a specialized connective tissue.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements about aponeuroses.
o: Flattened sheets of dense connective tissue
Composed of collagenous bundles and fibroblasts
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Aponeuroses are flat, tendon-like sheets of dense regular CT (collagen bundles + fibroblasts) that attach to muscle sheets — all three true, E.

questions.q: An epithelium has microvilli and cilia. This epithelium:
o: Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses
Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually
Was involved with secretion or absorption
Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required
questions.e: Microvilli (absorption) + cilia (motility) → a surface needing absorption and motility — D.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synchondroses are typically permanent joints that persist unchanged throughout life.
Reason (R): The epiphyseal plate, a synchondrosis, eventually ossifies and disappears once skeletal growth is complete.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.e: The Reason is true — the epiphyseal plate does ossify and disappear after growth — but this fact disproves the Assertion, since it shows synchondroses are typically temporary, not permanent.

questions.q: The following are characteristics of the vertebral column EXCEPT
o: It has a chain of 33 individual vertebrae with 23 intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage
Only the thoracic and sacral curvatures are well developed at birth and are termed as primary curvatures
About 1/4 of the length is contributed by the 23 intervertebral discs
In the adult there are 29 vertebrae; 27 mobile, 2 immobile, and 20 intervertebral discs
The sacral curvature positions the weight of the upper part of the body over the lower limbs, providing optimal balance during standing
questions.e: The adult vertebral column has 26 bones (24 individual vertebrae + fused sacrum + fused coccyx) with 23 intervertebral discs — not 29 vertebrae with 20 discs, making E the false/incorrect statement.

questions.q: The prominent bump on the lateral aspect of the leg at the ankle joint is the
o: A lateral extension of the tibia
questions.e: The lateral malleolus, a distal projection of the fibula, forms the bony prominence on the lateral ankle.

questions.q: Which factor does NOT directly influence the stability of a synovial joint, according to the lecture?
questions.e: Stability depends on articular surface shape, ligament number/position, and muscle tone — blood type has no role in joint stability.

questions.q: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve (V2) passes through which foramen?
questions.e: The maxillary division of the trigeminal nerve, V2, passes through the foramen rotundum of the sphenoid bone.

questions.q: A pathology slide shows an epithelium that is one cell layer thick, with cube-shaped cells, lining small ducts of a gland. Which classification correctly names this tissue?
o: Pseudostratified cuboidal epithelium (not a real category)
questions.e: A single layer (simple) of cube-shaped (cuboidal) cells lining small ducts describes simple cuboidal epithelium, commonly found in gland ducts and kidney tubules.

questions.q: The pubis is divided into a body and two rami. Which two rami are these?
questions.e: The pubis is composed of a body plus a superior ramus and an inferior ramus, which together help form the obturator foramen and pubic arch.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type performs a supportive, protective role around neuron cell bodies within ganglia, functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS?
questions.e: Satellite cells (amphicytes), located in the PNS, surround and protect neuron cell bodies within ganglia, performing a role functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS.

questions.q: In an adult X-ray, the thin radiopaque line marking the former site of the epiphyseal plate is called the:
questions.e: Once growth is complete, the epiphyseal plate ossifies and is seen radiographically as a thin epiphyseal line.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a cranial bone?
questions.e: The maxilla is a facial bone, not one of the 8 cranial bones (frontal, 2 parietal, 2 temporal, occipital, sphenoid, ethmoid).

questions.q: The xiphoid process of the sternum is composed of which tissue in youth, before ossifying around age 40?
questions.e: The xiphoid process is composed of hyaline cartilage in youth and typically ossifies around age 40, occasionally remaining bifid or perforated.

questions.q: Cartilage is different from bone in that:
o: Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in the adult skeleton
Cartilage contains about 80% water and is more resilient
questions.e: Cartilage is ~70–80% water, avascular and more resilient/flexible — A. (It CAN calcify, and it regenerates poorly, so D and E are false.)

questions.q: Which best explains why a biopsy of transitional epithelium taken from a fully distended (stretched) bladder would look noticeably different from one taken from an empty bladder?
o: Transitional epithelium is destroyed each time the bladder empties and regenerates from scratch
Transitional epithelium's cells flatten and the tissue appears thinner when stretched, compared to the more rounded, dome-shaped, thicker appearance when relaxed
There is no visible difference regardless of bladder fullness
The cell type completely changes from squamous to columnar upon stretching
questions.e: Transitional epithelium's distinctive feature is that its surface cells flatten and the whole layer thins out when stretched (as in a full bladder), compared to the thicker, more rounded, dome-shaped appearance seen when the tissue is relaxed (as in an empty bladder).

questions.q: A synarthrosis is best described as which type of joint?
o: A joint with a synovial cavity
questions.e: Synarthrosis literally means 'joined together' and refers to an immovable joint, such as a suture, gomphosis, or synchondrosis.

questions.q: An electrophysiologist notes that a myelinated axon conducts impulses considerably faster than a comparable unmyelinated axon of similar diameter. Which property of myelin best explains this speed advantage?
o: Myelin has no effect on conduction speed; the difference must be due to axon length alone
Myelin contains its own independent nervous system
Myelin insulates the axon and prevents leakage of electrical current, increasing conduction speed
Myelin actively pumps ions across the membrane
questions.e: Myelin acts as an insulating layer around the axon, preventing leakage of electrical current and thereby increasing the speed of impulse conduction compared to an unmyelinated axon of similar diameter.

questions.q: Which bursa of the elbow is implicated in 'student's elbow' or 'miner's elbow'?
questions.e: The subcutaneous (olecranon) bursa, located between the olecranon and overlying connective tissue, is implicated in olecranon bursitis, also called student's or miner's elbow.

questions.q: True or False: The hyoid bone articulates directly with the mandible above it.
questions.e: False. The hyoid bone is unique in that it does not articulate with any other bone; it is suspended in the neck by muscles and ligaments.

questions.q: Acquired hip dislocation is most commonly seen in which direction, and is associated with risk to which nerve?
questions.e: Posterior dislocation accounts for about 90% of acquired hip dislocations, since the joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, and this may injure the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The presence of microvilli and cilia on a cell usually indicates that the cell functions in:
questions.e: Microvilli → absorption; cilia → surface motility. Together = absorption and motility — C.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis is also commonly known as:
questions.e: Prepatellar bursitis, caused by inflammation and swelling of the prepatellar bursa, is commonly called housemaid's knee.

questions.q: True or False: The medial tibial condyle is more prominent than the lateral condyle.
questions.e: It is the lateral condyle that is more prominent than the medial condyle, the opposite of this statement.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones contains a sinus?
questions.e: The maxilla contains the large maxillary sinus, one of the paranasal sinuses.

questions.q: Arthritis is best described as:
o: A muscle disorder unrelated to joints
A form of rheumatism with joint swelling, stiffness, and pain
questions.e: Arthritis is a form of rheumatism characterized by swollen, stiff, and painful joints, with causes including infection, metabolic disorders, trauma, and immune disorders.

questions.q: Which bone cell type is the exception that does NOT originate from mesenchymal cells?
questions.e: Osteoclasts are derived from hematopoietic (blood-forming) precursor cells, unlike osteogenic cells, osteoblasts, osteocytes, and bone lining cells, which all arise from mesenchymal cells.

questions.q: The classification of bony pelvis shapes (gynecoid, android, anthropoid, platypelloid) is attributed to which classification system?
questions.e: The Caldwell and Moloy classification describes the four basic types of bony pelvis: gynecoid, android, anthropoid, and platypelloid.

questions.q: A joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule is termed a/an:
questions.e: A sprain is a joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves muscle or tendon injury.

questions.q: A Colles' fracture of the distal radius classically produces which deformity?
questions.e: In a Colles' fracture, the distal fragment of the radius is displaced and tilted posteriorly, producing the characteristic dinner fork (or silver fork) deformity of the wrist.

questions.q: Which of the following ribs is a true rib?
questions.e: True ribs (1–7) attach directly to the sternum via their own costal cartilage; rib 7 is the last true rib.

questions.q: True or False: Both the clavicle and the femur can be used to estimate a person's stature because their length correlates with overall body height.
questions.e: While the femur is most classically used for stature estimation (1/4 to 1/3 of body height), long bone length generally correlates with stature, and forensic methods may also use other long bones including the humerus or, in some methods, account for the clavicle, though the femur remains the gold standard.

questions.q: In adults, new surface epithelial cells and the epithelial cells lining the intestine are derived from:
o: Mitotic division of existing epithelial cells
questions.e: Intestinal/epithelial turnover comes from stem cells (in the crypts) that divide and differentiate — B.

questions.q: Compared to the radius, the ulna is described as the:
o: Equal in length but more lateral
Shorter and more lateral bone of the forearm
Longer and more medial bone of the forearm
questions.e: The ulna is the longer of the two forearm bones and lies on the medial side, in contrast to the shorter, laterally placed radius.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of bone's dry weight is made up of organic components such as collagen fibres and cells?
questions.e: Organic components make up about 35% of the dry weight of bone, including cells, mostly type I collagen fibres, and ground substance.

questions.q: Extracellular matrix is composed of:
questions.e: The ECM = fibres + ground substance. Cells are NOT part of the matrix — B.

questions.q: The 'unhappy (terrible) triad' of knee injuries involves the ACL, medial meniscus, and which other structure?
questions.e: The unhappy triad involves the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial meniscus, and the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, common in contact sports with lateral knee blows.

questions.q: A single mucus-secreting cell is found scattered among absorptive columnar cells lining the intestine. What is this cell called, and how is it classified as a gland?
o: An endocrine follicular cell; ductless gland
A sweat gland cell; a multicellular exocrine gland
An osteoblast; a connective tissue cell, not a gland
A goblet cell; a unicellular exocrine gland
questions.e: This scattered, mucus-secreting single cell is a goblet cell, classified as a unicellular exocrine gland since it is a single specialized secretory cell embedded within an epithelial layer.

questions.q: The muscular system:
o: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression
questions.e: Manipulation, locomotion & expression, posture and heat production are all muscular functions — E.

questions.q: True or False: The patella is a classic example of a sesamoid bone.
questions.e: True. The patella forms within the quadriceps tendon and is the textbook example of a sesamoid bone, protecting the tendon from compressive forces at the knee.

questions.q: The greater and lesser palatine foramina, located posterolaterally on the hard palate, transmit:
o: Nerves and vessels of the same name
questions.e: The greater and lesser palatine foramina transmit the greater and lesser palatine nerves and vessels respectively, supplying the palate.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a plane joint?
questions.e: The acromioclavicular joint is listed as a plane joint, alongside intertarsal, intercarpal, and 2nd–7th sternocostal joints.

questions.q: Which part of the vertebral column receives the most stress by bearing most of the weight of the body?
questions.e: The lumbar region bears the most body weight of the mobile spine, which is why its vertebral bodies are the largest/most massive.

questions.q: An action potential arrives at a muscle fiber's surface and must be conducted rapidly into the cell's interior, near the sarcoplasmic reticulum, to trigger contraction throughout the whole fiber almost simultaneously. Which structure specifically enables this rapid deep conduction?
o: The sarcolemma alone, without any specialized invagination
Transverse tubules, invaginations of the sarcolemma carrying the impulse into the fiber's interior
Terminal cisternae alone, without any surface connection
questions.e: T tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that extend into the fiber's interior, allowing the action potential to be conducted rapidly and deeply into the cell, close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, ensuring near-simultaneous activation throughout the fiber.

questions.q: How many bones make up the entire upper limb (one side), according to the standard count of arm, forearm, and hand bones?
questions.e: The upper limb has 30 bones: humerus (1), radius and ulna (2), and the hand with carpals (8), metacarpals (5), and phalanges (14) = 1+2+8+5+14 = 30.

questions.q: Which bone tissue is adapted to support weight and withstand tension stress?
questions.e: Compact (cortical) bone bears weight and resists bending/tension along the shaft — C.

questions.q: Unlike the other bone cell types, one type is not derived from mesenchymal cells but instead arises from blood-forming (hematopoietic) precursors related to monocytes, and its function is to break down (resorb) bone matrix. Which cell is this?
questions.e: Osteoclasts are the exception among bone cells, arising from hematopoietic precursors (related to monocytes) rather than mesenchymal cells, and their specific function is to resorb (break down) bone matrix, unlike the matrix-forming osteoblasts and osteocytes.

questions.q: Which of the following would you expect to find lining the ducts of a sweat gland, given that this location needs slightly more durability than a single-layer epithelium but is a relatively minor structural demand?
questions.e: Stratified cuboidal epithelium, though relatively uncommon, is found lining structures like sweat gland ducts, providing a sturdier lining than a simple epithelium would, appropriate for this modest structural demand.

questions.q: True or False: The fibula is a major weight-bearing bone of the lower limb.
questions.e: Despite forming synovial joints with the tibia above and the talus below, the fibula is NOT a weight-bearing bone; weight transmission occurs primarily through the tibia.

questions.q: Which historical discovery established that the heart pumps blood around the body in a single, continuous circuit rather than the blood being newly produced and consumed?
o: The invention of the compound microscope
questions.e: William Harvey demonstrated that blood circulates continuously, pumped by the heart, overturning the earlier belief that blood was continuously produced and consumed by the tissues.

questions.q: Which two types of arthritis are described as the most common?
questions.e: The lecture identifies rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis as the most common types of arthritis.

questions.q: The functions of the nervous system include:
o: Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction
Maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume
Responds to internal and external changes
questions.e: The nervous system detects and responds to internal and external stimuli — A. The others (growth, hormone transport, nutrient use, ECF volume) are endocrine/CV/renal roles.

questions.q: Comparing merocrine and holocrine secretion: a gland whose cells periodically rupture entirely, becoming the secreted product themselves, uses which mechanism — and what would you predict about that gland's need for cell replacement?
o: Merocrine secretion; no replacement is needed since cells remain intact
Holocrine secretion; the gland requires ongoing replacement of destroyed secretory cells
Apocrine secretion; only the nucleus is lost each cycle
None of the mechanisms involve cell loss
questions.e: Holocrine secretion involves complete destruction of the secretory cell as part of the secretion itself (as in the sebaceous gland), meaning such glands must continuously replace their secretory cells to sustain output.

questions.q: An imaging report describes a cut that passes through the body offset from the midline, producing a smaller anterior segment and a larger posterior segment. Which plane was used?
questions.e: A parasagittal plane is any sagittal cut that does not pass through the exact midline, so it necessarily produces unequal right and left portions — here shown by unequal anterior/posterior mass on either side, which only makes sense for an off-center sagittal cut.

questions.q: The side to which a scapula belongs can be determined from the following:
o: Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are located on the anterior surface
The acromion and glenoid cavity belong to the lower and lateral part of the scapula
The large concave surface is posterior
Coracoid process is located on the posterior surface
The spine projects from the posterior surface and extends laterally as the acromion
questions.e: The scapular spine projects from the posterior surface, extending laterally to become the acromion — a reliable landmark for determining side/orientation.

questions.q: Structurally, joints are classified based on what feature?
o: The shape of the surrounding muscles
What separates or binds the articulating bones
questions.e: Structural classification of joints depends on what separates or binds the articulating bones — fibers, cartilage, or a joint cavity — giving fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial categories.

questions.q: Which relationship between a tissue and its general function is NOT correct?
questions.e: The general role of epithelium is protection/absorption/secretion/lining — not "digestion" as such (that's a system-level function). The mismatched pair is A.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of cartilage?
o: Provision of an embryonic model prior to development of long bones
Allowing long bones to increase in length
Provision of a smooth surface for epiphyses of articulating joints
Provision of rigidity to soft tissues requiring support
Maintenance of a tubular shape of structures in the digestive tract
questions.e: Cartilage keeps the respiratory tract (trachea/bronchi) patent — not the digestive tract. So E is NOT a cartilage function.

questions.q: An epithelial membrane:
o: Contains simple or stratified epithelia and a basement membrane
Is formed of epithelium and smooth muscle
questions.e: An epithelial membrane = a sheet of epithelium (simple or stratified) resting on a basement membrane over connective tissue — C.

questions.q: Two students disagree about how a joint's shape relates to the movements it permits. Which anatomical principle are they discussing?
questions.e: The principle of complementarity of structure and function holds that a structure's form directly suits the function it performs — here, joint shape dictating the range of motion available.

questions.q: A middle-aged woman presents with chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread musculoskeletal pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, with no clear infectious cause. Which condition does this presentation most closely match?
questions.e: This presentation — chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, predominantly affecting women — matches fibromyositis (fibromyalgia).

questions.q: When the trunk of the body is subjected to physical trauma as happens in automobile accidents the most vulnerable organs are those within:
o: The abdominal cavity because the walls of the abdominal cavity are formed only by muscles without bone reinforcement
The thoracic cavity because they are well protected within the bony rib cage
The bony abdominal cavity because they have little protection
The thoracic cavity because they have little protection
The pelvic cavity because the walls of the pelvic cavity are formed only by muscles
questions.e: Unlike the thoracic cavity (protected by the rib cage) or pelvic cavity (protected by the bony pelvis), the abdominal cavity's walls are formed only by muscle, leaving its organs comparatively vulnerable to blunt trauma.

questions.q: Intervertebral discs exhibit a large amount of tensile strength to absorb shock because they possess:
questions.e: IV discs are fibrocartilage, packed with type I collagen fibres that give tensile strength — B.

questions.q: Which nasal concha(e) is a facial bone?
questions.e: Only the inferior nasal concha is an independent facial bone; the superior and middle conchae are projections of the ethmoid bone (a cranial bone).

questions.q: Which of the following would be the LEAST likely finding in a healthy sample of loose areolar connective tissue?
o: A tightly packed, parallel arrangement of collagen fibers with very little ground substance
Blood vessels running through the tissue
Scattered fibroblasts, macrophages, and mast cells within abundant ground substance
A sparse, loosely arranged network of collagen and elastic fibers
questions.e: A tightly packed, parallel fiber arrangement with minimal ground substance describes dense regular connective tissue (as in tendons), not the loosely arranged, ground-substance-rich structure characteristic of areolar connective tissue.

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae are described as having costal facets mainly for articulation with which structures?
questions.e: Thoracic vertebrae have costal facets on the body (and most also on transverse processes) for articulation with the heads and tubercles of the ribs.

questions.q: The superior portion of the sternum is the
questions.e: The sternum has three parts from superior to inferior: manubrium, body, and xiphoid process.

questions.q: Which scapular angle is formed at the junction of the lateral and superior borders?
questions.e: The lateral angle is the junction of the lateral and superior borders, and is thickened to form the head of the scapula bearing the glenoid cavity.

questions.q: The roughened anterior border of the pubis is named the:
questions.e: The pubic crest is the roughened ridge forming the anterior border of the pubic body, an attachment site for abdominal muscles.

questions.q: A physiologist compares the contraction speed of skeletal muscle (used for a sprinter's rapid stride) with that of the smooth muscle propelling food through the intestine. What functional difference would be predicted?
o: Skeletal muscle contracts rapidly for quick, powerful movements, while smooth muscle contracts slowly and sustains contraction over a longer period, suited to gradual propulsion
Neither tissue can sustain contraction for more than a fraction of a second
Smooth muscle contracts faster than skeletal muscle in all cases
questions.e: Skeletal muscle is adapted for rapid, powerful contractions suited to voluntary movements like sprinting, whereas smooth muscle is specialized for slow, sustained contraction, appropriate for the gradual, prolonged propulsion of substances through hollow organs like the intestine.

questions.q: A researcher identifies a lighter band within a sarcomere that contains only thin filaments, with no thick filament overlap. Which band is this, and what accounts for its lighter appearance?
o: The I band, appearing lighter because it contains only thin filaments without the additional density of overlapping thick filaments
The Z disc, which is defined by its complete absence of any protein
The A band, because it lacks any filaments at all
The H zone, which always appears darker than the A band
questions.e: The I band contains only thin (actin) filaments, without overlapping thick filaments, which is why it appears lighter under the microscope compared to the denser A band, where thick and thin filaments overlap.

questions.q: A physiotherapist instructs a patient to decrease the angle between the forearm and upper arm at the elbow. Which movement is being requested?
questions.e: Decreasing the angle between two body parts at a joint is, by definition, flexion — extension is the opposite, increasing that angle.

questions.q: Which ligaments of the shoulder joint stabilise the anterior aspect of the joint?
questions.e: The superior, middle, and inferior glenohumeral ligaments specifically stabilise the anterior aspect of the shoulder joint.

questions.q: Which type of epithelium is normally found in glands?
questions.e: Secretory (glandular) epithelium is typically simple cuboidal — D.

questions.q: The knee joint is best classified as a:
questions.e: The knee is described as a modified hinge joint and is the largest and most complicated joint in the body.

questions.q: Which of the following structures is the most difficult to observe on an X-Ray film?
questions.e: Tracheal (hyaline) cartilage is poorly mineralized/radiolucent, so it is far harder to visualize on X-ray than the dense bony structures listed.

questions.q: Bones united by hyaline cartilage, such as the epiphyseal plate, describe which type of joint?
questions.e: Synchondroses are primary cartilaginous joints in which bones are united by hyaline cartilage, with the epiphyseal plate as a key example.

questions.q: Children are often told to keep this process off the table while eating.
questions.e: The olecranon process of the ulna is the bony point of the elbow — the process children are told to keep off the table.

questions.q: Which cruciate ligament of the knee is described as weaker and more commonly injured?
questions.e: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is weaker and more commonly injured than the posterior cruciate ligament, and it blends with the medial meniscus.

questions.q: The vertebra which has no body is the
questions.e: The atlas (C1) is a ring of bone lacking a body, allowing the dens of the axis to occupy its anterior arch space.

questions.q: True or False: Infant skull bones are described as thin but somewhat flexible, making them less easily fractured than adult skull bones.
questions.e: True. The notes describe infant skull bones as thin but flexible, which makes them less easily fractured compared to the more rigid adult skull bones.

questions.q: Inflammation of the bursa covering the ischial tuberosity is termed:
questions.e: The ischial tuberosity is covered by a bursa that, when inflamed (often from prolonged sitting), causes ischial bursitis.

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the axial skeleton?
o: The skull, vertebral column and rib cage
The skull, vertebral column and pelvis
The skull, shoulder girdles and rib cage
questions.e: The axial skeleton comprises the skull, vertebral column, and rib cage/sternum — the body's central axis.

questions.q: True or False: Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in genetically susceptible individuals.
questions.e: True. Spina bifida is associated with folic acid deficiency in certain genetically susceptible individuals, which is why folic acid supplementation is recommended during pregnancy.

questions.q: Which combination of features would you expect in an epithelium specialized to both protect against significant abrasion and allow for a modest degree of secretion, as seen in parts of the oral cavity?
o: Simple squamous epithelium with abundant goblet cells
Stratified squamous epithelium, which still permits underlying glands to secrete through it via ducts
questions.e: Stratified squamous epithelium, particularly the non-keratinized moist variety lining much of the oral cavity, provides abrasion resistance from swallowed food or chewing while still allowing underlying glands to deliver secretions to the surface via ducts that penetrate the epithelium.

questions.q: Which four bones meet at the pterion, forming an H-shaped suture pattern?
questions.e: The pterion is the region where the frontal, sphenoid, temporal, and parietal bones meet, forming an H-shaped suture roughly 3-4 cm superior to the midpoint of the zygomatic arch.

questions.q: What are the three main components of connective tissue?
o: Alveoli, fibrous capsule, and secretory cells
questions.e: Connective tissue = cells + fibres + ground substance — A. (Fibres + ground substance together make the extracellular matrix.)

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares tight junctions and desmosomes in terms of their primary function?
o: Tight junctions provide mechanical anchorage, while desmosomes control paracellular passage
Both function identically, providing only mechanical strength
Neither junction type has any functional role in epithelium
Tight junctions primarily control what can pass between cells, while desmosomes primarily provide mechanical anchorage between cells
questions.e: Tight junctions are primarily barrier-forming, sealing the intercellular space to control paracellular passage, while desmosomes are primarily anchoring structures, providing mechanical strength between adjacent cells — distinct but complementary roles.

questions.q: Approximately how long is the adult vertebral column?
questions.e: The adult vertebral column is approximately 70 cm (28 inches) long, extending from the skull to the coccyx.

questions.q: The foramen magnum is a large hole in the base of the occipital bone that transmits the spinal cord. The homologous structure in an individual vertebra is the:
questions.e: The vertebral foramen of each vertebra (through which the spinal cord passes) is developmentally/functionally analogous to the foramen magnum of the skull.

questions.q: A pathologist examines a tumor biopsy under a microscope to determine the tissue of origin. Which subdivision of anatomy is she practicing?
questions.e: Examining tissue under magnification is histology, the microscopic study of tissue architecture, distinct from gross (naked-eye) anatomy.

questions.q: On the inferior surface of the clavicle's shaft, the conoid tubercle forms a synovial joint with which part of the scapula?
questions.e: The conoid tubercle, on the inferior surface of the clavicle, anchors the conoid ligament and corresponds to a synovial-type connection with the coracoid process of the scapula.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A 'sprain' and a 'strain' refer to the exact same type of soft-tissue injury.
Reason (R): A sprain involves tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves injury to muscle or tendon.
o: Both A and R are false
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.e: The Reason correctly distinguishes the two terms, which is precisely why the Assertion (claiming they are the same) is false.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly lists features associated with the PROXIMAL end of the humerus?
o: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle, intertrochanteric crest
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle, intertubercular groove
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter, bicipital groove
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa, olecranon fossa
questions.e: The proximal humerus bears the head, anatomical and surgical necks, and the greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular groove. Trochanters belong to the femur, not the humerus.

questions.q: An imaging study identifies a bundle of neuron processes running within the spinal cord itself, connecting different regions of the CNS. What is this type of bundle called, as opposed to the equivalent structure in the PNS?
questions.e: Within the CNS, a bundle of neuron processes is called a tract; the equivalent bundle located in the PNS is instead called a nerve.

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured, with tenderness elicited at the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.e: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand raises strong suspicion for a scaphoid fracture.

questions.q: Which of the following phrases best describes the function of the vertebral curves?
o: To improve cervical center of gravity
To accommodate the weight of the pelvic girdle
questions.e: The spine's alternating curves act like a coiled spring, giving it resilience and flexibility to absorb shock during movement.

questions.q: A body in anatomical position has the following characteristics EXCEPT:
o: Arms adjacent to sides with palms facing backward
Lower limbs close together with feet parallel and toes forward
questions.e: In anatomical position the palms face forward (supinated), not backward — so B is the incorrect (EXCEPT) statement.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which structure?
questions.e: The scapula articulates with the head of the humerus at the glenoid fossa, forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

questions.q: Comparing the terms 'superior' and 'cephalic': what is their relationship?
o: Superior applies only to the trunk, cephalic only to the limbs
They are essentially synonymous, both meaning toward the head end
questions.e: Superior and cephalic are essentially synonymous directional terms, both indicating a position toward the head end of the body.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the skeletal system:
o: Mineral storage and attachment of muscles
Protection, production of blood cells and filtration of blood
Only A and B are correct
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: A and B are true. C fails because "filtration of blood" is a spleen/kidney job, not a skeletal one — so only A and B (D).

questions.q: The enlargement of existing muscle fibres due to increasing diameters of cell but not increasing the number of new muscle fibres is known as
questions.e: Hypertrophy is growth in fiber SIZE (diameter) without an increase in fiber NUMBER; hyperplasia would involve more fibers.

questions.q: A ball-and-socket joint, formed when a spherical head fits into a concave socket, is classified functionally as:
questions.e: Ball-and-socket (spheroid) joints are multiaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, rotation, and circumduction — exemplified by the shoulder and hip.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae can be uniquely identified by the presence of
questions.e: Transverse foramina are unique to cervical vertebrae (all vertebrae have transverse/spinous/vertebral foramina/processes in general, but only cervical vertebrae have the foraminal openings in the transverse processes).

questions.q: The hip joint articulates between the head of the femur and which structure?
questions.e: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Synovial fluid contributes to the nutrition of articular cartilage.
Reason (R): Articular cartilage is avascular and relies on diffusion from synovial fluid for nourishment.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.e: Both statements are true. Because articular cartilage lacks its own blood supply, it depends on diffusion of nutrients from the surrounding synovial fluid, directly explaining the Assertion.

questions.q: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), being stronger, shorter, and broader than the ACL, primarily limits which movement?
o: Knee hyperflexion and posterior tibial dislocation
questions.e: The PCL limits knee hyperflexion and prevents posterior dislocation of the tibia relative to the femur.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world illustration of an axodendritic synapse specifically, as opposed to other synapse types?
o: An axon terminal of one neuron forming a synapse onto a dendrite of a second neuron, the most statistically common arrangement in the nervous system
Two axons synapsing directly onto each other with no dendrite involved
A motor neuron synapsing directly onto a skeletal muscle fiber
A dendrite synapsing directly onto another dendrite
questions.e: An axon terminal from one neuron synapsing onto the dendrite of a second neuron is the defining pattern of an axodendritic synapse, and this is also the most statistically common synapse type in the nervous system — distinguishing it from axoaxonic, dendrodendritic, or neuromuscular junction examples.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the femur?
o: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: The proximal femur/shaft region bears the gluteal tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest, along with the head, neck, and trochanters. Condyles (A, B) are distal features.

questions.q: The shaft of the radius has anterior, posterior, and lateral surfaces, along with anterior, posterior, and which other border?
questions.e: The radial shaft has three borders: anterior, posterior, and an interosseous border, the last of which gives attachment to the interosseous membrane (except near its proximal-most part).

questions.q: A physiologist stimulates an isolated tissue sample with a nerve impulse and observes it shorten. Which functional property of muscle tissue is being demonstrated?
questions.e: The tissue's response to a nerve impulse by contracting demonstrates excitability — its ability to respond to electrical stimulation with contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following is the largest of the paranasal sinuses?
questions.e: The maxillary sinuses are the largest of the paranasal sinuses, located within the maxillary bones.

questions.q: A patient with a suspected fracture but with a known dye/contrast allergy and no urgent need for cross-sectional detail is scheduled for baseline imaging. Which of the following would be the simplest, most direct first-line choice?
questions.e: For a straightforward suspected fracture, plain X-ray remains the simplest first-line imaging choice, using differences in tissue density to visualize bone, without requiring contrast dye.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The deltoid (medial) ligament of the ankle is more frequently torn than the lateral ligament.
Reason (R): The deltoid ligament is anatomically larger and stronger than the lateral ligament.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.e: Both statements are false. The lateral ligament, not the deltoid, is more frequently torn, precisely because the deltoid ligament is the stronger of the two — the opposite of what is asserted.

questions.q: Which one of these bones is not found in the pelvis?
questions.e: The hyoid is located in the neck, entirely unrelated to the pelvis.

questions.q: A comparison of skin (dense irregular connective tissue) and tendon (dense regular connective tissue) both under significant, but differently directed, mechanical stress would predict which outcome?
o: The tendon would tolerate multidirectional stress better than the skin
The skin would tolerate multidirectional stress well due to its randomly oriented fibers, while a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be more vulnerable to injury
Both tissues perform identically regardless of stress direction
Neither tissue type is affected by the direction of applied stress
questions.e: Because dense irregular tissue (skin) has randomly oriented fibers suited to multidirectional stress, while dense regular tissue (tendon) has fibers aligned to resist force along one specific direction, a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be comparatively more vulnerable to injury than skin facing the same off-axis stress.

questions.q: A biopsy shows tissue with cells packed tightly together and almost no space between them for extracellular material. Which basic tissue type does this most likely represent?
questions.e: Epithelial tissue is defined by cells packed closely with minimal extracellular matrix, the opposite arrangement to connective tissue, which has abundant matrix and sparse cells.

questions.q: Which digit does not have a middle phalanx?
questions.e: Digit I (the thumb/pollex) has only a proximal and distal phalanx — no middle phalanx.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser trochanter of the femur is larger and more laterally placed than the greater trochanter.
questions.e: This is reversed: the greater trochanter is the larger, laterally placed prominence, while the lesser trochanter is smaller and located medially/posteriorly.

questions.q: The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is best described functionally as:
o: The least movable but most stable joint
questions.e: The shoulder joint is highly movable but is also the least stable major joint of the body, owing to its shallow socket.

questions.q: True or False: To correctly orient an isolated hip bone, the obturator foramen should be positioned posteriorly and pointing upward.
questions.e: To orient a hip bone correctly, the obturator foramen should face anteriorly and is positioned inferiorly (below and in front), not posteriorly or upward.

questions.q: The thumb and the great toe are known as
questions.e: In anatomical terminology, the thumb is the pollex and the great toe is the hallux.

questions.q: Goblet cells are found in each of the following organs EXCEPT the:
questions.e: The stomach lining is simple columnar mucous epithelium WITHOUT discrete goblet cells. Intestine and bronchus have them — so the exception is A.

questions.q: The sternum:
o: Is a bony plate anterior to the heart
Is an irregular bone that is divided into 3 regions: manubrium, body and xiphoid process
Is also known as the "breastbone" and its xiphoid process is a plate of hyaline cartilage until about age 40
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: All three statements correctly describe the sternum.

questions.q: Specimen A: surface under severe mechanical stress. Specimen B: surface where filtration/diffusion occurs. Specimen C: internal chamber needing absorption AND motility. A, B, C are from:
o: Skin, alveoli of lungs, efferent ductules
Hard palate, respiratory bronchioles and oesophagus
Filiform papillae of tongue, endothelium of blood vessels and skin
Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and vagina
Soles of feet, visceral layer of renal corpuscle and oesophagus
questions.e: A = mechanical stress → keratinised stratified squamous → skin. B = diffusion → simple squamous → alveoli. C = absorption + motility → the efferent ductules (absorptive cells + ciliated cells that move sperm). Oesophagus (option D) does neither, so C wins.

questions.q: The primary centre of ossification in endochondral bone formation typically appears in which part of the developing bone?
questions.e: The primary centre of ossification appears around the 7th to 12th week, in the middle of the diaphysis, where mesenchymal tissue, osteoblasts, and blood vessels initiate bone formation.

questions.q: The superior orbital fissure is formed in the sphenoid bone, whereas the inferior orbital fissure is formed between the sphenoid and
questions.e: The inferior orbital fissure lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the zygomatic (and maxilla), with the zygomatic bone as the key second contributor here.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow attaches the radius firmly so it cannot rotate within it during pronation and supination.
questions.e: False. The annular ligament holds the head of the radius in place against the radial notch of the ulna while still permitting the radial head to rotate within it, enabling pronation and supination.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS possess
o: Hyaline cartilage that absorbs compressive forces
Hyaline cartilage at the ends of the opposing bones
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Synovial joints have articular (hyaline) cartilage on opposing bone ends that absorbs compressive loads, plus a fluid-filled joint cavity.

questions.q: The floor of the anatomical snuffbox is formed by which two carpal bones?
questions.e: The anatomical snuffbox, a triangular depression on the radial side of the wrist, has the scaphoid and trapezium forming its floor.

questions.q: The upper end of the femur consists of the head, neck, and two trochanters. Which trochanters are these?
questions.e: The proximal femur bears the head and neck plus the greater trochanter (lateral, larger) and lesser trochanter (medial, smaller), both serving as muscle attachment sites.

questions.q: Which structure forms the coracoacromial arch that prevents superior (upward) displacement of the humeral head?
o: Coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament
questions.e: The coracoacromial arch is formed by the coracoid process, the acromion, and the coracoacromial ligament, and it blocks superior displacement of the humeral head.

questions.q: Estrogen replacement therapy in postmenopausal women, while reducing bone loss risk, is associated with an increased risk of which of the following?
o: Heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer
questions.e: Although estrogen decline increases postmenopausal bone loss risk, estrogen replacement therapy itself is associated with an increased risk of heart attack, stroke, and breast cancer.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Bursae located near a joint can sometimes become distended when the joint itself produces excess synovial fluid.
Reason (R): Some bursae, such as the suprapatellar bursa at the knee, directly communicate with the synovial cavity of the adjacent joint.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
questions.e: Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion: because certain bursae like the suprapatellar bursa communicate directly with the joint cavity, excess synovial fluid in the joint can flow into and distend the bursa.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a synchondrosis?
questions.e: The first sternocostal joint (between the first rib and the sternum) is cited as a synchondrosis, alongside epiphyseal plates and the costochondral joint.

questions.q: True or False: Clubfoot is described as a congenital defect in which the soles of the foot face medially and the talus points inferiorly.
questions.e: Clubfoot (talipes equinovarus) is a congenital condition in which the soles face medially (inward) and the talus points inferiorly, consistent with the inverted, adducted, plantar-flexed positioning.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the humerus?
o: Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tubercle, Lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
questions.e: The proximal humerus bears the greater and lesser tubercles separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove. Trochanters belong to the femur, not the humerus.

questions.q: Disc herniation classically occurs posterolaterally rather than directly posteriorly because of the protective action of the:
questions.e: The posterior longitudinal ligament prevents herniation from proceeding directly posteriorly, so herniation usually occurs posterolaterally instead.

questions.q: A patient suffers a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes before resuscitation. Given what is known about neurons' tolerance for oxygen deprivation, what would be the most likely neurological consequence?
o: Only glial cells would be affected, sparing all neurons
No neurological effect, since neurons can survive indefinitely without oxygen
Significant neuronal death, since neurons typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen due to their high metabolic demand
Neurons would simply pause activity and resume normally with no damage after any duration
questions.e: Because neurons have a high metabolic rate and typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen, a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes would be expected to cause significant neuronal death, an important basis for the urgency of resuscitation.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world example of dense irregular connective tissue in action, based on its multidirectional fiber arrangement?
o: A tendon transmitting force from a single muscle in one direction
The wall of a large elastic artery stretching with each heartbeat
Hyaline cartilage at the end of a long bone
The dermis of the skin, resisting pulling and stretching forces from many directions during movement
questions.e: The dermis, composed of dense irregular connective tissue with randomly oriented collagen fibers, is well suited to resisting mechanical stress from multiple directions, unlike the single-direction force resisted by dense regular tissue in a tendon.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is/are not weight bearing?
questions.e: The fibula bears minimal body weight; it mainly serves as a muscle attachment site and stabilizer of the ankle.

questions.q: On the inferior aspect of the skull cap (calvaria), pits formed by arachnoid granulations, marking sites of CSF transfer, are called:
