questions.e: Granular foveolae are pits on the inner skull cap formed by arachnoid granulations, which are sites of cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) transfer into the venous system.

questions.q: Body cavities and Membranes
o: The serous pericardium is associated with the pericardial cavity and the lungs
The thoracic cavity contains two pleural cavities and a thick band of organs called the mediastinum
The abdominal cavity contains the stomach, urinary bladder, uterus and the prostate gland
Synovial cavities are enclosed within fibrous capsules that fill the sutures of the skull
The ventral body cavity is subdivided into a cranial cavity and a vertebral cavity
questions.e: The thoracic cavity correctly contains two pleural cavities flanking the mediastinum (which houses the heart, great vessels, trachea, and esophagus). The other options misplace structures (bladder/uterus/prostate are pelvic, not abdominal; pericardium relates to the heart not lungs; synovial cavities are at joints not sutures).

questions.q: An increased Q-angle is considered a risk factor for several knee disorders. Which group typically has a greater Q-angle, owing to wider pelves?
questions.e: The Q-angle is greater in adult females than males, owing to females generally having wider pelves.

questions.q: A student claims that all three muscle types are voluntary. Which single fact most directly disproves this claim?
o: Smooth and cardiac muscle are both classified as involuntary, unlike skeletal muscle
questions.e: Since both smooth and cardiac muscle are functionally classified as involuntary — not under conscious control — the claim that all three muscle types are voluntary is directly disproved by this fact.

questions.q: In which anatomic region of the abdomen would you expect to locate the gall bladder?
questions.e: The gallbladder lies beneath the liver in the right hypochondriac region of the abdomen.

questions.q: The canal that runs through the core of each osteon is the principal site of:
questions.e: The central (Haversian) canal at the core of each osteon contains blood vessels and nerve fibres that nourish and innervate the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: Given that hormone signaling in the endocrine system generally has a slower onset but longer duration than nervous signaling, which of the following body functions would be better suited to endocrine rather than nervous control?
o: Millisecond-scale coordination of a sprinter's muscles
Long-term regulation of growth over months to years
Rapid withdrawal of a hand from a hot surface
questions.e: Long-term processes like growth regulation benefit from the slower-onset, longer-lasting nature of hormonal control, whereas split-second actions like reflexes or sprinting require the nervous system's rapid signaling.

questions.q: Articular cartilage at the very surface of a joint lacks a perichondrium. Given cartilage's usual reliance on this membrane for nutrition, how does articular cartilage obtain nutrients instead?
o: By diffusion from the surrounding synovial fluid
It does not require nutrients since it is composed of dead cells
It receives nutrients directly from the bone marrow through the matrix
It has its own direct blood supply, unlike other cartilage
questions.e: Lacking a perichondrium at the joint surface, articular cartilage instead relies on diffusion of nutrients from the surrounding synovial fluid within the joint cavity.

questions.q: Osteomyelitis is best described as:
o: Inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria
Caused by altered vitamin D metabolism only
Caused purely by hyperactivity of osteoclasts
questions.e: Osteomyelitis is inflammation of bone caused by pus-forming bacteria, distinguishing it from metabolic bone diseases like rickets or osteomalacia.

questions.q: True or False: A fractured femoral neck can interrupt the blood supply to the head of the femur, risking avascular necrosis.
questions.e: The blood supply to the femoral head largely depends on retinacular vessels running along the neck; a femoral neck fracture can disrupt this supply, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Comparing myelin formation in the CNS versus the PNS: which pairing of glial cell and location is correct?
o: Astrocytes myelinate both CNS and PNS axons
Microglia myelinate CNS axons; ependymal cells myelinate PNS axons
Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons
questions.e: The correct pairing is oligodendrocytes forming myelin in the CNS, and Schwann cells forming myelin in the PNS — the reverse or other pairings listed are incorrect.

questions.q: What does the acronym RICE, used in management of soft tissue joint injuries, stand for?
questions.e: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard immediate management for soft tissue joint injuries.

questions.q: A stroke damages CNS tissue, and astrocytes at the injury site respond by proliferating and forming dense scar tissue. What consequence does this astrocyte-driven scarring have for axon regrowth at the injury site?
o: It has no effect on axon regrowth whatsoever
It blocks axon regrowth and, along with released inhibitory chemicals, contributes to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after injury
It converts damaged axons directly into new, functional oligodendrocytes
It actively promotes and accelerates axon regrowth across the injury
questions.e: Astrocyte-produced scar tissue physically blocks axon regrowth across the injury site, and astrocytes also release chemicals that further inhibit regrowth — together contributing to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after significant injury.

questions.q: An exocrine gland's cells remain completely intact throughout secretion, releasing their product purely through vesicle fusion with the plasma membrane. Which mode of secretion is this, and which of the three modes is most common among exocrine glands?
o: None of the three modes describes intact-cell secretion
Holocrine secretion; the least damaging mode
Merocrine secretion; and yes, it is the most common mode among exocrine glands
Apocrine secretion; also the most common mode
questions.e: Merocrine secretion releases the product by exocytosis with the cell remaining fully intact, and it is indeed the most common secretory mechanism among exocrine glands generally.

questions.q: True or False: The shaft of the tibia is the most frequent site of an open fracture, commonly resulting from motorcycle accidents.
questions.e: Because the tibial shaft lies just beneath the skin with little soft tissue covering anteriorly, it is the most common site for open (compound) fractures, frequently from motorcycle accidents.

questions.q: What fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the acetabulum in the hip joint?
questions.e: The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous collar that deepens the acetabulum, improving congruency with the femoral head.

questions.q: The tuberosity of the ulna serves as an attachment site for which muscle?
questions.e: The ulnar tuberosity is a roughened area distal to the coronoid process that receives the insertion of the brachialis muscle.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the LEAST consistent finding with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, given that this disease specifically demyelinates CNS axons?
o: Slowed conduction velocity in affected CNS pathways
Variable neurological symptoms depending on which CNS tracts are affected
Progressive damage to myelin produced by oligodendrocytes
Damage strictly limited to Schwann-cell-produced myelin in peripheral nerves, sparing the CNS entirely
questions.e: Because multiple sclerosis is specifically a CNS demyelinating disease targeting oligodendrocyte-produced myelin, a presentation strictly limited to peripheral (Schwann-cell) myelin damage while sparing the CNS entirely would be the least consistent finding with this diagnosis.

questions.q: Intramembranous ossification occurs in the
o: A, B, C are all correct
questions.e: Per the marked answer key, intramembranous (direct) ossification is credited here for the clavicle, sternum and scapula.

questions.q: Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can damage its accompanying artery and lead to which complication?
questions.e: The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery, and rupture of the ligament can damage this artery, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Which of the following bones does not articulate directly with any other bone in the skeleton?
questions.e: As established earlier, the hyoid bone articulates with no other bone in the skeleton.

questions.q: Which best summarizes the overall functional division of labor between neurons and neuroglia in the nervous system?
o: Neurons are the excitable, signal-transmitting cells; neuroglia are nonexcitable cells that support, protect, nourish, and insulate neurons, among other roles
Neurons and neuroglia perform identical functions with complete redundancy
Neither cell type has any specialized function
Neuroglia transmit all electrical signals, while neurons provide only structural support
questions.e: The fundamental division of labor is that neurons are the excitable cells specialized for transmitting electrical signals, while neuroglia are nonexcitable supporting cells that nourish, protect, insulate, and otherwise support neurons in their signaling role.

questions.q: True or False: A lumbar rib is sometimes referred to as a gorilla rib because gorillas typically possess an extra rib at this vertebral level.
questions.e: A lumbar rib (an extra rib articulating with a lumbar vertebra) is nicknamed the gorilla rib because gorillas normally have 13 pairs of ribs, including one attached to the first lumbar vertebra.

questions.q: The lower end of the femur has two spirally curved condyles separated by which structure?
questions.e: The two distal femoral condyles (medial and lateral) are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar fossa (notch), which provides attachment for the cruciate ligaments of the knee.

questions.q: A textbook diagram labels a neuron's telodendria at the very tip of its longest process. Which process is being illustrated, and what do the telodendria lead to?
o: A dendrite; the telodendria are branches leading back to the cell body
The axon hillock; telodendria mark where the axon originates
A node of Ranvier; telodendria are gaps in the myelin sheath
The axon; the telodendria are its terminal branches, ending in axon terminals
questions.e: Telodendria are the terminal branches found at the very end of an axon (not a dendrite), and these branches lead to the axon terminals (synaptic boutons), where synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter.

questions.q: How many bones comprise the skull?
questions.e: The skull consists of 22 bones: 8 cranial bones and 14 facial bones.

questions.q: Compression of the median nerve as it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist produces which condition?
questions.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, the space bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: Given that roughly 99% of neurons have numerous dendrites and a single axon, which structural type accounts for the vast majority of neurons in the nervous system?
o: None of these; most neurons have no processes at all
questions.e: Multipolar neurons, with numerous dendrites and a single axon, make up approximately 99% of neurons — the dominant structural type in the nervous system.

questions.q: True or False: The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are typically filled with red bone marrow.
questions.e: True. The spaces between trabeculae in spongy bone are filled with red bone marrow, which is involved in blood cell formation.

questions.q: Membranous gaps between cranial bones that make up the calvaria of a foetus are called:
questions.e: Fontanelles are the membranous gaps between cranial bones in the developing foetal/infant calvaria, before they fuse into rigid sutures.

questions.q: Which of the following abnormal curve(s) is often seen in obese men with "potbellies" as they attempt to preserve their center of gravity?
questions.e: An anterior abdominal weight shift (as with a "potbelly") is often compensated by an exaggerated lumbar curvature — lordosis.

questions.q: The side of the intervertebral disc where herniation most commonly occurs is the:
questions.e: The posterolateral part of the intervertebral disc is where herniation most commonly occurs, due to the protective effect of the posterior longitudinal ligament centrally.

questions.q: The bulk of the sternum, whose sides are notched for articulation with costal cartilages of ribs 2-7, is called the:
questions.e: The body forms the bulk of the sternum, with notched sides for articulation with the costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7.

questions.q: Small spaces between lamellae that house mature bone cells are called:
questions.e: Lacunae are small spaces between lamellae that contain mature bone cells, the osteocytes. Canaliculi are the tiny channels that radiate from lacunae.

questions.q: True or False: Elderly individuals are prone to fracturing the neck of the femur even after only a minor fall.
questions.e: Due to age-related osteoporosis, elderly individuals are particularly susceptible to femoral neck fractures even from relatively minor falls.

questions.q: A slightly movable joint is functionally termed:
questions.e: Amphiarthrosis describes a slightly movable joint, with the symphysis and syndesmosis given as examples in the lecture.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina are found going through the sphenoid bone?
o: Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen magnum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, jugular foramen and foramen magnum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
questions.e: The sphenoid bone contains the optic canal plus foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum (the stylomastoid, jugular foramina and foramen magnum belong to the temporal/occipital bones).

questions.q: A tissue sample shows a single layer of cells, all of which touch the basement membrane, yet the nuclei are staggered at different heights, giving a false impression of multiple layers. Which epithelial type is this?
questions.e: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is actually a single layer (simple), but because all the cells vary in height and their nuclei sit at staggered levels, it gives a false appearance of stratification.

questions.q: Which of these joints is classified as a condyloid (ellipsoid) joint?
questions.e: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is a condyloid joint, along with metacarpophalangeal, metatarsophalangeal, and temporomandibular joints.

questions.q: Which connective tissue is described as hard, dense, and forms most of the adult skeleton?
questions.e: Bone, or osseous tissue, is the hard, dense connective tissue that forms most of the adult skeleton. Cartilage is more flexible and is found at joints and a few other sites, not throughout most of the skeleton.

questions.q: The smooth, slightly depressed area located just superior to the nasion, on the frontal bone, is called the:
questions.e: The glabella is a smooth, slightly depressed area on the frontal bone located just superior to the nasion, between the eyebrows.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why a transverse plane through the abdomen and a transverse plane through the head both use the same term, despite being at very different heights on the body?
o: Transverse planes can only occur at the level of the abdomen
Transverse planes are actually a type of sagittal plane
The term changes name depending on which body region is cut
'Transverse' refers to the orientation of the cut at any level, not to a single fixed height
questions.e: The term 'transverse' describes the plane's orientation — perpendicular to the body's long axis — which can occur at any level of the body, from head to feet, not a single fixed location.

questions.q: The functions of the respiratory system:
o: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Responsible for the sense of smell
A, B, C and D are all functions of the respiratory system
questions.e: Gas exchange, phonation (larynx), olfaction and air filtration (nasal hairs/mucus) are all respiratory roles — E.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser tubercle of the humerus is located posteriorly, while the greater tubercle is anterior.
questions.e: This is reversed: the greater tubercle is lateral/posterior in position while the lesser tubercle is anterior, with the intertubercular groove lying between them.

questions.q: Articular facets on vertebrae form joints between adjacent vertebrae, also known as:
questions.e: Articular facets form the zygapophyseal (facet) joints between adjacent vertebrae, guiding and limiting spinal movement.

questions.q: True or False: The inferior angle of the scapula is formed at the junction of the medial and lateral borders.
questions.e: The inferior angle marks the meeting point of the medial and lateral borders of the scapular body at the lowest point of the bone.

questions.q: Why are endocrine glands described as 'ductless,' and how does their secretion actually reach its target?
o: They lack ducts and instead release their secretions directly into a rich network of surrounding blood capillaries
They release secretions only onto the skin surface
They rely entirely on nerve fibers to transport hormones
They are not ductless; all glands have ducts
questions.e: Endocrine glands lack a duct system; instead, their hormonal secretions are released directly into the dense network of blood capillaries surrounding the gland, allowing distribution throughout the body via the bloodstream.

questions.q: Damage to the epiphyseal plate following a long bone fracture in a child may lead to:
questions.e: Because the epiphyseal plate is responsible for longitudinal bone growth, damage to it in a child can disrupt growth and lead to shortening of the affected limb.

questions.q: A protein fiber in connective tissue allows a stretched structure, like the wall of a large elastic artery, to spring back to its original length. Which type of fiber is primarily responsible for this recoil property?
questions.e: Elastic fibers, rich in the protein elastin, give tissue the capacity to stretch and then recoil back to its original shape — the property responsible for the resilience of structures like elastic artery walls.

questions.q: Mesenchymal cells are most commonly found in which type of connective tissue?
questions.e: Mesenchyme IS embryonic connective tissue, where mesenchymal cells predominate — C.

questions.q: The posterior drawer sign, classically caused by a 'dashboard injury,' assesses tearing of which ligament?
questions.e: The posterior drawer sign tests for PCL tear, occurring when a large force is applied to the shins of a flexed knee, pushing the tibia posteriorly — classically in dashboard injuries.

questions.q: The pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs both experience substantial compressive load and must resist shearing forces, particularly during activities like childbirth or heavy lifting. Which cartilage type, reinforced with thick collagen bundles, is adapted to these structural demands?
questions.e: Fibrocartilage, reinforced by thick bundles of collagen fibers, provides the strength needed to withstand compressive load and resist shearing forces at sites like the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

questions.q: The posterior fontanelle ossifies how soon after birth, and its point of fusion is called what?
questions.e: The posterior fontanelle ossifies 2-3 months after birth, with its point of fusion being the lambda.

questions.q: The mucus-secreting cells prevalent in simple columnar epithelium are known as:
questions.e: Goblet cells are the mucus-secreting cells wedged among columnar cells — A.

questions.q: How many distinct curvatures give the adult vertebral column its characteristic S-shape?
questions.e: Four distinct curvatures give the vertebral column its S-shape: the cervical, thoracic, lumbar, and sacral curvatures.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina, all passing through the sphenoid bone, are correctly grouped together?
o: Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale, foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, foramen magnum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen, foramen spinosum
questions.e: The sphenoid bone transmits structures through the optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale, and foramen spinosum, all associated with branches of the trigeminal nerve and middle meningeal vessels.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'ankle ring' concept described in the lecture?
o: The ankle mortise behaves like a flexible band that never fractures
The talus can dislocate without bony injury
A ring, when broken, usually breaks in two places
The ankle joint has no ligamentous support
questions.e: The 'ankle ring' analogy describes how the bony-ligamentous ring of the ankle, like any ring, usually breaks (fractures) in two places when subjected to significant force, as seen in Pott's fracture.

questions.q: A basal epithelial cell is torn away from the underlying basement membrane during a biopsy, seemingly detaching more easily than its neighboring cells detach from each other. Which junction type, connecting cells specifically to the basement membrane rather than to each other, was most likely compromised?
questions.e: Hemidesmosomes specifically anchor the basal surface of an epithelial cell to the underlying basement membrane, distinct from desmosomes, which link adjacent cells to one another.

questions.q: Which nerve can be stretched and damaged by downward displacement of the humerus in shoulder dislocation, in addition to the axillary nerve?
questions.e: The lecture notes that downward displacement of the humerus can stretch and damage the radial nerve, in addition to the axillary nerve.

questions.q: Pott's fracture of the ankle, caused by forced eversion of the foot, typically involves which malleoli?
questions.e: Pott's fracture involves a bimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli) or trimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli plus distal tibia) fracture pattern, resulting from forced eversion of the foot.

questions.q: True or False: Intramembranous ossification forms most of the long bones of the limbs.
questions.e: False. Intramembranous ossification forms most of the flat bones of the skull, the mandible, the sternum, and the clavicle, whereas long bones form mainly via endochondral ossification.

questions.q: Which cells, located in the periosteum and endosteum, persist as stem cells throughout life and can be activated for fracture repair?
questions.e: Osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells reside in the periosteum and endosteum, persisting as stem cells that can later differentiate to aid in bone repair, such as after a fracture.

questions.q: A patient presents with skeletal-muscle spasms that progress to muscle weakness, accompanied by an abnormal heart rhythm. Which muscular dystrophy variant does this combination most specifically suggest?
questions.e: Myotonic dystrophy is specifically characterized by skeletal-muscle spasms progressing to weakness, together with abnormal heart rhythm — this combination of features distinguishes it from Duchenne muscular dystrophy and the other listed conditions.

questions.q: At the knee, lateral and medial rotation can only occur when the knee is in which position?
questions.e: Medial and lateral rotation at the knee can only occur when the knee is flexed; if the knee is extended, such rotation occurs instead at the hip joint.

questions.q: Which observation about a tissue sample would most clearly indicate specialized rather than connective tissue proper — cartilage, bone, or blood — rather than one of the connective tissue proper subtypes?
o: The presence of fibroblasts within a loose fiber network
Randomly oriented collagen fibers, as in the dermis
Parallel collagen fibers, as in a tendon
A mineralized matrix, a firm non-mineralized avascular matrix with chondrocytes, or a fluid matrix with suspended cells
questions.e: The specialized connective tissues — bone, cartilage, and blood — are distinguished by matrix properties not seen in connective tissue proper: bone's mineralization, cartilage's firm avascular non-mineralized matrix with chondrocytes, and blood's fluid plasma matrix, versus the fibrous, cellular connective tissue proper subtypes.

questions.q: A researcher examines two muscle samples: one is striated and involuntary, the other is striated and voluntary. Which two muscle types does this pair most likely represent?
o: Cardiac muscle and skeletal muscle, respectively
Both samples must be skeletal muscle
Smooth muscle and cardiac muscle, respectively
Skeletal muscle and smooth muscle, respectively
questions.e: Cardiac muscle is striated yet involuntary, while skeletal muscle is striated and voluntary — matching the described pair; smooth muscle, in contrast, is non-striated.

questions.q: Movements of inversion and eversion of the foot take place primarily at which joints, NOT at the ankle joint itself?
questions.e: The lecture specifically notes that inversion and eversion occur at the tarsal joints, not at the ankle (talocrural) joint, which itself permits dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

questions.q: A patient with four lumbar vertebrae and 6 fused sacral vertebrae, but an otherwise normal spine, most likely shows which condition?
questions.e: Sacralisation occurs when the lowest lumbar vertebra fuses with the sacrum, effectively reducing lumbar vertebrae to four and increasing fused sacral vertebrae to six.

questions.q: A specimen: epithelial-cell clusters embedded in CT; some dark serous, some pale mucous; UNBRANCHED ducts link them to a surface. The specimen is:
o: Is a gland that secretes a watery product rich in enzymes
A simple exocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
Contains both simple squamous and simple cuboidal epithelial tissues
A simple endocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
Is from an organ which secretes both endocrine and exocrine products
questions.e: Ducts opening onto a surface = exocrine; unbranched ducts = simple; both serous and mucous units = mixed (seromucous). That's C.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones is/are part of the hard palate?
questions.e: The hard palate is formed anteriorly by the palatine processes of the maxillae (and posteriorly by the palatine bones).

questions.q: A 16th-century anatomist corrected many long-standing errors in anatomical texts by insisting on direct human dissection rather than relying on older, unverified sources. Who is most closely associated with this shift?
questions.e: Andreas Vesalius produced a landmark, meticulously illustrated anatomical text based on direct human dissection, correcting many inherited errors from earlier authorities.

questions.q: Unlike most connective tissue, one specialized type is notably avascular, relying entirely on diffusion for nutrient exchange. Which specialized connective tissue is this?
questions.e: Cartilage is the notable exception among connective tissues in being avascular; it depends on diffusion of nutrients through the perichondrium (or synovial fluid at joint surfaces), unlike the generally well-vascularized bone and connective tissue proper.

questions.q: The ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur) runs from the acetabular fossa to which structure?
questions.e: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) passes from the acetabular fossa to the fovea on the femoral head, enclosing a branch of the obturator artery.

questions.q: On the lower part of the anterior surface of the radial shaft, a roughened oblique line marks the:
questions.e: The pronator ridge is a rough, obliquely placed line on the lower anterior surface of the radius, providing attachment for part of pronator quadratus.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a tissue?
o: A group of cells that have a similar structure and function
A group of organs working together for a common purpose
The collection of all organelles in a cell
Organs such as the heart or liver
A group of macromolecules within a cell
questions.e: A tissue = a group of cells of similar structure and function — B. (A group of organs = a system.)

questions.q: Which carpal bone bears a hook-like projection (the hook of hamate)?
questions.e: The hamate carpal bone is named for and characterized by its hook (hamulus), a projection on its palmar surface that anchors part of the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: Within the lateral collateral ligament complex of the elbow, which component is described as the main stabilizer?
questions.e: The lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) is described as the main stabilizer of the lateral elbow, protecting against varus force.

questions.q: The skull bone that provides the major passageway for the brain to communicate with the rest of the body is the
questions.e: The occipital bone contains the foramen magnum, the major passageway connecting the brain (via the spinal cord) to the rest of the body.

questions.q: The costal groove, found at the inferior border of the inner rib surface, contains which neurovascular structures, in order from superior to inferior?
questions.e: The costal groove contains the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve arranged from superior to inferior, remembered by the mnemonic VAN.

questions.q: Examination of brown adipose tissue shows that it:
o: Has an extremely rich supply of capillaries
Is unilocular and mainly found in adults
Is found both in adults and infants
Is multilocular and mainly found in adults
questions.e: Brown fat is multilocular and packed with mitochondria and a rich capillary supply (the source of its brown colour) — D. (Note: option E is also true in modern understanding — active brown fat does persist in adults — but D is the distinctive histological answer the paper wants.)

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding epithelia.
o: Pseudostratified epithelia consist of several layers of cuboidal cells
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of at least two layers of cells stacked on top of one another
Stratified epithelia are present where protection from abrasion is important
Stratified epithelia are tall, narrow cells
questions.e: Stratified epithelia occur where abrasion protection matters — C. (Pseudostratified is a single layer; simple epithelia are selectively permeable, not impermeable.)

questions.q: Which two carpals articulate with the radius to form the wrist joint?
questions.e: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is formed by the distal radius articulating mainly with the scaphoid and lunate.

questions.q: Posterior to the foramen magnum lies a midline bony ridge known as the:
questions.e: Posterior to the foramen magnum, the internal occipital crest and internal occipital protuberance can be identified within the posterior cranial fossa.

questions.q: You think an unknown cartilage is from the pinna of the ear because:
o: It contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
Numerous chondroblasts arranged into isogenous groups
questions.e: The pinna (auricle) is made of elastic cartilage — D. (Alternating collagen layers = fibrocartilage.)

questions.q: An elongated bursa that wraps around a tendon subjected to friction is termed a:
questions.e: A tendon sheath is an elongated bursa that wraps around tendons of certain muscles, occurring only where tendons are subjected to friction.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A suture is classified as an amphiarthrosis.
Reason (R): A suture is found only in the skull and is held by short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
questions.e: The Reason is true (it correctly describes a suture), but the Assertion is false — a suture is classified as a synarthrosis (immovable joint), not an amphiarthrosis.

questions.q: Which of the bones below is the first to ossify in pregnancy?
questions.e: The clavicle is the first bone in the body to begin ossifying in the embryo (around week 5–6).

questions.q: The femur:
o: The upper end consists of a head, a neck, greater tubercle and a lesser tubercle
Is the longest and heaviest bone of the body.
In the standing position the femur transmits weight from the hip bone to the tibia
The lower end consists of two condyles and two trochanters
questions.e: A and B correctly describe the femur. C and D incorrectly assign tubercles/trochanters to the wrong ends (trochanters are proximal, condyles are distal).

questions.q: Endochondral ossification occurs in the
questions.e: Most bones of the body (ribs, phalanges, fibula, and other long/irregular bones) develop via endochondral ossification (cartilage model first).

questions.q: Which of the following best summarizes the key contrast between the general structure of epithelial tissue and connective tissue?
o: Epithelial tissue has densely packed cells with minimal matrix; connective tissue has abundant matrix and comparatively sparse cells
Epithelial tissue always contains a mineralized matrix like bone
Only connective tissue contains cells at all
Both have abundant matrix and sparse cells
questions.e: The core structural contrast is that epithelial tissue packs cells tightly with very little matrix, while connective tissue is defined by its abundant extracellular matrix surrounding relatively few cells.

questions.q: Factors in preventing osteoporosis include:
questions.e: Of these flawed options, increasing dietary vitamin C (needed for collagen in bone matrix) is the only sound one — C. (You should INCREASE weight-bearing exercise and sun exposure, so B and D are wrong.)

questions.q: A dentist notes that a patient habitually juts the lower jaw forward when concentrating. Which term describes this forward gliding movement of the mandible?
questions.e: Protraction is an anterior (forward) gliding movement; retraction is the reverse, pulling the structure posteriorly back to its original position.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a synarthrotic joint?
questions.e: Sutures of the skull are classic synarthroses (immovable joints). The pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis, the knee is a freely movable diarthrosis, and a syndesmosis is generally classified as amphiarthrotic.

questions.q: True or False: The capitulum of the humerus articulates with the ulna, while the trochlea articulates with the radius.
questions.e: This is reversed: the capitulum articulates with the radius (specifically the head of radius), while the trochlea articulates with the ulna (at the trochlear notch).

questions.q: A physiology exam asks students to identify the CNS structures analogous to the PNS's ganglia and nerves. Which pairing is correct?
o: Nuclei and tracts are unrelated to ganglia and nerves
Ganglia and nerves exist only in the CNS, not the PNS
questions.e: The correct analogy is that CNS nuclei correspond to PNS ganglia (clusters of neuron cell bodies), while CNS tracts correspond to PNS nerves (bundles of neuron processes) — matching structure type across the two divisions.

questions.q: Which group of ribs is described as atypical due to their dissimilar features?
questions.e: The 1st, 2nd, and 10th-12th ribs are considered atypical because they are dissimilar in shape and articulation compared to the typical 3rd-9th ribs.

questions.q: The primary functions of the vertebral column include
o: Conducting nervous impulses from the brain.
Transmission of weight from the trunk to the lower limbs.
questions.e: The vertebral column protects the spinal cord and transmits body weight from the trunk down to the lower limbs (via the pelvis); it does not itself conduct nerve impulses.

questions.q: Continuing the dissection, the surgeon next separates the muscle into smaller bundles, each wrapped in its own connective tissue layer. What is each of these individual bundles called, and which layer wraps it?
o: A fascicle, wrapped by the perimysium
A myofibril, wrapped by the epimysium
A sarcomere, wrapped by the endomysium
A motor unit, wrapped by the sarcolemma
questions.e: Each bundle of muscle fibers is called a fascicle, and it is wrapped by the perimysium, the connective tissue layer intermediate between the epimysium (whole muscle) and endomysium (individual fiber).

questions.q: The saddle-shaped bony formation that houses and guards the pituitary gland, located on the body of the sphenoid, is the:
questions.e: The sella turcica is a saddle-like formation on the sphenoid that houses and guards the pituitary gland, flanked by anterior and posterior clinoid processes.

questions.q: The hip bone (os coxae) is formed by the fusion of three bones, all meeting at the acetabulum. Which three bones are these?
questions.e: The os coxae (hip bone) forms from fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis, which converge and fuse at the acetabulum, the socket for the femoral head.

questions.q: The anterior cruciate ligament primarily functions to:
o: Limit knee hyperextension and prevent anterior tibial dislocation
questions.e: The ACL limits knee hyperextension and prevents anterior dislocation of the tibia on the femur.

questions.q: The ridge just superior to the supraorbital margin, more pronounced in males, is the:
questions.e: The superciliary arch is a prominent ridge just above the supraorbital margin, typically more pronounced in males, corresponding to the brow ridge.

questions.q: True ribs (vertebrosternal ribs) refer to which pairs, articulating directly with the sternum anteriorly?
questions.e: True ribs, or vertebrosternal ribs, are the upper 7 pairs of ribs that articulate directly with the sternum anteriorly via their own costal cartilages.

questions.q: The skull
o: The opening that connects the cranial cavity to the spinal column is the foramen magnum
The bone surrounding the foramen magnum is the occipital bone
The lambdoid suture separates the two parietal bones from the frontal bone
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: A and B are correct. C is false — the lambdoid suture separates the parietal bones from the occipital bone, not the frontal bone (that is the coronal suture).

questions.q:
Assertion (A): All synovial joints are functionally classified as diarthroses.
Reason (R): Diarthroses are freely movable joints, and synovial joints possess a joint cavity that permits free movement.
o: Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true
questions.e: Both statements are true. The presence of a synovial (joint) cavity is precisely what allows synovial joints to move freely, which is why they are universally classified as diarthroses.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The shoulder joint's rotator cuff muscles contribute significantly to its stability.
Reason (R): The rotator cuff is a sheath of tendons from the subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus that covers and blends with most of the joint capsule.
o: A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are false
Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
questions.e: Both statements are true, and the Reason explains the Assertion: by enveloping and blending with the joint capsule, the rotator cuff musculotendinous sheath provides crucial dynamic stability to an otherwise structurally unstable joint.

questions.q: A motor neuron forms a specialized synapse directly onto a skeletal muscle fiber, rather than onto another neuron. What is this specific type of synapse called?
questions.e: A synapse formed specifically between a neuron and a muscle cell — as in this motor neuron/muscle fiber scenario — is termed a neuromuscular junction, distinct from the neuron-to-neuron synapse types.

questions.q: A trauma patient needs rapid bedside imaging of possible internal bleeding, without moving them to a scanner suite. Which modality is best suited to this point-of-care scenario?
o: Plain X-ray exclusively, since it is the only portable modality
Ultrasound, since portable units allow real-time bedside imaging
questions.e: Ultrasound units are commonly portable and provide real-time images at the bedside, making it well suited to rapid trauma assessment (as in the FAST exam for internal bleeding) without needing to transport the patient.

questions.q: The knee joint consists of two articulations enclosed within a single joint cavity. These are the tibiofemoral and:
questions.e: The knee joint consists of the tibiofemoral (a condylar joint) and patellofemoral (a saddle joint) articulations, both enclosed within a single joint cavity.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common clinical feature of developmental dysplasia of the hip?
o: Limb length discrepancy with the affected limb shorter
Increased range of abduction at the hip
questions.e: Common features of DDH include limited abduction, limb length discrepancy (affected limb shorter), and asymmetrical gluteal or thigh skin folds.

questions.q: Which motor neuron subtype would be responsible for stimulating smooth muscle in the gut wall to contract, as part of the autonomic nervous system's control over digestion?
questions.e: Visceral (autonomic) motor neurons innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands — including the smooth muscle of the gut wall involved in digestive motility — distinguishing them from somatic motor neurons, which innervate skeletal muscle.

questions.q: An epithelial cell's apical and basal surfaces differ structurally and functionally from one another. What is this property called?
questions.e: This apical-versus-basal structural and functional asymmetry is termed polarity, a hallmark feature of epithelial cells.

questions.q: Shoulder dislocation most commonly displaces the humeral head in which direction relative to the infraglenoid tubercle?
questions.e: Anterior dislocation accounts for about 95% of shoulder dislocations, making it by far the most common direction, although the overall displacement is described as downward (inferior).

questions.q: By approximately what age does fusion of the three hip bone components become complete?
questions.e: Fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis begins between 15 and 17 years of age and is generally complete between 20 and 25 years of age.

questions.q: All synovial joints fall under which functional category?
questions.e: Diarthroses are freely movable joints, and the lecture states that all synovial joints belong to this functional category.

questions.q: When the distal part of a bone deviates more medially than normal at a joint, this is termed:
questions.e: Varus describes angulation where the distal part is positioned more medially than it should be.

questions.q: How many facial bones are there in total, according to the notes?
questions.e: There are 14 facial bones in total: 2 unpaired (mandible, vomer) and 6 pairs (maxillae, zygomatic, nasal, lacrimal, palatine, and inferior nasal conchae).

questions.q: The anterior drawer sign is used to assess injury to which ligament?
questions.e: The anterior drawer sign tests for ACL tear, where hyperextension with anterior force on the tibia (partly flexed knee) produces excessive anterior tibial translation.

questions.q: Which best explains why simple epithelium (rather than stratified) is typically found lining sites specialized for diffusion, filtration, secretion, or absorption?
o: A single cell layer offers the shortest possible path for substances to cross, maximizing efficiency for these exchange-related functions
Simple epithelium is always thicker than stratified epithelium
Stratified epithelium contains no basement membrane
questions.e: A single-cell-layer (simple) epithelium minimizes the distance substances must cross, making it functionally efficient for diffusion, filtration, secretion, and absorption — functions less suited to the multiple layers of stratified epithelium.

questions.q: The skeleton with the highest number of bones is that of:
questions.e: A newborn has roughly 300 separate bone/cartilage elements — many that later fuse (e.g., skull, sacrum, hip bones) are still separate, giving infants more discrete bones than adults (~206).

questions.q: The lateral meniscus of the knee is approximately what fraction of a circle, and how does its mobility compare to the medial meniscus?
o: 4/5 of a circle; smaller and more mobile
questions.e: The lateral meniscus is about 4/5 of a circle and is smaller and more mobile than the medial meniscus.

questions.q: True or False: Hammer toe and claw toe both describe abnormalities in the alignment of toe joints, similar in concept to deformities seen in fingers.
questions.e: Hammer toe and claw toe describe flexion deformities at the interphalangeal joints of the toes, conceptually paralleling deformities like boutonniere or swan-neck seen in the fingers, though the specific joints and mechanisms differ.

questions.q: The forearm (antebrachium) consists of the radius and ulna, connected along their length by which structure?
questions.e: The radius (lateral) and ulna (medial) are connected throughout their shafts by a fibrous interosseous membrane, which also provides attachment for forearm muscles.

questions.q: What is the major function of the intervertebral discs?
questions.e: Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilaginous cushions whose main role is shock absorption between vertebral bodies.

questions.q: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior articular surface of the tibia, and which bone?
questions.e: The talocrural (ankle) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior surface of the tibia, and the talus.

questions.q: The mental foramen, located inferior to the second premolar, transmits the mental nerve and vessels, and lies on which part of the mandible?
questions.e: The mental foramen is located on the body (horizontal portion) of the mandible, inferior to the second premolar tooth.

questions.q: A researcher proposes that connective tissue's overall diversity (from blood to bone to tendon) arises mainly from variation in one structural component. Which component's variation best accounts for this diversity?
o: Connective tissue diversity is actually due to variation in epithelial cells, not connective tissue itself
The extracellular matrix — its composition and fiber content varies dramatically across connective tissue types, producing very different mechanical properties
The cell membrane, which is identical to all other cell types in the body
The presence or absence of a nucleus in the cells
questions.e: Connective tissue's remarkable functional diversity — from the fluid matrix of blood to the mineralized matrix of bone to the fiber-dense matrix of tendon — largely stems from variation in the extracellular matrix's composition and fiber content, which produces very different mechanical and functional properties across types.

questions.q: The skull bone that is connected to the rest of the cranium posteriorly via the coronal suture is the
questions.e: Per the marked answer key: the occipital region relationship was indicated as C. (Note: the coronal suture itself directly joins the frontal and parietal bones — students should also know this classic relationship.)

questions.q: Which of the following statements best describes connective tissue?
o: Always arranged in a single layer of cells
Usually contains a large amount of matrix
questions.e: (Repeat of Q58.) Connective tissue is defined by its abundant matrix — A.

questions.q: The axis (C2) has a peg-like projection called the dens, which articulates with the atlas to allow which movement?
questions.e: The dens of the axis articulates with the atlas at a pivot joint, helping rotate the head, as in shaking the head to say 'no'. The transverse ligament secures the dens in place.

questions.q: True or False: When examining a wet footprint, the medial margin from the heel to the first metatarsal head normally leaves no print because the medial longitudinal arch curves above the ground.
questions.e: In a person with a normal medial longitudinal arch, the wet footprint shows no impression along the medial margin between heel and first metatarsal head, since that part of the foot is elevated off the ground by the arch.

questions.q: Approximately what fraction of homicides by strangulation result in a fractured hyoid bone, according to the notes?
questions.e: According to the lecture notes, the hyoid bone is fractured in one-third of all homicides by strangulation.

questions.q: NONAXIAL JOINTS
o: Is found between articular processes of vertebrae and between tarsal bones
Does not involve rotation around any axis
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Nonaxial (plane/gliding) joints allow only short gliding movements without rotation, found e.g. between vertebral articular processes and between tarsal bones.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the tibia:
o: Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: The proximal tibia bears the medial and lateral condyles (articulating with the femur) and the tibial tuberosity (patellar ligament attachment).

questions.q: Which connective tissue membrane lines the internal surfaces of bone, including the medullary cavity, as opposed to the membrane covering bone's external surface?
questions.e: The endosteum lines the internal surfaces of bone (including the medullary cavity), in contrast to the periosteum, which covers the external surface of bone.

questions.q: The membranous area between the occipital and parietal bones of the foetal skull is called
questions.e: This membranous gap at the junction of the sagittal and lambdoid sutures (between the occipital and parietal bones) is the posterior fontanelle.

questions.q: Which best explains the functional logic behind classifying epithelial tissue partly by the shape of its surface cells (squamous, cuboidal, columnar)?
o: Cell shape has no functional significance and is purely descriptive
Only squamous cells can form glands
Columnar cells are always ciliated, unlike other shapes
Cell shape correlates with function: thin squamous cells favor diffusion, while cuboidal/columnar cells with more cytoplasm favor secretion and absorption
questions.e: Cell shape correlates meaningfully with function — flatter squamous cells minimize diffusion distance, while cuboidal and columnar cells, with more cytoplasmic volume and organelles, are better equipped for the active processes of secretion and absorption.

questions.q: The antebrachium is composed of which of the following two bones?
questions.e: "Antebrachium" is the anatomical term for the forearm, composed of the radius and ulna.

questions.q: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle is made up of which two bones?
questions.e: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle is made up of the scapula and the clavicle, connecting the upper limb to the axial skeleton.

questions.q: The femur is described as the longest and heaviest bone of the body, with its length ranging approximately what fraction of total body height?
questions.e: The femur's length typically ranges from about one-quarter to one-third of total body height/stature, which is why stature can be estimated from femur length in forensic contexts.

questions.q: Which of the following forms the largest portion of the hip bone?
questions.e: The ilium is the largest of the three bones (ilium, ischium, pubis) that fuse to form the hip bone.

questions.q: Which location would you NOT expect to find smooth muscle, based on its typical distribution in the walls of hollow organs and specific structures like the eye?
o: The wall of a blood vessel
questions.e: The femur shaft is composed of bone tissue, not smooth muscle; smooth muscle is characteristically found in the walls of hollow organs (blood vessels, stomach, intestines) and specialized structures like the intrinsic muscles of the eye (e.g., the iris).

questions.q: The patella:
o: Is a sesamoid bone that articulates with the femur, tibia and fibula
Enclosed in the tendon that secures the anterior muscles of the thigh to the tibia
Has an apex that is directed superiorly and a base that is inferior
questions.e: The patella, embedded in the quadriceps tendon, primarily functions to protect the knee joint anteriorly (it articulates only with the femur, and its apex points inferiorly, not superiorly).

questions.q: At birth, an infant has roughly how many separate bony elements before later fusion reduces the number?
questions.e: At birth, infants have about 270 separate bones; this number decreases over time due to gradual fusion of separate bony elements into the adult total of 206.

questions.q: A newly discovered gland secretes its product by pinching off part of its apical cytoplasm, similar to how some mammary gland cells release milk fat components. Which secretion mode does this match?
o: None of the above; this is a description of exocytosis only
questions.e: This description — the cell losing part of its apical cytoplasm along with the secreted product while surviving — matches apocrine secretion, a mode also seen in some mammary gland cells during lactation.

questions.q: Granular tissue formed after a fracture is infiltrated by which cells, according to the notes?
questions.e: Granular tissue at the fracture site is infiltrated by blood capillaries and fibroblasts, along with macrophages, osteoclasts, and osteogenic cells, which together prepare the site for callus formation.

questions.q: The adult human skeleton normally contains how many bones?
questions.e: The adult skeleton has 206 bones. At birth there are about 270 separate bony elements, several of which fuse together during growth, reducing the number to 206 by adulthood.

questions.q: Which bone type is thin, flattened, usually curved, and serves as an attachment site for muscles while protecting internal organs?
questions.e: Flat bones such as the skull, ribs, and sternum are thin and flattened with compact bone surrounding spongy bone, providing protection and muscle attachment.

questions.q: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the upper and lower limbs, plus their attachments to the axial skeleton at the:
questions.e: The appendicular skeleton includes limb bones along with their attachment points to the axial skeleton at the pectoral girdle (upper limb) and pelvic girdle (lower limb).

questions.q: Which end of the clavicle articulates with the manubrium of the sternum?
questions.e: The medial end of the clavicle is the sternal end, which articulates with the manubrium of the sternum to form the sternoclavicular joint.

questions.q: Which accessory structures are associated with synovial joints?
o: Fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, tendons
questions.e: Accessory structures of synovial joints include fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, and tendons.

questions.q: Which abdominopelvic region is located directly beneath the umbilical region?
questions.e: Directly inferior to the umbilical region is the hypogastric (pubic) region — E.

questions.q: The distal end of the ulna includes the head and its styloid process. Where is the ulnar styloid process located relative to the head?
questions.e: The styloid process of the ulna is small, conical, and palpable, situated medial and posterior to the rest of the ulnar head.

questions.q: In synovial joints, what covers the ends of the opposing bones and acts as a shock absorber?
questions.e: Articular cartilage covers the ends of opposing bones, decreases in thickness with age, and functions as a shock absorber that also reduces friction.

questions.q: Rickets, caused by inadequate dietary calcium or vitamin D in children, primarily causes:
questions.e: Rickets results from insufficient calcium or vitamin D in children, causing inadequate mineralisation of bone and characteristic bowing of the skeleton (bowed legs).

questions.q: Which fibrous joint is found exclusively in the skull, held by short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges?
questions.e: A suture is held together by very short interconnecting fibers with interlocking bone edges, and it is found only in the skull.

questions.q: Fibrous joints possess a true joint cavity.
questions.e: False. Fibrous joints have no joint cavity; the bones are connected directly by tough fibrous connective tissue.

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the temporal bone?
o: External acoustic meatus, styloid process, jugular foramen and carotid canal
Squamous suture, zygomatic process, mandibular fossa and stylomastoid foramen
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, hypoglossal canal and foramen ovale
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: A and B correctly list temporal bone features. C mixes in sphenoid (optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale) and occipital (hypoglossal canal) features, so it is incorrect.

questions.q: The fibula:
o: Several muscles originate from the fibula but it does not bear weight
Its malleolus forms the medial bulge of the ankle and articulates with the talus bone of the foot
Is a thin bone with two expanded ends and
questions.e: The fibula is thin with expanded ends and serves as a muscle attachment site without bearing significant weight. B is wrong — the fibula's malleolus is LATERAL, not medial.

questions.q: The vertebral arch projects from the body via paired structures called:
questions.e: Pedicles project from the vertebral body to form the sides of the vertebral arch, while laminae unite posteriorly to form the spinous process.

questions.q: The suprapatellar and semimembranosus bursae of the knee can become distended if excess synovial fluid accumulates within the joint, because they communicate with the joint cavity.
questions.e: True. Both the suprapatellar and semimembranosus bursae communicate with the knee joint and may distend when synovial fluid accumulates excessively.

questions.q: Which term reflects the epithelial tissue lining blood and lymphatic vessels?
questions.e: Endothelium lines blood and lymphatic vessels (mesothelium lines serous cavities). — B.

questions.q: Sexual differences in the human skeleton
o: The male pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep than the female pelvis
The female cranium is about 10% larger on the average
The sacrum is a long narrow triangle with a less pronounced sacral curvature in the female
The mandible is larger and more robust in the female
Male bones are heavier with prominent bone markings
questions.e: Correct: the male pelvis has a heart-shaped inlet, is narrower, and relatively deeper than the female pelvis (which is broader and shallower for childbearing). The mandible/bones/cranium statements in A, B, E are reversed or incorrect for sex differences.

questions.q: Which component of the lateral ankle ligament is described as the weakest, making it the most commonly injured?
questions.e: The anterior talofibular part of the lateral ligament is the weakest component, followed by the calcaneofibular ligament, making it the most frequently injured in ankle sprains.

questions.q: The anterior fontanelle closes during the second year of life and is then known as the:
questions.e: The anterior fontanelle sits at the junction of the coronal and sagittal sutures — the bregma — and typically closes by 18–24 months.

questions.q: The endosteum is best described as:
o: An avascular membrane found only in flat bones
A non-cellular fibrous capsule around joints
A double-layered membrane covering the outer bone surface
A single-layered, osteogenic membrane lining inner bone surfaces
questions.e: The endosteum is single-layered, lines the inner bone surfaces, is osteogenic, and contributes to new bone formation, unlike the periosteum which covers outer surfaces.

questions.q: Given that cilia require significant cellular energy (ATP) to beat continuously, which epithelial cell would you expect to contain a particularly high density of mitochondria to support this activity?
o: A squamous cell lining a capillary
An unciliated cuboidal cell in a small gland duct
A keratinized surface cell of the epidermis
A ciliated columnar cell in the respiratory tract
questions.e: Because ciliary beating is energy-intensive, ciliated columnar cells of the respiratory tract are expected to contain a relatively high density of mitochondria to supply the ATP needed for continuous, coordinated ciliary movement.

questions.q: The prominent bony knobs on each side of the ankle joint are
o: The medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula
The medial malleolus of the fibula and the lateral malleolus of the tibia
The epicondyles of the tibia and fibula
The styloid processes of the tibia and fibula
The head of the fibula and the tuberosity of the tibia
questions.e: The ankle "bony knobs" are the medial malleolus (of the tibia) and lateral malleolus (of the fibula).

questions.q: What distinguishes dislocation from subluxation?
o: Dislocation is a complete loss of articular surface contact, while subluxation is a partial loss
questions.e: A dislocation (luxation) is a complete displacement of articulating bone surfaces from one another, while subluxation is only a partial displacement.

questions.q: The major function(s) of the thoracic cage is (are)
o: To help expand the thoracic cavity during breathing
questions.e: The thoracic cage both protects the thoracic organs (lungs, heart) and, via rib movement, helps expand the thoracic cavity during breathing.

questions.q: The following are features of the humerus EXCEPT:
o: It consists of a shaft and two ends
The distal end consists of the two condyles, a medial trochlea and a lateral capitulum
The proximal end consists of the condyle, the medial epicondyle and the lateral epicondyle
It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder
The proximal end consists of the head, anatomical neck, and two tubercles
questions.e: The condyle and epicondyles are DISTAL humeral features, not proximal — making C the incorrect (EXCEPT) statement.

questions.q: A neurosurgeon distinguishes structures protected within the skull and vertebral column from those running through the limbs and torso. Which two divisions of the nervous system does this distinction correspond to?
o: The central nervous system and peripheral nervous system
The somatic and autonomic nervous systems
questions.e: This distinction matches the CNS (brain and spinal cord, protected within the skull and vertebral column) versus the PNS (cranial and spinal nerves running through the limbs and torso, outside this bony protection).

questions.q: The constricted portion of a typical rib located between the head and tubercle is called the:
questions.e: The neck of a typical rib is the constricted portion located between the head and the tubercle.

questions.q: Unlike skeletal or cardiac muscle cells, isolated smooth muscle cells retain a capacity that allows tissues like the uterus to increase muscle mass substantially during pregnancy. Which capacity is this?
o: Complete resistance to any hormonal influence
The ability to divide, increasing cell number
The ability to fuse into multinucleated fibers
questions.e: Smooth muscle cells are unusual among muscle types in retaining the capacity to divide (proliferate), which allows tissues like the uterine wall to substantially increase muscle mass through hyperplasia, such as during pregnancy.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion that selectively destroys interneurons within a specific spinal reflex circuit, while leaving the sensory and motor neurons of that circuit intact. What would you predict about the reflex's ability to function?
o: Only the sensory portion of the reflex would be affected, with motor output entirely unaffected
Destroying interneurons would have no measurable effect on any neural circuit
The reflex would likely be disrupted or altered, since interneurons provide the integrative link between the sensory input and motor output within the circuit
The reflex would function completely normally, since interneurons are not involved in any reflex circuits
questions.e: Because interneurons provide the integrative connection between sensory input and motor output within a reflex circuit (and make up the vast majority of neurons overall), their selective destruction would be expected to disrupt or alter the reflex, even with sensory and motor neurons themselves intact.

questions.q: A patient with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes shows early signs of sarcopenia despite being only in their 50s. Which best describes what is happening, based on the definition of this term?
o: An infection specific to muscle tissue
A benign, reversible increase in muscle mass
Accelerated muscle wasting, involving a decline in the number of muscle fibers and an increase in relative connective tissue, occurring earlier than typical age-related expectations
A congenital muscle disorder present since birth
questions.e: Sarcopenia refers to muscle wasting — a decline in muscle fiber number and mass with a relative increase in connective tissue — and though it is typically age-related, the same underlying process can be accelerated by conditions like poorly controlled diabetes, appearing earlier than expected.

questions.q: Which category of bone is typically longer than wide, has a shaft with heads at both ends, and functions mainly as a lever?
questions.e: Long bones are tubular, longer than wide, contain mostly compact bone, and act as levers for movement when muscles contract, e.g. the femur and humerus.

questions.q: Elastic connective tissue:
o: Is present in the vocal ligaments of the larynx
Contains stellate fibroblasts and a mucoid ground substance
Is typical of the umbilical cord and placenta
Is present in adults and foetuses
Contains jelly-like intercellular substance with collagenous fibers
questions.e: Dense elastic connective tissue forms the vocal ligaments, ligamenta flava, etc. — B. (Umbilical cord/stellate cells/jelly describe mucous CT = Wharton's jelly.)

questions.q: A less common synapse type is found where an axon terminal directly contacts the cell body (soma) of the next neuron, rather than its dendrites. What is this synapse type called?
questions.e: An axosomatic synapse is formed between an axon terminal and the cell body (soma) of another neuron, distinguishing it from the more common axodendritic synapse.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly matches a muscle type with its typical location, based on functional and structural adaptation?
o: Smooth muscle — attached to the femur via a tendon
Cardiac muscle — the wall of the stomach
Smooth muscle — the wall of a blood vessel
questions.e: Smooth muscle is correctly matched to the wall of a blood vessel, where it controls vessel diameter; the other pairings mismatch tissue type and location (cardiac muscle belongs to the heart wall, and skeletal muscle typically attaches to bone via tendons).

questions.q: Which hormone, produced by the parathyroid gland, increases blood calcium by stimulating osteoclast activity?
questions.e: Parathyroid hormone increases blood calcium levels by stimulating osteoclasts to resorb bone, releasing calcium into the bloodstream.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS
o: Have a synovial membrane of loose connective tissue
Have a fibrous capsule of dense irregular connective tissue
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Synovial joints have a two-layered articular capsule: an outer fibrous layer (dense irregular connective tissue) and an inner synovial membrane (loose connective tissue).

questions.q: Which tissue(s) would be most affected by chemotherapy?
questions.e: Chemotherapy targets rapidly dividing cells. Epithelium has the highest turnover (constantly renewing), so it's most affected — B.

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Hip joint pathology may sometimes present clinically as knee pain.
Reason (R): The obturator nerve supplies sensory branches to both the hip and the knee joints.
o: Both A and R are true, but R is NOT the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true
A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are false
questions.e: Both statements are true, and shared innervation by the obturator nerve across both joints directly explains why hip disease can refer pain to the knee.

questions.q: True or False: Temporary lordosis can be seen in obese individuals and pregnant women.
questions.e: True. Temporary lordosis is commonly observed in obese individuals and pregnant women due to the shifted centre of gravity.

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.e: Lumbar vertebrae have the largest, most massive vertebral bodies, adapted for weight-bearing.

questions.q: After a reflex is processed within the spinal cord, a signal travels from the CNS out to a skeletal muscle to produce a motor response. Functionally, which category of neuron carries this outgoing signal?
o: Interneuron only, since interneurons directly contract muscle
None of these; only sensory neurons exist in a reflex arc
questions.e: A neuron carrying a signal away from the CNS toward an effector organ such as skeletal muscle is functionally classified as a motor (efferent) neuron.

questions.q: A neuron's single long process, emerging from a specific point on the soma, conducts an impulse away from the cell body toward a distant target. From which specific point does this process originate?
questions.e: The axon hillock is the specific point on the soma from which the axon emerges, marking the origin of the process that conducts impulses away from the cell body.

questions.q: The coccyx is composed of how many rudimentary fused bones, oriented downward and ventrally?
questions.e: The coccyx has 4 rudimentary bones fused together according to the notes, directed downwards and ventrally, with laterally projecting rudimentary transverse processes. (Note: while commonly cited as 3-5 segments, this deck specifies 4 fused bones for the coccyx structure described.)

questions.q: Stereocilia are present in epithelial linings of the following organs:
o: Trachea, epididymis, penile urethra, membranous urethra
Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles, membranous urethra
Primary bronchi and gallbladder, vas deferens, penile urethra
questions.e: True stereocilia (long, non-motile microvilli) line the epididymis and ductus (vas) deferens — and sensory hair cells of the ear. Only E lists both without a wrong organ.

questions.q: An epithelium: cells taller than wide, appearing >1 layer thick, all attached to the membrane; some with apical microvilli; NO goblet cells or cilia; contained some bipolar neurons. Most likely:
o: Located in the olfactory and respiratory segments
A modified type of respiratory epithelium with sensory neurons
A, B and C are correct
Only B and C are correct
questions.e: Bipolar neurons = olfactory receptor cells → this is the olfactory mucosa (pseudostratified, with supporting-cell microvilli). Answer C.

questions.q: Which of the following would most directly compromise an epithelium's ability to serve as a selective barrier (controlling exactly what passes between the external and internal environments)?
o: A change from simple to stratified epithelium
An increase in the number of goblet cells
Disruption of tight junctions between adjacent cells
questions.e: Since tight junctions are what seal the intercellular space and prevent free paracellular passage, their disruption most directly undermines the epithelium's selective barrier function, allowing uncontrolled leakage between cells.

questions.q: The intervertebral disc consists of an outer rim of fibrocartilage called annulus fibrosus and a central gelatinous core called:
questions.e: The intervertebral disc has an outer annulus fibrosus and an inner gelatinous core called the nucleus pulposus, which together act as shock absorbers.

questions.q: The hyoid bone is unique because it is:
o: Covered with mucosa and epithelial tissue
Attached to the sternal angle at the T4 vertebral level
Shaped like a right-angled triangle on its side
A sesmoid bone formed in connective tissue under pressure
The only bone that does not articulate with any other bone
questions.e: The hyoid is suspended by muscles and ligaments in the neck and is the only bone in the body that does not directly articulate with any other bone.

questions.q: A bulging fontanelle in an infant is typically a sign of:
questions.e: A bulging fontanelle indicates increased pressure on the brain (raised intracranial pressure), whereas a depressed fontanelle indicates dehydration.

questions.q: Intervertebral discs account for what proportion of the height of the vertebral column?
questions.e: Intervertebral discs account for 20-25% of the height of the vertebral column, acting as cushion-like shock absorbers between vertebral bodies.

questions.q: Which best describes the relationship between the basement membrane and epithelial regeneration after superficial injury?
o: Only connective tissue, not the basement membrane, guides epithelial regeneration
The basement membrane plays no role in regeneration
The basement membrane must be destroyed before regeneration can occur
As long as the basement membrane remains intact, new epithelial cells can migrate and proliferate across it to resurface the wound relatively efficiently
questions.e: An intact basement membrane provides a structural scaffold that guides the migration and proliferation of new epithelial cells during regeneration after superficial injury, supporting relatively efficient resurfacing of the wound.

questions.q: Why is bone able to heal relatively efficiently after a fracture, in contrast to the poor healing capacity of cartilage discussed earlier?
o: Bone matrix contains no cells at all, so there is nothing to regenerate
Bone fractures never actually require cellular repair
Bone is richly vascularized, unlike avascular cartilage, allowing efficient delivery of repair cells, oxygen, and nutrients to the fracture site
Bone cells divide faster than any other cell type in the body
questions.e: Bone's extensive vascular supply — in sharp contrast to avascular cartilage — allows efficient delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and repair-related cells to a fracture site, underlying its comparatively efficient healing.

questions.q: A researcher disrupts the cells that form the blood-brain barrier, causing substances that normally cannot cross into brain tissue to leak through. Which glial cell type has most likely been disrupted?
questions.e: Astrocytes contribute significantly to forming the blood-brain barrier, so their disruption would be expected to compromise this barrier, allowing abnormal substance leakage into brain tissue.

questions.q: Proximally, the ulna articulates with the humerus and, more distally, it also relates to which structures?
o: The carpals directly and the humerus laterally
Only the radius, with no distal articulation
The articular disc below and the radius laterally
questions.e: The ulna articulates with the humerus proximally, and distally relates to an articular disc (of the wrist) below and the radius laterally via the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.q: A flatten sheet of tendon is called
questions.e: An aponeurosis is a broad, flattened sheet of tendinous tissue.

questions.q: Posterior to the central incisors, a small depression with paired canals for the nasopalatine nerves is the:
questions.e: The incisive fossa, located posterior to the central incisors, contains the incisive canals which transmit the nasopalatine nerves.

questions.q: The hard palate is formed by the palatine processes of the maxillae together with which other structure?
o: The pterygoid plates of the sphenoid
The horizontal plates of the palatine bone
questions.e: The hard palate is formed anteriorly by the palatine processes of the maxillae and posteriorly by the horizontal plates of the palatine bone.

questions.q: Adhering to the outer surface of the limiting membrane of the granular endoplasmic reticulum is/are the:
questions.e: "Granular"/rough ER is granular precisely because ribosomes stud its outer surface — C.

questions.q: The fibre type that gives connective tissue GREAT TENSILE STRENGTH is:
questions.e: Collagen fibres provide great tensile strength — B.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the tibia:
o: Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
questions.e: The distal tibia has the fibular notch (articulating with the fibula) and the medial malleolus, which forms the medial bulge of the ankle.

questions.q: If you see a foramen in the transverse process of a vertebra, which type of vertebra are you observing?
questions.e: Transverse foramina (which transmit the vertebral artery/vein) are a defining feature unique to cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: In the anatomical position the:
o: The thumb is medial to the little finger
Body is erect and palms face anterior
Palms of the hands face posteriorly
Arms are extended away from the body
Body is in a foetal position.
questions.e: In standard anatomical position, the body stands erect, arms at the sides, palms facing anteriorly (forward).

questions.q: The maxillae:
o: Form the upper jaw and the central part of the facial skeleton
Form the bony roof of the oral cavity/mouth
Do not articulate with the mandible
A, C and D are correct
questions.e: A, C, D correctly describe the maxillae. B is incorrect — the maxillae do not articulate with every facial bone (e.g., not with the mandible).

questions.q: On the inferior aspect of the skull, three parts of the sphenoid bone can be appreciated. Which structure lies between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates?
questions.e: The pterygoid fossa is located between the medial and lateral pterygoid plates of the sphenoid bone, visible on the inferior skull view.

questions.q: A peripheral nerve is dissected in layers, from the innermost connective tissue wrapping a single axon, outward to a wrapping around a bundle of axons, and finally to the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve. In order from innermost to outermost, what are these three layers called?
questions.e: From innermost to outermost, a peripheral nerve's connective tissue layers are: the endoneurium (around a single axon), the perineurium (around a fascicle/bundle of axons), and the epineurium (the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve).

questions.q: Perforating (Volkmann's) canals are oriented in what direction relative to the central (Haversian) canals?
