questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Compared to the male sacrum, the female sacrum is generally:
questions.e: The female sacrum is generally wider and shorter than the male sacrum, with a shallower concavity, adapted for the wider female pelvis.

questions.q: The coccyx is composed of how many rudimentary fused bones, oriented downward and ventrally?
questions.e: The coccyx has 4 rudimentary bones fused together according to the notes, directed downwards and ventrally, with laterally projecting rudimentary transverse processes. (Note: while commonly cited as 3-5 segments, this deck specifies 4 fused bones for the coccyx structure described.)

questions.q: The bulk of the sternum, whose sides are notched for articulation with costal cartilages of ribs 2-7, is called the:
questions.e: The body forms the bulk of the sternum, with notched sides for articulation with the costal cartilages of ribs 2 through 7.

questions.q: The xiphoid process of the sternum is composed of which tissue in youth, before ossifying around age 40?
questions.e: The xiphoid process is composed of hyaline cartilage in youth and typically ossifies around age 40, occasionally remaining bifid or perforated.

questions.q: How many pairs of false ribs are present in the skeleton?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The costal groove, found at the inferior border of the inner rib surface, contains which neurovascular structures, in order from superior to inferior?
questions.e: The costal groove contains the intercostal vein, artery, and nerve arranged from superior to inferior, remembered by the mnemonic VAN.

questions.q: The constricted portion of a typical rib located between the head and tubercle is called the:
questions.e: The neck of a typical rib is the constricted portion located between the head and the tubercle.

questions.q: The only group of vertebrae that articulates with the ribs is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which ribs are described as having only one facet and articulating with a single vertebra, with no neck or tubercle?
questions.e: The 10th and 12th ribs have only one facet and articulate with a single vertebra, and the 11th and 12th ribs are short with no neck or tubercle.

questions.q: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the upper and lower limbs, plus their attachments to the axial skeleton at the:
questions.e: The appendicular skeleton includes limb bones along with their attachment points to the axial skeleton at the pectoral girdle (upper limb) and pelvic girdle (lower limb).

questions.q: The common names for the scapula, clavicle, sternum, calvaria and patella are the:
o: Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, hip bone and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, knee cap, collar bone, breast bone and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, hip bone, collar bone, knee cap and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, collar bone, breast bone, skull cap and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, collar bone and knee cap respectively
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which structure?
questions.e: The scapula articulates with the head of the humerus at the glenoid fossa, forming the glenohumeral (shoulder) joint.

questions.q: Compression of the median nerve as it passes deep to the flexor retinaculum at the wrist produces which condition?
questions.e: Carpal tunnel syndrome results from compression of the median nerve within the carpal tunnel, the space bounded by the carpal bones and the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: The following are features of the humerus EXCEPT:
o: It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder
The distal end consists of the two condyles, a medial trochlea and a lateral capitulum
It consists of a shaft and two ends
The proximal end consists of the head, anatomical neck, and two tubercles
The proximal end consists of the condyle, the medial epicondyle and the lateral epicondyle
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The shaft of the tibia is the most frequent site of an open fracture, commonly resulting from motorcycle accidents.
questions.e: Because the tibial shaft lies just beneath the skin with little soft tissue covering anteriorly, it is the most common site for open (compound) fractures, frequently from motorcycle accidents.

questions.q: Which tarsal bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which carpal bone is most frequently fractured, with tenderness elicited at the anatomical snuffbox?
questions.e: The scaphoid is the most commonly fractured carpal bone. Tenderness over the anatomical snuffbox after a fall on an outstretched hand raises strong suspicion for a scaphoid fracture.

questions.q: On the shaft of the humerus, the deltoid tuberosity is located:
o: Laterally, for attachment of the deltoid muscle
questions.e: The deltoid tuberosity is a roughened prominence on the lateral aspect of the humeral shaft that serves as the insertion site for the deltoid muscle.

questions.q: The appendicular skeleton includes the bones of the limbs together with the structures that attach them to the axial skeleton. Which pair correctly matches limb to its girdle?
o: Upper limb - pelvic girdle; Lower limb - pectoral girdle
Upper limb - pectoral girdle; Lower limb - pelvic girdle
Upper limb has no girdle attachment
Both limbs attach via the pectoral girdle
Both limbs attach via the pelvic girdle
questions.e: The upper limb attaches to the axial skeleton at the pectoral (shoulder) girdle, while the lower limb attaches at the pelvic girdle.

questions.q: True or False: The medial epicondyle of the humerus has the ulnar nerve passing immediately behind it, making it vulnerable to injury (the 'funny bone' phenomenon).
questions.e: The ulnar nerve runs in a groove just posterior to the medial epicondyle, which is why striking this area produces the tingling sensation commonly called hitting the 'funny bone'.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements concerning the radius:
o: It is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
It articulates with the carpus proximally and the ulna medially
The proximal end consists of a head, neck and tuberosity
The distal end is expanded and bears a pointed process known as the styloid process
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the humerus?
o: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: In standard anatomical position, which bone of the forearm lies laterally?
questions.e: In anatomical position (forearm supinated, palm facing forward), the radius lies lateral and the ulna lies medial.

questions.q: Which bone is not part of the pelvic girdle?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: What kind of tissue serves as a model for long bones in the embryo?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The bony pelvis:
o: All the above are features of the bony pelvis
Consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx
In the female it is generally wider, shallower and lighter and adapted for childbearing
The outlet is bounded anteriorly by the pubic arch, laterally by the ischial tuberosities, posteriorly by the sacrum and coccyx
Has a pelvic inlet and pelvic outlet
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which carpal bone bears a hook-like projection (the hook of hamate)?
questions.e: The hamate carpal bone is named for and characterized by its hook (hamulus), a projection on its palmar surface that anchors part of the flexor retinaculum.

questions.q: True or False: The supraspinous fossa is found on the costal (anterior) surface of the scapula.
questions.e: The supraspinous fossa is on the dorsal (posterior) surface of the scapula, above the spine. The costal surface instead bears the subscapular fossa.

questions.q: The lesser trochanter, intertrochanteric crest and gluteal tuberosity are found on the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: By approximately what age does fusion of the three hip bone components become complete?
questions.e: Fusion of the ilium, ischium, and pubis begins between 15 and 17 years of age and is generally complete between 20 and 25 years of age.

questions.q: True or False: A lumbar rib is sometimes referred to as a gorilla rib because gorillas typically possess an extra rib at this vertebral level.
questions.e: A lumbar rib (an extra rib articulating with a lumbar vertebra) is nicknamed the gorilla rib because gorillas normally have 13 pairs of ribs, including one attached to the first lumbar vertebra.

questions.q: The thumb (pollex) corresponds to which numbered metacarpal?
questions.e: Metacarpals are numbered 1 to 5 from lateral (thumb side) to medial; the thumb (pollex) corresponds to metacarpal I.

questions.q: A Colles' fracture of the distal radius classically produces which deformity?
questions.e: In a Colles' fracture, the distal fragment of the radius is displaced and tilted posteriorly, producing the characteristic dinner fork (or silver fork) deformity of the wrist.

questions.q: Which of the following forms the largest portion of the hip bone?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not correct anatomically?
o: The Axis is inferior to the Atlas
The eye brow is superior to the eye lid
The index finger is medial to the pollex
The distal end of the radius lies lateral in a pronated antebrachium
The carpal bones are arranged into a proximal and distal rows of four bones each
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which digit does not have a middle phalanx?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The femur is described as the longest and heaviest bone of the body, with its length ranging approximately what fraction of total body height?
questions.e: The femur's length typically ranges from about one-quarter to one-third of total body height/stature, which is why stature can be estimated from femur length in forensic contexts.

questions.q: The roughened anterior border of the pubis is named the:
questions.e: The pubic crest is the roughened ridge forming the anterior border of the pubic body, an attachment site for abdominal muscles.

questions.q: How many epiphyseal centres typically develop in the clavicle, and at which end?
o: Three, at the shaft and both ends
None — it ossifies entirely from a single primary centre
questions.e: Only one epiphyseal centre develops in the clavicle, located at the sternal (medial) end, appearing during adolescent years.

questions.q: True or False: The lesser tubercle of the humerus is located posteriorly, while the greater tubercle is anterior.
questions.e: This is reversed: the greater tubercle is lateral/posterior in position while the lesser tubercle is anterior, with the intertubercular groove lying between them.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the humerus?
o: Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On the inferior surface of the clavicle's shaft, the conoid tubercle forms a synovial joint with which part of the scapula?
questions.e: The conoid tubercle, on the inferior surface of the clavicle, anchors the conoid ligament and corresponds to a synovial-type connection with the coracoid process of the scapula.

questions.q: In anatomical position, the scapula lies posterolateral to which ribs?
questions.e: The scapula is a large, flattened triangular bone that lies posterolateral to the 2nd through 7th ribs in the normal anatomical position.

questions.q: The major function(s) of the thoracic cage is (are)
o: To help expand the thoracic cavity during breathing
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Characteristics of the ulna include:
o: The ulna is the longer and more lateral bone of the forearm
It articulates with the humerus proximally and the radius laterally
The proximal end includes the olecranon, the trochlear notch and the radial notch
The distal end includes the head and the styloid process
B, C and D are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The greater tubercle of the humerus is palpable laterally and contributes to the rounded contour of the shoulder.
questions.e: The greater tubercle, situated laterally on the proximal humerus, is a palpable bony landmark that contributes to the lateral contour of the shoulder.

questions.q: The ilium contributes what fraction of the acetabulum?
questions.e: The ilium, the largest and uppermost of the three hip bone components, contributes about two-fifths (2/5th) of the acetabulum.

questions.q: Which neck of the humerus joins the proximal end to the shaft, and is clinically significant because fractures here can injure the axillary nerve?
questions.e: The surgical neck joins the proximal end of the humerus to the shaft. It is clinically important because the axillary nerve and posterior circumflex humeral vessels wrap around it closely and are vulnerable in fractures here.

questions.q: On which bone is the head found at the distal end?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The wing-like flared portion of the ilium is called the:
questions.e: The flared, wing-shaped portion of the ilium is called the ala (Latin for 'wing'), which provides broad surface area for gluteal muscle attachment.

questions.q: Just below the head of the femur lies a small pit. What is this pit called and what attaches there?
o: The trochanteric fossa, for obturator externus
The fovea, for the ligament of the head of femur
The intertrochanteric crest, for quadratus femoris
The linea aspera, for adductor muscles
questions.e: The fovea is a small pit just below and slightly posterior to the femoral head, marking the attachment of the ligament of the head of the femur (ligamentum teres).

questions.q: Which of the following bones is/are not weight bearing?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: During a pudendal nerve block performed to relieve perineal pain in childbirth, the nerve wraps around which structure before giving its branches?
questions.e: The pudendal nerve curves around the ischial spine and sacrospinous ligament before dividing into its terminal branches, making this region the target for a pudendal nerve block.

questions.q: In the same mnemonic, which carpal bone is represented by the word "Peter"?
questions.e: The proximal row from lateral to medial is Scaphoid (So), Lunate (Luke), Triquetrum (Took), Pisiform (Peter) — "Peter" corresponds to the pisiform.

questions.q: The proximal row of carpal bones includes which of the following?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The pubis is divided into a body and two rami. Which two rami are these?
questions.e: The pubis is composed of a body plus a superior ramus and an inferior ramus, which together help form the obturator foramen and pubic arch.

questions.q: Which of these bones would bear a ring?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which two tubercles of the proximal humerus are separated by the intertubercular (bicipital) groove?
questions.e: The greater tubercle (laterally) and lesser tubercle (anteriorly) are separated by the intertubercular groove (sulcus), through which the long head of biceps tendon runs.

questions.q: The ischium consists of a body and a ramus, and the free lower end of the body forms which prominent landmark?
questions.e: The free lower end of the ischial body forms the ischial tuberosity, the bony prominence that bears the body's weight during sitting.

questions.q: The pubic tubercle, an important landmark in the lower abdominal wall, is located at the:
o: Upper medial part of the pubis
Lower lateral part of the pubis
questions.e: The pubic tubercle lies at the lower lateral part of the pubic body and is a key surface landmark used to identify the superficial inguinal ring and to differentiate inguinal from femoral hernias.

questions.q: The subpubic (pubic) angle in females is generally:
questions.e: Females typically have a broader pubic angle, greater than 100 degrees between the pubic bones, compared to the narrower angle in males.

questions.q: True or False: A Colles' fracture is a classic injury sustained after a fall onto an outstretched hand.
questions.e: Colles' fracture of the distal radius is a very common injury resulting from a fall onto an outstretched hand (FOOSH), particularly in older adults with osteoporotic bone.

questions.q: True or False: Elderly individuals are prone to fracturing the neck of the femur even after only a minor fall.
questions.e: Due to age-related osteoporosis, elderly individuals are particularly susceptible to femoral neck fractures even from relatively minor falls.

questions.q: A fracture involving the surgical neck of the humerus would most likely affect which nerve?
questions.e: The axillary nerve winds closely around the surgical neck of the humerus, making it the nerve most at risk in fractures at this site (in contrast to the radial nerve, which is at risk in mid-shaft fractures at the spiral groove).

questions.q: The carpal bones are arranged in two rows of four. Which carpal bone is unusual in having very few articular facets, unlike the rest?
questions.e: Most carpal bones have several articular facets for neighbouring bones, but the pisiform is an exception, articulating mainly with the triquetrum and acting like a sesamoid bone within the flexor carpi ulnaris tendon.

questions.q: True or False: The gynecoid pelvis shape is considered the type least favorable for vaginal childbirth.
questions.e: The gynecoid pelvis is the classic rounded shape considered most favorable for vaginal delivery; the android and platypelloid types are generally considered less favorable.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the femur?
o: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: In females, the sacrum and coccyx show greater curvature, arcing further into the pelvic outlet compared to males.
questions.e: It is the male sacrum and coccyx that arc more sharply into the pelvic outlet; the female sacrum and coccyx show LESS curvature, helping to enlarge the pelvic outlet for childbirth.

questions.q: The lower end of the femur has two spirally curved condyles separated by which structure?
questions.e: The two distal femoral condyles (medial and lateral) are separated posteriorly by the intercondylar fossa (notch), which provides attachment for the cruciate ligaments of the knee.

questions.q: The side to which a scapula belongs can be determined from the following:
o: The large concave surface is posterior
The acromion and glenoid cavity belong to the lower and lateral part of the scapula
The spine projects from the posterior surface and extends laterally as the acromion
Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are located on the anterior surface
Coracoid process is located on the posterior surface
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The upper limb is described as having four segments — the shoulder girdle, arm, forearm, and hand.
questions.e: The upper limb is classically divided into the shoulder girdle, arm (brachium), forearm (antebrachium), and hand, giving it four functional segments.

questions.q: The oblique groove on the posterior shaft of the humerus, which transmits the radial nerve, is also called the:
questions.e: The radial groove (spiral groove) runs obliquely across the posterior surface of the humeral shaft and houses the radial nerve and profunda brachii vessels.

questions.q: "Stove-in-chest" is another name for which condition?
questions.e: Flail chest, caused by multiple adjacent rib fractures in more than one place, is also called a stove-in-chest because the loose segment moves paradoxically with breathing.

questions.q: The styloid processes of the radius and ulna are normally separated by approximately how much, a fact used in diagnosing distal radius fractures?
o: They are normally at the exact same level
questions.e: Normally, the radial and ulnar styloid processes are about 1 cm apart, with the radial styloid more distal; disruption of this relationship helps diagnose fractures of the distal radius.

questions.q: The lateral third of the clavicular shaft is described as flattened, while the medial two-thirds is described as:
questions.e: The shaft's lateral third is flattened, whereas the medial two-thirds has a rounded, hammer-like cross-sectional shape.

questions.q: True or False: Hammer toe and claw toe both describe abnormalities in the alignment of toe joints, similar in concept to deformities seen in fingers.
questions.e: Hammer toe and claw toe describe flexion deformities at the interphalangeal joints of the toes, conceptually paralleling deformities like boutonniere or swan-neck seen in the fingers, though the specific joints and mechanisms differ.

questions.q: On the radius, where is the radial tuberosity located relative to the neck?
o: Posterior and distal to the neck
Lateral and proximal to the head
Anterior and medial, distal to the neck
On the posterior border of the shaft
questions.e: The radial tuberosity lies on the anteromedial aspect of the radius, just distal to the neck, marking the boundary between the upper end and the shaft, and serves as the insertion for biceps brachii.

questions.q: The shaft of the radius has anterior, posterior, and lateral surfaces, along with anterior, posterior, and which other border?
questions.e: The radial shaft has three borders: anterior, posterior, and an interosseous border, the last of which gives attachment to the interosseous membrane (except near its proximal-most part).

questions.q: True or False: The transverse arch of the foot runs from the heel to the toes, while the longitudinal arches run side to side.
questions.e: This is reversed: the longitudinal arches (medial and lateral) run from front to back (heel to toes), while the transverse arch runs side to side across the foot.

questions.q: The bones of the hand are grouped into carpals, metacarpals, and phalanges. How many bones are in each group respectively?
questions.e: The hand has 8 carpal bones (wrist), 5 metacarpals (palm), and 14 phalanges (fingers), totalling 27 bones.

questions.q: Using the mnemonic "So Luke Took Peter To The Church Hall" for the carpal bones from lateral to medial (proximal then distal row), which bone does "Church" represent?
questions.e: In the mnemonic, the distal row from lateral to medial is Trapezium (To), Trapezoid (The), Capitate (Church), Hamate (Hall) — so "Church" stands for the capitate bone.

questions.q: How many bones make up the entire upper limb (one side), according to the standard count of arm, forearm, and hand bones?
questions.e: The upper limb has 30 bones: humerus (1), radius and ulna (2), and the hand with carpals (8), metacarpals (5), and phalanges (14) = 1+2+8+5+14 = 30.

questions.q: The bone(s) of the leg which bears no weight is/are
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A fall onto the shoulder classically fractures the clavicle at which location?
o: The midpoint of the lateral third
The junction of the medial two-thirds and lateral one-third
questions.e: The clavicle most commonly fractures at the junction between its medial two-thirds and lateral one-third, a relatively weak transition point, after a fall onto the shoulder.

questions.q: The scapula articulates with the humerus at which feature?
questions.e: The glenoid fossa (glenoid cavity), located on the lateral angle of the scapula, is the shallow socket that articulates with the head of the humerus to form the glenohumeral joint.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the femur?
o: Lateral condyle, medial condyle and adductor tubercle
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: True or False: The inferior angle of the scapula is formed at the junction of the medial and lateral borders.
questions.e: The inferior angle marks the meeting point of the medial and lateral borders of the scapular body at the lowest point of the bone.

questions.q: Which of the bones below is the first to ossify in pregnancy?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Inflammation of the bursa covering the ischial tuberosity is termed:
questions.e: The ischial tuberosity is covered by a bursa that, when inflamed (often from prolonged sitting), causes ischial bursitis.

questions.q: The obturator foramen is bounded by which three structures?
questions.e: The obturator foramen is bounded by the pubis, the ischium, and their respective rami, and is closed by the obturator membrane except at the obturator groove/canal.

questions.q: On the lower part of the anterior surface of the radial shaft, a roughened oblique line marks the:
questions.e: The pronator ridge is a rough, obliquely placed line on the lower anterior surface of the radius, providing attachment for part of pronator quadratus.

questions.q: At puberty, the three hip bone components are separated by a characteristically shaped cartilage. What shape is this cartilage?
questions.e: At puberty, a Y-shaped (triradiate) cartilage still separates the ilium, ischium, and pubis at the acetabulum before final fusion occurs.

questions.q: Sexual differences in the human skeleton
o: The mandible is larger and more robust in the female
The sacrum is a long narrow triangle with a less pronounced sacral curvature in the female
Male bones are heavier with prominent bone markings
The male pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep than the female pelvis
The female cranium is about 10% larger on the average
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which scapular angle is formed at the junction of the lateral and superior borders?
questions.e: The lateral angle is the junction of the lateral and superior borders, and is thickened to form the head of the scapula bearing the glenoid cavity.

questions.q: The pectoral girdle is composed of the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Where is the articular circumference of the proximal radius widest, and why?
o: It has uniform width all around
Laterally, where it meets the capitulum
Medially, where it articulates with the ulna
questions.e: The articular circumference of the radial head is widest medially, the side that articulates with the radial notch of the ulna, allowing pronation and supination.

questions.q: Which one of these bones is not found in the pelvis?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The clavicle is the only bony link between which two structures?
o: The scapula and the vertebral column
The axial skeleton and the pectoral appendicular skeleton
The manubrium and the first rib
questions.e: The clavicle extends from the manubrium of the sternum to the acromion of the scapula, forming the only bony connection between the axial skeleton and the pectoral (shoulder) girdle of the appendicular skeleton.

questions.q: If the distal fragment in a distal radius fracture is displaced anteriorly instead of posteriorly, the injury is termed:
questions.e: Anterior displacement of the distal fragment, opposite to the classic Colles' pattern, is termed a reverse Colles' fracture, also known as a Smith's fracture.

questions.q: Which of the following bones does not articulate directly with any other bone in the skeleton?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which part of the vertebral column receives the most stress by bearing most of the weight of the body?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The femur:
o: Is the longest and heaviest bone of the body.
In the standing position the femur transmits weight from the hip bone to the tibia
The upper end consists of a head, a neck, greater tubercle and a lesser tubercle
The lower end consists of two condyles and two trochanters
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The superior portion of the sternum is the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: On the costal (anterior) surface of the scapular body, the shallow concavity is called the:
questions.e: The costal surface of the scapular body is concave, forming the subscapular fossa, which gives origin to the subscapularis muscle.

questions.q: Proximally, the ulna articulates with the humerus and, more distally, it also relates to which structures?
o: The articular disc below and the radius laterally
The carpals directly and the humerus laterally
Only the radius, with no distal articulation
questions.e: The ulna articulates with the humerus proximally, and distally relates to an articular disc (of the wrist) below and the radius laterally via the distal radioulnar joint.

questions.q: The anterior fontanelle closes during the second year of life and is then known as the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The antebrachium is composed of which of the following two bones?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Joints are classified functionally according to which criterion?
o: The blood supply to the joint
The amount of movement permitted at the joint
The number of bones meeting at the joint
The embryological origin of the bones
questions.e: The functional classification of joints is based purely on the amount of movement allowed at the joint, giving the categories synarthrosis, amphiarthrosis, and diarthrosis.

questions.q: BIAXIAL JOINT
o: An example is the metacarpophalangeal joint
An example is the wrist joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a synarthrotic joint?
questions.e: Sutures of the skull are classic synarthroses (immovable joints). The pubic symphysis is an amphiarthrosis, the knee is a freely movable diarthrosis, and a syndesmosis is generally classified as amphiarthrotic.

questions.q: A slightly movable joint is functionally termed:
questions.e: Amphiarthrosis describes a slightly movable joint, with the symphysis and syndesmosis given as examples in the lecture.

questions.q: SYNOVIAL JOINTS possess
o: Hyaline cartilage at the ends of the opposing bones
Hyaline cartilage that absorbs compressive forces
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Structurally, joints are classified based on what feature?
o: The shape of the surrounding muscles
What separates or binds the articulating bones
questions.e: Structural classification of joints depends on what separates or binds the articulating bones — fibers, cartilage, or a joint cavity — giving fibrous, cartilaginous, and synovial categories.

questions.q: An autoimmune disorder in which joints are affected bilaterally and which involves pannus formation and gradual joint immobilization is
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: All synovial joints have the following structural characteristics
o: The inner layer is the synovial membrane
The outer layer is the fibrous capsule
Articular cartilage covers the surfaces of the bones forming the joint
The joint surfaces are enclosed by a two-layered articular capsule
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A synostosis occurs when:
o: Two bones fuse and the boundary between them disappears
questions.e: Synostosis is a bony joint where two bones fuse together such that the original boundary between them is lost.

questions.q: Which fibrous joint binds bones using a sheet (interosseous membrane) or bundle (interosseous ligament) of dense connective tissue?
questions.e: A syndesmosis binds bones via an interosseous membrane or interosseous ligament, as seen between the tibia and fibula.

questions.q: A BALL AND SOCKET JOINT
o: The spherical head of one bone fits into a round socket in another
Permits universal movement in all axes including rotation
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of these is given as an example of a synchondrosis?
questions.e: The first sternocostal joint (between the first rib and the sternum) is cited as a synchondrosis, alongside epiphyseal plates and the costochondral joint.

questions.q: Secondary cartilaginous joints (symphyses) are united by which tissue?
questions.e: Symphyses are secondary cartilaginous joints in which the bones are united by fibrocartilage, e.g., the pubic symphysis and intervertebral joints.

questions.q: Which of the following is a classic example of a symphysis?
questions.e: The pubic symphysis is the prototypical secondary cartilaginous joint (symphysis), uniting the two pubic bones via fibrocartilage.

questions.q: In synovial joints, what covers the ends of the opposing bones and acts as a shock absorber?
questions.e: Articular cartilage covers the ends of opposing bones, decreases in thickness with age, and functions as a shock absorber that also reduces friction.

questions.q: Which layer of the articular capsule is composed of dense irregular connective tissue and strengthens the joint?
questions.e: The outer fibrous capsule consists of dense irregular connective tissue and provides strength to the joint.

questions.q: Which of the following are responsible for nodding ‘yes’ and for shaking your head ‘no’?
o: Occipital condyles and odontoid process respectively
Odontoid process and occipital condyles respectively
Occipital condyles and odontoid process of atlas respectively
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Synovial fluid contains phagocytes that remove microbes and cellular debris from the joint cavity.
questions.e: True. Synovial fluid contains phagocytic cells that clear microbes and debris, in addition to lubricating and nourishing the joint.

questions.q: According to the lecture, synovial fluid prevents separation of bone ends much like:
o: A little water between two glass surfaces
questions.e: The lecture compares synovial fluid's cohesive effect to a little water between two glass surfaces, which resists separation of the surfaces.

questions.q: Which accessory structures are associated with synovial joints?
o: Fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, tendons
questions.e: Accessory structures of synovial joints include fat pads, menisci, ligaments, bursae, and tendons.

questions.q: An elongated bursa that wraps around a tendon subjected to friction is termed a:
questions.e: A tendon sheath is an elongated bursa that wraps around tendons of certain muscles, occurring only where tendons are subjected to friction.

questions.q: Synovial joints are classified according to the shape of the articulating surfaces and the type of movement they permit. Which of these is a uniaxial joint type?
questions.e: Hinge (ginglymus) joints are uniaxial, permitting movement (flexion/extension) in a single plane only, e.g., the elbow and knee.

questions.q: A plane joint, formed when two flat surfaces meet, characteristically allows which type of movement?
questions.e: Plane joints are formed by two flat articulating surfaces and allow gliding or sliding movements, e.g., intertarsal and intercarpal joints.

questions.q: Which of the following is an example of a plane joint?
questions.e: The acromioclavicular joint is listed as a plane joint, alongside intertarsal, intercarpal, and 2nd–7th sternocostal joints.

questions.q: Pivot joint
o: Joint in which the rounded end of one bone fits into a ring formed by another bone
A, B, and C are all correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which joint is formed when a round surface fits into a ring created by a ligament and a depression in another bone?
questions.e: A pivot (trochoid) joint is formed in exactly this manner; the atlanto-axial joint is a classic example, allowing rotation of the head.

questions.q: Saddle joints, where concave and convex surfaces meet at right angles, allow which category of movement?
questions.e: Saddle joints are biaxial, permitting flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and circumduction, as seen at the carpometacarpal joint of the thumb.

questions.q: Which joint allows opposition of the thumb?
questions.e: The first carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is a saddle joint that uniquely allows the movement of opposition.

questions.q: A condyloid (ellipsoid) joint is formed when a convex oval surface fits into an elliptical concavity. Which movement is NOT typically permitted at this joint?
questions.e: Condyloid joints are biaxial and allow flexion, extension, abduction, adduction, and slight circumduction, but they do not permit axial rotation.

questions.q: NONAXIAL JOINTS
o: Does not involve rotation around any axis
Is found between articular processes of vertebrae and between tarsal bones
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: MULTIAXIAL JOINT
o: Universal movement is allowed in all axes
Rotation is allowed in all axes
An example is the shoulder joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of these joint pairs are BOTH classic examples of ball-and-socket joints?
questions.e: The shoulder (glenohumeral) and hip joints are the two principal ball-and-socket joints highlighted in the lecture.

questions.q: The joint formed at the carpometacarpal joint of the pollex (thumb) is a typical example of which joint type?
questions.e: The carpometacarpal joint of the thumb is the textbook example of a saddle joint, allowing the unique movement of opposition.

questions.q: UNIAXIAL JOINTS
o: An example is the ankle joint
An example is the Interphalangeal joint
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Rheumatism is best defined as:
o: A type of synovial fluid abnormality
Any painful disorder of supporting structures not caused by infection or injury
A fracture of the epiphyseal plate
questions.e: Rheumatism is defined as any painful disorder of the body's supporting structures that is NOT due to infection or injury.

questions.q: Which two carpals articulate with the radius to form the wrist joint?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which two types of arthritis are described as the most common?
questions.e: The lecture identifies rheumatoid arthritis and osteoarthritis as the most common types of arthritis.

questions.q: Muscle tone, important for maintaining posture, is best defined as:
o: Tension present in a relaxed muscle
The size of a muscle belly
questions.e: Muscle tone refers to the baseline tension present in a relaxed muscle, which is important for joint stability and posture.

questions.q: A joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule is termed a/an:
questions.e: A sprain is a joint injury involving tearing of ligaments or the joint capsule, whereas a strain involves muscle or tendon injury.

questions.q: What does the acronym RICE, used in management of soft tissue joint injuries, stand for?
questions.e: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression, and Elevation — the standard immediate management for soft tissue joint injuries.

questions.q: The stability of a joint depends on all of the following EXCEPT:
o: Tone of muscles around the joint
Synovial membrane and fluid in the joint
Shape and size of articular surfaces
questions.e: While synovial membrane and fluid lubricate and nourish the joint, the lecture identifies articular surface shape/arrangement, muscle tone, and ligaments as the key determinants of joint stability — not the synovial membrane/fluid.

questions.q: The glenohumeral (shoulder) joint is best described functionally as:
o: The least movable but most stable joint
questions.e: The shoulder joint is highly movable but is also the least stable major joint of the body, owing to its shallow socket.

questions.q: Ankylosis means
o: Immobility of a joint due to fusion of the articular surfaces
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The prominent bump on the lateral aspect of the leg at the ankle joint is the
o: A lateral extension of the tibia
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which structure deepens the glenoid cavity to improve shoulder joint stability?
questions.e: The glenoid labrum is a fibrocartilaginous ring that deepens the shallow glenoid cavity, improving the fit of the humeral head.

questions.q: Which muscle of the rotator cuff is described as the strongest?
questions.e: Among the rotator cuff muscles (subscapularis, teres minor, supraspinatus, and infraspinatus), the supraspinatus is described as the strongest.

questions.q: Which structure forms the coracoacromial arch that prevents superior (upward) displacement of the humeral head?
o: Coracoid process, acromion, and coracoacromial ligament
questions.e: The coracoacromial arch is formed by the coracoid process, the acromion, and the coracoacromial ligament, and it blocks superior displacement of the humeral head.

questions.q: Shoulder dislocation most commonly displaces the humeral head in which direction relative to the infraglenoid tubercle?
questions.e: Anterior dislocation accounts for about 95% of shoulder dislocations, making it by far the most common direction, although the overall displacement is described as downward (inferior).

questions.q: Injury to the axillary nerve following shoulder dislocation can cause paralysis of the deltoid muscle and loss of sensation over the 'regimental badge' area.
questions.e: True. The axillary nerve is vulnerable in shoulder dislocation, and its injury classically produces deltoid paralysis and sensory loss over the regimental badge area of the lateral shoulder.

questions.q: Which articulation of the elbow is classified as a hinge joint?
questions.e: The humero-ulnar articulation, between the trochlea of the humerus and the trochlear notch of the ulna, is a hinge joint.

questions.q: At the superior radio-ulnar joint, the head of the radius is held in place by which ligament?
questions.e: The tough annular (orbicular) ligament holds the head of the radius in place at the superior radio-ulnar joint, classified as a pivot joint.

questions.q: Which band of the medial collateral ligament of the elbow is considered the main stabilizer against valgus stress?
questions.e: The anterior oblique band of the medial collateral ligament is the main stabilizer of the elbow, protecting against excessive valgus forces and internal rotation stress.

questions.q: Within the lateral collateral ligament complex of the elbow, which component is described as the main stabilizer?
questions.e: The lateral ulnar collateral ligament (LUCL) is described as the main stabilizer of the lateral elbow, protecting against varus force.

questions.q: In orthopaedic terminology, when the distal part of a bone deviates more laterally than normal, this angulation is called:
questions.e: Valgus describes angulation where the distal part is positioned more laterally than it should be.

questions.q: When the distal part of a bone deviates more medially than normal at a joint, this is termed:
questions.e: Varus describes angulation where the distal part is positioned more medially than it should be.

questions.q: Which bursa of the elbow is implicated in 'student's elbow' or 'miner's elbow'?
questions.e: The subcutaneous (olecranon) bursa, located between the olecranon and overlying connective tissue, is implicated in olecranon bursitis, also called student's or miner's elbow.

questions.q: Most elbow dislocations occur in which direction, named by the position of the ulna and radius?
questions.e: Elbow dislocations are mostly posterior, and are named according to the position of the ulna and radius relative to the humerus, not the humerus itself.

questions.q: The carrying angle of the elbow is the acute angle between the median axes of the arm and forearm, measured in which position?
questions.e: The carrying angle is measured with the elbow in full extension and the forearm supinated, and it allows the forearm to clear the hips during walking.

questions.q: Junctional complexes are located on the:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A supracondylar fracture of the humerus, typically from a fall onto an outstretched hand, can result in uncontrolled flexion of the hand due to fibrosis of flexor muscles. This complication is called:
questions.e: Volkmann's ischaemic contracture is the complication of uncontrolled hand flexion arising from fibrotic, shortened flexor muscles following a supracondylar fracture with vascular compromise.

questions.q: 'Nursemaid's elbow' refers to which condition?
o: Radial head subluxation pulled out of the annular ligament
questions.e: Nursemaid's elbow (radial head subluxation) occurs when the radial head is traumatically pulled out of its normal position within the annular ligament, common in young children pulled by the arm.

questions.q: The hip joint articulates between the head of the femur and which structure?
questions.e: The hip joint is a ball-and-socket joint between the head of the femur and the acetabulum of the hip bone.

questions.q: What fibrocartilaginous structure deepens the acetabulum in the hip joint?
questions.e: The acetabular labrum is a fibrocartilaginous collar that deepens the acetabulum, improving congruency with the femoral head.

questions.q: The ligamentum teres (ligament of the head of femur) runs from the acetabular fossa to which structure?
questions.e: The ligament of the head of femur (ligamentum teres) passes from the acetabular fossa to the fovea on the femoral head, enclosing a branch of the obturator artery.

questions.q: Rupture of the ligament of the head of femur can damage its accompanying artery and lead to which complication?
questions.e: The ligamentum teres encloses a branch of the obturator artery, and rupture of the ligament can damage this artery, leading to avascular necrosis of the femoral head.

questions.q: Which extracapsular ligament of the hip joint is described as the strongest ligament in the body?
questions.e: The iliofemoral ligament (of Bigelow), which is Y-shaped or an inverted V, is described as the strongest ligament in the body and prevents hyperextension of the hip when standing.

questions.q: Which hip ligament spans from the superior pubic rami to the intertrochanteric line, preventing excessive abduction and extension?
questions.e: The pubofemoral ligament has a triangular shape and reinforces the capsule anteriorly and inferiorly, preventing excessive abduction and extension.

questions.q: Which extracapsular hip ligament is described as the weakest of the three, reinforcing the capsule posteriorly?
questions.e: The ischiofemoral ligament, running from the body of the ischium to the greater trochanter, is the weakest of the three main hip ligaments and reinforces the capsule posteriorly.

questions.q: Which nerve, in addition to the sciatic, supplies the hip joint and also the skin of the front and medial sides of the thigh, explaining referred thigh pain in hip disease?
questions.e: The femoral nerve supplies both the hip joint and the skin of the anterior and medial thigh, which is why hip joint pathology can refer pain to those regions.

questions.q: Which nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, explaining why hip disease can cause referred pain in the knee?
questions.e: The obturator nerve supplies both the hip and knee joints, which explains why hip joint disease sometimes presents with referred pain felt in the knee.

questions.q: Developmental dysplasia of the hip (DDH) occurs due to:
o: A shallow acetabulum from failure to develop properly in utero
Premature fusion of the epiphyseal plate
questions.e: DDH occurs when the acetabulum is shallow as a result of failure to develop properly in utero, leading to instability or dislocation of the hip.

questions.q: Which of the following is a common clinical feature of developmental dysplasia of the hip?
o: Limb length discrepancy with the affected limb shorter
Increased range of abduction at the hip
questions.e: Common features of DDH include limited abduction, limb length discrepancy (affected limb shorter), and asymmetrical gluteal or thigh skin folds.

questions.q: DDH is typically treated using which device?
questions.e: Developmental dysplasia of the hip is usually treated with a Pavlik harness, which holds the hips in a flexed and abducted position.

questions.q: Acquired hip dislocation is most commonly seen in which direction, and is associated with risk to which nerve?
questions.e: Posterior dislocation accounts for about 90% of acquired hip dislocations, since the joint is least stable when flexed and adducted, and this may injure the sciatic nerve.

questions.q: The patella:
o: Is a sesamoid bone that articulates with the femur, tibia and fibula
Has an apex that is directed superiorly and a base that is inferior
Enclosed in the tendon that secures the anterior thigh muscles to the tibia
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The knee joint consists of two articulations enclosed within a single joint cavity. These are the tibiofemoral and:
questions.e: The knee joint consists of the tibiofemoral (a condylar joint) and patellofemoral (a saddle joint) articulations, both enclosed within a single joint cavity.

questions.q: Clinically, the articular surfaces of the medial and lateral condyles of the tibia are often referred to as:
questions.e: The medial and lateral condyles of the tibia are clinically referred to as the medial and lateral tibial plateaus.

questions.q: Which collateral ligament of the knee is thicker, stronger, and attached to the medial meniscus, so that injury to it may also injure the meniscus?
questions.e: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament is thicker and stronger than the fibular collateral, and because it attaches to the medial meniscus, injury to it may involve the meniscus too.

questions.q: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament resists which type of deforming force?
questions.e: The tibial (medial) collateral ligament limits extension and abduction of the leg, resisting valgus-producing (outward bending) forces.

questions.q: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament of the knee resists which type of force?
questions.e: The fibular (lateral) collateral ligament limits extension and adduction of the leg, resisting varus-producing (inward bending) forces.

questions.q: Which cruciate ligament of the knee is described as weaker and more commonly injured?
questions.e: The anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) is weaker and more commonly injured than the posterior cruciate ligament, and it blends with the medial meniscus.

questions.q: The posterior cruciate ligament (PCL), being stronger, shorter, and broader than the ACL, primarily limits which movement?
o: Knee hyperflexion and posterior tibial dislocation
questions.e: The PCL limits knee hyperflexion and prevents posterior dislocation of the tibia relative to the femur.

questions.q: The anterior cruciate ligament primarily functions to:
o: Limit knee hyperextension and prevent anterior tibial dislocation
questions.e: The ACL limits knee hyperextension and prevents anterior dislocation of the tibia on the femur.

questions.q: The knee menisci primarily function to deepen the articular surface of the tibial condyles and:
o: Increase stability and act as shock absorbers
Replace the need for collateral ligaments
questions.e: Menisci deepen the articular surface of the tibial condyles, increasing joint stability, and act as shock absorbers by increasing surface area to dissipate forces.

questions.q: Which meniscus of the knee is described as almost a semicircle (C-shaped), relatively immobile, and more likely to be damaged?
o: Neither — menisci are not classified this way
questions.e: The medial meniscus is C-shaped, broader posteriorly, attached to the medial collateral ligament and joint capsule, making it relatively immobile and more prone to damage.

questions.q: The lateral meniscus of the knee is approximately what fraction of a circle, and how does its mobility compare to the medial meniscus?
o: 4/5 of a circle; smaller and more mobile
questions.e: The lateral meniscus is about 4/5 of a circle and is smaller and more mobile than the medial meniscus.

questions.q: Prepatellar bursitis is also commonly known as:
questions.e: Prepatellar bursitis, caused by inflammation and swelling of the prepatellar bursa, is commonly called housemaid's knee.

questions.q: Infrapatellar bursitis (superficial) is commonly known as:
questions.e: Infrapatellar bursitis is commonly called clergyman's knee, reflecting the kneeling posture historically associated with the condition.

questions.q: A cleaning staff member at the anatomy department developed housemaid's knee due to irritation. Which bursa is most likely involved?
questions.e: Housemaid's knee specifically involves the prepatellar (subcutaneous) bursa, resulting from prolonged kneeling and friction over the front of the knee.

questions.q: A footballer was kicked on the lateral side of the knee while standing on that leg, and MRI revealed a torn tibial collateral ligament. Which other structure is most likely also injured?
questions.e: Because the tibial (medial) collateral ligament is attached to the medial meniscus, injury to the MCL from a lateral blow (valgus force) commonly also involves the medial meniscus.

questions.q: Which structure on the tibia prevents sideways displacement of the femur on the tibia, contributing to knee stability?
questions.e: The intercondylar eminence of the tibia helps prevent sideways slipping of the femur on the tibia, contributing to overall knee stability.

questions.q: The anterior drawer sign is used to assess injury to which ligament?
questions.e: The anterior drawer sign tests for ACL tear, where hyperextension with anterior force on the tibia (partly flexed knee) produces excessive anterior tibial translation.

questions.q: The posterior drawer sign, classically caused by a 'dashboard injury,' assesses tearing of which ligament?
questions.e: The posterior drawer sign tests for PCL tear, occurring when a large force is applied to the shins of a flexed knee, pushing the tibia posteriorly — classically in dashboard injuries.

questions.q: The 'unhappy (terrible) triad' of knee injuries involves the ACL, medial meniscus, and which other structure?
questions.e: The unhappy triad involves the anterior cruciate ligament, the medial meniscus, and the tibial (medial) collateral ligament, common in contact sports with lateral knee blows.

questions.q: An increased Q-angle is considered a risk factor for several knee disorders. Which group typically has a greater Q-angle, owing to wider pelves?
questions.e: The Q-angle is greater in adult females than males, owing to females generally having wider pelves.

questions.q: The ankle (talocrural) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior articular surface of the tibia, and which bone?
questions.e: The talocrural (ankle) joint is formed by the articulation of the malleoli, the inferior surface of the tibia, and the talus.

questions.q: Movements of inversion and eversion of the foot take place primarily at which joints, NOT at the ankle joint itself?
questions.e: The lecture specifically notes that inversion and eversion occur at the tarsal joints, not at the ankle (talocrural) joint, which itself permits dorsiflexion and plantarflexion.

questions.q: The ankle joint is most stable in which position and least stable in which other position?
o: Stable in inversion; unstable in eversion
Stable in dorsiflexion; unstable in plantarflexion
Stable in plantarflexion; unstable in dorsiflexion
questions.e: The ankle joint is stable in dorsiflexion and unstable in plantarflexion, since the wider anterior part of the talus fits snugly into the mortise during dorsiflexion.

questions.q: The prominent bony knobs on each side of the ankle joint are
o: The medial malleolus of the fibula and the lateral malleolus of the tibia
The epicondyles of the tibia and fibula
The styloid processes of the tibia and fibula
The medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula
The head of the fibula and the tuberosity of the tibia
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The deep and superficial parts of the medial (deltoid) ligament primarily resist which movement of the foot?
questions.e: The deltoid ligament resists over-eversion of the foot. Because it is the stronger ligament, one is more likely to forcibly invert the ankle (sprain) than evert it.

questions.q: Which ligament of the ankle is weaker than its counterpart and thus more commonly damaged in ankle sprains?
questions.e: The lateral ligament of the ankle is weaker than the medial (deltoid) ligament, making it more susceptible to damage in ankle sprains, particularly from forced inversion.

questions.q: Which component of the lateral ankle ligament is described as the weakest, making it the most commonly injured?
questions.e: The anterior talofibular part of the lateral ligament is the weakest component, followed by the calcaneofibular ligament, making it the most frequently injured in ankle sprains.

questions.q: Which test is used clinically to assess ankle ligament integrity by evaluating forced inversion?
questions.e: The talar tilt test, also called the inversion stress test, evaluates the integrity of the lateral ankle ligaments under forced inversion.

questions.q: Pott's fracture of the ankle, caused by forced eversion of the foot, typically involves which malleoli?
questions.e: Pott's fracture involves a bimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli) or trimalleolar (medial and lateral malleoli plus distal tibia) fracture pattern, resulting from forced eversion of the foot.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the 'ankle ring' concept described in the lecture?
o: A ring, when broken, usually breaks in two places
The ankle joint has no ligamentous support
The talus can dislocate without bony injury
The ankle mortise behaves like a flexible band that never fractures
questions.e: The 'ankle ring' analogy describes how the bony-ligamentous ring of the ankle, like any ring, usually breaks (fractures) in two places when subjected to significant force, as seen in Pott's fracture.

questions.q: The annular ligament of the elbow attaches the radius firmly so it cannot rotate within it during pronation and supination.
questions.e: False. The annular ligament holds the head of the radius in place against the radial notch of the ulna while still permitting the radial head to rotate within it, enabling pronation and supination.

questions.q: The subscapular bursae communicate with the shoulder joint cavity.
questions.e: True. The lecture states that the subscapular bursae communicate with the shoulder joint, which has clinical relevance for joint effusions and bursal pathology.

o: Have a fibrous capsule of dense irregular connective tissue

questions.q: The shoulder joint capsule's laxity, combined with the disproportion between the shallow glenoid cavity and the large humeral head, contributes to its wide range of motion but reduced stability.
questions.e: True. A roughly 1:4 disproportion between the glenoid surface and humeral head, plus capsular laxity, gives the shoulder excellent mobility at the cost of stability.

questions.q: The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperflexion of the hip joint.
questions.e: False. The iliofemoral ligament prevents hyperextension of the hip joint when standing, not hyperflexion.

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Posterior dislocation of the hip is far more common than anterior dislocation.

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q:

questions.q: A biopsy shows tissue with cells packed tightly together and almost no space between them for extracellular material. Which basic tissue type does this most likely represent?
questions.e: Epithelial tissue is defined by cells packed closely with minimal extracellular matrix, the opposite arrangement to connective tissue, which has abundant matrix and sparse cells.

questions.q: A pathologist notes that a sampled epithelium shows no blood vessels running through it at all, yet the cells appear healthy and well-nourished. How is this possible?
o: The sample must have been mishandled, since living epithelium always contains vessels
The cells are actually dead and do not need nutrients
All epithelium secretes its own blood supply
It is avascular and fed by diffusion from below
questions.e: Epithelial tissue is characteristically avascular; it relies on diffusion of nutrients and oxygen from blood vessels in the adjacent connective tissue across the basement membrane, rather than containing its own vessels.

questions.q: An epithelial cell's apical and basal surfaces differ structurally and functionally from one another. What is this property called?
questions.e: This apical-versus-basal structural and functional asymmetry is termed polarity, a hallmark feature of epithelial cells.

questions.q: A researcher wants to identify the specific junction type responsible for mechanically binding epidermal cells together so the skin can resist friction and stretching without cells tearing apart. Which junction is most directly responsible?
questions.e: Desmosomes are spot-like junctions that mechanically anchor adjacent cells together, giving epithelium (such as the epidermis) resistance to mechanical stress like friction and stretching.

o: Not epithelium at all — only connective tissue can perform absorption
questions.e: Cuboidal cells, with more cytoplasm and organelle content than thin squamous cells, are well suited to the active secretion and absorption occurring in structures like kidney tubules, which require substantial cellular machinery.
