questions.q: Comparing merocrine and holocrine secretion: a gland whose cells periodically rupture entirely, becoming the secreted product themselves, uses which mechanism — and what would you predict about that gland's need for cell replacement?
o: None of the mechanisms involve cell loss
Apocrine secretion; only the nucleus is lost each cycle
Merocrine secretion; no replacement is needed since cells remain intact
Holocrine secretion; the gland requires ongoing replacement of destroyed secretory cells
questions.e: Holocrine secretion involves complete destruction of the secretory cell as part of the secretion itself (as in the sebaceous gland), meaning such glands must continuously replace their secretory cells to sustain output.

questions.q: A gland loses only the apical portion of its cytoplasm along with its secreted product, while the rest of the cell survives and repairs itself. Which secretion mode does this describe?
questions.e: Apocrine secretion involves the cell losing only its apical cytoplasm (along with the product) while the remainder of the cell survives, distinguishing it from merocrine (no cell loss) and holocrine (complete cell destruction) secretion.

questions.q: A gland has a duct system that branches multiple times before reaching secretory units, some of which are tube-shaped and others sac-shaped. How would this gland be classified structurally?
questions.e: A branching (compound) duct system with secretory units combining both tubular and acinar (sac-like) shapes describes a compound tubuloacinar gland, the classification matching structures like the salivary glands.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding multicellular exocrine glands
o: Merocrine glands release their secretion by pinching off part of the cell.
The secretory cells of holocrine glands release their product by rupturing.
Compound glands are so called because they are constructed from more than one cell type.
Compound glands are always constructed from mucous cells.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: If a gland's secretory cells were arranged in hollow, sphere-like clusters called follicles, richly surrounded by capillaries, and secreted directly into the blood, which organ does this description most closely match?
questions.e: The thyroid gland is composed of follicles — hollow, sphere-like clusters of epithelial cells — richly supplied by capillaries, secreting hormones directly into the blood, matching this endocrine gland description.

questions.q: Which best explains why hormonal effects, once triggered, often persist longer than a typical nervous system response, even though the nervous system generally acts faster?
o: Hormones travel by direct nerve fibers, which are slower than blood vessels
Hormones travel in blood and act more gradually
There is no real difference between the two systems' durations
Nervous signals cannot be turned off once started
questions.e: Because hormones travel through the blood and act more gradually on distant target tissues, their effects tend to build up and persist over a longer duration, in contrast to the fast, brief, on/off nature of direct nervous system signaling.

questions.q: A tissue engineer wants to grow an epithelial sheet capable of significant stretching (to be used for a distensible organ). Based on functional matching, which native epithelial type would best inform this design?
questions.e: Transitional epithelium is specifically adapted to withstand significant stretching without damage, as seen in the urinary bladder, making it the most relevant functional model for a distensible tissue design.

questions.q: Which of the following would most directly compromise an epithelium's ability to serve as a selective barrier (controlling exactly what passes between the external and internal environments)?
o: Disruption of tight junctions between adjacent cells
A change from simple to stratified epithelium
An increase in the number of goblet cells
questions.e: Since tight junctions are what seal the intercellular space and prevent free paracellular passage, their disruption most directly undermines the epithelium's selective barrier function, allowing uncontrolled leakage between cells.

questions.q: A gland is unbranched, with a straight tubular secretory portion — matching the sweat gland's basic pattern, though sweat glands are actually coiled. What is the correct structural classification for an unbranched, straight-tubed exocrine gland?
questions.e: A gland with a single, unbranched duct and a tube-shaped secretory portion is classified as a simple tubular gland; the sweat gland itself is a simple coiled tubular variant of this pattern.

questions.q: Which pairing of gland type with its defining structural feature is INCORRECT?
o: Acinar (alveolar) gland — flask or sac-shaped secretory unit
Tubular gland — always found only in the endocrine system
questions.e: This pairing is incorrect: tubular refers to the shape of an exocrine gland's secretory portion (a tube), and tubular glands are exocrine, not endocrine — endocrine glands are ductless and classified differently.

questions.q: A basal lamina:
o: Is a cellular layer secreted by epithelial tissues only
Is a noncellular layer between adjacent epithelial cells
Contains PAS positive glycoproteins and lies between epithelium and connective tissue
Is believed to be secreted by the muscle and epithelial cells only
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: You are given an epithelium from an unknown location, the epithelium has microvilli and cilia. This epithelium
o: Was involved with secretion or absorption
Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required
Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually.
Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Blood vessels lining the inner wall of an artery are covered by a single layer of extremely thin cells. Which epithelial classification does this endothelial lining represent?
questions.e: The endothelium lining blood vessels is a simple squamous epithelium — a single layer of thin, flat cells — well suited to the vessel wall's need for efficient diffusion and a smooth, low-friction surface for blood flow.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about the mode of secretion of exocrine glands?
o: Apocrine cells are destroyed, then replaced, after secretion.
Apocrine cells retain their secretory products
Holocrine cells are slightly damaged by the secretory process, but repair themselves.
Merocrine glands are not altered by the secretory process.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The presence of microvilli and cilia on a cell usually indicates that the cell junctions in
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which best explains why stratified epithelium, rather than simple epithelium, lines the outer skin and the oral cavity?
o: Only stratified epithelium can produce a basement membrane
These sites face mechanical wear and need layers
These sites need efficient diffusion above all else
questions.e: Areas exposed to significant abrasion, like the skin and oral cavity, benefit from stratified epithelium's multiple cell layers, which provide mechanical protection at the cost of the diffusion efficiency a single-layer epithelium would offer.

questions.q: Multicellular exocrine glands can be classified
o: Functionally into secreting or nonsecreting types
Structurally into alveolar and acinar types
Functionally into merocrine, holocrine, and apocrine divisions
Structurally into vascular and avascular types
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Merocrine secretion from cells of exocrine glands:
o: Involves exocytosis via the apical membrane of cells
Involves secretion of part of the apical cytoplasm of cells
Involves secretion of whole cells and their contents
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: If a mutation prevented hemidesmosomes from forming properly in skin epithelium, what would be the most likely structural consequence?
o: Adjacent skin cells would fail to communicate electrically
The skin would become more resistant to abrasion than normal
Tight junctions would compensate completely with no effect
The epidermis would separate from the dermis
questions.e: Since hemidesmosomes anchor the basal epithelial layer to the underlying basement membrane, their failure would weaken this attachment, predisposing the epidermis to separate (blister) from the dermis under mechanical stress — a mechanism seen in certain blistering skin diseases.

questions.q: Given that epithelial tissue has a notably high regenerative capacity, which everyday clinical observation does this best explain?
o: Bone fractures healing within a few days
Nerve cells regenerating fully after spinal cord injury
Superficial scrapes and sunburn healing quickly
Cartilage regrowing rapidly after joint injury
questions.e: Epithelial tissue's high regenerative capacity explains why superficial skin injuries, such as scrapes and mild sunburn — which damage epithelial layers — tend to heal relatively quickly compared to tissues with lower regenerative capacity like cartilage or nerve.

questions.q: A pathology slide shows an epithelium that is one cell layer thick, with cube-shaped cells, lining small ducts of a gland. Which classification correctly names this tissue?
o: Pseudostratified cuboidal epithelium (not a real category)
questions.e: A single layer (simple) of cube-shaped (cuboidal) cells lining small ducts describes simple cuboidal epithelium, commonly found in gland ducts and kidney tubules.

questions.q: A specimen with a meshwork of irregular polygonal profiles of cells was described as adult white fat cells. These cells have:
o: Centrally located nuclei and many small lipid droplets within the cells
Numerous flattened basal nuclei per cell with small peripheral cytoplasm
Flattened basal nuclei and single large droplets of lipid within the cells
Centrally placed nuclei with large amounts of cytoplasm
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: You are given a specimen with several clusters of epithelial cells embedded completely in connective tissue. Some of the cell clusters were dark-stained with central round nuclei whereas others were pale-stained with peripheral flattened nuclei. In addition epithelially-lined passages that link the cell clusters to an epithelially-lined surface were present. The passages were unbranched.The specimen is
o: A simple exocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
Contains both simple squamous and simple cuboidal epithelial tissues
Is a gland that secretes a watery product rich in enzymes
Is from an organ which secretes both endocrine and exocrine products
A simple endocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Suppose a novel gland is discovered whose duct branches repeatedly, and whose final secretory units are tube-shaped throughout, with no sac-like (acinar) portions. How should this gland be classified?
questions.e: A branching duct system (compound) with entirely tube-shaped secretory units (tubular), and no sac-like portions, is classified as a compound tubular gland.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding epithelia.
o: Pseudostratified epithelia consist of several layers of cuboidal cells
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of at least two layers of cells stacked on top of one another.
Stratified epithelia are tall, narrow cells.
Stratified epithelia are present where protection from abrasion is important.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location revealed cells that were taller than wide and appeared to be more than one-cell layer thick. However all the cells were attached to the basement membrane and some of the cells had extensive apical microvilli. Goblets cells and cilia were absent. The epithelium also contained some bipolar neurons. This epithelium is most likely to be:
o: Located in the olfactory and respiratory segments
A modified type of respiratory epithelium with sensory neurons
A, B and C are correct
Only B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following would most strongly suggest that a tissue sample is epithelial rather than connective tissue, based purely on general microscopic appearance?
o: Densely packed cells with almost no matrix
Abundant fibers with widely spaced cells
A fluid matrix with cells suspended in it
A mineralized matrix with cells in lacunae
questions.e: Densely packed cells with minimal visible extracellular matrix is the hallmark general appearance of epithelial tissue, in contrast to connective tissue's characteristic abundant matrix (fibrous, fluid, or mineralized) surrounding sparser cells.

questions.q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissues is normally found in glands?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which statement correctly compares tight junctions and desmosomes in terms of their primary function?
o: Neither junction type has any functional role in epithelium
Both function identically, providing only mechanical strength
Tight junctions provide mechanical anchorage, while desmosomes control paracellular passage
Tight junctions primarily control what can pass between cells, while desmosomes primarily provide mechanical anchorage between cells
questions.e: Tight junctions are primarily barrier-forming, sealing the intercellular space to control paracellular passage, while desmosomes are primarily anchoring structures, providing mechanical strength between adjacent cells — distinct but complementary roles.

questions.q: A multilayered epithelium with cuboidal basal cells and flat cells at its surface would be classified as
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A cell biologist observes that removing calcium from a tissue culture medium causes desmosomes between epithelial cells to weaken and cells to separate more easily. What does this suggest about desmosome function?
o: Desmosomes only function in connective tissue, not epithelium
This observation is irrelevant to desmosome structure
questions.e: This observation is consistent with desmosomes relying on calcium-dependent adhesion molecules (cadherins) to mechanically link adjacent cells; removing calcium would be expected to weaken this calcium-dependent binding.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes glandular epithelium from covering/lining epithelium as the two broad functional categories of epithelial tissue?
o: There is no meaningful distinction between the two categories
Glandular epithelium is specialized for secretion
Glandular epithelium never contains a basement membrane
Covering epithelium can only be found in the skin
questions.e: Covering and lining epithelium covers external body surfaces and lines internal cavities and vessels, while glandular epithelium is specialized for secretion, forming the functional tissue of glands — the two broad functional categories of epithelial tissue.

questions.q: Why might a clinician be concerned about a biopsy showing loss of normal polarity in an epithelial layer (apical and basal surfaces no longer clearly distinguishable)?
o: It can be an early sign of malignant change
It confirms the tissue is functioning normally
It indicates the tissue has become connective tissue
Loss of polarity has no clinical significance
questions.e: Loss of normal epithelial polarity is often regarded as a marker of disorganized, potentially abnormal or malignant cellular architecture, making it a feature of clinical concern on histological examination.

questions.q: If a gland lost its ability to form a duct during development but still retained the capacity to secrete a product, what would you predict about how its secretion reaches its target?
o: It would become a unicellular gland automatically
It would secrete into surrounding blood vessels
Secretion would be impossible without a duct
It would secrete onto the nearest epithelial surface regardless of duct absence
questions.e: A gland lacking a duct system, by definition, must rely on releasing its product into the surrounding vasculature rather than through a channel to a surface — this ductless secretion pattern is exactly what characterizes endocrine glands.

questions.q: Which of the following best illustrates the concept that epithelial classification depends on BOTH the number of layers AND the surface cell shape, rather than either alone?
o: Simple and stratified always refer to different cell shapes, never the same one
Cell shape alone fully determines classification, with layering being irrelevant
Simple squamous and stratified squamous share the same cell shape but differ in the number of layers
Layering alone fully determines classification, with cell shape being irrelevant
questions.e: Simple squamous and stratified squamous epithelium share the same surface cell shape (squamous) but differ in the number of layers (one versus several), illustrating that full classification requires specifying both criteria together.

questions.q: A hormone assay detects a substance at high concentration in the blood but never finds it concentrated in any single duct or on any epithelial surface. What type of gland most likely produced this substance?
o: An exocrine gland with a blocked duct
questions.e: Finding a secreted substance concentrated in the blood, with no duct or surface concentration, is the expected pattern for an endocrine gland, whose hormone is released directly into surrounding capillaries rather than transported via a duct.

questions.q: Which is the best explanation for why the moist lining of the esophagus is classified as non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, rather than simple columnar like the stomach just below it?
o: The esophagus needs both the abrasion resistance of multiple squamous layers and a moist surface, unlike the stomach, which prioritizes secretion and absorption via a thinner, glandular simple columnar lining
Non-keratinized epithelium cannot exist anywhere except the esophagus
The esophagus and stomach actually share identical epithelium
There is no functional reason; the difference is arbitrary
questions.e: The esophagus's functional demand — resisting abrasion from swallowed food while remaining moist — is met by non-keratinized stratified squamous epithelium, in contrast to the stomach's need for active secretion and absorption, met by a thinner simple columnar epithelium with a glandular component.

questions.q: An epithelial membrane:
o: Is formed of epithelium and smooth muscle
Contains simple or stratified epithelia and a basement membrane
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which best captures why the thyroid gland, despite being made of epithelial tissue arranged in follicles, is classified functionally as endocrine rather than exocrine?
o: It has no epithelial cells at all
It secretes hormones into surrounding capillaries
Endocrine glands must always be shaped like follicles
The thyroid actually has a duct that has simply never been observed
questions.e: Despite being epithelial in origin, the thyroid is functionally endocrine because its follicular cells secrete hormones directly into the surrounding rich capillary network rather than through a duct system to an epithelial surface — duct presence or absence is the defining functional criterion.

questions.q: Which of the following tissue types would you expect to find on a surface of the body that is subject to friction?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Examination of three different specimens from unknown locations, showed that specimen A was taken from a chamber that changes its volume continually, specimen B was from a surface where both absorption and secretion are required and specimen C was from an internal surface where friction may occur. Specimens A, B, C were obtained from:
o: Ureter, ductuli efferentes and cornea respectively
Uterus, ileum and anal canal respectively
Penile urethra, jejunum, laryngeal surface of epiglottis respectively
Urinary bladder, duodenum and vagina respectively
Vas deferens, small intestine and pharynx respectively
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Excretory glands are classified as simple branched tubular and merocrine by the:
o: Presence or absence of ducts and mechanism of secretion
Shape of secretory units and types of ducts only
Nature of the ducts, shape of secretory unit and mechanism of secretion
Mechanism of secretion and shape of secetory units
Types of secretory products and mechanism of secretion
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A researcher damages the tight junctions in a segment of intestinal epithelium in a lab model. Which downstream consequence would be most expected?
o: Leakage of luminal contents past the seal
No consequence, since tight junctions are only found in skin
Immediate conversion of the tissue into connective tissue
Improved nutrient absorption due to fewer barriers
questions.e: Because tight junctions normally seal the space between adjacent intestinal epithelial cells, damaging them would be expected to allow uncontrolled paracellular leakage of luminal contents into the underlying tissue, rather than any functional improvement.

questions.q: Which best explains why glandular epithelium, despite arising from covering/lining epithelium during development, can end up structurally quite different from a flat surface lining?
o: Glandular epithelium is not really epithelium but connective tissue in disguise
Glandular tissue always loses its basement membrane
It cannot actually differ, since all epithelium looks identical
It folds inward to form tubes, sacs or follicles
questions.e: During development, glandular epithelium typically forms by invagination of the original surface epithelium, folding inward and specializing for secretion, which is why mature glands take on tube-, sac-, or follicle-shaped structures quite different from the flat sheet of the original surface lining.

questions.q: Which the following statements best describes connective tissue?
o: Usually contains a large amount of matrix
Always arranged in a single layer of cells
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The shape of the external ear is maintained by
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Elastic connective tissue:
o: Contains jelly-like intercellular substance with collagenous fibers
Is present in adults and foetuses
Is present in the vocal ligaments of the larynx
Contains stellate fibroblasts and a mucoid ground substance
Is typical of the umbilical cord and placenta
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is TRUE of connective tissue?
o: Elastin fibers are sometimes called white fibers.
When connective tissue is stretched, collagen gives it the ability to snap back.
Ground substance is thick and semi-rigid
Reticular fibers form thick, ropelike structures.
Collagen fibers provide high tensile strength.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Removing the fine, branching fiber network that forms the structural framework (stroma) of the spleen would primarily disrupt which fiber-dependent function?
o: Providing tensile strength to resist stretching, like a tendon
Supporting free cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages within a soft organ's framework
Allowing the organ to stretch and recoil like an artery wall
questions.e: This fine, branching network is formed by reticular fibers, whose primary role in organs like the spleen and lymph nodes is to provide a supportive framework (stroma) that houses free cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages — not tensile strength or elasticity.

questions.q: What are the three main components of connective tissue?
o: Alveoli, fibrous capsule, and secretory cells
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: At a site of bacterial infection, a connective tissue cell type engulfs and destroys invading pathogens and cellular debris. Which cell is primarily responsible for this phagocytic defense?
questions.e: Macrophages are the phagocytic cells of connective tissue, engulfing and destroying pathogens, debris, and dead cells as part of the tissue's immune defense.

questions.q: A patient experiences a sudden allergic reaction, with localized swelling and redness at the site of an insect sting. Which connective tissue cell type, releasing histamine and heparin from its granules, is most directly responsible for triggering this response?
questions.e: Mast cells release histamine and heparin from their granules during allergic and inflammatory responses, directly producing the swelling and redness characteristic of a localized allergic reaction.

questions.q: A connective tissue cell type is specialized to store lipid as a long-term energy reserve, and its abundance in a tissue sample would be the defining feature of adipose tissue. Which cell type is this?
questions.e: Adipocytes are specialized for lipid storage as an energy reserve, and their predominance is what defines adipose tissue as a distinct connective tissue type.

questions.q: A patient's blood test shows elevated antibody levels following a recent infection. Which connective tissue-derived cell type is responsible for producing these antibodies?
questions.e: Plasma cells, derived from B lymphocytes, are the cells responsible for synthesizing and secreting antibodies as part of the immune response, distinguishing them from the other connective tissue cell types listed.

questions.q: Comparing a ligament (bone to bone) with the dermis of the skin: both are dense connective tissue, yet the ligament resists a single predictable direction of pull, while the dermis must resist stress from many directions. Which structural difference accounts for this functional contrast?
o: The ligament has no collagen at all, unlike the dermis
The ligament has parallel collagen fibers, while the dermis has randomly oriented collagen fibers
Both tissues have identical fiber arrangements, and the difference is due to cell type alone
The dermis is actually cartilage, not connective tissue proper
questions.e: Dense regular connective tissue, as in ligaments and tendons, has collagen fibers running in parallel, ideal for resisting force from one predictable direction, whereas dense irregular connective tissue, as in the dermis, has randomly arranged fibers that resist stress applied from multiple directions.

questions.q: Mesenchymal cells are most commonly found in which type of connective tissue?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A patient loses significant subcutaneous fat after prolonged illness, resulting in reduced insulation and cushioning beneath the skin. Which connective tissue type has been most directly depleted?
questions.e: Adipose tissue, a loose connective tissue dominated by adipocytes, provides insulation, cushioning, and energy storage beneath the skin; its depletion during illness explains the loss of these protective functions.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Cartilage's matrix remains firm yet flexible under normal conditions, in contrast to bone's rigid, calcified matrix. What underlies this key difference?
o: Bone's matrix contains only collagen and no minerals
There is no real difference; both matrices are identical
Cartilage has no matrix at all
Cartilage's matrix is not mineralized under normal conditions, while bone's matrix is hardened by mineral salt deposition
questions.e: The key distinction is mineralization: bone's matrix is hardened by deposition of mineral salts (largely calcium phosphate), giving it rigidity, while cartilage's matrix remains uncalcified under normal conditions, allowing it to stay firm yet flexible.

questions.q: An articular cartilage injury in the knee is notorious for healing slowly, if at all, compared to a bone fracture in the same limb. What structural feature of cartilage best explains this poor healing capacity?
o: Cartilage cannot be damaged, so there is nothing to heal
Cartilage is avascular, limiting the delivery of repair cells and nutrients compared to well-vascularized bone
Cartilage chondrocytes divide faster than any other cell type, which somehow impairs healing
Cartilage has more blood vessels than bone, which paradoxically slows healing
questions.e: Because cartilage is avascular, it must rely on slow diffusion (largely through the perichondrium or synovial fluid) for nutrient and repair-cell delivery, in sharp contrast to well-vascularized bone, which receives these directly via blood vessels — explaining cartilage's comparatively poor healing.

questions.q: Pieces of cartilage were examined by an Anatomy Prosector and classified as elastic cartilage. He concluded that the samples were obtained from the:
o: Intervertebral discs and the epiglottis only
Corniculate and cuneiform cartilages of the larynx and the pinna of ear
Arytenoid cartilage of the larynx and corniculate cartilage of the larynx
Symphsis pubis and cricoid cartilage of the larynx
Thyroid cartilage of the larynx and the pinna of ear
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs both experience substantial compressive load and must resist shearing forces, particularly during activities like childbirth or heavy lifting. Which cartilage type, reinforced with thick collagen bundles, is adapted to these structural demands?
questions.e: Fibrocartilage, reinforced by thick bundles of collagen fibers, provides the strength needed to withstand compressive load and resist shearing forces at sites like the pubic symphysis and intervertebral discs.

questions.q: Chondroblasts
o: Within the cartilage divide and secrete new matrix
Are mature cartilage cells located in spaces called lacunae
Located deep to the perichondrium divide and secrete new matrix on the internal portions of the cartilage
Never lose their ability to divide
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: You are given cartilage from an unknown location, you think it is from the pinna of the ear because:
o: Numerous chondroblasts that are arranged into isogenous groups
It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
It contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of cartilage?
o: Provision of an embryonic model prior to developmnt of long bones.
Maintenance of a tubular shape of structures in the digestive tract
Provision of a smooth surface for epiphyses of articulating joints
Allowing long bones to increase in length
Provision of rigidity to soft tissues requiring support.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A bone-forming cell actively synthesizes new bone matrix during growth or after a fracture, but once fully surrounded by matrix, it matures into a different, less active cell type residing in a lacuna. What are these two successive cell types called?
questions.e: An osteoblast actively synthesizes new bone matrix; once it becomes surrounded by the matrix it has produced, it matures into an osteocyte, the less active, matrix-maintaining cell housed within a lacuna.

questions.q: Unlike the other bone cell types, one type is not derived from mesenchymal cells but instead arises from blood-forming (hematopoietic) precursors related to monocytes, and its function is to break down (resorb) bone matrix. Which cell is this?
questions.e: Osteoclasts are the exception among bone cells, arising from hematopoietic precursors (related to monocytes) rather than mesenchymal cells, and their specific function is to resorb (break down) bone matrix, unlike the matrix-forming osteoblasts and osteocytes.

questions.q: After a fracture, new bone-forming cells are needed at the injury site. Given that mature osteocytes cannot readily divide, which cell population, found in the periosteum and endosteum, provides this regenerative capacity?
o: Osteoprogenitor cells, which act as stem cells able to differentiate into osteoblasts
questions.e: Osteoprogenitor (osteogenic) cells persist as a stem cell population in the periosteum and endosteum, retaining the capacity to differentiate into active osteoblasts when new bone formation is needed, such as during fracture repair.

questions.q: Why is bone able to heal relatively efficiently after a fracture, in contrast to the poor healing capacity of cartilage discussed earlier?
o: Bone cells divide faster than any other cell type in the body
Bone is richly vascularized, unlike avascular cartilage, allowing efficient delivery of repair cells, oxygen, and nutrients to the fracture site
Bone matrix contains no cells at all, so there is nothing to regenerate
Bone fractures never actually require cellular repair
questions.e: Bone's extensive vascular supply — in sharp contrast to avascular cartilage — allows efficient delivery of oxygen, nutrients, and repair-related cells to a fracture site, underlying its comparatively efficient healing.

questions.q: Which best explains why blood, despite being fluid, is still classified as a connective tissue rather than forming its own separate category?
o: Blood is actually classified as a type of epithelial tissue
Connective tissue must always be solid, so blood does not truly qualify
Blood contains no cells, matching the definition of connective tissue matrix alone
Blood follows the general connective tissue pattern of cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — in blood's case, the fluid matrix is plasma
questions.e: Blood fits the defining connective tissue pattern — cells suspended within an extracellular matrix — even though its matrix (plasma) is fluid rather than solid or gel-like, which is why it is classified as a specialized connective tissue.

questions.q: Regarding the characteristics of HYALINE CARTILAGE evaluate the following statements:
o: It has a smooth appearance and contains abundant ground substance and isogenous groups of chondrocytes
It contains collagen type II fibres and abundant ground substance and is found in the intervertebral discs and the epiglottis only
Its chondrocytes occur singly and it is the main supporting framework of the epiglottis, cuneiform cartilage of the larynx and the intrapulmonary bronchi
It contains collagen type I fibres, few chondrocytes arranged in rows and a fluid small ground
It contains more elastic fibres than collagen type II fibres and is found in the thyroid, cricoid and corniculate cartilages of the larynx
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A structural engineer studying biological materials notes that compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units, each centered on a canal carrying blood vessels. What is the name of this repeating structural unit?
questions.e: Compact bone is organized into repeating cylindrical units called osteons (Haversian systems), each built around a central canal that carries blood vessels supplying the surrounding bone tissue.

questions.q: The following features are observed during intramembranous ossification: i. Modulation of osteoprogenitor ii. Secretion of matrix iii. Formation of spicules iv. Confluence of spicules v. Transformation of spongy bone to compact bone
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Tiny channels radiate outward from each lacuna in bone tissue, connecting neighboring osteocytes to one another. What are these channels called, and what is their functional purpose?
o: Trabeculae; they provide mechanical support only
Endomysium; they surround muscle fibers, not bone cells
Perichondrium; they nourish cartilage, not bone
Canaliculi; they allow exchange of nutrients, waste, and signals between osteocytes
questions.e: Canaliculi are the tiny channels radiating from each lacuna, connecting neighboring osteocytes and enabling the exchange of nutrients, waste products, and signaling molecules between these otherwise isolated cells.

questions.q: Which connective tissue membrane lines the internal surfaces of bone, including the medullary cavity, as opposed to the membrane covering bone's external surface?
questions.e: The endosteum lines the internal surfaces of bone (including the medullary cavity), in contrast to the periosteum, which covers the external surface of bone.

questions.q: A tendon is torn from its attachment to bone. Which membrane, providing an attachment site for tendons and containing osteogenic cells for repair, is most directly involved at the injury site?
questions.e: The periosteum covers the outer surface of bone and serves as the attachment site for tendons and ligaments, while also containing osteogenic (osteoprogenitor) cells important for bone growth and repair — making it central to this type of injury.

questions.q: Connective tissue fibres and glycosaminoglycans (acid mucopolysaccharides) are synthesized by:
o: Plasma cells, fibroblats and reticular cells
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The structure of bone tissue suits its functions. Which of the following bone tissues is adapted to support weight and withstand tension stress?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The most generalized type of connective tissue with the greatest variety of connective tissue components is/are:
o: Reticular connective tissue and loose connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue and hyaline cartilage
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A ligament sprain heals more slowly than a typical skin cut. Considering what you know about the vascularity of dense regular connective tissue compared to epithelial tissue, what is the most likely explanation?
o: Dense regular connective tissue like ligaments is less richly vascularized than epithelial tissue, slowing nutrient and repair-cell delivery, and epithelial tissue also regenerates especially quickly
Skin cuts never actually heal faster than ligament injuries
Ligaments contain no cells and therefore cannot heal at all
Dense regular connective tissue has a higher regenerative capacity than epithelium
questions.e: Dense regular connective tissue such as ligament is less vascularized than skin's richly vascularized, high-turnover epithelium, which combined with epithelium's notably high regenerative capacity, explains why superficial skin injuries typically heal faster than ligament injuries.

questions.q: The cell responsible for secreting the matrix of bone is the:

questions.q: A researcher wants to selectively increase bone resorption (breakdown) in an experimental model to study osteoporosis. Which cell type's activity would need to be stimulated?
questions.e: Osteoclasts are specifically responsible for resorbing (breaking down) bone matrix, so stimulating their activity would be the relevant target for modeling increased bone resorption, as occurs in osteoporosis.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world example of dense irregular connective tissue in action, based on its multidirectional fiber arrangement?
o: Hyaline cartilage at the end of a long bone
The wall of a large elastic artery stretching with each heartbeat
The dermis of the skin, resisting pulling and stretching forces from many directions during movement
A tendon transmitting force from a single muscle in one direction
questions.e: The dermis, composed of dense irregular connective tissue with randomly oriented collagen fibers, is well suited to resisting mechanical stress from multiple directions, unlike the single-direction force resisted by dense regular tissue in a tendon.

questions.q: Which best explains the functional advantage of reticular connective tissue's fine, branching fiber network specifically within lymph nodes?
o: It prevents any cells from moving through the tissue at all
It functions identically to dense regular connective tissue in tendons
It provides an open, supportive meshwork that allows free immune cells, like lymphocytes, to move through and be housed within the organ
It mineralizes to protect the lymph node from injury
questions.e: Reticular fibers form a fine, branching, relatively open meshwork that supports and houses mobile immune cells such as lymphocytes and macrophages within organs like lymph nodes, unlike the dense, tightly packed fiber arrangement of tendons.

questions.q: Which combination of features would make a tissue sample most clearly identifiable as blood rather than another connective tissue type under the microscope?
o: Cells suspended in a fluid matrix, with no fixed fiber network visible
Densely packed cells with almost no matrix
Cells suspended in a solid, mineralized matrix
questions.e: Blood is uniquely identifiable among connective tissues by its fluid matrix (plasma) containing suspended formed elements (cells), without the fixed fiber network or mineralization seen in other connective tissue types.

questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: If a patient's mast cells were pharmacologically stabilized (prevented from releasing their granule contents), which of the following symptoms of an allergic reaction would most directly be reduced?
o: Bone pain from an unrelated fracture
Localized swelling, redness, and itching mediated by histamine release
questions.e: Since mast cells release histamine (among other mediators) responsible for the swelling, redness, and itching of an allergic response, stabilizing mast cells to prevent this release would most directly reduce these specific symptoms.

questions.q: Which best explains why adipose tissue, though classified as loose connective tissue, looks quite different under the microscope from areolar connective tissue, despite both belonging to the same broad category?
o: Areolar tissue is mineralized, unlike adipose tissue
Adipose tissue actually contains no cells at all
There is no real difference between the two tissues

Adipose tissue is dominated by large, lipid-storing adipocytes that make up most of the tissue volume, while areolar tissue has a more varied population of cells within a looser fiber and ground substance framework
questions.e: While both are loose connective tissue subtypes, adipose tissue is distinguished by being dominated by large, lipid-filled adipocytes that occupy most of the tissue's volume, giving it a very different microscopic appearance from the more varied cellular and fibrous composition of areolar connective tissue.

questions.q: How is hyaline cartilage DIFFERENT from elastic or fibrocartilage?

questions.q: Which best explains why the walls of large elastic arteries (like the aorta) would be structurally unsuited to serving as a tendon, despite both containing dense connective tissue?
o: Tendons are actually more elastic than arteries

Elastic artery walls are built for repeated stretch and recoil, while tendons are built to resist stretch and transmit force efithout much elongation — reversing these roles would compromise both structures' functions
Arteries contain no connective tissue at all
There is no structural difference between the two tissues
questions.e: The mechanical demands are essentially opposite: elastic artery walls need to stretch and recoil repeatedly (favoring elastic fibers), while tendons need to resist stretch to efficiently transmit muscle force (favoring collagen fibers) — swapping their fiber composition would compromise each structure's specific function.

questions.q: Which best explains why osteocytes, despite being described as less metabolically active than osteoblasts, are still essential for maintaining healthy bone tissue?
o: Osteocytes have no function at all once embedded in matrix
Osteocytes actively resorb bone matrix, unlike osteoclasts
Osteocytes continue to monitor and help maintain the surrounding matrix and communicate with neighboring cells via canaliculi, contributing to bone's ongoing upkeep and response to mechanical stress
Osteocytes are responsible for producing red blood cells within the matrix
questions.e: Although less active than osteoblasts in matrix synthesis, osteocytes remain essential because they continue to monitor and maintain the surrounding matrix and communicate with neighboring cells via the canalicular network, contributing to bone's ongoing maintenance and its response to mechanical loading.

questions.q: Cartilage is different from bone in that
o: Cartilage contains about 80% water and is more resilient
Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in the adult skeleton.
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which best explains why a deficiency in vitamin C, which is required for proper collagen synthesis, would be expected to cause widespread connective tissue problems (as seen in scurvy), including poor wound healing and fragile blood vessels?
o: Vitamin C has no relationship to connective tissue function

Collagen is a major structural component across many connective tissue types, so impaired collagen synthesis would compromise the structural integrity of tissues ranging from skin and blood vessel walls to bone
Vitamin C is only relevant to muscle tissue, not connective tissue
Collagen deficiency only affects cartilage, with no other tissue impact
questions.e: Since collagen is a major structural fiber found throughout many connective tissue types (skin, blood vessel walls, bone, tendons), impaired collagen synthesis from vitamin C deficiency would be expected to compromise structural integrity broadly across these tissues, consistent with the widespread symptoms seen in scurvy.

questions.q: The following cell types are likely to be seen in areolar connective tissue EXCEPT.

questions.q: Which observation would most strongly support the conclusion that a given connective tissue sample is dense regular, rather than dense irregular, connective tissue?
o: The tissue contains large numbers of adipocytes
The tissue contains abundant ground substance and few fibers
The fibers appear tightly packed and running in clearly parallel bundles
The fibers appear randomly oriented in many directions
questions.e: Tightly packed collagen fibers running in clearly parallel bundles is the defining microscopic feature of dense regular connective tissue, distinguishing it from the randomly oriented fibers of dense irregular connective tissue.

questions.q: A researcher proposes that connective tissue's overall diversity (from blood to bone to tendon) arises mainly from variation in one structural component. Which component's variation best accounts for this diversity?
o: The cell membrane, which is identical to all other cell types in the body
The extracellular matrix — its composition and fiber content varies dramatically across connective tissue types, producing very different mechanical properties
Connective tissue diversity is actually due to variation in epithelial cells, not connective tissue itself
The presence or absence of a nucleus in the cells
questions.e: Connective tissue's remarkable functional diversity — from the fluid matrix of blood to the mineralized matrix of bone to the fiber-dense matrix of tendon — largely stems from variation in the extracellular matrix's composition and fiber content, which produces very different mechanical and functional properties across types.

questions.q: If a bone sample showed abnormally low osteoclast activity relative to normal osteoblast activity over a prolonged period, what would be the most likely long-term structural consequence?
o: No change, since osteoclasts have no effect on bone density
Progressive loss of bone density (osteoporosis-like thinning)
Immediate conversion of bone into cartilage
Progressive excessive bone density, since resorption would not be keeping pace with formation
questions.e: Since osteoclasts are responsible for resorbing bone matrix, abnormally low osteoclast activity relative to ongoing osteoblast-driven formation would tip the balance toward excessive bone accumulation over time, rather than bone loss.

questions.q: A comparison of skin (dense irregular connective tissue) and tendon (dense regular connective tissue) both under significant, but differently directed, mechanical stress would predict which outcome?
o: The skin would tolerate multidirectional stress well due to its randomly oriented fibers, while a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be more vulnerable to injury
Neither tissue type is affected by the direction of applied stress
The tendon would tolerate multidirectional stress better than the skin
Both tissues perform identically regardless of stress direction
questions.e: Because dense irregular tissue (skin) has randomly oriented fibers suited to multidirectional stress, while dense regular tissue (tendon) has fibers aligned to resist force along one specific direction, a tendon subjected to stress from an unexpected angle would be comparatively more vulnerable to injury than skin facing the same off-axis stress.

questions.q: The tibia is formed from which of the following during foetal life?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A physiologist stimulates an isolated tissue sample with a nerve impulse and observes it shorten. Which functional property of muscle tissue is being demonstrated?
questions.e: The tissue's response to a nerve impulse by contracting demonstrates excitability — its ability to respond to electrical stimulation with contraction.

questions.q: After contracting, a muscle is stretched back to its resting length by the pull of an opposing muscle. Which property allows the muscle to be stretched in this way without damage?
questions.e: Extensibility is the property that allows a muscle to be stretched back to its original length, typically by the action of an opposing muscle.

questions.q: A muscle that has just been stretched springs back toward its original shape once the stretching force is removed. Which property is responsible for this recoil?
questions.e: Elasticity is specifically the property allowing a muscle to recoil back toward its original shape after being stretched, distinct from extensibility (the capacity to BE stretched in the first place).

questions.q: Shivering in cold weather generates warmth as a secondary effect of repeated muscle contraction. Which general function of muscle tissue does this represent?
questions.e: Shivering illustrates thermogenesis — heat generation as a byproduct of muscle contraction — one of muscle tissue's general functions distinct from producing visible, purposeful motion.

questions.q: A histologist examines a muscle biopsy under the microscope and sees clear light and dark cross-banding across the cells. Based on this feature alone, which muscle type(s) could this be?
o: None; no muscle type shows this banding
questions.e: Visible cross-striations are the hallmark of striated muscle, a category that includes both skeletal and cardiac muscle; smooth muscle, by contrast, lacks this banding pattern.

questions.q: A patient can consciously decide to contract this type of muscle to lift a weight, but cannot consciously will their intestinal walls to contract in the same deliberate way. What distinguishes these two muscle types functionally?
o: Skeletal muscle is involuntary; smooth muscle is voluntary
Neither is under any form of nervous control
Both are voluntary in identical ways
Skeletal muscle is voluntary; smooth muscle in the gut wall is involuntary
questions.e: Skeletal muscle is functionally classified as voluntary, under conscious control, whereas smooth muscle (such as in the intestinal wall) is involuntary, not subject to deliberate conscious control.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the skeletal system
o: Mineral storage and attachment of muscles
Protection, production of blood cells and filtration of blood
Only A and B are correct
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A muscle fiber sample shows multiple nuclei located just beneath the plasma membrane, near the cell's periphery, in a long cylindrical, non-branching cell. Which muscle type does this describe?
o: None of these; this pattern does not occur in muscle
questions.e: Peripherally located, multiple nuclei within a long, cylindrical, non-branching fiber is characteristic of skeletal muscle, distinguishing it from cardiac muscle's typically single, central nucleus and smooth muscle's spindle shape.

questions.q: Skeletal muscle fibers end up containing many nuclei because of a specific developmental process. What is this process?
o: Absorption of nearby satellite cells after birth
Repeated mitotic division of a single myoblast nucleus without cell division
Direct transformation from cardiac muscle cells
Fusion of many individual myoblasts into a single fiber during development
questions.e: Skeletal muscle fibers become multinucleated because they form through the fusion of many individual myoblasts during development, combining their nuclei into one large, multinucleated fiber.

questions.q: A severely damaged skeletal muscle fiber cannot repair itself through division of the mature fiber itself, since mature fibers do not divide. Which cell population, located between the fiber's plasma membrane and its external lamina, provides this repair capacity instead?
questions.e: Satellite cells, positioned between the plasma membrane of a mature skeletal muscle fiber and its external lamina, serve as a stem cell population capable of assisting in the repair of damaged muscle fibers, since the mature fibers themselves cannot divide.

questions.q: A surgeon dissecting toward a skeletal muscle first cuts through a dense connective tissue layer surrounding the entire muscle, through which the major nerve and blood supply enter. Which layer has just been cut?
questions.e: The epimysium is the dense regular connective tissue layer surrounding an entire skeletal muscle, and it is through this outer layer that the major vascular and nerve supply typically penetrates.

questions.q: A fibrous sheath that surrounds and protects individual fascicles of a muscle is called
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Finally, the thinnest connective tissue layer, wrapping each single muscle fiber individually, is exposed. What is this innermost layer called?
questions.e: The endomysium is the thin connective tissue layer surrounding each individual muscle fiber, the innermost of the three nested connective tissue sheaths of skeletal muscle.

questions.q: A flat, sheet-like tendon attaches a broad, flat muscle (such as the external oblique) to underlying structures, rather than the muscle narrowing to a cord-like tendon. What is this sheet-like tendon called?
questions.e: An aponeurosis is specifically a flat, sheet-like tendon, appropriate for broad, flat muscles, distinguishing it from a typical cord-like tendon.

questions.q: Which connective tissue structure is responsible for holding multiple functional muscle units together as a group, lining the body wall and limbs more broadly than the epimysium of a single muscle?
questions.e: Fascia is a broader dense irregular connective tissue that lines the body wall and limbs, holding groups of functional muscle units together, distinct from the epimysium, which wraps only a single individual muscle.

questions.q: A cardiologist explains that heart muscle cells, unlike skeletal muscle fibers, can pass electrical signals directly between adjacent cells through specialized junctions, allowing the whole heart to contract almost as a single unit. What is the structure responsible for this electrical coupling called?
questions.e: Intercalated discs, the specialized junctions connecting adjacent cardiac muscle cells, contain gap junctions that allow electrical signals to pass directly between cells, enabling the heart to function as a coordinated unit.

questions.q: A heart continues beating for a short time even when completely removed from the body and disconnected from all nerve input, as long as it is kept oxygenated. Which property of cardiac muscle explains this observation?
o: Autorhythmicity — cardiac muscle can generate its own action potentials without needing external nerve impulses
Its dependence on skeletal muscle for coordination
questions.e: Autorhythmicity is the property that allows cardiac muscle to generate its own action potentials via a built-in pacemaker system, meaning the heart can continue beating rhythmically even without external nerve input, as long as it remains oxygenated.

questions.q: A patient suffers significant cardiac muscle damage during a heart attack. Why is this damage generally considered permanent, in contrast to a comparable skeletal muscle injury that might partially recover?
o: Skeletal muscle also never regenerates, making the comparison meaningless
Cardiac muscle has no nuclei to guide repair
Cardiac muscle shows essentially no regenerative activity under normal conditions, unlike skeletal muscle's partial repair capacity via satellite cells
Cardiac muscle regenerates faster than skeletal muscle
questions.e: Cardiac muscle shows essentially no regenerative capacity under normal conditions, unlike skeletal muscle, which retains some repair capacity through satellite cells — explaining why cardiac muscle damage after a heart attack tends to be permanent, often replaced by scar tissue.

questions.q: What feature distinguishes cardiac muscle from skeletal muscle in microscopic sections?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A tissue sample shows narrow, spindle-shaped cells lying roughly parallel to one another, each with a single central nucleus, and no visible cross-striations. Which muscle type does this describe?
questions.e: Narrow, spindle-shaped, non-striated cells with a single central nucleus arranged roughly parallel to one another is the characteristic microscopic appearance of smooth muscle.

questions.q: Factors in preventing osteoporosis include:
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A physiologist compares the contraction speed of skeletal muscle (used for a sprinter's rapid stride) with that of the smooth muscle propelling food through the intestine. What functional difference would be predicted?
o: Skeletal muscle contracts rapidly for quick, powerful movements, while smooth muscle contracts slowly and sustains contraction over a longer period, suited to gradual propulsion
Smooth muscle contracts faster than skeletal muscle in all cases
Neither tissue can sustain contraction for more than a fraction of a second
questions.e: Skeletal muscle is adapted for rapid, powerful contractions suited to voluntary movements like sprinting, whereas smooth muscle is specialized for slow, sustained contraction, appropriate for the gradual, prolonged propulsion of substances through hollow organs like the intestine.

questions.q: Which location would you NOT expect to find smooth muscle, based on its typical distribution in the walls of hollow organs and specific structures like the eye?
o: The wall of a blood vessel
questions.e: The femur shaft is composed of bone tissue, not smooth muscle; smooth muscle is characteristically found in the walls of hollow organs (blood vessels, stomach, intestines) and specialized structures like the intrinsic muscles of the eye (e.g., the iris).

questions.q: An action potential arrives at a muscle fiber's surface and must be conducted rapidly into the cell's interior, near the sarcoplasmic reticulum, to trigger contraction throughout the whole fiber almost simultaneously. Which structure specifically enables this rapid deep conduction?
o: Transverse tubules, invaginations of the sarcolemma carrying the impulse into the fiber's interior
Terminal cisternae alone, without any surface connection
The sarcolemma alone, without any specialized invagination
questions.e: T tubules are invaginations of the sarcolemma that extend into the fiber's interior, allowing the action potential to be conducted rapidly and deeply into the cell, close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum, ensuring near-simultaneous activation throughout the fiber.

questions.q: A drug blocks calcium release from a specific organelle within skeletal muscle fibers, preventing contraction despite normal electrical stimulation. Which structure, specialized for calcium storage and release, is most likely the drug's target?
o: The terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum
questions.e: The terminal cisternae, specialized regions of the sarcoplasmic reticulum, store calcium ions and release them to trigger contraction; blocking this release would prevent contraction despite otherwise normal electrical stimulation of the fiber.

questions.q: Adhering to the outer surface of the limiting membrane of the granular endoplasmic reticulum is/are the
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A sarcomere is bounded on either side by structures that anchor its thin filaments and mark where one contractile unit ends and the next begins. What are these boundary structures called?
questions.e: Z discs anchor the thin filaments and mark the boundary between adjacent sarcomeres, defining the limits of each individual contractile unit along a myofibril.

questions.q: Within the region of a sarcomere where thick and thin filaments overlap, each thick (myosin) filament is typically surrounded by a specific number of thin (actin) filaments in a hexagonal arrangement. How many thin filaments typically surround each thick filament in this zone?
questions.e: In the overlap zone of a sarcomere, each thick filament is typically surrounded by six thin filaments in a characteristic hexagonal pattern, reflecting the precise, repeating molecular architecture of the contractile apparatus.

questions.q: A muscle biopsy from a patient shows normal-looking sarcomeres but with the muscle progressively replaced by fat and connective tissue over years, along with muscle weakness. This pattern, combined with a sex-linked recessive inheritance, most strongly suggests which condition?
o: Myotonic dystrophy specifically, given its distinct cardiac features
questions.e: Progressive degeneration of muscle with replacement by fat and connective tissue, combined with sex-linked recessive inheritance, is characteristic of Duchenne muscular dystrophy, distinguishing it from the other listed conditions.

questions.q: A patient with a severe heart defect had to undergo an emergency surgery, the Doctor decides to open the chest wall to access the heart, this procedure is known as?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A middle-aged woman presents with chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread musculoskeletal pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, with no clear infectious cause. Which condition does this presentation most closely match?
questions.e: This presentation — chronic fatigue, disrupted sleep, and widespread pain involving muscle, its connective tissue coverings, and nearby joint capsules, predominantly affecting women — matches fibromyositis (fibromyalgia).

questions.q: An 80-year-old patient shows measurably reduced muscular strength compared to earlier decades, along with a biopsy showing increased connective tissue relative to the number of muscle fibers. Which age-related process best explains these combined findings?
o: Sarcopenia, the age-related decline in muscle fibers and mass, accompanied by a relative increase in connective tissue
Fibromyositis, which requires an inflammatory trigger
Muscular dystrophy, which is not age-related
questions.e: Sarcopenia refers to age-related muscle wasting, characterized by a decline in the number of muscle fibers and overall muscle mass, with a corresponding relative increase in connective tissue — matching this patient's findings.

questions.q: A patient reports diffuse muscle pain without describing any weakness or structural disease. Which precise medical term best captures this specific symptom, as opposed to a broader disease diagnosis?
questions.e: Myalgia is the precise term for muscle pain itself, whereas myopathy is the broader term for any disease of muscle tissue — the patient's symptom alone (pain, without a named disease) is best captured by myalgia.

questions.q: A clinician uses a broad term to refer to any disease process affecting muscle tissue, without specifying the exact condition. Which term is this?
questions.e: Myopathy is the general term referring to any disease of muscle tissue, serving as an umbrella term under which specific conditions (like muscular dystrophy or fibromyositis) fall.

questions.q: A weightlifter's biceps visibly enlarge after months of resistance training, though the total number of muscle fibers remains essentially unchanged. Which process best explains this increase in muscle size?
questions.e: Hypertrophy refers to an increase in tissue size due to the enlargement of individual existing cells, which is the primary mechanism behind resistance-training-induced muscle growth in adult skeletal muscle, where fiber number remains largely fixed.

questions.q: In contrast to hypertrophy, a tissue increases in size because its cells have increased in number, with individual cell size remaining roughly constant. Which process does this describe?
questions.e: Hyperplasia is the process by which tissue size increases due to a rise in the number of cells, in contrast to hypertrophy, where size increases due to enlargement of existing cells without necessarily increasing their number.

questions.q: Under the electron microscope, a sarcomere's dark band, corresponding to the full length of the thick filaments (including the region where they overlap with thin filaments), is identified. Which band is this?
o: H zone exclusively, distinct from the A band
questions.e: The A band is the dark band of a sarcomere, corresponding to the full length of the thick (myosin) filaments, including the central region where they overlap with the thin filaments.

questions.q: A researcher identifies a lighter band within a sarcomere that contains only thin filaments, with no thick filament overlap. Which band is this, and what accounts for its lighter appearance?
o: The Z disc, which is defined by its complete absence of any protein
The I band, appearing lighter because it contains only thin filaments without the additional density of overlapping thick filaments
The H zone, which always appears darker than the A band
The A band, because it lacks any filaments at all
questions.e: The I band contains only thin (actin) filaments, without overlapping thick filaments, which is why it appears lighter under the microscope compared to the denser A band, where thick and thin filaments overlap.

questions.q: A developmental biologist observes individual myoblasts fusing together in the embryo to form a single elongated cell with many nuclei. What is the end product of this fusion process?
questions.e: This fusion of multiple individual myoblasts is exactly the developmental process that produces a mature, multinucleated skeletal muscle fiber — a hallmark distinguishing skeletal muscle development from cardiac or smooth muscle.

questions.q: Which protein forms the thin filaments of a sarcomere, working in conjunction with the thick filament protein during the sliding filament mechanism of contraction?
questions.e: Actin is the protein that forms the thin filaments of a sarcomere, interacting with the thick filament protein myosin to generate the sliding motion underlying muscle contraction.

questions.q: Which protein forms the thick filaments of a sarcomere, and is responsible (along with actin) for generating the pulling force of muscle contraction?
questions.e: Myosin is the protein forming the thick filaments of a sarcomere; together with actin (the thin filament protein), it generates the force of muscle contraction through the sliding filament mechanism.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly matches a muscle type with its typical location, based on functional and structural adaptation?
o: Smooth muscle — attached to the femur via a tendon
Smooth muscle — the wall of a blood vessel
Cardiac muscle — the wall of the stomach
questions.e: Smooth muscle is correctly matched to the wall of a blood vessel, where it controls vessel diameter; the other pairings mismatch tissue type and location (cardiac muscle belongs to the heart wall, and skeletal muscle typically attaches to bone via tendons).

questions.q: Smooth muscle, unlike cardiac muscle is UNSTRIATED because:
o: Its myofilaments are not regularly arranged
It has more sarcoplasm so the striations are not prominent
Myosin filaments are attached to the sarcolemma
It lacks many of the filaments found in cardiac muscle
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following would be expected to have the SLOWEST, most sustained pattern of contraction among the three muscle types, well suited to gradually moving substances through a tube-like organ?
o: None of the three; all contract identically
questions.e: Smooth muscle is specialized for slow, sustained contraction, an adaptation well suited to gradually propelling substances (such as food or urine) through the tube-like hollow organs where it is found.

questions.q: Why would damage to a large area of a limb's skeletal muscle likely heal with a mixture of muscle regeneration and scar tissue formation, rather than complete regeneration alone?
o: Satellite cells can assist limited repair, but severe or extensive damage often exceeds this limited regenerative capacity, leading to some replacement by connective tissue
Skeletal muscle has unlimited regenerative capacity, so scarring never occurs
Skeletal muscle cannot regenerate at all under any circumstances
Satellite cells convert directly into scar tissue
questions.e: While satellite cells provide some capacity for skeletal muscle repair, this capacity is limited; extensive damage often exceeds what satellite cells can fully regenerate, resulting in partial regeneration combined with some replacement by connective tissue (scar formation).

questions.q: Which structural feature allows a single motor neuron's action potential, once it reaches the T tubules, to trigger near-simultaneous calcium release and contraction throughout the ENTIRE fiber, not just near the surface?
o: The aponeurosis at the muscle's end
The T tubule network penetrating deep into the fiber, positioned close to the sarcoplasmic reticulum's terminal cisternae throughout the cell
The connective tissue sheaths (epimysium, perimysium, endomysium)
Satellite cells located at the fiber's periphery
questions.e: Because T tubules extend deep into the fiber's interior and lie close to the terminal cisternae of the sarcoplasmic reticulum throughout the cell, they allow the action potential to trigger calcium release (and thus contraction) nearly simultaneously throughout the whole fiber, not just at the surface.

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the striated or brush border?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which finding would most strongly suggest a biopsy sample is skeletal rather than cardiac muscle, based purely on nuclear count and position per cell?
o: Multiple nuclei positioned at the cell periphery
Nuclei clustered only at one end of the cell
A single central nucleus per cell
questions.e: Multiple, peripherally positioned nuclei per cell is characteristic of skeletal muscle fibers, distinguishing them from cardiac muscle cells, which typically have a single, centrally located nucleus.

questions.q: Given that smooth muscle can divide (proliferate) while skeletal and cardiac muscle largely cannot, which of the following age-related or pathological scenarios would be uniquely possible in smooth muscle but not in mature skeletal or cardiac muscle?
o: Contraction in response to a nerve impulse
Significant new muscle cell formation through cell division in the wall of a hollow organ
The presence of an extracellular matrix nearby
questions.e: Because smooth muscle cells retain the capacity to divide, significant new muscle cell formation via cell proliferation is uniquely possible in smooth muscle, unlike mature skeletal or cardiac muscle, which largely lack this capacity.

questions.q: A pharmacologist wants to design a drug that selectively relaxes blood vessel walls to lower blood pressure, without significantly affecting skeletal muscle contraction. Which type of muscle tissue must the drug specifically target?
o: All three muscle types equally, since selectivity is impossible
questions.e: Since blood vessel walls are composed of smooth muscle, a drug intended to selectively relax vessel walls (lowering blood pressure) without affecting skeletal muscle would need to specifically target smooth muscle mechanisms distinct from those of skeletal muscle.

questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A patient with long-standing, poorly controlled diabetes shows early signs of sarcopenia despite being only in their 50s. Which best describes what is happening, based on the definition of this term?
o: Accelerated muscle wasting, involving a decline in the number of muscle fibers and an increase in relative connective tissue, occurring earlier than typical age-related expectations
An infection specific to muscle tissue
A congenital muscle disorder present since birth
A benign, reversible increase in muscle mass
questions.e: Sarcopenia refers to muscle wasting — a decline in muscle fiber number and mass with a relative increase in connective tissue — and though it is typically age-related, the same underlying process can be accelerated by conditions like poorly controlled diabetes, appearing earlier than expected.

questions.q: Which best explains why fibromyositis (fibromyalgia) predominantly affects women and produces widespread, rather than localized, symptoms?
o: Fibromyositis is caused exclusively by a bacterial infection localized to one joint

The condition, as described, involves diffuse inflammation of muscle, its connective tissue coverings, tendons, and nearby joint capsules, rather than an isolated single-site process, and the pattern of predominance in women is a described epidemiological feature
This information is not established; fibromyositis affects only a specific single muscle in a highly localized way
It is a purely psychological condition with no described physical involvement
questions.e: Fibromyositis, as described, involves diffuse inflammation spanning muscle, its connective tissue coverings, tendons, and nearby joint capsules — consistent with its widespread rather than localized symptom pattern — and it predominantly affects women as an epidemiological feature of the condition.

questions.q: Which best distinguishes 'myalgia' from 'myopathy' as clinical terms?
o: Myalgia refers to bone disease, myopathy to muscle disease
Myalgia specifically denotes muscle pain, a symptom, while myopathy is the broader term for any disease process affecting muscle tissue
Myopathy specifically denotes muscle pain, while myalgia is the broader disease term
They are exact synonyms with no distinction
questions.e: Myalgia specifically refers to the symptom of muscle pain, while myopathy is a broader term encompassing any disease of muscle tissue — myalgia may be a symptom of a myopathy, but the two terms are not interchangeable in scope.

questions.q: The enlargement of existing muscle fibres due to increasing diameters of cell but not increasing the number of new muscle fibres is known as
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best experimental evidence that a novel tissue sample is smooth rather than skeletal muscle?
o: Long, cylindrical, non-branching, multinucleated fibers with peripheral nuclei
Presence of visible cross-striations under the microscope
Presence of intercalated discs connecting adjacent cells
Spindle-shaped cells with a single central nucleus and no visible striations, capable of dividing in culture
questions.e: Spindle-shaped, non-striated cells with a single central nucleus and retained capacity to divide is characteristic of smooth muscle, clearly distinguishing it from the striated, multinucleated, peripherally-nucleated fibers of skeletal muscle or the intercalated-disc-containing cells of cardiac muscle.

questions.q: Given that skeletal muscle is described as having limited regenerative capacity via satellite cells, while cardiac muscle shows essentially none, which tissue would be predicted to have the WORST long-term functional outcome after a severe, extensive injury?
o: Neither tissue type is affected by severe injury
Cardiac muscle, due to its essentially absent regenerative capacity under normal conditions
Skeletal muscle, due to its limited but still-present satellite cell repair capacity
questions.e: Because cardiac muscle shows essentially no regenerative activity under normal conditions — in contrast to skeletal muscle's limited but present satellite-cell-mediated repair — cardiac muscle would be predicted to have the worse long-term functional outcome after a severe, extensive injury, typically resulting in permanent scar tissue rather than functional muscle replacement.

questions.q: Which best explains the functional logic behind skeletal muscle's three nested connective tissue layers (epimysium, perimysium, endomysium) rather than just a single surrounding sheath?
o: The layers exist solely to prevent the muscle from ever being able to contract

The nested layers allow force generated by individual fibers to be transmitted and combined efficiently up through fascicles to the whole muscle and ultimately to the tendon, while also providing a path for blood vessels and nerves to reach every fiber
