Only the outermost layer, the epimysium, has any real function
The layers exist purely for aesthetic organization with no functional role
questions.e: The nested arrangement of epimysium, perimysium, and endomysium allows the force generated by individual fibers to be transmitted and progressively combined at each level (fiber to fascicle to whole muscle) up to the tendon, while also providing routes for blood vessels and nerves to reach every individual fiber.

questions.q: Which of the following best distinguishes the trigger for smooth muscle contraction in a blood vessel from the trigger for skeletal muscle contraction at a neuromuscular junction?
o: Smooth muscle cannot be influenced by any external signal
Both tissue types respond only to direct mechanical pressure, never to nerves or hormones

Smooth muscle in vessel walls can be influenced by autonomic nerve impulses, hormones, and local metabolites, whereas skeletal muscle contraction is triggered specifically by a somatic motor neuron at the neuromuscular junction
Skeletal muscle responds to hormones exclusively, never to nerve impulses
questions.e: Smooth muscle contraction (as in a blood vessel) can be modulated by autonomic nerve impulses, circulating hormones, and local metabolites, offering more varied control pathways than skeletal muscle, whose contraction is triggered specifically by a somatic motor neuron acting at the neuromuscular junction.

questions.q: A patient with an autoimmune condition develops antibodies that specifically attack proteins at the neuromuscular junction, impairing signal transmission from nerve to muscle. Which muscle type would be most directly and immediately affected by this specific attack?
o: Cardiac muscle exclusively, since it relies on autorhythmicity rather than nerve input
None of the muscle types would be affected
Skeletal muscle, since it relies specifically on the neuromuscular junction for activation
questions.e: Because skeletal muscle contraction is triggered specifically via the neuromuscular junction (unlike cardiac muscle's autorhythmicity or smooth muscle's multiple modulating inputs), an autoimmune attack on neuromuscular junction proteins would most directly and immediately impair skeletal muscle activation.

questions.q: A neurosurgeon distinguishes structures protected within the skull and vertebral column from those running through the limbs and torso. Which two divisions of the nervous system does this distinction correspond to?
o: The somatic and autonomic nervous systems
The central nervous system and peripheral nervous system
questions.e: This distinction matches the CNS (brain and spinal cord, protected within the skull and vertebral column) versus the PNS (cranial and spinal nerves running through the limbs and torso, outside this bony protection).

questions.q: A glial cell tumor (glioma) is found to be growing rapidly, consistent with the fact that this cell type, unlike most neurons, retains the ability to divide. Which broad cell category does the tumor arise from?
questions.e: A glioma arises from glial (neuroglial) cells, which — unlike most mature neurons — retain the capacity to divide, consistent with their potential to form rapidly growing tumors.

questions.q: A patient suffers a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes before resuscitation. Given what is known about neurons' tolerance for oxygen deprivation, what would be the most likely neurological consequence?
o: No neurological effect, since neurons can survive indefinitely without oxygen
Only glial cells would be affected, sparing all neurons
Significant neuronal death, since neurons typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen due to their high metabolic demand
Neurons would simply pause activity and resume normally with no damage after any duration
questions.e: Because neurons have a high metabolic rate and typically die after about 5 minutes without oxygen, a period of cardiac arrest lasting several minutes would be expected to cause significant neuronal death, an important basis for the urgency of resuscitation.

questions.q: A researcher observes that damaged mature neurons in the brain, unlike epithelial cells in the skin, generally do not get replaced by new cell division after injury. Which property of neurons explains this?
o: Neurons regenerate faster than any other cell type
questions.e: Neurons are largely amitotic, meaning most cannot divide to replace themselves if destroyed — a key contrast with tissues like epithelium, which regenerate readily through ongoing cell division.

questions.q: Within a neuron's cell body, clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes are visible under the microscope, responsible for renewing the cell's membranes. What is the specific name for these clusters?
questions.e: Chromatophilic bodies, also called Nissl bodies, are clusters of rough endoplasmic reticulum and free ribosomes within the neuron's cell body, responsible for renewing the cell's membranes through ongoing protein synthesis.

questions.q: A pathologist finds a cluster of neuron cell bodies within the substance of the spinal cord itself. What is this type of cluster properly called, as distinct from a similar cluster located outside the CNS?
questions.e: A cluster of neuron cell bodies located within the CNS is called a nucleus; the equivalent cluster located in the PNS, along a peripheral nerve, is instead called a ganglion.

questions.q: Following the previous scenario, if the same type of cell body cluster were instead found along a peripheral nerve outside the spinal cord, what would it be called?
questions.e: A cluster of neuron cell bodies located in the PNS, along a peripheral nerve, is specifically called a ganglion — distinct from a nucleus, which is the equivalent term used within the CNS.

questions.q: An imaging study identifies a bundle of neuron processes running within the spinal cord itself, connecting different regions of the CNS. What is this type of bundle called, as opposed to the equivalent structure in the PNS?
questions.e: Within the CNS, a bundle of neuron processes is called a tract; the equivalent bundle located in the PNS is instead called a nerve.

questions.q: A neuron receives incoming signals from several other neurons through highly branched processes, then integrates these signals and conducts them toward its own cell body. Which structure is performing this receptive role?
questions.e: Dendrites are the extensively branching processes specialized as receptive sites, receiving signals from other neurons and conducting electrical signals toward the cell body — matching this integrative, receptive role.

questions.q: A neuron's single long process, emerging from a specific point on the soma, conducts an impulse away from the cell body toward a distant target. From which specific point does this process originate?
questions.e: The axon hillock is the specific point on the soma from which the axon emerges, marking the origin of the process that conducts impulses away from the cell body.

questions.q: A drug interferes with protein synthesis specifically within a neuron's axon, but leaves protein synthesis in the cell body and dendrites unaffected. Why would this drug have essentially no additional effect on the axon itself?
o: Because axons already lack chromatophilic bodies and normally do not perform protein synthesis, unlike the cell body and dendrites
Because axons contain no ribosomes at all under any interpretation, making this drug irrelevant everywhere in the cell
Because this scenario is impossible; axons synthesize just as much protein as the cell body
Because axons have the highest rate of protein synthesis in the neuron
questions.e: Axons characteristically lack chromatophilic (Nissl) bodies and do not normally carry out protein synthesis (unlike the cell body and dendrites, which do), so a drug specifically blocking axonal protein synthesis would have little additional effect, since this process was not occurring there to begin with.

questions.q: An electron microscopist examines the very tip of an axon, at its terminal branches, and finds small membrane-bound sacs clustered near the plasma membrane, ready to release their contents. What are these structures, and what do they release?
o: Neurofibrils, releasing calcium directly into the cell body
questions.e: Synaptic vesicles, clustered within axon terminals, contain and release neurotransmitters into the synapse when the neuron is stimulated to fire — matching this description of vesicle-mediated release at the axon tip.

questions.q: A neuron conducts a signal toward a synapse and releases neurotransmitter, which then acts on a second neuron on the other side of the gap. Which neuron is functioning as the 'presynaptic' neuron in this scenario?
o: The first neuron, conducting the signal toward the synapse and releasing neurotransmitter
Neither; presynaptic only applies to sensory neurons
The second neuron, receiving the signal
questions.e: The presynaptic neuron is, by definition, the one conducting a signal toward the synapse and releasing neurotransmitter — matching the first neuron's role in this scenario, as opposed to the second (postsynaptic) neuron receiving the signal.

questions.q: Which structure specifically separates the plasma membranes of the presynaptic and postsynaptic neurons at a typical chemical synapse, requiring neurotransmitter to diffuse across it?
questions.e: The synaptic cleft is the physical gap separating the presynaptic and postsynaptic membranes, across which neurotransmitter must diffuse to relay the signal from one neuron to the next.

questions.q: A motor neuron forms a specialized synapse directly onto a skeletal muscle fiber, rather than onto another neuron. What is this specific type of synapse called?
questions.e: A synapse formed specifically between a neuron and a muscle cell — as in this motor neuron/muscle fiber scenario — is termed a neuromuscular junction, distinct from the neuron-to-neuron synapse types.

questions.q: Statistically, the vast majority of synapses in the nervous system occur between the axon terminals of one neuron and the dendrites of the next. What is this most common synapse type called?
questions.e: The axodendritic synapse, formed between axon terminals and dendrites, is the most common synapse type in the nervous system.

questions.q: A less common synapse type is found where an axon terminal directly contacts the cell body (soma) of the next neuron, rather than its dendrites. What is this synapse type called?
questions.e: An axosomatic synapse is formed between an axon terminal and the cell body (soma) of another neuron, distinguishing it from the more common axodendritic synapse.

questions.q: A researcher examines the retina and finds a neuron with exactly one dendrite and one axon extending from opposite poles of the cell body. Given that this structural pattern is relatively uncommon overall, which structural neuron type is this most likely to be?
questions.e: A neuron with exactly one dendrite and one axon is structurally classified as bipolar — a relatively rare pattern found in specialized sensory locations such as the retina, inner ear, and olfactory epithelium.

questions.q: The functions of the nervous system include the following
o: Responds to internal and external changes
Maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume
Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction
Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A sensory neuron's cell body is found not within the CNS, but in a ganglion just outside it, with a single process splitting into a peripheral branch (toward the receptor) and a central branch (into the CNS). Which structural neuron type does this describe?
o: None of these categories apply to sensory neurons
questions.e: This description — a cell body located in a peripheral ganglion, with one process splitting into peripheral and central branches — is characteristic of unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons, which serve mainly as sensory neurons of the PNS.

questions.q: A sensory receptor in the skin detects a painful stimulus and the resulting signal is conducted toward the spinal cord. Functionally, which category of neuron is carrying this signal?
o: None of these; sensory information does not require dedicated neurons
questions.e: A neuron conducting a signal from a peripheral tissue (skin) toward the CNS (spinal cord) is functionally classified as a sensory (afferent) neuron.

questions.q: After a reflex is processed within the spinal cord, a signal travels from the CNS out to a skeletal muscle to produce a motor response. Functionally, which category of neuron carries this outgoing signal?
o: Interneuron only, since interneurons directly contract muscle
None of these; only sensory neurons exist in a reflex arc
questions.e: A neuron carrying a signal away from the CNS toward an effector organ such as skeletal muscle is functionally classified as a motor (efferent) neuron.

questions.q: Within a simple reflex arc, a neuron located entirely within the spinal cord processes information between the incoming sensory signal and the outgoing motor signal. Which functional category of neuron performs this integrative role, and what fraction of all neurons does this category represent?
o: Interneurons; about 99.98% of all neurons in the body
questions.e: Interneurons, confined entirely to the CNS, perform this integrative role between sensory input and motor output, and they represent the vast majority of neurons in the body — approximately 99.98%.

questions.q: A motor neuron specifically innervates skeletal muscle under voluntary control, as opposed to smooth muscle or glands. Which functional subtype of motor neuron is this?
o: Sensory motor neuron (not a real category)
questions.e: A motor neuron innervating skeletal muscle specifically is classified as a somatic motor neuron, in contrast to visceral (autonomic) motor neurons, which innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands.

questions.q: Which motor neuron subtype would be responsible for stimulating smooth muscle in the gut wall to contract, as part of the autonomic nervous system's control over digestion?
questions.e: Visceral (autonomic) motor neurons innervate smooth muscle, cardiac muscle, and glands — including the smooth muscle of the gut wall involved in digestive motility — distinguishing them from somatic motor neurons, which innervate skeletal muscle.

questions.q: A tumor selectively destroys the CNS's resident phagocytic cells, impairing the brain's ability to clear debris and pathogens. Which type of glial cell has been affected?
questions.e: Microglia function as the resident phagocytes (macrophages) of the CNS, so their destruction would specifically impair the brain's capacity to clear debris and pathogens via phagocytosis.

questions.q: A patient's cerebrospinal fluid production is impaired due to dysfunction of the epithelial-like cells lining the brain's ventricles that help form the choroid plexus. Which glial cell type is most directly implicated?
questions.e: Ependymal cells line the ventricles and central canal, helping form the choroid plexuses that secrete cerebrospinal fluid, making them the glial cell type most directly implicated in this scenario.

questions.q: An autoimmune disease selectively targets the CNS glial cells responsible for forming myelin sheaths around axons, each capable of myelinating segments of several different axons at once. Which glial cell type is under attack?
questions.e: Oligodendrocytes form the myelin sheaths around axons in the CNS, and uniquely, a single oligodendrocyte can extend processes to myelinate segments of several different nearby axons — matching this description.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type performs a supportive, protective role around neuron cell bodies within ganglia, functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS?
questions.e: Satellite cells (amphicytes), located in the PNS, surround and protect neuron cell bodies within ganglia, performing a role functionally comparable to astrocytes in the CNS.

questions.q: Which PNS glial cell type forms the myelin sheath and neurolemma around a single axon at a time, in contrast to its CNS counterpart, which can myelinate multiple axon segments simultaneously?
questions.e: Schwann cells form the myelin sheath and neurolemma in the PNS, and each Schwann cell myelinates only a single axon segment — in contrast to oligodendrocytes in the CNS, which can myelinate segments of multiple different axons.

questions.q: Following a peripheral nerve injury, a severed axon successfully regrows and eventually reconnects with its target. Which structure, provided by Schwann cells, forms the physical guiding tube that made this regrowth possible?
questions.e: The neurolemma, the cytoplasmic covering provided by Schwann cells, forms a regeneration tube that guides the regrowth of a severed axon in the PNS — the structure responsible for enabling successful reconnection in this scenario.

questions.q: Comparing myelin formation in the CNS versus the PNS: which pairing of glial cell and location is correct?
o: Oligodendrocytes myelinate CNS axons; Schwann cells myelinate PNS axons
Microglia myelinate CNS axons; ependymal cells myelinate PNS axons
Astrocytes myelinate both CNS and PNS axons
Schwann cells myelinate CNS axons; oligodendrocytes myelinate PNS axons
questions.e: The correct pairing is oligodendrocytes forming myelin in the CNS, and Schwann cells forming myelin in the PNS — the reverse or other pairings listed are incorrect.

questions.q: A demyelinating disease progressively damages the myelin sheaths of axons specifically within the brain and spinal cord (not peripheral nerves). Which condition, and which glial cell type's product, is most directly implicated?
o: Multiple sclerosis; damage to myelin produced by oligodendrocytes
Multiple sclerosis; damage to myelin produced by Schwann cells
questions.e: Multiple sclerosis is a demyelination disease affecting the CNS specifically, where the myelin normally produced by oligodendrocytes (not the PNS's Schwann cells) is progressively damaged.

questions.q: An electrophysiologist notes that a myelinated axon conducts impulses considerably faster than a comparable unmyelinated axon of similar diameter. Which property of myelin best explains this speed advantage?
o: Myelin actively pumps ions across the membrane
Myelin contains its own independent nervous system
Myelin has no effect on conduction speed; the difference must be due to axon length alone
Myelin insulates the axon and prevents leakage of electrical current, increasing conduction speed
questions.e: Myelin acts as an insulating layer around the axon, preventing leakage of electrical current and thereby increasing the speed of impulse conduction compared to an unmyelinated axon of similar diameter.

questions.q: Along a myelinated peripheral axon, small gaps interrupt the otherwise continuous myelin sheath at regular intervals. What are these gaps called, and why do they occur at these specific points?
o: Nodes of Ranvier; they occur where the myelin sheath is not continuous because it is formed by a series of individual Schwann cells
Terminal boutons; they occur only at the axon's very end
Synaptic clefts; they occur between every pair of neurons
Chromatolytic zones; they occur only after nerve injury
questions.e: Nodes of Ranvier are the gaps interrupting the myelin sheath at regular intervals along a PNS axon, occurring because the myelin sheath is formed by a series of individual Schwann cells, each myelinating only one axon segment, leaving small gaps between them.

questions.q: A brain slice appears grayish in some regions and whitish in others. Which combination of tissue composition explains the gray appearance specifically?
o: Predominantly myelinated axons, giving the whitish color from myelin
Densely packed collagen fibers, similar to a tendon
Neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, and neuroglia, with Nissl bodies imparting a gray color and little myelin present
Only cerebrospinal fluid, with no cellular content
questions.e: Gray matter's grayish appearance arises from its composition — neuronal cell bodies, dendrites, unmyelinated axons, and neuroglia — where Nissl (chromatophilic) bodies impart a gray color and there is little or no myelin present, unlike the myelin-rich white matter.

questions.q: All the following are bilateral organs EXCEPT?
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: A peripheral nerve is dissected in layers, from the innermost connective tissue wrapping a single axon, outward to a wrapping around a bundle of axons, and finally to the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve. In order from innermost to outermost, what are these three layers called?
questions.e: From innermost to outermost, a peripheral nerve's connective tissue layers are: the endoneurium (around a single axon), the perineurium (around a fascicle/bundle of axons), and the epineurium (the tough outer sheath around the whole nerve).

questions.q: A stroke damages CNS tissue, and astrocytes at the injury site respond by proliferating and forming dense scar tissue. What consequence does this astrocyte-driven scarring have for axon regrowth at the injury site?
o: It blocks axon regrowth and, along with released inhibitory chemicals, contributes to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after injury
It actively promotes and accelerates axon regrowth across the injury
It has no effect on axon regrowth whatsoever
It converts damaged axons directly into new, functional oligodendrocytes
questions.e: Astrocyte-produced scar tissue physically blocks axon regrowth across the injury site, and astrocytes also release chemicals that further inhibit regrowth — together contributing to the CNS's generally poor capacity for repair after significant injury.

questions.q: Roughly one to two days after a peripheral nerve injury, a neuron's Nissl bodies break up into fine granular masses, a process visible under the microscope. What is this specific early post-injury change called?
questions.e: Chromatolysis is the breakup of Nissl (chromatophilic) bodies into fine granular masses, occurring about 1-2 days after injury to a peripheral neuron's process — an early, specific post-injury change distinct from the later Wallerian degeneration of the distal axon segment.

questions.q: Following the same peripheral nerve injury, by around day 3 to 5, the distal segment of the severed axon (and its myelin) begins to break down, with macrophages clearing the resulting debris while the neurolemma remains intact. What is this later process called?
o: Gliosis, restricted to the CNS only
questions.e: Wallerian degeneration is the process by which the distal segment of an injured axon (and its myelin sheath) degenerates, typically occurring by the 3rd to 5th day post-injury, with macrophages phagocytizing the resulting debris while the neurolemma remains intact to guide eventual regrowth.

questions.q: After Wallerian degeneration clears the distal axon segment, Schwann cells on either side of the injury proliferate and form a guiding structure that a new axon can grow through, from the proximal stump toward its distal target. What is this guiding structure called?
questions.e: The regeneration tube, formed by proliferating Schwann cells on either side of the injury, provides the structural guide through which a new axon can grow from the proximal stump back toward its distal target.

questions.q: Two patients suffer similar-sized peripheral nerve injuries, but one has a very large gap at the injury site that becomes filled with collagen fibers before regeneration can occur, while the other has a small, clean gap. Which patient is predicted to have a poorer outcome for successful axon regrowth, and why?
o: Both patients would have identical outcomes regardless of gap size
The patient with the small, clean gap, since larger gaps always heal better
Neither patient's axons can ever regenerate under any circumstances
The patient with the large, collagen-filled gap, since axons will not regrow successfully if the gap is too large or becomes filled with collagen fibers
questions.e: New axons fail to regrow successfully across gaps that are too large, or that become filled with collagen fibers before regeneration can occur — predicting a poorer outcome for the patient with the large, collagen-filled gap compared to the one with a small, clean gap.

questions.q: A stroke patient shows significant functional recovery over months, attributed partly to the brain's capacity to sprout new dendrites and alter synaptic connections in response to rehabilitation therapy, despite limited neuron replacement. Which broad property of the nervous system underlies this kind of recovery?
questions.e: Neural plasticity refers to the nervous system's capacity to change based on experience — including sprouting new dendrites and altering synaptic contacts — providing a mechanism for functional recovery even when neuron replacement itself remains limited.

questions.q: Given that regenerating peripheral axons grow toward their distal targets at roughly 1.5 mm per day, approximately how long would you predict it might take an axon to regrow across a 3 cm gap, assuming ideal conditions (intact neurolemma, small gap)?
o: Regrowth speed is unrelated to distance
questions.e: At a rate of approximately 1.5 mm per day, regrowth across a 3 cm (30 mm) gap would be predicted to take roughly 20 days under otherwise ideal regenerative conditions.

questions.q: Which of the following best explains why glial cells vastly outnumber neurons yet receive comparatively less attention in basic descriptions of 'thinking' or signal transmission?
o: Glial cells cannot be found within the brain at all
Glial cells actually transmit all electrical signals, while neurons are purely structural

Glial cells outnumber neurons roughly 10 to 1 and make up about half of brain mass, but neurons — not glia — are the excitable cells specialized to transmit the electrical signals underlying nervous system communication
Neurons are outnumbered by glia by a factor of only 2 to 1, not 10 to 1
questions.e: Although glial cells outnumber neurons roughly 10 to 1 and comprise about half of brain mass, it is neurons — the excitable cells specialized for electrical signal transmission — that are typically emphasized in descriptions of nervous system communication, since glia serve primarily supportive rather than signal-transmitting roles.

questions.q: A physiology exam asks students to identify the CNS structures analogous to the PNS's ganglia and nerves. Which pairing is correct?
o: Ganglia and nerves exist only in the CNS, not the PNS
Nuclei and tracts are unrelated to ganglia and nerves
questions.e: The correct analogy is that CNS nuclei correspond to PNS ganglia (clusters of neuron cell bodies), while CNS tracts correspond to PNS nerves (bundles of neuron processes) — matching structure type across the two divisions.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the LEAST consistent finding with a diagnosis of multiple sclerosis, given that this disease specifically demyelinates CNS axons?
o: Progressive damage to myelin produced by oligodendrocytes
Damage strictly limited to Schwann-cell-produced myelin in peripheral nerves, sparing the CNS entirely
Variable neurological symptoms depending on which CNS tracts are affected
Slowed conduction velocity in affected CNS pathways
questions.e: Because multiple sclerosis is specifically a CNS demyelinating disease targeting oligodendrocyte-produced myelin, a presentation strictly limited to peripheral (Schwann-cell) myelin damage while sparing the CNS entirely would be the least consistent finding with this diagnosis.

questions.q: A student incorrectly states that 'all neurons have exactly the same shape.' Which observation from neuron classification most directly refutes this?
o: All neurons are technically classified as identical, so the statement is correct
Neurons are classified into distinct structural types — multipolar, bipolar, and unipolar — based on differing numbers of processes extending from the cell body
Only glial cells show shape variation; neurons are uniform
Neuron shape is determined solely by age, not by type
questions.e: The existence of distinct structural neuron types — multipolar (many dendrites, one axon), bipolar (one dendrite, one axon), and unipolar (a single process splitting into two branches) — directly refutes the claim that all neurons share exactly the same shape.

questions.q: Which best explains why a unipolar (pseudounipolar) sensory neuron is described as having started out bipolar during development?
o: Unipolar neurons begin development with two separate processes, which later fuse close to the cell body into what appears to be a single process splitting into peripheral and central branches
Unipolar neurons never actually change shape during development
Bipolar and unipolar neurons are entirely unrelated developmentally
Unipolar neurons develop directly from multipolar neurons by losing dendrites
questions.e: Unipolar (pseudounipolar) neurons begin development as bipolar cells with two separate processes, which subsequently fuse close to the cell body during development, producing the single process that then splits into peripheral and central branches characteristic of the mature unipolar neuron.

questions.q: Which of the following would be the best real-world illustration of an axodendritic synapse specifically, as opposed to other synapse types?
o: A dendrite synapsing directly onto another dendrite
An axon terminal of one neuron forming a synapse onto a dendrite of a second neuron, the most statistically common arrangement in the nervous system
Two axons synapsing directly onto each other with no dendrite involved
A motor neuron synapsing directly onto a skeletal muscle fiber
questions.e: An axon terminal from one neuron synapsing onto the dendrite of a second neuron is the defining pattern of an axodendritic synapse, and this is also the most statistically common synapse type in the nervous system — distinguishing it from axoaxonic, dendrodendritic, or neuromuscular junction examples.

questions.q: Which combination of features would you expect to observe if a researcher successfully isolated and examined a genuine multipolar neuron under the microscope?
o: No axon at all, only dendrites
Numerous dendrites and a single axon
Exactly one dendrite and one axon
questions.e: A multipolar neuron is defined by having numerous dendrites together with a single axon — this is the structural pattern that would be observed, and it represents the most common neuron type overall.

questions.q: A patient has a lesion that selectively destroys interneurons within a specific spinal reflex circuit, while leaving the sensory and motor neurons of that circuit intact. What would you predict about the reflex's ability to function?
o: Only the sensory portion of the reflex would be affected, with motor output entirely unaffected
The reflex would function completely normally, since interneurons are not involved in any reflex circuits
The reflex would likely be disrupted or altered, since interneurons provide the integrative link between the sensory input and motor output within the circuit
Destroying interneurons would have no measurable effect on any neural circuit
questions.e: Because interneurons provide the integrative connection between sensory input and motor output within a reflex circuit (and make up the vast majority of neurons overall), their selective destruction would be expected to disrupt or alter the reflex, even with sensory and motor neurons themselves intact.

questions.q: Which of the following would most strongly suggest, on a nerve biopsy, that microglia (rather than macrophages from elsewhere in the body) are responsible for clearing debris at a site of CNS injury?
o: The clearing cells are found exclusively in peripheral nerves, never in the CNS
The clearing cells are confined to the CNS and are of a lineage related to blood-derived monocytes, appearing early in embryonic development as resident phagocytes
The clearing cells produce myelin rather than performing phagocytosis
The clearing cells are neurons, not glia
questions.e: Microglia are specifically the CNS's resident phagocytes, derived from blood-related monocyte lineage but established early in embryonic development and confined to the CNS — distinguishing their role from peripheral macrophages or other glial cell types with different functions.

questions.q: Which best summarizes the overall functional division of labor between neurons and neuroglia in the nervous system?
o: Neuroglia transmit all electrical signals, while neurons provide only structural support
Neurons and neuroglia perform identical functions with complete redundancy
Neither cell type has any specialized function
Neurons are the excitable, signal-transmitting cells; neuroglia are nonexcitable cells that support, protect, nourish, and insulate neurons, among other roles
questions.e: The fundamental division of labor is that neurons are the excitable cells specialized for transmitting electrical signals, while neuroglia are nonexcitable supporting cells that nourish, protect, insulate, and otherwise support neurons in their signaling role.

questions.q: A researcher wants to specifically block new cerebrospinal fluid production without affecting neuron signaling or myelin formation. Which glial cell type's function should be targeted?
questions.e: Since ependymal cells help form the choroid plexuses responsible for secreting cerebrospinal fluid, targeting their function specifically would block CSF production without directly affecting oligodendrocyte-mediated myelination or Schwann cell function in the PNS.

questions.q: Which best explains why damage limited to peripheral nerve myelin (Schwann-cell-derived) generally carries a better prognosis for recovery than comparable damage to CNS myelin (oligodendrocyte-derived)?
o: There is no difference in prognosis between PNS and CNS demyelination
PNS neurons cannot be remyelinated under any circumstances, unlike CNS neurons
CNS myelin regenerates faster than PNS myelin in all cases
PNS axons associated with an intact neurolemma can regenerate under favorable conditions, whereas CNS repair is generally limited by astrocyte scarring and inhibitory chemical signals
questions.e: The generally better prognosis for peripheral nerve damage reflects the PNS's capacity for axon regrowth guided by an intact neurolemma under favorable conditions, in contrast to the CNS, where repair is typically limited by astrocyte-produced scar tissue and inhibitory chemical signals that block regrowth.

questions.q: A textbook diagram labels a neuron's telodendria at the very tip of its longest process. Which process is being illustrated, and what do the telodendria lead to?
o: A node of Ranvier; telodendria are gaps in the myelin sheath
The axon; the telodendria are its terminal branches, ending in axon terminals
A dendrite; the telodendria are branches leading back to the cell body
The axon hillock; telodendria mark where the axon originates
questions.e: Telodendria are the terminal branches found at the very end of an axon (not a dendrite), and these branches lead to the axon terminals (synaptic boutons), where synaptic vesicles release neurotransmitter.

questions.q: The ovaries are suspended in the broad ligament of the uterus by an attachment called the:
questions.e: The ovaries are suspended by the mesovarium, a special fold of peritoneum that conveys blood vessels to the ovaries.

questions.q: Each ovary weighs approximately:
questions.e: Each ovary is an almond-shaped body about 3 cm long, weighing approximately 14 g.

questions.q: The ovary is covered by which epithelium?
questions.e: The ovary is covered by the germinal epithelium, which is simple cuboidal or squamous.

questions.q: The fibrous capsule of the ovary, composed of dense irregular collagenous connective tissue, is called the:
questions.e: Beneath the germinal epithelium lies the tunica albuginea, a fibrous capsule of dense irregular collagenous connective tissue.

questions.q: The ovary is divided into which two regions?
questions.e: The ovary is divided into the cortex (containing follicles at various stages) and the medulla (loose CT, large vessels, lymphatics, nerves).

questions.q: The production of ova/gametes in the ovary is called:
questions.e: The production of gametes in the ovary is called oogenesis; developing gametes are oocytes, mature gametes are ova.

questions.q: Which hormone is primarily responsible for growth and maturation of internal/external sex organs and female secondary sex characteristics?
questions.e: Estrogens drive growth and maturation of the sex organs and are responsible for the female secondary sex characteristics that develop at puberty.

questions.q: Which hormone prepares the uterus for pregnancy and the mammary gland for lactation via lobular proliferation?
questions.e: Progesterone prepares the uterus for pregnancy and promotes lobular proliferation in the mammary gland in preparation for lactation.

questions.q: At approximately 3 months' gestation, a fetal ovary contains about how many primordial oocytes?
questions.e: The fetal ovary at 3 months contains approximately 5 million primordial oocytes.

questions.q: Approximately how many primordial oocytes remain present at birth?
questions.e: Of the ~5 million primordial oocytes present at 3 months' gestation, approximately 1 million remain at birth after atresia begins.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the female reproductive system
o: Production of ova and hormones and elimination of nitrogenous waste products
Provision of a site for fertilization and implantation
Nourishment and development of the preimplantation embryo
Only B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The earliest stage of follicular development, first appearing during the 3rd month of fetal development, is the:
questions.e: The primordial follicle is the earliest stage, appearing during the 3rd month of fetal development, found beneath the tunica albuginea.

questions.q: A primordial follicle consists of an oocyte surrounded by:
o: A single layer of squamous follicle cells
questions.e: The primordial follicle has a single layer of squamous follicle cells surrounding a large oocyte with a prominent nucleolus.

questions.q: A follicle is identified as a primary (unilaminar) follicle once the follicle cells become:
questions.e: As the primordial follicle develops, its squamous follicle cells proliferate and become cuboidal, marking the primary unilaminar stage.

questions.q: The zona pellucida is best described as:
o: A blood clot within the antrum
A layer of smooth muscle around the follicle
The outer connective tissue capsule of the ovary
An extracellular glycoprotein coat around the oocyte
questions.e: As the oocyte grows, it secretes glycoproteins that assemble into the zona pellucida, an extracellular coat between the oocyte and adjacent follicle cells.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein permits sperm binding and triggers the acrosome reaction?
questions.e: ZP3 permits the binding of spermatozoa and facilitates the acrosome reaction.

questions.q: After fertilization, which enzyme is secreted by the ovum to degrade ZP2 and prevent polyspermy?
questions.e: After fertilization, the ovum secretes ovastacin, which degrades ZP2, preventing further sperm binding to the zona pellucida.

questions.q: In a late primary (multilaminar) follicle, connective tissue cells surrounding the follicle form the:
questions.e: Stromal cells immediately surrounding the follicle form the theca folliculi, a sheath of connective tissue external to the basal lamina.

questions.q: Which layer of the theca folliculi is highly vascularized, contains cuboidal secretory cells with LH receptors, and synthesizes androgens in response to LH?
questions.e: The theca interna is highly vascularized, rich in LH receptors, and its cells synthesize and secrete androgens (precursors of estrogen) in response to LH stimulation.

questions.q: The theca externa is composed mainly of:
questions.e: The theca externa is the outer connective tissue layer, containing mainly smooth muscle cells and bundles of collagen fibers.

questions.q: In response to FSH, granulosa cells convert theca-derived androgens into:
questions.e: Androgens transported to the granulosa cells' smooth endoplasmic reticulum are converted to estrogens under FSH stimulation, which in turn stimulates granulosa cell proliferation.

questions.q: A secondary (antral) follicle is distinguished from a primary follicle mainly by the presence of:
o: A single layer of squamous cells
questions.e: The secondary (antral) follicle is characterized by a fluid-containing antrum, which forms once the granulosa layer reaches 6–12 cell layers.

questions.q: Ovulation occurs in direct response to:
questions.e: Ovulation occurs in response to the LH surge, causing release of the secondary oocyte and its corona radiata cells from the ruptured follicle.

questions.q: Immediately after ovulation, the remnant of the Graafian follicle becomes the:
questions.e: The remnant of the ruptured Graafian follicle first becomes the corpus hemorrhagicum, which is then transformed into the corpus luteum.

questions.q: In the corpus hemorrhagicum, which cells dispose of the blood clot and cellular debris before conversion to the corpus luteum?
questions.e: Macrophages, along with connective tissue elements, enter the region and dispose of the blood clot and cellular debris in the corpus hemorrhagicum.

questions.q: The process by which granulosa and theca interna cells differentiate into granulosa luteal and theca luteal cells is called:
questions.e: Luteinization is the process by which granulosa and theca interna cells differentiate into granulosa luteal and theca luteal cells during corpus luteum formation.

questions.q: During luteinization, luteal cells undergo dramatic morphologic change, notably:
o: Enlarging and filling with lipid droplets
questions.e: Luteal cells increase in size and fill with lipid droplets, showing features typical of steroid-secreting cells.

questions.q: The corpus luteum, a highly vascularized structure in the ovarian cortex, mainly secretes:
questions.e: The corpus luteum secretes progesterone (which prepares the uterus for pregnancy) and estrogens.

questions.q: If fertilization and implantation do not occur, the corpus luteum of menstruation remains functional for about:
questions.e: Without fertilization/implantation, the corpus luteum of menstruation remains active for only about 14 days before degenerating.

questions.q: The white scar left after the corpus luteum degenerates is called the:
questions.e: After degeneration and autolysis of the luteal cells, a white scar called the corpus albicans forms and slowly sinks deeper into the ovarian cortex over months.

questions.q: In pregnancy, which hormone from the syncytiotrophoblast maintains the corpus luteum for about the first 3 months?
questions.e: hCG, produced by the syncytiotrophoblast of the developing placenta, maintains the corpus luteum of pregnancy for about 3 months, after which the placenta takes over hormone production.

questions.q: Which luteal hormone facilitates parturition?
questions.e: Relaxin, one of the hormones secreted by the corpus luteum, facilitates parturition.

questions.q: The uterine (fallopian) tubes are located at the upper free border of which structure?
questions.e: The uterine tubes are located at the upper free border of the broad ligament, in a portion called the mesosalpinx.

questions.q: Which part of the uterine tube is the longest and widest, and the usual site of fertilization?
questions.e: The ampulla (about 5 cm) is the longest and widest part of the uterine tube, following a tortuous course, and is the usual site of fertilization.

questions.q: Which part of the uterine tube bears the finger-like fimbriae that sweep the ovarian surface?
questions.e: The infundibulum is the lateral, expanded part with an abdominal opening surrounded by fimbriae, which sweep the ovarian surface to facilitate ovum entry.

questions.q: Which part of the uterine tube is embedded within the uterine wall and opens into the uterine cavity?
questions.e: The intramural/interstitial portion (about 1 cm) is embedded in the uterine wall and opens into the uterus at the superior-lateral angles.

questions.q: The medial 2/3 of the uterine tube receives its blood supply from the:
questions.e: The medial 2/3 of the fallopian tube is supplied by the uterine artery, a branch of the internal iliac artery.

questions.q: The lateral 1/3 of the uterine tube receives its blood supply from the:
questions.e: The lateral 1/3 of the fallopian tube is supplied by the ovarian artery, which arises from the abdominal aorta.

questions.q: The wall of the uterine tube consists of which three coats?
questions.e: The uterine tube wall has three coats: mucosa, muscularis, and serosa/visceral peritoneum.

questions.q: The mucosal secretory cells of the uterine tube that nourish spermatozoa and the preimplantation embryo are called:
questions.e: Peg cells are secretory cells of the tubal mucosa that secrete a nutrient-rich medium nourishing spermatozoa and the preimplantation embryo.

questions.q: Which hormone increases the number of peg cells in the uterine tube mucosa, making them predominant during the luteal phase?
questions.e: Progesterone increases the number of peg cells, which predominate during the luteal (secretory) phase.

questions.q: Which hormone increases the number and ciliary motion of ciliated cells in the uterine tube, making them numerous during the follicular phase?
questions.e: Estrogen increases the number of cilia and the intensity of their motion; ciliated cells are therefore numerous during the follicular phase, when epithelial height is also greatest.

questions.q: In nulliparous women, the uterus typically measures approximately:
questions.e: In nulliparous women, the uterus measures approximately 8 x 5 x 3 cm and weighs 30–50 g.

questions.q: Which part of the uterus is the rounded superior portion above the entrance of the uterine tubes, and the usual site of implantation?
questions.e: The fundus is the rounded superior portion of the uterus above the tubal openings, and is the usual site of implantation.

questions.q: The constricted part of the uterus between the body and the cervix, corresponding to the internal os, is the:
questions.e: The isthmus is the constricted part of the uterus between the body and the cervix, corresponding to the internal os.

questions.q: "Anteflexed" describes a uterine position in which:
o: The cervix tilts forward relative to the vaginal axis
The body of the uterus tilts forward relative to the cervix
questions.e: Anteflexion (120–170°) describes the body of the uterus tilting forward relative to the cervix, as distinct from anteversion (the cervix tilting forward relative to the vagina).

questions.q: The muscular system:
o: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Which ligament extends from the lateral aspect of the cervix and upper vagina to the lateral pelvic wall and prevents downward displacement of the uterus?
questions.e: The cardinal (transverse cervical, or Mackenrodt's) ligament extends from the cervix/upper vagina to the lateral pelvic wall and prevents downward uterine displacement.

questions.q: Listed from outer to inner, the layers of the uterine wall are:
questions.e: From outer to inner, the uterine wall layers are: perimetrium (visceral peritoneum), myometrium (smooth muscle), and endometrium (mucosal lining).

questions.q: The myometrium's middle circular layer is notable for being:
questions.e: The thick middle circular layer of the myometrium is richly vascularized, and is known as the stratum vasculare.

questions.q: Near the end of pregnancy, the myometrium develops numerous gap junctions between smooth muscle cells in order to:
questions.e: Gap junctions that develop late in pregnancy coordinate contraction of the myometrial smooth muscle cells during parturition.

questions.q: Contractions of the myometrium at parturition are triggered mainly by:
o: FSH and LH from the pituitary
questions.e: At parturition, the myometrium undergoes powerful contractions triggered by oxytocin and prostaglandins.

questions.q: The endometrium is lined by which type of epithelium?
questions.e: The endometrium is lined by a simple columnar epithelium containing both secretory and ciliated cells.

questions.q: Which endometrial layer is thick, superficial, and sloughed and rebuilt monthly?
questions.e: The stratum functionalis (functional layer) is the thick superficial layer sloughed and reestablished monthly under hormonal control.

questions.q: Which endometrial layer is preserved during menstruation and contains glands for re-epithelialization?
questions.e: The stratum basalis (basal layer), about 1 mm or less thick, is preserved during menstruation and contains glands that re-epithelialize the endometrium after the functional layer sheds.

questions.q: Which arteries supply the stratum functionalis and undergo cyclic changes during the menstrual cycle?
questions.e: Spiral (coiled) arteries supply the stratum functionalis and undergo cyclic changes throughout the menstrual cycle.

questions.q: The menstrual cycle begins on:
o: The last day of the secretory phase
The first day of blood flow
The day the corpus luteum forms
questions.e: The menstrual cycle begins on the day of the first blood flow (day 1 of the menstrual phase).

questions.q: During the menstrual phase (days 1–5), blood levels of estrogen, progesterone, FSH, and LH are:
o: Unchanged from the secretory phase peak
questions.e: At the start of the menstrual phase, blood levels of estrogen, progesterone, FSH, and LH are all very low.

questions.q: The menstrual phase is triggered by spasms of contraction and relaxation of which vessels?
questions.e: Menstruation is triggered by spasms of contraction and relaxation of the coiled (spiral) arteries, leading to ischemia, necrosis, and eventually rupture with hemorrhage.

questions.q: In a 28-day cycle, the proliferative (follicular) phase of the uterine cycle runs approximately from:
questions.e: The proliferative phase runs from about day 5 to day 15, continuing until 1 day after ovulation (day 14 in a 28-day cycle).

questions.q: Which hormone is the principal driver of the proliferative phase of the endometrium?
questions.e: Rising blood levels of estrogen are the principal hormonal driver responsible for the endometrial proliferative phase.

questions.q: At the end of the proliferative phase, the endometrium is approximately how thick?
questions.e: By the end of the proliferative phase, the endometrium is approximately 3 mm thick.

questions.q: During the proliferative phase, the endometrial glands are described as:
o: Straight, simple columnar, with a narrow lumen
questions.e: During the proliferative phase, glands are straight and lined by simple columnar epithelium with a narrow lumen.

questions.q: The secretory (luteal) phase of the uterine cycle is regulated mainly by:
questions.e: The secretory phase, characterized by endometrial thickening from edema and glandular secretion, is regulated by progesterone.

questions.q: At the end of the secretory phase, the endometrium is approximately how thick?
questions.e: By the end of the secretory phase, the endometrium is somewhat edematous and approximately 6–7 mm thick.

questions.q: During the secretory phase, endometrial glands become:
o: Coiled, with lumina filled with glycogen secretion
questions.e: In the secretory phase, glands become coiled and their lumina fill with a glycogen-rich secretion.

questions.q: In the ovarian cycle (usually 28 days), the follicular phase, driven by FSH, spans approximately:
questions.e: In the ovarian cycle, FSH begins development of the follicle during the follicular phase, spanning approximately days 1–13.

questions.q: Ovulation, caused by the LH surge, typically occurs on which day of a standard 28-day ovarian cycle?
questions.e: Ovulation, caused by the LH surge, occurs on day 14 of a standard 28-day ovarian cycle.

questions.q: Which phase of the ovarian cycle is more constant in length — the follicular phase or the luteal phase?
questions.e: The luteal phase (approximately 14 days) is more constant in length than the follicular phase, which varies more between cycles and individuals.

questions.q: The length of the menstrual cycle is calculated as:
questions.e: Length of the menstrual cycle = Follicular Phase (FP) + Luteal Phase (LP).

questions.q: The cervix differs from the rest of the uterus in that it:
o: Sheds its epithelium monthly like the endometrium
Is not involved in menstruation and lacks spiral arteries
Is directly involved in menstruation and has spiral arteries
questions.e: The cervix is not involved in menstruation and lacks the spiral arteries characteristic of the endometrium.

questions.q: The endocervical canal is lined by which epithelium?
questions.e: The endocervical canal has a simple columnar, mucus-secreting epithelium interspersed with ciliated cells.

questions.q: The inferior portion of the cervix, continuous with the vaginal lining, is covered by:
questions.e: The inferior portion of the cervix, continuous with the vaginal lining, is covered by stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium.

questions.q: Cervical mucus secretion increases by roughly how much near the time of ovulation?
questions.e: Branched cervical glands secrete a voluminous secretion — about a 10-fold increase near the time of ovulation — facilitating sperm entry.

questions.q: During pregnancy, cervical glands produce a secretion that is:
o: Thick and viscous, hindering sperm entry
questions.e: During pregnancy, cervical secretion becomes thick and viscous, hindering the entry of spermatozoa and microbes into the uterus.

questions.q: Prior to parturition, the cervix dilates and softens due to lysis of collagen fibers in response to which hormone?
questions.e: Prior to parturition, relaxin causes lysis of collagen fiber bundles in the cervix, leading to dilation and softening.

questions.q: The vaginal mucosa is lined by which epithelium?
questions.e: The vaginal mucosa has a stratified squamous non-keratinized epithelium overlying a fibroelastic lamina propria.

questions.q: Vaginal epithelial cells accumulate glycogen under the influence of which hormone, greatest at ovulation?
questions.e: Estrogen (during the follicular phase) drives glycogen accumulation in vaginal epithelium, greatest around the time of ovulation.

questions.q: Vaginal bacteria use glycogen to produce lactic acid, giving the vagina a normal pH of approximately:
questions.e: Bacterial metabolism of glycogen to lactic acid lowers the vaginal pH to about 3.5–4.0, which inhibits pathogen invasion.

questions.q: The vagina, unlike most tubular organs, lacks:
questions.e: The vagina lacks glands throughout its length; lubrication is provided by cervical secretion instead.

questions.q: The recess between the cervix and vaginal wall, of which the posterior portion is the deepest and acts as a semen reservoir, is the:
questions.e: The fornix is the recess between the cervix and vaginal wall; the posterior fornix is the deepest and acts as a natural semen reservoir after ejaculation.

questions.q: The lower one-third of the vagina, including the region of the vaginal orifice, is supplied by which nerve for touch sensitivity?
questions.e: The lower 1/3 of the vagina is extremely sensitive to touch and is supplied by the pudendal nerve, via the inferior rectal and posterior labial branches.

questions.q: The external genitalia (vulva/pudendum) includes all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: The vulva consists of the mons pubis, labia majora, labia minora, clitoris, vestibule, vestibular bulb, and greater vestibular glands. The corpus luteum is part of the ovary, not the external genitalia.

questions.q: The mons pubis overlies the pubic symphysis and, after puberty, is covered by pubic hair; it primarily contains:
questions.e: The mons pubis overlies the pubic symphysis and contains adipose tissue, covered by pubic hair after puberty.

questions.q: The labia majora are homologous to which male structure?
questions.e: The labia majora are the homologue of the male scrotum, containing adipose tissue and large sebaceous follicles.

questions.q: The space between the labia majora is called the:
questions.e: The space between the labia majora is called the pudendal cleft.

questions.q: The vestibule, bounded by the labia minora, contains the openings of all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: The vestibule contains the openings of the vagina, external urethra, greater vestibular glands, and para-urethral glands. Lactiferous ducts belong to the breast, not the vulva.

questions.q: The clitoris is erectile tissue homologous to the penis, and is divided into which three parts?
questions.e: The clitoris is divided into the glans, body (two corpora cavernosa), and crura, and is hooded by a fold of skin called the prepuce.

questions.q: Para-urethral (Skene's) glands are homologous to which male structure and discharge near the urethral opening for lubrication and antimicrobial protection?
questions.e: Skene's (para-urethral) glands are homologous to the male prostate gland; they discharge into the urethra near its external opening, lubricating it and protecting against UTIs.

questions.q: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands are homologous to which male structure?
questions.e: The greater vestibular (Bartholin's) glands are homologous to the bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands in the male.

questions.q: The ducts of the Bartholin's glands typically open into the vestibule at approximately which clock positions?
questions.e: The ducts of the Bartholin's glands normally open at approximately 5 and 7 o'clock in the vestibule, between the labium minora and the hymen.

questions.q: The bulbs of the vestibule are erectile tissue equivalent to which structure in the male?
questions.e: The bulbs of the vestibule are two masses of erectile tissue equivalent to the corpus spongiosum of the male, located around the vaginal opening.

questions.q: The mammary gland is best described developmentally as a modified:
questions.e: The mammary gland is a modified sweat gland, located in the subcutaneous tissue over pectoralis major and serratus anterior.

questions.q: The dorsal cavity is lined with a three-membrane layer called?
o: A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Approximately 50% of breast cancers occur in which quadrant?
questions.e: About 50% of breast cancer cases occur in the upper lateral quadrant, which includes the axillary tail extending toward the axilla.

questions.q: Each lobe of the mammary gland opens onto the nipple via a duct that enlarges into a reservoir for milk called the:
questions.e: Each lactiferous duct enlarges near the nipple to form a lactiferous sinus, which serves as a reservoir for milk during lactation.

questions.q: The fibrous bands connecting the dermis of the skin to the deep fascia through the breast, which help maintain its shape in youth, are the:
questions.e: Cooper's (suspensory) ligaments are fibrous strands connecting the dermis to the deep fascia through the breast; with age-related atrophy they loosen, allowing the breast to become pendulous.

questions.q: The areolar glands (glands of Montgomery) are a type of:
questions.e: Glands of Montgomery are sebaceous glands in the areola that produce oily secretions to lubricate and protect the nipple/areola, minimizing cracking during nursing.

questions.q: The breast receives most of its blood supply from which artery?
questions.e: The breast receives blood mainly from the lateral thoracic artery, along with contributions from the internal thoracic, posterior intercostal, and thoracoacromial arteries.

questions.q: During late pregnancy, glandular epithelium prepares for lactation; which cells surround the enlarging alveoli?
questions.e: Myoepithelial cells surround the alveoli of the mammary gland as they enlarge and prepare for lactation in late pregnancy.

questions.q: Failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum is called:
questions.e: Cryptorchidism is the failure of one or both testes to descend into the scrotum.

questions.q: The functions of the cardiovascular system:
o: Transport of oxygen and carbon dioxide
Transport of nutrients and waste products
Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
A, B, C are all functions of the cardiovascular system
Only A and B are functions of the cardiovascular system
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Each testis is surrounded by a thick, dense connective tissue capsule called the:
questions.e: The tunica albuginea is the thick, dense CT capsule surrounding each testis.

questions.q: The loose connective tissue layer lying anterolaterally, inner to the tunica albuginea, is the:
questions.e: The tunica vasculosa is the inner loose connective tissue layer lying anterolaterally.

questions.q: Posteriorly, the tunica albuginea thickens and projects inward as the:
questions.e: Posteriorly, the tunica albuginea thickens and projects inward as the mediastinum testis.

questions.q: Each testis is divided by incomplete connective tissue septa into approximately how many lobules?
questions.e: Each testis is divided into approximately 250 lobules by incomplete CT septa projecting from the capsule.

questions.q: Each testicular lobule typically contains how many seminiferous tubules?
questions.e: Each lobule of the testis consists of one to four seminiferous tubules, plus a connective tissue stroma containing Leydig cells.

questions.q: A seminiferous tubule is typically how long?
questions.e: A seminiferous tubule is 30 to 70 cm long, with a diameter of 150 to 250 µm.

questions.q: The seminiferous tubule is surrounded by which layer of peritubular tissue?
questions.e: The seminiferous tubule is surrounded by the tunica (lamina) propria, also called peritubular tissue.

questions.q: The tunica propria contains 3 to 5 layers of contractile cells called:
questions.e: The tunica propria is multilayered connective tissue containing 3 to 5 layers of myoid cells, flattened contractile peritubular cells.

questions.q: Myoid cells of the tunica propria secrete which of the following?
questions.e: Myoid cells secrete the external lamina and fibrillar collagen of the tunica propria.

questions.q: The germinal (seminiferous) epithelium contains which two populations of cells?
o: Leydig cells and myoid cells only
questions.e: The seminiferous epithelium contains proliferating spermatogenic (germ) cells and non-proliferating supporting (Sertoli) cells.

questions.q: Within the seminiferous epithelium, which spermatogenic cells are the most immature and rest on the basal lamina?
questions.e: Spermatogonia are the most immature spermatogenic cells and rest on the basal lamina of the seminiferous epithelium.

questions.q: Which spermatogenic cells are the most mature, attached to the apical Sertoli cell surface bordering the lumen?
questions.e: Spermatids are the most mature spermatogenic cells present, attached to the apical portion of the Sertoli cell near the tubule lumen.

questions.q: Sertoli cells are best described morphologically as:
o: Flattened squamous cells with flat nuclei
Cuboidal cells with dense, dark nuclei
Round cells lacking a visible nucleolus
questions.e: Sertoli cells are slender, elongated cells with an oval nucleus and a dark nucleolus, extending from the basement membrane to the tubule lumen.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of Sertoli cells?
o: Support, protect, and nourish developing sperm
Release mature sperm into the tubule lumen
questions.e: Sertoli cells support, phagocytose residual bodies, and release mature sperm — but testosterone is produced by Leydig cells, not Sertoli cells.

questions.q: Sertoli cells synthesize androgen-binding protein (ABP), which functions to:
o: Bind LH receptors on Leydig cells
Decrease FSH production by the pituitary
questions.e: Androgen-binding protein (ABP), synthesized by Sertoli cells, keeps testosterone levels high within the seminiferous tubules.

questions.q: Which hormone, secreted by Sertoli cells, decreases FSH production by the anterior pituitary?
questions.e: Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which decreases follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) production in the anterior pituitary.

questions.q: Sertoli cells no longer undergo mitosis after which life stage?
questions.e: Sertoli cells are columnar, extend from the basal lamina to the lumen, and no longer undergo mitosis after puberty.

questions.q: The blood-testis barrier is formed by which structures between adjacent Sertoli cells?
questions.e: Interdigitating Sertoli cell processes form tight junctions (zonulae occludentes) near their bases, which constitute the blood-testis barrier.

questions.q: The blood-testis barrier divides the seminiferous tubule lumen into which two compartments?
questions.e: The tight junctions of the blood-testis barrier divide the tubule into a basal compartment and an adluminal compartment.

questions.q: Which cells are restricted to the basal compartment of the seminiferous tubule?
o: Sertoli cells and Leydig cells only
questions.e: Spermatogonia and early primary spermatocytes are restricted to the basal compartment, outside the blood-testis barrier.

questions.q: Which cells are restricted to the adluminal compartment of the seminiferous tubule?
o: Spermatogonia resting on the basal lamina
questions.e: More mature spermatocytes and spermatids are restricted to the adluminal compartment, protected by the blood-testis barrier.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the lymphatic system
o: Body immunity and filtration of lymph
Absorption of fats and collection of cellular debris
Drainage of tissue fluid and production of lymphocytes
Only A and C are correct
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Sperm-specific antibodies are sometimes seen clinically after which procedure, due to breakdown of BTB isolation?
questions.e: After vasectomy, sperm-specific antibodies may be produced as immune cells become exposed to spermatozoa leaking from the cut ductus deferens.

questions.q: Leydig (interstitial) cells produce testosterone in direct response to which pituitary hormone?
questions.e: Leydig cells are endocrine cells that produce testosterone in response to luteinizing hormone (LH) released by the pituitary gland.

questions.q: Spermatogenesis is initiated shortly before puberty by:
questions.e: A rise in gonadotropins shortly before puberty initiates spermatogenesis.

questions.q: Spermatogenesis is divided into which three phases, in order?
questions.e: Spermatogenesis proceeds through spermatocytogenesis (spermatogonial phase), then meiosis (spermatocyte phase), then spermiogenesis (spermatid phase).

questions.q: Spermatocytogenesis refers to:
o: Capacitation of sperm in the female tract
questions.e: Spermatocytogenesis is the spermatogonial phase — differentiation of spermatogonia into primary spermatocytes via mitosis.

questions.q: The meiotic (spermatocyte) phase of spermatogenesis reduces the diploid chromosomal complement of primary spermatocytes to form:
questions.e: Meiosis reduces the diploid complement of primary spermatocytes, forming haploid spermatids via Meiosis I and Meiosis II.

questions.q: Spermiogenesis (spermatid phase) refers to the:
o: Storage of sperm in the epididymis
questions.e: Spermiogenesis is the process of cytodifferentiation that transforms spermatids into spermatozoa.

questions.q: Which subtype of spermatogonia is mitotically inactive and serves as a reserve population with dark-staining nuclei?
questions.e: Dark type A spermatogonia are reserve spermatogonial stem cells with dark nuclei that do not usually undergo active mitosis.

questions.q: Which subtype of spermatogonia is mitotically active starting at puberty and gives rise to more of its own type plus type B cells?
questions.e: Pale type A spermatogonia have a pale-staining nucleus, are mitotically active from puberty, and give rise to more pale type A cells and type B spermatogonia.

questions.q: Which subtype of spermatogonia undergoes mitosis to directly give rise to primary spermatocytes?
questions.e: Type B spermatogonia undergo mitosis to give rise to primary spermatocytes.

questions.q: The spermatogonial stem cell (type A spermatogonium) is unique in that it:
o: It differentiates into a Sertoli cell
It immediately undergoes the first meiotic division
Always differentiates directly into a spermatocyte
It can divide or stay dormant as a reserve
questions.e: The spermatogonial stem cell does not differentiate into a spermatocyte; instead it continues dividing into other spermatogonia or remains dormant, maintaining a reserve population.

questions.q: Primary spermatocytes are:
o: Small haploid cells lying near the lumen
Large diploid cells undergoing meiosis I
Precursors of the Sertoli cell population
Non-motile mature sperm in the lumen
questions.e: Primary spermatocytes are large diploid cells that undergo the first (reductional) meiotic division to form secondary spermatocytes.

questions.q: Secondary spermatocytes are haploid cells that:
o: Directly become spermatozoa without further division
Undergo mitosis to form more secondary spermatocytes
Quickly undergo the 2nd meiotic division to form spermatids
questions.e: Secondary spermatocytes are haploid and quickly undergo the second meiotic division to form spermatids.

questions.q: Spermatogenesis, from spermatogonium to mature spermatozoon release, takes approximately:
questions.e: Spermatogenesis takes 65–75 days, occurring at different times in different regions of the testis to ensure even, continuous sperm production.

questions.q: Spermatogenesis proceeds in the testis via wavelike sequences of maturation known as:
o: Repeating cycles of the ovarian follicle
questions.e: Spermatogenesis does not occur simultaneously throughout all tubules but rather in wavelike sequences called cycles of the seminiferous epithelium.

questions.q: In the Golgi phase of spermiogenesis, granules accumulate in the Golgi complex to form the:
questions.e: In the Golgi phase, granules accumulate in the spermatid's Golgi complexes, forming an acrosomal granule enclosed within an acrosomal vesicle.

questions.q: During the Golgi phase, centrioles migrate to the posterior pole of the spermatid to form the:
questions.e: Centrioles migrate from the juxtanuclear region to the posterior pole of the spermatid to form the flagellar axoneme.

questions.q: In the cap phase of spermiogenesis, the acrosomal vesicle expands over much of the nucleus to form the:
questions.e: The cap phase is characterized by expansion of the acrosomal vesicle over much of the nucleus, forming the acrosomal cap.

questions.q: During the acrosomal phase, mitochondria aggregate around the proximal flagellum to form the:
questions.e: In the acrosomal phase, mitochondria aggregate around the proximal portion of the flagellum, which develops into the middle piece of the tail.

questions.q: The temporary cylinder of microtubules that aids elongation of the spermatid during the acrosomal phase is the:
questions.e: The manchette is a temporary cylinder of microtubules that aids spermatid elongation during the acrosomal phase.

questions.q: During the maturation phase of spermiogenesis, discarded excess cytoplasm from spermatids is disposed of by:
o: Being expelled directly into the bloodstream
questions.e: The discarded excess cytoplasm shed during the maturation phase is phagocytosed by Sertoli cells.

questions.q: At the end of the maturation phase, spermatozoa are released into the tubule lumen in which orientation, and in what motility state?
questions.e: The maturation phase ends with nonmotile spermatozoa released tail first into the lumen of the seminiferous tubule.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as an intratesticular duct?
questions.e: The intratesticular ducts are the straight tubules (tubuli recti), the rete testis, and the proximal portion of the efferent ductules.

questions.q: Which of the following is classified as an extratesticular duct?
questions.e: Extratesticular ducts include the distal portion of the efferent ductules, ductus epididymis, ductus (vas) deferens, ejaculatory ducts, and urethra.

questions.q: In the straight tubules (tubuli recti), the proximal half is lined by which cell type?
questions.e: The proximal half of the straight tubules is lined by Sertoli cells; the distal half is lined by cuboidal cells.

questions.q: Which structures are devoid of spermatogenic cells and lack smooth muscle in their wall?
o: The ductus deferens and its ampulla
The seminal vesicle and its duct
questions.e: Both the straight tubules and the rete testis are devoid of spermatogenic cells and have no smooth muscle.

questions.q: The rete testis is located within the:
questions.e: The rete testis is an irregular, anastomosing network of tubules located within the mediastinum testis.

questions.q: The epithelium of the rete testis is:
questions.e: The rete testis has a simple cuboidal epithelium with microvilli as well as a single luminal flagellum (cilium).

questions.q: The efferent ductules (ductuli efferentes) have a characteristic luminal margin described as:
questions.e: Efferent ductules have a saw-toothed luminal margin, produced by alternating tall ciliated columnar and short unciliated cuboidal cells.

questions.q: In the efferent ductules, non-ciliated cuboidal cells function mainly to:
questions.e: Non-ciliated cells of the efferent ductules reabsorb testicular fluid, while the ciliated cells propel the still-immobile sperm toward the epididymis.

questions.q: The epithelium of the ductus epididymis is best described as:
o: Pseudostratified ciliated columnar with goblet cells
questions.e: The ductus epididymis has a pseudostratified columnar stereociliated (non-motile) epithelium.

questions.q: Within the ductus epididymis epithelium, which cell type is round and serves as the precursor of principal cells?
questions.e: Basal cells are round and serve as precursors of the principal cells in the epididymal epithelium.

questions.q: The stereocilia of the ductus epididymis mainly function to:
o: Form part of the blood-testis barrier
Propel sperm along by ciliary beating
questions.e: Stereocilia (which are non-motile, unlike true cilia) increase the epithelial surface area for reabsorption of about 90% of the luminal fluid.

questions.q: Why is a large volume of fluid secreted by Sertoli cells needed to help move sperm out of the seminiferous tubule?
o: Because sperm are too large to move on their own
Because sperm are initially non-motile as they leave the tubule
Because the tubule lumen is completely blocked otherwise
questions.e: Sperm are initially non-motile as they leave the seminiferous tubule, so a large secreted fluid volume (from Sertoli cells) helps propel them toward the epididymis.

questions.q: Along the length of the epididymis, which of the following changes occur from head to tail?
o: No structural changes occur along its length
Epithelial height and stereocilia increase; muscularis decreases
questions.e: Along the epididymis, epithelial cell height and stereocilia height decrease, while the muscularis increases from 1 to 3 layers.

questions.q: Which part of the epididymis serves as the principal reservoir for sperm storage?
questions.e: The tail of the epididymis is the principal reservoir for sperm storage, while the head and body move sperm via peristaltic contraction.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of the ductus epididymis?
o: Temporary storage and maturation of sperm
Production of glycoprotein inhibiting premature capacitation
questions.e: The epididymis stores/matures sperm, absorbs fluid, and secretes an inhibitory glycoprotein — but testosterone synthesis is a function of Leydig cells, not the epididymis.

questions.q: The modification of the sperm head by decapacitation-factor-containing glycoconjugates during epididymal transit is called:
questions.e: Decapacitation is the process during epididymal maturation in which the sperm head is modified by surface-associated decapacitation-factor glycoconjugates.

questions.q: Stereocilia are present in epithelial linings of the following organs:
o: Trachea, epididymis, penile urethra, membranous urethra
Primary bronchi and gallbladder, vas deferens, penile urethra
Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles, membranous urethra
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The ductus deferens has a muscularis composed of how many smooth muscle layers, and what characteristic lumen shape?
o: 1 layer only; a round, regular lumen
No muscularis at all; irregular lumen
questions.e: The ductus deferens has a 3-layered muscularis (inner longitudinal, middle circular, outer longitudinal) and a characteristic star-shaped lumen.

questions.q: Compared to the rest of the vas deferens, the ampulla of the ductus deferens is characterized by:
o: A larger lumen with folded mucosa
A smaller lumen and smooth mucosa
questions.e: The ampulla of the ductus deferens has a larger lumen, highly folded mucosa, and glandular diverticula/crypts, with a comparatively thinner muscle layer.

questions.q: The ejaculatory duct is lined by which epithelium, and what substitutes for its lack of a true muscularis?
o: Stratified squamous epithelium; smooth muscle of the bladder
Simple columnar epithelium; fibromuscular tissue of the prostate
questions.e: The ejaculatory duct has a simple columnar epithelium and no smooth muscle of its own — the fibromuscular tissue of the prostate substitutes for muscle.

questions.q: In the male embryo, the genital duct system develops from which paired ducts (as opposed to the paramesonephric ducts of the female)?
questions.e: In the indifferent stage, both sexes have mesonephric (wolffian) and paramesonephric (müllerian) ducts; the male genital duct system develops from the mesonephric (wolffian) ducts.

questions.q: The male urethra serves as the terminal duct for which two systems?
questions.e: The male urethra serves as the terminal duct for both the urinary and genital systems.

questions.q: The male urethra is approximately how long?
questions.e: The male urethra is about 20 cm long, considerably longer than the female urethra (3–5 cm).

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in all the following EXCEPT
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location, showed 3 layers of cells that were taller than wide. The cells lacked surface specialization. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
