o: Ureter, spongy urethra and prostatic urethra
Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and ureter
Membranous urethra and fossa navicularis of the penis
questions.e: ⭐ Past exam question. Straight from a past paper on this topic.

questions.q: The membranous urethra is surrounded by skeletal muscle of the deep perineal pouch, forming the:
questions.e: Skeletal muscle of the deep perineal pouch surrounding the membranous urethra forms the external (voluntary) sphincter of the urethra.

questions.q: The penile (spongy) urethra is surrounded by which erectile body as it passes through the length of the penis?
questions.e: The penile (spongy) urethra is surrounded by the corpus spongiosum as it passes through the length of the penis.

questions.q: Near its distal end, the penile urethra's epithelium changes to:
questions.e: At its distal end, the penile urethra is lined with stratified squamous epithelium continuous with the skin of the penis.

questions.q: Which glands' ducts empty into the penile urethra, contributing mucus-secreting glandular openings along its length?
questions.e: Ducts of the bulbourethral glands and the mucus-secreting urethral glands (glands of Littré) empty into the penile urethra.

questions.q: Compared with the male urethra, the female urethra is:
o: Longer and lined by transitional epithelium throughout
questions.e: The female urethra is short (3–5 cm), lined primarily by stratified squamous epithelium, with patches of pseudostratified columnar epithelium.

questions.q: The penis contains three masses of erectile tissue: two corpora cavernosa and:
o: The rete testis of the mediastinum
A second pair of corpora cavernosa
The tunica vasculosa of the testis
questions.e: The penis contains two corpora cavernosa plus a single corpus spongiosum (corpus cavernosum urethrae), through which the penile urethra passes.

questions.q: The vascular spaces of the corpora cavernosa are lined by:
o: A continuous layer of endothelial cells
questions.e: The corpora cavernosa contain irregular vascular spaces lined by a continuous layer of endothelial cells, separated by CT/smooth muscle trabeculae.

questions.q: Compared with the corpora cavernosa, the corpus spongiosum's trabeculae contain:
o: More elastic fibers and less smooth muscle
More smooth muscle and fewer elastic fibers
questions.e: Corpus spongiosum trabeculae contain more elastic fibers and less smooth muscle than those of the corpora cavernosa, and its vascular spaces are of uniform size.

questions.q: The dilated distal end of the corpus spongiosum is called the:
questions.e: The glans penis is the dilated distal end of the corpus spongiosum, covered by the retractable prepuce.

questions.q: The retractable skin covering the glans penis is called the:
questions.e: The prepuce is the retractable skin covering the glans penis, lined by stratified squamous lightly keratinized epithelium.

questions.q: The thick fibrous CT sheath surrounding both the corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum of the penis is the:
questions.e: The tunica albuginea is the thick fibrous connective tissue sheath surrounding the paired corpora cavernosa and the corpus spongiosum.

questions.q: During erection, engorgement of the vascular spaces results from which type of nervous impulse?
o: Purely hormonal signals with no nervous input
questions.e: During erection, vascular spaces become engorged with blood as a result of parasympathetic impulses, which constrict arteriovenous shunts and dilate the helicine arteries.

questions.q: Semen contains fluid and sperm from the testis, along with secretory products from all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: Semen contains secretions from the epididymis, ductus deferens, prostate, seminal vesicles, and bulbourethral glands — not the kidneys.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of semen?
o: Provides DNA identical to body cells
Serves as a transport medium for sperm
questions.e: Semen transports sperm, neutralizes acidity, liquefies the coagulum, and activates sperm — sperm are haploid, not identical in genetic content to somatic cells.

questions.q: The prostate gland produces a fluid best described as:
questions.e: The prostate gland produces a clear/watery, slightly alkaline fluid.

questions.q: Which prostatic secretion is specifically responsible for liquefying semen?
questions.e: Fibrinolysin, secreted by the prostate, liquefies semen.

questions.q: Prostate-specific antigen (PSA), used clinically as a tumor marker, is normally a secretory product of the:
questions.e: PSA is a normal secretory component of prostatic fluid, though it is used clinically as a marker that can be elevated in prostate disease.

questions.q: Histologically, the prostate gland shows:
o: A honeycomb appearance similar to seminal vesicles
questions.e: The prostate gland is composed of prostatic acini/glandular alveoli in a fibromuscular connective tissue stroma, and does NOT show the honeycomb appearance seen in seminal vesicles.

questions.q: Prostatic concretions (corpora amylacea) are:
o: Composed purely of calcium with no organic material
questions.e: Prostatic concretions (corpora amylacea) increase in number with age, forming by precipitation of secretory material around cell fragments, and may become calcified.

questions.q: As the prostate enlarges, which urethral segment is most directly compressed, producing urinary symptoms?
questions.e: Prostate enlargement narrows the prostatic urethra, which passes directly through the gland, producing obstructive urinary symptoms.

questions.q: Which of the following is a listed urinary symptom of prostate enlargement?
o: Immediate kidney failure in all patients
Complete absence of any urinary symptoms
questions.e: Prostate enlargement is associated with symptoms including increased night-time frequency, urgency, poor/thin stream, and sense of incomplete emptying, among others.

questions.q: Seminal vesicle secretions contribute approximately what proportion of total semen volume?
questions.e: Seminal vesicle secretions make up approximately 70% of semen volume.

questions.q: Which of the following is a component of seminal vesicle secretion?
o: Prostatic acid phosphatase and citric acid
questions.e: Seminal vesicles produce a whitish-yellow viscous fluid containing fructose, fibrinogen, amino acids, ascorbic acid, and prostaglandins.

questions.q: Histologically, the seminal vesicle is distinguished by its:
questions.e: The seminal vesicle shows a honeycomb appearance, with highly branched folds of mucosa and mucosal crypts.

questions.q: The seminal vesicle epithelium is best described as:
questions.e: The seminal vesicle has a pseudostratified columnar, low columnar, or cuboidal epithelium, arranged with mucosal crypts.

questions.q: The seminal vesicle wall contains which muscle layers?
o: Three layers identical to the vas deferens
Only a single circular layer of muscle
questions.e: The seminal vesicle wall has inner circular and outer longitudinal smooth muscle layers, within 3 coats overall.

questions.q: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) gland secretion is best described as:
o: Identical in composition to prostatic fluid
Composed mainly of fructose and citrate
questions.e: Bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands produce a clear, mucous-like secretion that lubricates the penile urethra just prior to the emission of semen.

questions.q: Which of the following is a listed component of bulbourethral gland secretion?
questions.e: Bulbourethral gland secretions contain galactose, galactosamine, galacturonic acid, sialic acid, and methylpentose.

questions.q: The bulbourethral (Cowper's) glands are histologically composed of:
o: Mucous glands with a fibroelastic capsule
Honeycomb glandular alveoli identical to seminal vesicles
questions.e: Bulbourethral glands are mucous glands with simple cuboidal or columnar epithelium, surrounded by a fibroelastic capsule containing skeletal muscle, with CT septa.

questions.q: Sperm movement through the female reproductive tract is driven by:
o: Muscular contractions of the uterus/uterine tubes plus their own propulsion
Ciliary beating exclusively, with no sperm motility
questions.e: Sperm movement is driven by muscular contractions of the uterus and uterine tubes, together with the sperm's own propulsion.

questions.q: The trip of sperm from the cervix to the oviduct requires a minimum of:
questions.e: The trip from the cervix to the oviduct requires a minimum of 2–7 hours.

questions.q: After reaching the isthmus, sperm:
o: Become less motile and pause their migration
questions.e: After reaching the isthmus, sperm become less motile and cease their migration until ovulation.

questions.q: At ovulation, sperm become motile again largely due to:
o: Chemoattractants produced by the cumulus cells
questions.e: At ovulation, sperm regain motility due to chemoattractants produced by the cumulus cells, and swim to the ampulla.

questions.q: Thermotaxis describes how sperm are guided through most of the fallopian tube by:
o: Temperature — the tube with the ovulated oocyte is slightly warmer
questions.e: Thermotaxis: sperm are guided by temperature through most of the tube, since the tube containing the ovulated oocyte is slightly warmer, before switching to chemical guidance near the egg.

questions.q: Before a spermatozoon is capable of fertilizing, it must undergo which three changes?
o: Capacitation, hyperactivation, and the acrosomal reaction
questions.e: Pre-fertilization changes required are capacitation, hyperactivation, and the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Capacitation occurs in the uterine tubes and lasts approximately:
questions.e: Capacitation is a period of conditioning in the female reproductive tract, occurring in the uterine tubes and lasting approximately 7 hours.

questions.q: During capacitation, which of the following is removed from the plasma membrane surrounding the acrosomal region?
o: Glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins
questions.e: Capacitation involves removal of the glycoprotein coat and seminal plasma proteins from the plasma membrane surrounding the acrosomal region of the sperm.

questions.q: Only capacitated sperm can:
o: Pass through the cells of the corona radiata to undergo the acrosomal reaction
questions.e: Only capacitated sperm can pass through the cells of the corona radiata to undergo the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Hyperactivation refers to the sperm's ability to:
o: Swim faster and more vigorously, easing zona pellucida penetration
Fuse with the oocyte membrane directly
questions.e: Hyperactivation is the ability of the spermatozoon to swim faster and more vigorously, making it easier to penetrate the zona pellucida.

questions.q: The acrosomal reaction is induced by:
questions.e: The acrosomal reaction occurs after the sperm binds to the zona pellucida and is induced by zona proteins.

questions.q: The acrosomal reaction releases which enzymes needed for zona pellucida penetration?
questions.e: The acrosomal reaction releases enzymes, including acrosin and trypsin-like enzymes, needed to penetrate the zona pellucida.

questions.q: Fertilization usually takes place within which structure?
o: The isthmus of the uterine tube
questions.e: Fertilization usually takes place within the ampulla of the oviduct.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of sperm deposited in the vagina enter the cervix?
questions.e: Only about 1% of the sperm deposited in the vagina enter the cervix.

questions.q: Spermatozoa may remain viable within the female reproductive tract for about:
questions.e: Spermatozoa may remain viable in the female reproductive tract for approximately 5 days.

questions.q: Fertilization consists of three phases; which is Phase 1?
o: Fusion of oocyte and sperm cell membranes
questions.e: Phase 1 of fertilization is penetration of the corona radiata.

questions.q: Of the 200–300 million sperm deposited in the vagina, approximately how many reach the ampulla?
questions.e: Of the 200–300 million sperm deposited in the vagina, only 300 to 500 reach the ampulla.

questions.q: The many sperm that do not fertilize the oocyte serve what role?
o: They aid the fertilizing sperm in penetrating the corona radiata and zona pellucida
They compete to reach the uterus first
They fertilize the polar body instead
questions.e: The remaining, non-fertilizing spermatozoa aid the fertilizing sperm in penetrating the barriers (corona radiata and zona pellucida) protecting the egg.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, preventing additional sperm from binding?
questions.e: ZP1 cross-links ZP2 with ZP3, thereby preventing more spermatozoa from binding.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein permits sperm binding and facilitates the acrosome reaction?
questions.e: ZP3 permits the binding of spermatozoa and facilitates occurrence of the acrosome reaction.

questions.q: Which zona pellucida glycoprotein has an unknown function?
questions.e: ZP4's function is unknown, unlike ZP1, ZP2, and ZP3.

questions.q: After fertilization, the ovum secretes ovastacin, which:
o: Degrades ZP2, preventing additional sperm binding
questions.e: After fertilization, the ovum secretes the enzyme ovastacin, which degrades ZP2, preventing binding of additional spermatozoa to the zona pellucida.

questions.q: In Phase 2 of fertilization, release of acrosin allows the sperm to:
o: Penetrate the zona pellucida and contact the oocyte's plasma membrane
questions.e: Release of acrosin, the acrosomal enzyme, allows the sperm to penetrate the zona pellucida, bringing it into contact with the oocyte's plasma membrane.

questions.q: In Phase 3 of fertilization, initial adhesion of sperm to oocyte is partly mediated by:
o: Integrins on the oocyte and disintegrins on the sperm
questions.e: Initial adhesion is partly mediated by interaction of integrins on the oocyte and their ligands, disintegrins, on the sperm.

questions.q: Cleavage is best defined as:
o: A series of mitotic divisions fractionating the zygote into numerous normal-size cells
A single meiotic division of the oocyte
questions.e: Cleavage is a series of mitotic divisions by which the large zygote is fractionated into numerous 'normal size' cells.

questions.q: Each daughter cell produced during cleavage is called a:
questions.e: Each daughter cell of the cleavage process is termed a blastomere.

questions.q: Cleavage begins with the zygote and, via compaction and the morula stage, terminates at the start of the:
questions.e: Cleavage begins with a zygote, progresses through compaction to a morula stage, and terminates at the start of the blastocyst (blastula) stage.

questions.q: Until the 8-cell stage, blastomeres form:
questions.e: Until the eight-cell stage, the blastomeres form a loosely arranged clump.

questions.q: After the 3rd cleavage, blastomeres maximize contact with each other, forming a compact ball held together by tight junctions — this process is called:
questions.e: Compaction is the process by which, after the 3rd cleavage, blastomeres maximize mutual contact, forming a compact ball held by tight junctions.

questions.q: Compaction differentiates blastomeres into which two populations?
o: Inner and outer cells with different fates
questions.e: The process of compaction differentiates blastomeres into inner and outer cells with different developmental missions.

questions.q: Approximately 3 days after fertilization, the compacted embryo forms a 16-cell structure known as the:
questions.e: Approximately 3 days after fertilization, cells of the compacted embryo divide again to form a 16-cell morula (named for its resemblance to a mulberry).

questions.q: Inner cells of the morula constitute the:
questions.e: Inner cells of the morula constitute the inner cell mass, while surrounding cells compose the outer cell mass.

questions.q: The inner cell mass of the morula gives rise to:
questions.e: The inner cell mass gives rise to tissues of the embryo proper, while the outer cell mass forms the trophoblast, contributing later to the placenta.

questions.q: During cleavage, individual blastomeres:
o: Do not grow — cell size is reduced by almost half at each division
Double in size at each division
questions.e: Individual blastomeres do not grow during cleavage; the size of the cell is reduced by almost half at each division.

questions.q: The first cleavage division occurs how many days following ovulation?
questions.e: The first cleavage division occurs 1 to 5 days following ovulation.

questions.q: After the first division, cells divide about once every:
questions.e: Thereafter, cells divide about once every 12 hours, with up to 8 generations of mitoses occurring without intervening cytoplasmic growth.

questions.q: As fluid from the uterine tube penetrates the zona pellucida into the intercellular spaces of the inner cell mass, these spaces become confluent and form a single cavity called the:
questions.e: The intercellular spaces gradually become confluent, forming a single cavity — the blastocoel — at which point the embryo is called a blastocyst.

questions.q: In the blastocyst, cells of the outer cell mass (trophoblast) flatten to form:
o: The epithelial wall of the blastocyst
questions.e: Cells of the outer cell mass (trophoblast) flatten and form the epithelial wall of the blastocyst, while inner cell mass (embryoblast) cells sit at one pole.

questions.q: Disappearance of the zona pellucida in the blastocyst allows:
questions.e: The zona pellucida disappears, allowing implantation of the blastocyst to begin.

questions.q: Which cell adhesion molecule on trophoblast cells mediates initial attachment of the blastocyst to the uterine epithelium?
questions.e: L-selectin (CD62L), a cell adhesion molecule on trophoblast cells, and its carbohydrate receptors on the uterine epithelium mediate initial blastocyst attachment.

questions.q: Monozygotic twins arise from:
o: 1 oocyte fertilized by a single spermatozoon
A single oocyte fertilized by 2 sperm
Two separate ovulations in the same cycle, each fertilized separately
questions.e: Monozygotic (identical) twins arise from 1 oocyte fertilized by a single spermatozoon.

questions.q: Dizygotic twins are always:
o: The same sex, with identical blood groups
Potentially the same or different sex, with separate placentas
questions.e: Dizygotic twins arise from 2 oocytes and 2 spermatozoa, may be the same or different sex, have different blood groups, and always have separate placentas.

questions.q: Monozygotic twins may share a placenta (monochorionic) or have separate placentas because:
o: They always have separate placentas, like dizygotic twins
Depending on when the single zygote splits, the placenta may or may not be shared
Placenta type depends on maternal blood group
Twin placentation is random and unrelated to zygosity
questions.e: Depending on the timing of the split, monozygotic twins may share a common placenta (monochorionic) or develop separate placentas (dichorionic).

questions.q: Which factor is associated with a higher likelihood of dizygotic twinning?
questions.e: A family history of fraternal twins increases the chance of conceiving twins, along with older maternal age, African-American race, obesity, greater height, breastfeeding during conception, and reproductive technologies.

questions.q: In one type of monozygotic twinning, the zygote divides into two separate cells (embryos) at:
questions.e: One pattern of monozygotic twinning occurs when the zygote divides into two separate cells (embryos) at the first cleavage division.

questions.q: Siamese (conjoined) twins result when:
o: Two inner cell masses form and separate completely
A single inner cell mass forms, divides incompletely
Two separate zygotes fuse at fertilization
The zona pellucida fails to disappear
questions.e: Conjoined twins result when a single inner cell mass forms and divides incompletely, giving rise to two incompletely separated embryos.

questions.q: By day 8 of development, the trophoblast differentiates into which two layers?
questions.e: On day 8, the trophoblast differentiates into the cytotrophoblast (inner mononucleated layer) and syncytiotrophoblast (outer multinucleated layer).

questions.q: Mitotic figures are found in which trophoblast layer, but NOT the other?
questions.e: Mitotic figures are found in the cytotrophoblast but not the syncytiotrophoblast; cytotrophoblast cells divide and migrate into the syncytiotrophoblast, fusing and losing their individual membranes.

questions.q: On day 8, the embryoblast (inner cell mass) differentiates into which two layers?
questions.e: The embryoblast differentiates into the hypoblast (small cuboidal cells adjacent to the blastocyst cavity) and the epiblast (high columnar cells adjacent to the amniotic cavity).

questions.q: The hypoblast and epiblast, together with the cytotrophoblast and syncytiotrophoblast, form:
questions.e: Together, these 4 layers form a flat, bilaminar disc.

questions.q: A small cavity appearing within the epiblast on day 8 enlarges to become the:
questions.e: A small cavity appears within the epiblast and enlarges to become the amniotic cavity.

questions.q: Epiblast cells adjacent to the cytotrophoblast that line the amniotic cavity are called:
questions.e: Epiblast cells adjacent to the cytotrophoblast are called amnioblasts, and together with the rest of the epiblast, they line the amniotic cavity.

questions.q: Day 9 of development is known as the lacunar stage because:
o: Lacunae (fused vacuoles) appear in the syncytium at the embryonic pole
The blastocyst first attaches to the endometrium
questions.e: On day 9, vacuoles appear in the syncytium at the embryonic pole and fuse to form large lacunae — the lacunar stage of trophoblast development.

questions.q: At the abembryonic pole on day 9, flattened hypoblast-derived cells form the:
questions.e: At the abembryonic pole, flattened cells from the hypoblast form the exocoelomic (Heuser's) membrane, lining the inner surface of the cytotrophoblast.

questions.q: On days 11–12, syncytiotrophoblast cells erode maternal capillaries, which become congested and dilated and are then called:
questions.e: Eroded maternal capillaries, congested and dilated, are known as sinusoids.

questions.q: When syncytial lacunae become continuous with sinusoids and maternal blood enters the lacunar system, this establishes the:
questions.e: Continuity between syncytial lacunae and sinusoids allows maternal blood to flow through the trophoblastic system, establishing uteroplacental circulation.

questions.q: Extraembryonic mesoderm, derived from the epiblast, eventually fills the space between the trophoblast and the amnion/exocoelomic membrane, and cavities within it become confluent to form the:
questions.e: Large cavities in the extraembryonic mesoderm become confluent, forming the extraembryonic coelom, or chorionic cavity.

questions.q: On day 13, cytotrophoblast cells proliferate into the syncytiotrophoblast, forming cellular columns known as:
questions.e: Cellular columns surrounded by syncytium, formed by cytotrophoblast proliferation into the syncytiotrophoblast, are known as primary villi.

questions.q: The secondary (definitive) yolk sac, formed on day 13 from additional hypoblast cells, is:
o: Larger than the primitive yolk sac
Much smaller than the primitive yolk sac (exocoelomic cavity)
Identical in size to the primitive yolk sac
questions.e: The secondary yolk sac is much smaller than the original exocoelomic cavity (primitive yolk sac).

questions.q: The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the inside of the cytotrophoblast is known as the:
questions.e: The extraembryonic mesoderm lining the cytotrophoblast is called the chorionic plate.

questions.q: The connecting stalk, traversed by extraembryonic mesoderm across the chorionic cavity, later develops into the:
questions.e: With development of blood vessels, the connecting stalk becomes the umbilical cord.

questions.q: By the end of the 2nd week, blood levels of hCG produced by the syncytiotrophoblast are sufficient for:
questions.e: By the end of week 2, hCG quantities are sufficient to be detected by radioimmunoassays, forming the basis of pregnancy testing.

questions.q: Which unusual MHC class IB molecule helps block maternal immune recognition of the conceptus as foreign?
questions.e: An unusual MHC class IB molecule, HLA-G, blocks recognition of the conceptus as foreign tissue, alongside immunosuppressive cytokines and proteins.

questions.q: Approximately what percentage of ectopic pregnancies occur in the uterine tube?
questions.e: 95% of ectopic pregnancies occur in the uterine tube, most often in the ampulla.

questions.q: Gastrulation marks the commencement of the embryonic period, which extends from:
questions.e: Gastrulation marks the commencement of the embryonic period, which extends from week 3 to week 8.

questions.q: Gastrulation transforms the bilaminar embryonic disc into a:
questions.e: Gastrulation results in transformation of the bilaminar embryonic disc into a trilaminar one, comprising ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm.

questions.q: Gastrulation begins with formation of the:
questions.e: Gastrulation begins with formation of the primitive (Spemann's) streak on the surface of the epiblast.

questions.q: The cranial end of the primitive streak expands to form the:
questions.e: The cranial end of the primitive streak is expanded as the primitive (Hensen's) node, containing the primitive pit.

questions.q: Formation of the primitive streak defines which body axes?
o: Cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, medial-lateral, and left-right axes
No axes are established by the streak
questions.e: Formation of the primitive streak defines all major body axes: cranial-caudal, dorsal-ventral, medial-lateral, and left-right.

questions.q: The inward movement of epiblast cells as they detach and slip beneath the epiblast at the primitive streak is called:
questions.e: This inward movement of epiblast cells is known as invagination.

questions.q: Cell migration and specification during gastrulation is controlled by which growth factor, synthesized by streak cells themselves?
questions.e: Cell migration and specification during gastrulation are controlled by fibroblast growth factor 8 (FGF8), synthesized by the streak cells themselves.

questions.q: Invaginated epiblast cells that displace the hypoblast create the:
questions.e: Once cells have invaginated, some displace the hypoblast, creating the embryonic endoderm.

questions.q: Cells that come to lie between the epiblast and the newly created endoderm form the:
questions.e: Other invaginating cells come to lie between the epiblast and newly created endoderm, forming the mesoderm.

questions.q: Cells remaining in the epiblast (that did not migrate through the streak) become the:
questions.e: Cells remaining in the epiblast form ectoderm — thus the epiblast is the ultimate source of all three germ layers.

questions.q: Cells migrating through the mid-streak level of the primitive streak become which mesoderm type?
questions.e: Cells migrating through the mid-streak level become intermediate (intraembryonic) mesoderm, which forms the urogenital system.

questions.q: Cells that ingress through the cranial region of the primitive node become the:
questions.e: Cells that ingress through the cranial region of the node become the notochord.

questions.q: The prechordal plate is a thickening of which germ layer, at the cranial end of the primitive streak?
questions.e: The prechordal plate is a thickening of the endoderm at the cranial end of the primitive streak.

questions.q: The prechordal plate later becomes important for:
o: Development of the notochord's blood supply
questions.e: The prechordal plate later becomes important for induction of the forebrain.

questions.q: The oropharyngeal membrane consists of tightly adherent ectoderm and endoderm and represents the future opening of the:
questions.e: The oropharyngeal membrane, at the cranial end, represents the future opening of the oral cavity.

questions.q: The intraembryonic mesoderm separates ectoderm from endoderm along the embryo's length except cranially (prechordal plate) and caudally at the:
questions.e: Caudally, intraembryonic mesoderm is absent at the cloacal membrane, the future site of the anus.

questions.q: By the end of which week does the primitive streak regress and disappear?
questions.e: The primitive streak regresses and disappears by the end of week 4.

questions.q: The notochordal process fuses transiently with endoderm to form the:
questions.e: The notochordal process fuses transiently with endoderm to form the notochordal plate.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a listed function of the notochord?
o: Forms a midline axis determining the antero-posterior axis
Induces formation of the neural tube
questions.e: The notochord forms the midline axis, induces neural tube formation, and persists as the nucleus pulposus — but it does not form the placenta.

questions.q: Remnants of notochordal tissue may give rise to tumors called:
questions.e: Remnants of notochordal tissue may give rise to tumors called chordomas.

questions.q: Paraxial mesoderm gives rise mainly to:
questions.e: Paraxial mesoderm undergoes segmentation into somitomeres and somites, giving rise to musculoskeletal structures.

questions.q: The number of somites present in an embryo is a useful indicator of:
questions.e: There are 42–44 pairs of somites, which do not all appear simultaneously; the number of somites provides a good index of embryonic age.

questions.q: The extraembryonic (fetal) membranes include all of the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: Fetal membranes include the chorion, amnion, yolk sac, allantois, and umbilical cord — the notochord is part of the embryo proper, not a fetal membrane.

questions.q: Primary villi consist of a cytotrophoblastic core covered by:
questions.e: By the beginning of week 3, the trophoblast is characterized by primary villi, consisting of a cytotrophoblastic core covered by a syncytial layer.

questions.q: A villus becomes a secondary villus once:
o: Mesodermal cells penetrate its cytotrophoblastic core
questions.e: Secondary villi form when mesodermal cells penetrate the core of primary villi and grow toward the decidua.

questions.q: A villus is termed tertiary (definitive placental villus) once mesodermal core cells differentiate into:
o: Blood cells and small blood vessels
questions.e: By the end of week 3, mesodermal cells in the villus core differentiate into blood cells and small blood vessels, forming the villous capillary system — the tertiary villus stage.

questions.q: Villi that extend from the chorionic plate to the decidua basalis are called:
questions.e: Villi extending from the chorionic plate to the decidua basalis are called stem or anchoring villi.

questions.q: The fetal component of the placenta develops from the chorionic plate, also called the:
questions.e: The fetal component of the placenta develops from the chorionic plate, the chorion frondosum, together with extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.q: The maternal component of the placenta develops from the endometrium, specifically the:
questions.e: The maternal component of the placenta develops from the decidua basalis, the endometrium to which the chorion frondosum is attached.

questions.q: On the abembryonic side (decidua capsularis), chorionic villi regress, leaving a smooth surface called the:
questions.e: On the decidua capsularis side, villi regress, leaving a smooth surface known as the chorion laeve (smooth chorion).

questions.q: Erosion of maternal spiral arteries to release blood into the intervillous spaces is accomplished by:
o: Direct action of the syncytiotrophoblast alone
questions.e: Cytotrophoblast cells undergo endovascular invasion of the spiral arteries, replacing maternal endothelial cells and creating hybrid vessels.

questions.q: Decidual septa divide the placenta into a number of compartments called:
questions.e: Decidual septa projecting into (but not reaching) the chorionic plate divide the placenta into 15–20 compartments, called cotyledons.

questions.q: The functional unit of the placenta, a villous tree perfused by a single spiral artery, is called the:
questions.e: The placentome (placental lobe) is the functional unit of the placenta — there are about 50–100 within a full placenta.

questions.q: Before 20 weeks, the layers of the placental membrane, from fetal to maternal side, are (in order):
o: Syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast, connective tissue, capillary endothelium
Capillary endothelium, connective tissue, cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast
Cytotrophoblast, syncytiotrophoblast, connective tissue, capillary endothelium
Connective tissue, capillary endothelium, syncytiotrophoblast, cytotrophoblast
questions.e: From fetal to maternal side, the placental membrane layers are: capillary endothelium of fetal capillaries, connective tissue of the villus, cytotrophoblast, and syncytiotrophoblast.

questions.q: The placental barrier does NOT exclude which of the following?
questions.e: The placental barrier does not exclude many potentially dangerous agents such as alcohol, nicotine, viruses, drugs, exogenous hormones, and heavy metals.

questions.q: Placenta previa is defined as:
o: Premature separation of a normally-positioned placenta
Abnormal placentation near or covering the internal cervical os
questions.e: Placenta previa is abnormal placentation near or covering the internal os of the uterine cervix, typically causing painless vaginal bleeding.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the humerus?
o: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
questions.e: Proximal humerus: greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and the intertubercular (bicipital) groove between them. Trochanters belong to the femur; the fossae are distal.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the humerus?
o: Greater trochanter, lesser tubercle and intertrochanteric crest
Greater tubercle, lesser tubercle and intertubercular groove
Lesser trochanter, greater trochanter and bicipital groove
Greater tuberosity, lesser tuberosity and intertrochanteric crest
Coronoid fossa, radial fossa and olecranon fossa
questions.e: Distal humerus bears three fossae: coronoid and radial (anterior) and olecranon (posterior).

questions.q: Which of the following statements about facial bones is FALSE?
o: The mandible is the largest and strongest bone of the face
The maxillae are considered as the keystone bones of the skeleton
The zygomatic bones are commonly called the cheekbones
The lacrimal bones contribute to the orbit's medial wall
The vomer is located in the orbit forming the inferior part of the orbit
questions.e: False: the vomer sits in the nasal septum, not the orbit. (Note: B is loosely worded — the maxillae are the keystone of the FACE, not the whole skeleton — but E is the clearly false statement intended.)

questions.q: The following are characteristics of the vertebral column EXCEPT
o: It has a chain of 33 individual vertebrae with 23 intervertebral discs of fibrocartilage
About ¼ of the length is contributed by the 23 intervertebral discs
Only the thoracic and sacral curvatures are well developed at birth and are termed primary curvatures
The sacral curvature positions the weight of the upper part of the body over the lower limbs, providing optimal balance during standing
In the adult there are 29 vertebrae; 27 mobile, 2 immobile, and 20 intervertebral discs
questions.e: False: the adult has 26 bones (24 mobile presacral vertebrae + sacrum + coccyx) with 23 discs — not 29 vertebrae as stated.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the DISTAL END of the tibia:
o: Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
questions.e: Distal tibia: fibular notch (for the fibula) and the medial malleolus. The lateral malleolus belongs to the fibula.

questions.q: Which of the following is associated with the PROXIMAL END of the tibia:
o: Intercondylar eminence, fibular notch and tibial tuberosity
Medial condyle, lateral condyle and tibial tuberosity
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Proximal tibia: intercondylar eminence + tibial tuberosity (option C), and the medial/lateral condyles (option B). correctedThe paper's key (D) is inconsistent — option A contains the fibular notch, which is a DISTAL feature, so 'A, B and C' cannot all be right. The clean pairing with Q8 makes C the intended answer.

questions.q: A 40-year old man has lordosis. This is
o: An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar region of the spine just above the sacrum
An abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column, common in obese men and pregnant women
questions.e: Lordosis = exaggerated lumbar (inward) curvature. Lateral curvature is scoliosis; exaggerated thoracic curvature is kyphosis (hunchback).

questions.q: A 14-year old girl has Scoliosis. This is
o: An exaggerated inward curvature of the lumbar region of the spine just above the sacrum
An abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column
questions.e: Scoliosis = abnormal lateral (side-to-side) curvature of the spine.

questions.q: The side to which an ulna belongs can be determined from the following:
o: The styloid process is proximal and lateral to the olecranon process
The olecranon process and coronoid process are located at the proximal end
On the lateral side of the olecranon process is the radial notch
The head and the styloid process are separated by a deep concavity known as the trochlear notch
questions.e: Both the olecranon and coronoid processes (forming the trochlear notch) sit at the proximal end of the ulna. The head and styloid are distal.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is not a facial bone?
questions.e: The hyoid is a neck bone (axial), not one of the 14 facial bones.

questions.q: Which of the following facial bones contains a sinus?
questions.e: The maxilla contains the maxillary sinus, the largest paranasal sinus.

questions.q: The vertebra which has no body is the
questions.e: The atlas (C1) is a ring of bone with no body — its 'body' fused to the axis to form the dens.

questions.q: How many pairs of false ribs are present in the skeleton?
questions.e: Ribs 8–12 are false ribs = 5 pairs (ribs 11 and 12 of these are also floating).

questions.q: If you see a foramen in the transverse process of a vertebra, which type of vertebra are you observing?
questions.e: Transverse foramina are unique to cervical vertebrae (they transmit the vertebral vessels).

questions.q: The pectoral girdle is composed of the
questions.e: The pectoral (shoulder) girdle = clavicle + scapula. The humerus is part of the free upper limb.

questions.q: Which digit does not have a middle phalanx?
questions.e: Digit I (the thumb / pollex) has only two phalanges — proximal and distal — so no middle phalanx.

questions.q: Children are often told to keep this process off the table while eating.
questions.e: The olecranon (point of the elbow) — 'keep your elbows off the table'.

questions.q: On which bone is the head found at the distal end?
questions.e: The ulna's head is at its DISTAL end; the radius' head is proximal.

questions.q: Which bone is not part of the pelvic girdle?
questions.e: The pelvic girdle = the two hip bones (ilium + ischium + pubis). The sacrum is part of the axial skeleton.

questions.q: The heel bone is called the
questions.e: The calcaneus is the heel bone and the largest tarsal bone.

questions.q: Which of the following abnormal curve(s) is often seen in obese men with ‘potbellies’ as they attempt to preserve their center of gravity?
questions.e: A heavy abdomen pulls the lumbar spine forward, exaggerating the lumbar curve — lordosis (swayback).

questions.q: Which of the following structures is the most difficult to observe on an X-Ray film?
questions.e: Cartilage is radiolucent (low density), so the tracheal cartilages are hardest to see on plain X-ray.

questions.q: The skeleton with the highest number of bones is that of:
questions.e: A newborn has roughly 270–300 bones; many later fuse, leaving 206 in the adult.

questions.q: The prominent bony knobs on each side of the ankle joint are
o: The styloid processes of the tibia and fibula
The medial malleolus of the fibula and the lateral malleolus of the tibia
The medial malleolus of the tibia and the lateral malleolus of the fibula
The epicondyles of the tibia and fibula
The head of the fibula and the tuberosity of the tibia
questions.e: Medial malleolus = tibia; lateral malleolus = fibula. (B swaps them.)

questions.q: The hyoid bone is unique because it is:
o: A sesmoid bone formed in connective tissue under pressure.
Attached to the sternal angle at the t4 vertebral level.
Covered with mucosa and epithelial tissue.
Shaped like a right-angled triangle on its side.
The only bone that does not articulate with another bone
questions.e: The hyoid is the only bone that forms no direct joint with another bone — it is slung by muscles and ligaments.

questions.q: The common names for the scapula, clavicle, sternum, calvaria and patella are the:
o: Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, hip bone and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, knee cap, collar bone, breast bone and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, collar bone, breast bone, skull cap and knee cap respectively
Shoulder blade, hip bone, collar bone, knee cap and skull cap respectively
Shoulder blade, breast bone, skullcap, collar bone and knee cap respectively
questions.e: Scapula = shoulder blade, clavicle = collar bone, sternum = breast bone, calvaria = skull cap, patella = knee cap.

questions.q: The foramen magnum is a large hole in the base of the occipital bone that transmits the spinal cord. The homologous structure in an individual vertebra is the:
questions.e: The vertebral foramen transmits the spinal cord — the segmental equivalent of the foramen magnum.

questions.q: The thumb and the great toe are known as
questions.e: Thumb = pollex; great toe = hallux.

questions.q: A patient had pain in an infected kidney in his lumbar region, a hernia in his inguinal region, haemorrhoids in his perineal region. These regions are the:
o: Loin, Groin, between the anus and external genitalia respectively
Loin, groin and genital region respectively
Genital region, loin and groin respectively
Abdomen, loin and genital region respectively
questions.e: Lumbar = loin, inguinal = groin, perineal = area between anus and external genitalia.

questions.q: A student fell off a motorcycle and broke bones in his coxal, femoral, acromial and crural regions and tore a nerve in his axillary region. These regions are the:
o: Armpit, hip, thigh, shoulder and leg respectively
Thigh, shoulder, leg, armpit and hip respectively
Hip, thigh, shoulder, armpit and leg respectively
Leg, armpit, hip, thigh and shoulder respectively
Hip, thigh, shoulder, leg and armpit respectively
questions.e: Coxal = hip, femoral = thigh, acromial = shoulder, crural = leg, axillary = armpit.

questions.q: The anterior fontanelle closes during the second year of life and is then known as the:
questions.e: Once ossified, the anterior fontanelle becomes the bregma (junction of coronal and sagittal sutures).

questions.q: Two of the fingers on Theresa's right hand are fused by a web of skin. Ten-year-old Joseph has a small streak of white hair on top of his head although the rest is black. Both Theresa and Joseph exhibit:
questions.e: Minor syndactyly and a white forelock are harmless anatomical variations, not diseases.

questions.q: Which of the following forms the largest portion of the hip bone?
questions.e: The ilium is the large, fan-shaped superior portion of the hip bone.

questions.q: The membranous area between the occipital and parietal bones of the foetal skull is called
questions.e: Between the occipital and parietals lies the posterior fontanelle (becomes the lambda when closed).

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the axial skeleton?
o: The skull, vertebral column and pelvis
The skull, vertebral column and rib cage
The skull, shoulder girdles and rib cage
questions.e: Axial skeleton = skull + vertebral column + thoracic cage (ribs + sternum).

questions.q: The superior orbital fissure is formed in the sphenoid bone, whereas the inferior orbital fissure is formed between the sphenoid and
questions.e: The inferior orbital fissure lies between the greater wing of the sphenoid and the maxilla (with the palatine).

questions.q: What is the major function of the intervertebral discs?
questions.e: The discs act as shock-absorbing cushions between the vertebral bodies.

questions.q: Paranasal sinuses are found in which of these facial bones?
questions.e: Of the facial bones, the maxillae house paranasal (maxillary) sinuses.

questions.q: Which of the following is an abnormal lateral curvature of the vertebral column often seen in the thoracic region?
questions.e: Scoliosis is the abnormal lateral curvature.

questions.q: Which of the following ribs is a true rib?
questions.e: Ribs 1–7 are true (vertebrosternal) ribs, attaching directly to the sternum by their own costal cartilage.

questions.q: Which of the bones below is the first to ossify in pregnancy?
questions.e: The clavicle is the first bone to begin ossifying in the embryo (around week 5–6).

questions.q: A rounded opening in a bone is called
questions.e: A foramen is a round or oval hole through a bone (for vessels/nerves).

questions.q: Which of the following statements is not correct anatomically?
o: The index finger is medial to the pollex
The carpal bones are arranged into a proximal and distal rows of four bones each
The Axis is inferior to the Atlas
The eye brow is superior to the eye lid
The distal end of the radius lies lateral in a pronated antebrachium
questions.e: Incorrect: in pronation the radius crosses over the ulna, so its distal end lies MEDIALLY, not laterally.

questions.q: A flatten sheet of tendon is called
questions.e: An aponeurosis is a broad, flat sheet of tendon.

questions.q: A fibrous sheath that surrounds and protects individual fascicles of a muscle is called
questions.e: Perimysium wraps each fascicle; endomysium wraps single fibres; epimysium wraps the whole muscle.

questions.q: The prominent bump on the lateral aspect of the leg at the ankle joint is the
o: A lateral extension of the tibia
questions.e: The lateral malleolus (distal fibula) is the bony bump on the outer ankle.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the sacrum is false?
o: Is located on the posterior aspect of the pelvis
Articulates with L5 superiorly and the coccyx inferiorly
Its alae articulate with the two hip bones
Consists of six sacral vertebrae and four anterior foramina
questions.e: False: the sacrum has FIVE fused vertebrae and FOUR PAIRS (eight) of anterior sacral foramina.

questions.q: The enlargement of existing muscle fibres due to increasing diameters of cell but not increasing the number of new muscle fibres is known as
questions.e: Hypertrophy = larger existing fibres. Hyperplasia would be more fibres.

questions.q: How many cervical vertebrae are typically present in the body?
questions.e: There are 7 cervical vertebrae (C1–C7).

questions.q: Which one of these bones is not found in the pelvis?
questions.e: The hyoid is in the neck, not the pelvis.

questions.q: In which anatomic region of the abdomen would you expect to locate the gall bladder?
questions.e: The gall bladder sits under the liver in the right hypochondriac region.

questions.q: Barbara is 3 months pregnant and her doctor wants to measure the foetal head. Newton is suspected of a brain tumour. The imaging techniques used are:
o: Transabdominal ultrasonography and Positron emission tomography respectively
Positron emission tomography and Transvaginal ultrasonography respectively
Transabdominal ultrasonography and Magnetic resonance imaging respectively
Computed tomography and Transabdominal ultrasonography respectively
questions.e: Ultrasound (no radiation) for the foetus; MRI gives the best soft-tissue detail for a brain tumour.

questions.q: Body cavities and Membranes
o: The ventral body cavity is subdivided into a cranial cavity and a vertebral cavity
The thoracic cavity contains two pleural cavities and a thick band of organs called the mediastinum
The abdominal cavity contains the stomach, urinary bladder, uterus and the prostate gland
The serous pericardium is associated with the pericardial cavity and the lungs
Synovial cavities are enclosed within fibrous capsules that fill the sutures of the skull
questions.e: True: the thoracic cavity holds two pleural cavities plus the mediastinum. (A describes the dorsal cavity; the bladder/uterus/prostate are pelvic, not abdominal.)

questions.q: When the trunk is subjected to physical trauma as in automobile accidents, the most vulnerable organs are those within:
o: The pelvic cavity because the walls are formed only by muscles
The bony abdominal cavity because they have little protection
The thoracic cavity because they are well protected within the bony rib cage
The abdominal cavity because the walls are formed only by muscles without bone reinforcement
The thoracic cavity because they have little protection
questions.e: Abdominal organs are least protected — the wall is muscular with no bony cage.

questions.q: Which canal and three foramina are found going through the sphenoid bone?
o: Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, foramen ovale and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, jugular foramen and foramen spinosum
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, foramen ovale and foramen magnum
Optic canal, stylomastoid foramen, jugular foramen and foramen magnum
questions.e: Sphenoid openings: optic canal + foramen rotundum + foramen ovale + foramen spinosum.

questions.q: Which of the following are associated with the ethmoid bone?
o: Crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate and superior nasal conchae
Styloid process, inferior nasal conchae, jugular foramen and carotid canal
Optic canal, foramen rotundum, hypoglossal canal and foramen ovale
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Ethmoid: crista galli, cribriform plates, perpendicular plate, superior & middle nasal conchae.

questions.q: Which nasal concha(e) is a facial bone?
questions.e: The inferior nasal concha is a separate facial bone; superior and middle conchae are parts of the ethmoid (a cranial bone).

questions.q: Demifacets are a characteristic of which type of vertebrae?
questions.e: Thoracic vertebrae bear costal demifacets for rib heads.

questions.q: On which bone is the head found at the distal end?
questions.e: The ulnar head is distal (the radial head is proximal).

questions.q: The lesser trochanter, intertrochanteric crest and gluteal tuberosity are found on the
questions.e: These are all markings of the femur.

questions.q: Which tarsal bone is the keystone of the medial longitudinal arch?
questions.e: This paper's key names the navicular. noteMany textbooks give the head of the TALUS as the true keystone of the medial longitudinal arch — worth knowing both.

questions.q: Assume the body is sectioned along a median sagittal, a frontal or a transverse plane at the level of each organ. Which organs would not be visible in all three cases?
questions.e: The lungs and kidneys are paired and lie off the midline, so a median (mid-sagittal) plane would miss them.

questions.q: Place the following from darkest (black) to lightest (white) as they appear on X-ray film: 1. Soft tissue 2. Femur 3. Air in the lungs 4. Gold metal filling
questions.e: Radiolucent → radiodense: air (darkest) → soft tissue → bone → metal (whitest): 3, 1, 2, 4.

questions.q: The proximal row of carpal bones includes which of the following?
questions.e: Proximal row (lateral→medial): scaphoid, lunate, triquetrum, pisiform.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is/are not weight bearing?
questions.e: The fibula transmits little/no body weight; it mainly serves for muscle attachment and ankle stability.

questions.q: Which portion of the fibula articulates with the talus?
questions.e: The lateral malleolus of the fibula forms the lateral wall of the ankle mortise, articulating with the talus.

questions.q: How many bones comprise the skull?
questions.e: 22 bones: 8 cranial + 14 facial.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is not an integral bone of the skull and is not attached by sutures to the remainder of the skull bones
questions.e: The mandible joins the skull at the mobile temporomandibular joint, not by sutures.

questions.q: The skull bone that is connected to the rest of the cranium posteriorly via the coronal suture is the
questions.e: The paper's key is the parietal (its anterior border meets the frontal at the coronal suture).

questions.q: The skull bone that provides the major passageway for the brain to communicate with the rest of the body is the
questions.e: The occipital bone contains the foramen magnum, through which the brainstem/spinal cord passes.

questions.q: Which structure serves as a ‘seat’ of the endocrine system by supporting the pituitary gland?
o: Greater wings of the sphenoid bone
Lesser wings of the sphenoid bone
questions.e: The sella turcica of the sphenoid cradles the pituitary gland.

questions.q: Which of the following bones does not articulate directly with any other bone in the skeleton?
questions.e: The hyoid forms no bony joint — it is suspended by muscles and ligaments.

questions.q: How many bones make up the adult vertebral column?
questions.e: 26 bones: 24 individual vertebrae (7C, 12T, 5L) + sacrum + coccyx.

questions.q: Which phrase best describes the function of the vertebral curves?
o: To improve cervical center of gravity
To accommodate the weight of the pelvic girdle
questions.e: The curves act like springs, giving the column resilience and flexibility while supporting weight.

questions.q: Which part of the vertebral column receives the most stress by bearing most of the weight of the body?
questions.e: The lumbar vertebrae carry the most weight (hence their massive bodies).

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.e: Only thoracic vertebrae have costal facets/demifacets for the ribs.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.e: Transverse foramina are the hallmark of cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae differ from the other vertebrae in that they have
questions.e: Lumbar vertebrae have large, thick (massive) bodies to bear weight.

questions.q: What is the major function of the axial skeleton?
o: Provide an attachment point for muscles that allow movement
Provide central support for the body and protect internal organs
Provide a space for the major digestive organs
questions.e: The axial skeleton supports the body's long axis and protects the brain, spinal cord and thoracic organs.

questions.q: The antebrachium is composed of which of the following two bones?
questions.e: Antebrachium = forearm = radius + ulna.

questions.q: The ‘true wrist’ or carpus consists of
o: A group of eight short bones united by ligaments
The styloid processes of the radius and ulna
A group of eight short bones and the metacarpals
questions.e: The carpus is the 8 carpal bones bound by ligaments in two rows.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the paranasal sinuses?
o: Paranasal sinuses open into the oral cavity.
Paranasal sinuses enhance the resonance of the voice and lighten the skull.
Paranasal sinuses contain passages acting as one-way valves.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, ethmoid, and lacrimal bones.
Paranasal sinuses are found in maxillary, frontal and lacrimal bones.
questions.e: Sinuses lighten the skull and add resonance to the voice. (They occur in frontal, ethmoid, sphenoid and maxillary bones — not the lacrimal.)

questions.q: Which bone contains diaphysis and epiphysis areas and is proportionally more compact than spongy bone?
questions.e: A long bone — the humerus — has a diaphysis and epiphyses and is predominantly compact bone.

questions.q: Cervical vertebrae can be uniquely identified by the presence of
questions.e: Transverse foramina are unique to cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: Which of the following are responsible for nodding ‘yes’ and for shaking your head ‘no’?
o: Occipital condyles and odontoid process respectively
Odontoid process and occipital condyles respectively
Occipital condyles and odontoid process of atlas respectively
questions.e: 'Yes' = atlanto-occipital (atlas); 'no' = atlanto-axial rotation (axis).

questions.q: The only group of vertebrae that articulates with the ribs is
questions.e: Only thoracic vertebrae articulate with ribs.

questions.q: Which of the following organs lies directly posterior to the sternum?
questions.e: The heart (in the mediastinum) lies just behind the sternum.

questions.q: Which two carpals articulate with the radius to form the wrist joint?
questions.e: The scaphoid and lunate articulate with the distal radius at the radiocarpal (wrist) joint.

questions.q: Which of these bones would bear a ring?
questions.e: A ring is worn on a finger — around a (proximal) phalanx.

questions.q: Which of the following bones is capable of bearing the greatest physical stress?
questions.e: The femur is the strongest, largest weight-bearing bone.

questions.q: The bone(s) of the leg which bears no weight is/are
questions.e: The fibula bears essentially no body weight.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a cranial bone?
questions.e: The maxilla is a facial bone; the other four are cranial.

questions.q: The side to which a scapula belongs can be determined from the following:
o: The large concave surface is posterior
The spine projects from the posterior surface and extends laterally as the acromion
The acromion and glenoid cavity belong to the lower and lateral part of the scapula
Supraspinous and infraspinous fossae are located on the anterior surface
Coracoid process is located on the posterior surface
questions.e: On the posterior surface, the spine runs laterally and expands into the acromion — the key orientation clue.

questions.q: The following are features of the humerus EXCEPT:
o: It articulates with the scapula at the shoulder
It consists of a shaft and two ends
The proximal end consists of the condyle, the medial epicondyle and the lateral epicondyle
The proximal end consists of the head, anatomical neck, and two tubercles
The distal end consists of the two condyles, a medial trochlea and a lateral capitulum
questions.e: Wrong: the condyle and epicondyles are DISTAL features, not proximal.

questions.q: The bony pelvis:
o: Consists of the two hip bones, sacrum and coccyx
In the female it is generally wider, shallower and lighter and adapted for childbearing
Has a pelvic inlet and pelvic outlet
The outlet is bounded anteriorly by the pubic arch, laterally by the ischial tuberosities, posteriorly by the sacrum and coccyx
All the above are features of the bony pelvis
questions.e: All the statements are correct descriptions of the bony pelvis.

questions.q: The patella:
o: Is a sesamoid bone that articulates with the femur, tibia and fibula
Enclosed in the tendon that secures the anterior thigh muscles to the tibia
Has an apex that is directed superiorly and a base that is inferior
questions.e: The patella protects the front of the knee. (It articulates only with the femur; its apex points DOWN, base up — so A and D are wrong.)

questions.q: The foot:
o: Consists of the tarsals, metacarpals and phalanges
Has 2 arches; medial longitudinal arch and lateral longitudinal arch
It has 7 tarsal bones, 5 metatarsal bones and 12 phalanges
It has 3 cuneiforms; superior, inferior and intermediate cuneiforms
questions.e: The foot has a medial and a lateral longitudinal arch (plus a transverse arch). (A says metacarpals; the foot has 14 phalanges; the cuneiforms are medial/intermediate/lateral.)

questions.q: In the anatomical position the:
o: Arms are extended away from the body
Palms of the hands face posteriorly
Body is erect and palms face anterior
Body is in a foetal position.
The thumb is medial to the little finger
questions.e: Anatomical position: standing erect, arms at sides, palms facing forward (anteriorly).

questions.q: If Robert's left kidney was deep to his last two left lower ribs, these ribs will be
questions.e: 'Deep to' is the opposite of 'superficial' — so relative to the kidney, the ribs are superficial.

questions.q: The tibia is formed from which of the following during foetal life?
questions.e: Long bones like the tibia form by endochondral ossification: mesenchyme condenses into a cartilage model that is replaced by bone.

questions.q: All synovial joints have the following structural characteristics
o: The joint surfaces are enclosed by a two-layered articular capsule
The inner layer is the synovial membrane
The outer layer is the fibrous capsule
Articular cartilage covers the surfaces of the bones forming the joint
questions.e: All are defining features of synovial joints.

questions.q: Sexual differences in the human skeleton
o: The mandible is larger and more robust in the female
Male bones are heavier with prominent bone markings
The male pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep than the female pelvis
The sacrum is a long narrow triangle with a less pronounced sacral curvature in the female
The female cranium is about 10% larger on the average
questions.e: True: the male pelvis is narrower/deeper with a heart-shaped inlet; the female pelvis is wider and shallower. (Male bones/mandible are more robust; male cranium is larger.)

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Humerus
Match to the correct term: Sternum
Match to the correct term: Vertebrae
Match to the correct term: Clavicle
questions.e: The clavicle is classed as a long bone (it has a shaft and two ends), even though it is short and curved.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Has a medial ankle projection
questions.e: The calcaneus bears the sustentaculum tali, a medial shelf-like projection. (The tibia's medial malleolus is not one of the options here.)

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Bone of the axial skeleton to which the pectoral girdle attaches
questions.e: The pectoral girdle attaches to the axial skeleton only at the sternum (sternoclavicular joint).

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Markings include glenoid cavity and acromion
Match to the correct term: Features include ala, crest and greater sciatic notch
Match to the correct term: Doubly curved; acts as shoulder strut
Match to the correct term: Pelvic girdle bone that articulates with the axial skeleton
questions.e: The ilium meets the sacrum at the sacroiliac joint.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: The sit-down bone
questions.e: The ischial tuberosities bear your weight when sitting.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Bone that carries the hand
questions.e: The hand hangs from the radius via the radiocarpal joint.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Is the largest, longest bone of the upper limb
Match to the correct term: Its distal end articulates with the radius and ulna
Match to the correct term: Is the longer and more medial bone of the forearm
questions.e: The ulna is the longer, medial forearm bone.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Part of it forms the heel of the foot
questions.e: The calcaneus (a tarsal) forms the heel.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: This bone is thin at its proximal end and widens distally
questions.e: The radius has a small proximal head and a broad distal end.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Its head is shaped like the head of a nail
questions.e: The radial head is a flat disc, like a nail-head.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Transmits weight to the foot
Match to the correct term: Made up of seven bones
questions.e: There are 7 tarsal bones.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Major forearm bone contributing to the wrist joint
Match to the correct term: Contributes more heavily to the elbow joint
questions.e: The ulna's trochlear notch is the main forearm contribution at the elbow.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Its distal end bears a head and a styloid process
questions.e: The ulna's distal end has both a head and a styloid process.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: This bone grips the humerus to form a stable hinge joint
questions.e: The ulna's trochlear notch wraps the trochlea of the humerus.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: From its styloid process a ligament extends to the wrist
Match to the correct term: Anteriormost bone of the pelvic girdle
Match to the correct term: Part of the vertebral column
Match to the correct term: Articulates with the acetabulum and tibia
questions.e: The femur head sits in the acetabulum; its distal end meets the tibia.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Consists of 2 rows of bones
Match to the correct term: Forms the lateral aspect of the ankle
Match to the correct term: The wrist bones
Match to the correct term: Triangular bone which shapes the posterior wall of the pelvis
Match to the correct term: The bone that strengthens and stabilizes the pelvis
Match to the correct term: It is formed by five fused vertebrae in the adult
Match to the correct term: Its inferior end has an enlarged external opening
questions.e: The sacral canal ends inferiorly at the sacral hiatus.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: The bodies of these bones are joined by a fibrocartilage disc
questions.e: The two pubic bones are joined at the pubic symphysis by an interpubic fibrocartilage disc.

questions.q: Match to the correct term: Is the largest, strongest and longest bone in the body
Match to the correct term: It does not bear weight but several muscles originate from it
questions.e: The fibula is non-weight-bearing but gives many muscle origins.

questions.q: The mandible is considered as the keystone bone of the facial skeleton.
questions.e: The maxilla is the keystone of the face. The mandible is the largest/strongest facial bone.

questions.q: The zygomatic bones are commonly known as the cheekbones.
The lacrimal bones contain a sac that gathers tears.
questions.e: The lacrimal fossa lodges the lacrimal sac.

questions.q: The vomer is located within the nasal cavity forming the inferior part of the nasal septum.
The lacrimal bones are very small bones which form the medial wall of each orbit.
Failure of the maxillae to fuse causes a condition known as cleft palate.
The temporal bone houses the apparatus of the internal and middle ear.
The sphenoid bone is a wing-shaped bone that extends behind the eyes and forms part of the floor of the cranial vault.
The Maxillae are the bones that contain teeth.
questions.e: They hold the upper teeth (the mandible holds the lower).

questions.q: The Lacrimal bone contains a passageway into the nasal cavity.
questions.e: The nasolacrimal duct drains tears into the nasal cavity.

questions.q: The axis or C2 vertebra has a projection called the dens that allows the axis to pivot.
questions.e: The dens is the pivot about which the atlas (and head) rotate.

questions.q: The hyoid acts as an attachment point for muscles in the neck region to connect the muscles in the lower jaw region.
The hyoid serves as a movable base for the tongue.
The horns of the hyoid are attachment points for neck muscles that raise and lower the larynx during speech and swallowing.
The xiphoid process is somewhat fragile and may break if pressed and puncture internal organs.
The maxillae are the largest and strongest bones of the face.
questions.e: The mandible is the largest and strongest facial bone.

questions.q: The female pelvis is broader with a heart-shaped inlet and relatively deep for childbearing.
questions.e: The female pelvis is broader but SHALLOWER, with a rounder/oval inlet. The heart-shaped, deep inlet is the male pattern.

questions.q: The sacrum is a long narrow triangle with a less pronounced sacral curvature in the male.
The fingers have two phalanges each whereas the thumb has three phalanges.
questions.e: Reversed: fingers have three phalanges, the thumb has two.

questions.q: The head of the humerus articulates with the glenoid fossa of the scapula.
The ulna is the forearm bone that articulates with most of the carpal bones.
questions.e: The RADIUS articulates with the carpals; the ulna is separated from them by an articular disc.

questions.q: Thoracic vertebrae have the thickest bodies and short blunt spinous processes.
questions.e: Lumbar vertebrae have the thickest bodies; thoracic spinous processes are long and point sharply downward.

questions.q: The coccyx is the fused rudimentary tailbone.
The axis is a circle of bone that articulates superiorly with the occipital condyles.
questions.e: That describes the ATLAS (C1).

questions.q: Lumbar vertebrae have articular facets for the ribs.
questions.e: Only thoracic vertebrae have costal facets.

questions.q: The lambdoid suture connects the frontal and parietal bones.
questions.e: The lambdoid connects the parietals to the occipital; the coronal connects frontal to parietals.

questions.q: The sagittal suture connects the parietal and occipital bones.
questions.e: The sagittal suture connects the two parietal bones to each other.

questions.q: The squamosal suture connects the temporal and parietal bones.
The coronal suture connects the right and left parietal bones.
questions.e: That is the sagittal suture. The coronal connects the frontal to the parietals.

questions.q: The occipitomastoid suture connects the temporal and parietal bones.
questions.e: It connects the occipital bone to the mastoid part of the temporal bone.

questions.q: All of the bones of the skull, except the mandible, are united by sutures and are immovable.
The foramen magnum goes through the occipital bone.
The mastoid sinuses are located at a position in the skull where they are usually free from infections.
questions.e: The mastoid air cells communicate with the middle ear and are prone to infection (mastoiditis).

questions.q: The vertebral column is held in place primarily by the anterior and posterior longitudinal ligaments.
The last two ribs are floating ribs because they have no anterior attachments.
questions.e: Ribs 11 and 12 have no anterior (costal cartilage/sternal) attachment.

questions.q: The most common site of fracture in the humerus is the surgical neck.
The layman's name for the scapula is the collar bone.
questions.e: The scapula is the shoulder blade; the clavicle is the collar bone.

questions.q: A temporal bone protrusion riddled with sinuses is the styloid process.
questions.e: That describes the MASTOID process; the styloid is a thin spike with no air cells.

questions.q: Costal cartilages join most ribs to the sternum.
The tubercle of a rib articulates with the transverse process of a vertebra.
In women of childbearing age, the dimensions of the true pelvis are of utmost importance.
The term vertebrochondral ribs refers to ribs that attach to each other before they attach to the sternum.
questions.e: Vertebrochondral ribs (8–10) attach via cartilage to the rib above rather than directly to the sternum.

questions.q: In the anatomical position, the lateral forearm bone is the radius.
The vomer forms part of the nasal septum.
The cranial vault of the skull is also called the calvaria.
The lacrimal bones contain openings that provide a passage for the tear ducts.
The largest and strongest bone of the face is the maxilla.
questions.e: It is the mandible.

questions.q: There are seven cervical, twelve thoracic, and five lumbar vertebrae in the vertebral column.
Lordosis affects the thoracic vertebrae.
questions.e: Lordosis is a lumbar problem; kyphosis affects the thoracic region.

questions.q: All vertebrae possess a body, a spine, and transverse foramina.
questions.e: Only cervical vertebrae have transverse foramina, and the atlas has no body.

questions.q: The dens articulates with the axis.
questions.e: The dens is PART of the axis; it articulates with the anterior arch of the atlas.

questions.q: The ischium articulates with both the ilium and the pubis.
The talus is the heel bone.
questions.e: The heel bone is the calcaneus.

The largest foramen in the body is the obturator foramen.
The smallest short bone in the hand is the pisiform.
The styloid process of the radius points to the thumb.
questions.e: The radial styloid is on the lateral (thumb) side of the wrist.

questions.q: The femur, tibia, fibula, talus are weight-bearing bones.
questions.e: The fibula does not bear weight.

questions.q: The large fossa on the anterior aspect of the scapula is the subscapular fossa.
Only the lumbar vertebrae have transverse foramina.
questions.e: Transverse foramina belong to the cervical vertebrae.

questions.q: The vomer is the primary bone in the septum of the nose.
questions.e: The vomer (with the perpendicular plate of the ethmoid) forms the bony nasal septum.

questions.q: The ‘cheekbone’ is mostly formed from the zygomatic bone.
The vertebra prominens is a spinous process that is visible through the skin.
questions.e: It is the long spinous process of C7.

questions.q: The vertebra prominens can be used as a landmark for counting the vertebrae.
The lumbar curvature positions the weight of the trunk over the body's centre of gravity.
Scoliosis is the most serious vertebral curvature abnormality, due to the pressure that can be placed on the lungs and resulting breathing difficulties.
questions.e: Severe scoliosis can compress the thoracic cavity and impair breathing.

The flexibility fontanelles impart to the foetal skull helps to ease the delivery of the child.
The nucleus pulposus of intervertebral discs gives the discs elasticity and compressibility.
The anulus fibrosus of intervertebral discs limits expansion and holds successive vertebrae together.
The lower limbs carry the weight of the body and are subject to exceptional forces.
The lower limb bones are thicker and stronger whereas the upper limb bones are smaller and lighter, adapted for flexibility and mobility.
The pectoral girdle moves freely across the thorax and allows the upper limb a high degree of mobility.

The pelvic girdle is secured to the axial skeleton to provide strength and support.

The acetabulum of the pelvis is a deep socket.

The following features are observed during intramembranous ossification: i. Modulation of osteoprogenitor ii. Secretion of matrix iii. Formation of spicules iv. Confluence of spicules v. Transformation of spongy bone to compact bone
questions.e: Intramembranous ossification runs through all these steps, from osteoprogenitor differentiation to remodelling of spongy into compact bone.

questions.q: Endochondral ossification shows the following features: i. Zone of proliferation ii. Zone of cell maturation iii. Zone of calcifying cartilage
o: None of the above are correct
questions.e: The epiphyseal (growth) plate shows all these zones as cartilage is progressively replaced by bone.

questions.q: Suture
o: Joint in which bones are tightly bound by a minimal amount of fibrous connective tissue
The edges of the joining bones are wavy and interlock
Knits the bones together and allows growth at the edges
In adulthood the immobility of this joint is a protective adaptation
questions.e: All statements describe cranial sutures.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding epithelial tissues is FALSE?
o: Junctional complexes are found at numerous sites between adjacent epithelial cells
Stereocilia are extremely long form of microvilli
the principal function of microvilli is to increase greatly the surface area of cells
Desmosomes are sites of strong intercellular adhesion and provide points of attachment for elements of the cytoskeleton
Cilia constitute the characteristic brush border of the small intestine
questions.e: The brush (striated) border of the small intestine is made of microvilli, not cilia — so E is the false statement. Everything else is true, including the fact that stereocilia are really long, branching microvilli.

questions.q: Striated borders:
o: Consist of tightly packed cilia and usually line the respiratory tract
Consist of tightly packed microvilli and usually line blood vessels
Consist of tightly packed stereocilia and usually line the proximal segment of the nephron
Consist of tightly packed stereocilia and microvilli and usually line male reproductive tract
Consist of tightly packed microvilli and usually line intestinal absorptive cells
questions.e: Striated border = closely packed microvilli on intestinal absorptive cells (enterocytes). The kidney proximal tubule version is called a brush border; both are microvilli.

questions.q: Stereocilia are present in epithelial linings of the following organs:
o: Ileum, colon, trachea and respiratory bronchioles, membranous urethra
Primary bronchi and gallbladder, vas deferens, penile urethra
Trachea, epididymis, penile urethra, membranous urethra
questions.e: Stereocilia occur in only two places worth memorising: the epididymis and vas deferens (and the sensory hair cells of the inner ear). Every other option smuggles in a respiratory or gut site.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location, showed 3 layers of cells that were taller than wide. The cells lacked surface specialization. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
o: Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and ureter
Ureter, spongy urethra and prostatic urethra
Membranous urethra and fossa navicularis of the penis
questions.e: Several layers of tall (columnar) cells with no surface specialisation = stratified columnar epithelium — found in the membranous and spongy (penile) urethra. The ureter and bladder are transitional; the fossa navicularis is stratified squamous.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location revealed cells that were taller than wide and appeared to be more than one-cell layer thick. However all the cells were attached to the basement membrane and some had cilia. Goblets cells were also present. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
o: Nasal cavity, larynx and secondary bronchi
Trachea, membranous urethra and vas deferens
Primary bronchi, terminal bronchioles and the epiglottis
Penile urethra, primary bronchi and respiratory bronchioles
questions.e: Every cell touching the basement membrane while looking layered = pseudostratified; add cilia and goblet cells and it is respiratory epithelium — nasal cavity, larynx, trachea and bronchi down to the secondary bronchi. Terminal and respiratory bronchioles have lost their goblet cells, so C and E fail.

questions.q: Examination of three different specimens from unknown locations, showed that specimen A was taken from a chamber that changes its volume continually, specimen B was from a surface where both absorption and secretion are required and specimen C was from an internal surface where friction may occur. Specimens A, B, C were obtained from:
o: Uterus, ileum and anal canal respectively
Ureter, ductuli efferentes and cornea respectively
Penile urethra, jejunum, laryngeal surface of epiglottis respectively
