Urinary bladder, duodenum and vagina respectively
Vas deferens, small intestine and pharynx respectively
questions.e: Changing volume → transitional → urinary bladder. Absorption + secretion → simple columnar → duodenum. Internal surface exposed to friction → non-keratinised stratified squamous → vagina.

questions.q: Examination of three different specimens from unknown locations showed that specimen A was taken from a surface that was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses, specimen B was from a surface where either filtration or diffusion occurs and specimen C was from an internal chamber where absorption and motility are required. Specimens A, B, C were obtained from:
o: Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and vagina respectively
Hard palate, respirtory bronchioles and oesophagus respectively
Skin, alveoli of lungs, efferent ductules respectively
Soles of feet, visceral layer of renal corpuscle and oesophagus respectively
Filiform papillae of tongue, endothelium of blood vessels and skin respectively
questions.e: Severe mechanical stress → keratinised stratified squamous → skin. Diffusion → simple squamous → alveoli. Absorption plus motility (microvilli AND cilia together) → ductuli efferentes of the testis, the classic example.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium is found in all the following EXCEPT
questions.e: Urothelium runs from the renal pelvis through ureter, bladder and prostatic urethra, then stops. The membranous urethra is stratified/pseudostratified columnar.

questions.q: A basal lamina:
o: Is a cellular layer secreted by epithelial tissues only
Is a noncellular layer between adjacent epithelial cells
Is believed to be secreted by the muscle and epithelial cells only
Contains PAS positive glycoproteins and lies between epithelium and connective tissue
questions.e: The basal lamina is non-cellular, sits at the epithelium–connective tissue border, and stains PAS-positive because of its glycoproteins (laminin) and type IV collagen. Note type IV is a network collagen, not fibrillar, which kills option D.

questions.q: The muscular system:
o: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression
questions.e: Manipulation, locomotion and expression, posture, and heat generation are all standard muscular-system functions.

questions.q: Excretory glands are classified as simple branched tubular and merocrine by the:
o: Types of secretory products and mechanism of secretion
Shape of secretory units and types of ducts only
Presence or absence of ducts and mechanism of secretion
Mechanism of secretion and shape of secetory units
Nature of the ducts, shape of secretory unit and mechanism of secretion
questions.e: Unpack the name: simple = the duct is unbranched (nature of duct), branched tubular = shape of the secretory unit, merocrine = mechanism of secretion. Three criteria, so E.

questions.q: Specimens A and B are made up of secretory epithelial cells, ducts and connective tissue. Both specimens have a combination of tubular and spherical secretory units. The secretory units are dark-stained with round nuclei that were either central or basally located. A and B have ducts with several branches. Specimens A and B are surrounded by dense irregular connective tissue. Fibrous extensions from the connective tissue divide the specimens into compartments. In addition specimen B has small clusters of secretory cells that lack ducts and are closely associated with blood vessels.Which conclusion is correct?
o: Specimens A and B are both exocrine with serous secretory units.
Specimen A is solely serous-secreting whereas B is both exocrine and endocrine.
Specimens A and B are the parotid and pancreas respectively
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Branched ducts + tubuloacinar units + a capsule sending septa in = a compound gland. Dark serous units only → the parotid (specimen A). B has the same plus ductless cell clusters hugging capillaries — islets of Langerhans → the pancreas, which is both exocrine and endocrine. So B and C are right, which makes A ('both exocrine') incomplete.

questions.q: You are given a specimen with several clusters of epithelial cells embedded completely in connective tissue. Some of the cell clusters were dark-stained with central round nuclei whereas others were pale-stained with peripheral flattened nuclei. In addition epithelially-lined passages that link the cell clusters to an epithelially-lined surface were present. The passages were unbranched.The specimen is
o: Contains both simple squamous and simple cuboidal epithelial tissues
A simple endocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
A simple exocrine gland with serous and mucous secretory units
Is from an organ which secretes both endocrine and exocrine products
Is a gland that secretes a watery product rich in enzymes
questions.e: Ducts are present and unbranched → simple exocrine gland. Dark units with central round nuclei = serous; pale units with flattened peripheral nuclei = mucous. So a simple exocrine gland with both unit types (mixed/seromucous).

questions.q: Regarding the characteristics of HYALINE CARTILAGE evaluate the following statements:
o: It has a smooth appearance and contains abundant ground substance and isogenous groups of chondrocytes
It contains more elastic fibres than collagen type II fibres and is found in the thyroid, cricoid and corniculate cartilages of the larynx
It contains collagen type II fibres and abundant ground substance and is found in the intervertebral discs and the epiglottis only
It contains collagen type I fibres, few chondrocytes arranged in rows and a fluid small ground
Its chondrocytes occur singly and it is the main supporting framework of the epiglottis, cuneiform cartilage of the larynx and the intrapulmonary bronchi
questions.e: Hyaline cartilage looks glassy and smooth because its type II fibres are masked by abundant ground substance, and its chondrocytes sit in isogenous groups. D describes fibrocartilage; the epiglottis and cuneiform cartilage are elastic, killing C and E.

questions.q: The functions of the nervous system include the following
o: Responds to internal and external changes
Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction
Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
Maintenance of the extracellular fluid volume
questions.e: Detecting and responding to internal and external change is the defining nervous-system function. B, C, D and E are endocrine or urinary jobs.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location revealed several layers of cells. Only the basal layer of cells was attached to the basement membrane. The basal cells were taller than wide, the intermediate layers contained polyhedral cells and the superficial cell nuclei were flattened in a horizontal plane. The superficial cells were covered with an eosinophilic transluscent band that was anucleated. Parts of the surface also had fibrillar, anucleated, eosinophilic structures. Goblets cells, cilia, microvilli and stereocilia were absent.This epithelium is most likely to be located:
o: In the oesophagus, cornea, vagina and tongue
Tongue, soft palate, oral surface of lips and anal canal
In an internal environment that is subject to abrasion or the external environment
questions.e: This is stratified squamous epithelium showing both patterns at once: a non-keratinised translucent surface and patches of keratin. That combination is not one named organ — it is the general answer: any surface facing abrasion, internal or external.

questions.q: You are given cartilage from an unknown location, you think it is from the pinna of the ear because:
o: It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
It contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
Numerous chondroblasts that are arranged into isogenous groups
questions.e: The pinna (auricle) is the textbook site of elastic cartilage, along with the epiglottis, auditory tube and the corniculate and cuneiform cartilages.

questions.q: Which of the following tissue(s) would be most affected by chemotherapy?
questions.e: Chemotherapy hits rapidly dividing cells. Epithelium — gut lining, skin, hair follicles, bone marrow — turns over fastest, which is why mucositis and hair loss are the classic side effects.

questions.q: Cartilage is different from bone in that
o: Cartilage contains about 80% water and is more resilient
Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in the adult skeleton.
questions.e: Cartilage matrix is roughly 80% water bound to proteoglycans, which is exactly what makes it resilient under compression. It is avascular (killing C), it does calcify with age (D), and it heals far more slowly than bone (E).

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of cartilage?
o: Provision of an embryonic model prior to developmnt of long bones.
Provision of rigidity to soft tissues requiring support.
Allowing long bones to increase in length
Provision of a smooth surface for epiphyses of articulating joints
Maintenance of a tubular shape of structures in the digestive tract
questions.e: Cartilage keeps the airway tubular — trachea and bronchi — not the digestive tract, which stays patent by muscle tone. A, B, C and D are all real cartilage functions.

questions.q: Which of the following relationships between a tissue and its general function is NOT correct?
questions.e: Epithelium's general functions are protection, absorption, secretion and filtration. Digestion itself is the work of secreted enzymes and the gut as an organ, not a general epithelial function.

questions.q: An area in the body exposed to the external environment would be composed of which of the following tissue types?
questions.e: Every body surface and cavity that meets the outside world is covered by epithelium — that is its defining role.

questions.q: Which of the following tissue types would you expect to find on a surface of the body that is subject to friction?
questions.e: Surfaces facing friction are covered by epithelium — specifically stratified squamous, which sheds and replaces its surface cells.

questions.q: Which characteristic of epithelial tissues would you expect to find in a duct that is subject to a high degree of pressure?
questions.e: Extra layers are the epithelium's answer to mechanical stress — a large duct under pressure lines itself with stratified epithelium.

questions.q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissues is best suited for areas of the body where diffusion or filtration occurs?
questions.e: Simple squamous is one flat cell thick — the shortest possible diffusion path. Hence alveoli, endothelium and the renal corpuscle.

questions.q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissues is best adapted for a chamber which changes its volume continuously?
questions.e: Transitional epithelium's umbrella cells flatten and slide as the bladder distends, then dome up again when empty.

questions.q: Which of the following terms reflects the epithelial tissue found lining blood and lymphatic vessels?
questions.e: Endothelium lines blood and lymphatic vessels; mesothelium lines the serous cavities (pleura, pericardium, peritoneum); urothelium lines the urinary tract.

questions.q: Which of the following types of epithelial tissues is normally found in glands?
questions.e: Simple cuboidal is the standard secretory epithelium — glandular acini and small ducts.

questions.q: The mucus-secreting cells prevalent in simple columnar epithelium are known as
questions.e: Goblet cells are unicellular exocrine glands wedged among columnar cells, releasing mucin by merocrine exocytosis.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about epithelia?
o: Simple epithelia are commonly found in areas of high abrasion.
Stratified epithelia are associated with filtration.
Endothelium provides a slick surface lining all hollow cardiovascular organs
questions.e: Endothelium is the continuous, friction-free lining of heart chambers and every vessel. A is backwards (stratified handles abrasion), B and E swap filtration onto the wrong epithelia, and pseudostratified is never keratinised.

questions.q: The type of epithelium which appears to have two or three layers of cells, although all the cells are in contact with the basement membrane is
questions.e: That is the definition of pseudostratified: the nuclei sit at different heights so it looks layered, but every cell reaches the basement membrane.

questions.q: A multilayered epithelium with cuboidal basal cells and flat cells at its surface would be classified as
questions.e: Stratified epithelia are named for the shape of their surface cells — flat surface cells means stratified squamous, whatever the basal layer looks like.

questions.q: An epithelial membrane:
o: Is formed of epithelium and smooth muscle
Contains simple or stratified epithelia and a basement membrane
questions.e: An epithelial membrane is an epithelial sheet — simple or stratified — resting on its basement membrane and a thin layer of connective tissue. Mucous membranes are full of mucus-secreting cells, so D is wrong.

questions.q: Multicellular exocrine glands can be classified
o: Structurally into alveolar and acinar types
Structurally into vascular and avascular types
Functionally into merocrine, holocrine, and apocrine divisions
Functionally into secreting or nonsecreting types
questions.e: Structural classification is by the shape of the secretory unit — tubular, alveolar/acinar, or tubuloalveolar. noteOption C is also a real classification, but merocrine/apocrine/holocrine is a mode-of-secretion scheme rather than a functional one, which is why the paper takes A.

questions.q: Which of the following is TRUE about the mode of secretion of exocrine glands?
o: Merocrine glands are not altered by the secretory process.
Apocrine cells are destroyed, then replaced, after secretion.
Holocrine cells are slightly damaged by the secretory process, but repair themselves.
Apocrine cells retain their secretory products
questions.e: Merocrine secretion is pure exocytosis — the cell loses no substance and is unchanged. correctedThe tick on the paper sits between A and B, but B describes holocrine glands (whole cell destroyed and replaced); apocrine cells only shed a cap of apical cytoplasm. A is the true statement.

questions.q: In adults, new surface epithelial cells and the epithelial cells lining the intestine are derived from
o: Mitotic division of existing epithelial cells
questions.e: Replacement comes from a dedicated stem-cell population — in the gut, the cells at the base of the intestinal crypts, which divide and differentiate as they migrate up the villus.

questions.q: Which cells are commonly found wedged between simple columnar epithelial cells?
questions.e: Goblet cells sit interspersed among the columnar absorptive cells. Mast cells and macrophages live in connective tissue, not within the epithelium.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding epithelia.
o: Stratified epithelia are tall, narrow cells.
Stratified epithelia are present where protection from abrasion is important.
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of at least two layers of cells stacked on top of one another.
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of several layers of cuboidal cells
questions.e: Layers exist for protection against wear. Simple epithelia are built for exchange, not impermeability, and pseudostratified epithelia only look layered — nothing is stacked.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding multicellular exocrine glands
o: Compound glands are so called because they are constructed from more than one cell type.
The secretory cells of holocrine glands release their product by rupturing.
Merocrine glands release their secretion by pinching off part of the cell.
Compound glands are always constructed from mucous cells.
questions.e: Holocrine cells fill with product, die and rupture — the sebaceous gland pattern. 'Compound' refers to a branched duct, not cell types; exocrine glands are defined by having ducts; and pinching off apical cytoplasm is apocrine, not merocrine.

questions.q: Which of the following is not found in the matrix of cartilage but present in bone?
questions.e: Cartilage is avascular — it feeds by diffusion from the perichondrium. Bone is richly vascular, with vessels in Haversian and Volkmann's canals. Both have living cells in lacunae and collagen fibres.

questions.q: Intervertebral discs exhibit a large amount of tensile strength to absorb shock because they possess
questions.e: The anulus fibrosus is fibrocartilage — thick bundles of type I collagen, the fibre that supplies tensile strength.

questions.q: Which of the following tissues contains lacunae, calcium salts, and blood vessels?
questions.e: Only bone has all three at once. Cartilage has lacunae but no vessels and normally no calcium salts.

questions.q: Chondroblasts
o: Are mature cartilage cells located in spaces called lacunae
Within the cartilage divide and secrete new matrix
Located deep to the perichondrium divide and secrete new matrix on the internal portions of the cartilage
Never lose their ability to divide
questions.e: Chondroblasts inside the matrix divide and lay down new matrix — interstitial growth, which is how cartilage expands from within. A describes chondrocytes; C describes appositional growth from the perichondrium.

questions.q: What are glycosaminoglycans?
questions.e: GAGs are long unbranched polysaccharides carrying sulphate and carboxyl groups, so they are strongly negatively charged — which is why they pull in water and make ground substance hydrated.

questions.q: What are the three main components of connective tissue?
o: Alveoli, fibrous capsule, and secretory cells
questions.e: Cells + fibres + ground substance. The last two together are the extracellular matrix.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is TRUE of connective tissue?
o: Elastin fibers are sometimes called white fibers.
When connective tissue is stretched, collagen gives it the ability to snap back.
Collagen fibers provide high tensile strength.
Reticular fibers form thick, ropelike structures.
Ground substance is thick and semi-rigid
questions.e: Collagen = tensile strength. Collagen fibres are the white fibres and elastin the yellow ones (so A is swapped), snapping back is elastin's job (B), and reticular fibres are fine branching networks, not ropes (D).

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding the cells of connective tissue.
o: Connective tissue does not contain cells.
Chondroblasts are the main cell type of connective tissue proper.
“Blast” cells are undifferentiated, actively dividing cells
questions.e: The '-blast' suffix marks the immature, mitotically active, matrix-secreting cell; '-cyte' marks the mature maintenance cell. Fibroblasts, not chondroblasts, dominate connective tissue proper.

questions.q: Select the CORRECT statement regarding adipose tissue.
o: It is composed mostly of extracellular matrix.
Its primary function is nutrient storage.
Mature adipose cells are highly mitotic.
Most of the cell volume is occupied by the nucleus.
questions.e: Adipose stores energy as triglyceride. It is highly cellular rather than matrix-rich, richly vascular, and its mature cells barely divide — the nucleus is squashed flat against the rim by one huge lipid droplet.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes a tissue?
o: A group of organs working together for a common purpose
A group of cells that have a similar structure and function
The collection of all organelles in a cell
Organs such as the heart or liver
A group of macromolecules within a cell
questions.e: A tissue is a population of similar cells, with their matrix, performing a common function. Groups of organs make a system.

questions.q: How is hyaline cartilage DIFFERENT from elastic or fibrocartilage?
questions.e: Hyaline's type II fibres share the refractive index of the ground substance, so the matrix looks homogeneous and glassy. In elastic and fibrocartilage the fibres are obvious.

questions.q: Which the following statements best describes connective tissue?
o: Usually contains a large amount of matrix
Always arranged in a single layer of cells
questions.e: Abundant extracellular matrix with cells scattered through it is the hallmark of connective tissue — the opposite of epithelium, where cells are packed together with almost no matrix.

questions.q: Extracellular matrix is composed of
questions.e: Matrix = fibres + ground substance, by definition. Cells sit in the matrix but are not part of it.

questions.q: The following cell types are likely to be seen in areolar connective tissue EXCEPT.
questions.e: Chondroblasts live only in cartilage. Fibroblasts, macrophages, mast cells, plasma cells and reticular cells are all residents of areolar tissue.

questions.q: The fibre type that gives connective tissue GREAT TENSILE STRENGTH is
questions.e: Collagen resists pulling — gram for gram it is stronger than steel wire in tension. Elastic fibres give recoil, not strength.

questions.q: The shape of the external ear is maintained by
questions.e: Elastic cartilage holds the pinna's shape and lets it bend and spring back without breaking.

questions.q: Goblet cells are found in each of the following organs EXCEPT the
questions.e: The stomach has no goblet cells — its entire surface epithelium is made of mucous surface cells, so a separate goblet cell is unnecessary.

questions.q: Which of the following makes up the striated or brush border?
questions.e: Microvilli. Cilia are long and motile with a 9+2 axoneme; microvilli are short, non-motile actin-cored projections for absorption.

questions.q: Adhering to the outer surface of the limiting membrane of the granular endoplasmic reticulum is/are the
questions.e: The 'granular' in rough ER is the ribosomes studding its cytoplasmic surface — that is what makes the cytoplasm basophilic in protein-secreting cells.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following EXCEPT the
questions.e: The intervertebral disc is fibrocartilage. The other four are the standard elastic cartilage sites.

questions.q: The presence of microvilli and cilia on a cell usually indicates that the cell junctions in
questions.e: Microvilli = absorption; cilia = moving material along the surface. Together they mark the ductuli efferentes of the testis, which reabsorb fluid while sweeping sperm along.

questions.q: Evaluate the following statements about aponeuroses.
o: Flattened sheets of dense connective tissue
Composed of collagenous bundles and fibroblasts.
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: All three hold: an aponeurosis is a flat sheet of dense regular connective tissue — parallel collagen bundles with fibroblasts squeezed between them — attaching a flat muscle to bone or to another muscle.

questions.q: The function of a cell that has a basophilic cytoplasm, an eccentric nucleus and a juxtanuclear Golgi apparatus is
questions.e: That trio — deeply basophilic cytoplasm from packed rough ER, an off-centre clock-face nucleus, and a pale Golgi zone beside it — is the classic plasma cell, which makes antibodies. Histamine release would be a mast cell.

questions.q: The CORRECT sequential order of the components of a junctional complex is
o: A zonula occludens, a zonula adherens and a desmosome
A gap junction, a hemidesmosome and a tight junction
A tight junction, a hemidesmosome and a terminal web
A tight junction, a macula adherens and a terminal web
A zonula occludens, a macula adherens, a hemidesmosome and a gap junction
questions.e: From the apex downward: zonula occludens → zonula adherens → macula adherens (desmosome). Hemidesmosomes are at the base, not in the complex, which is what spoils B, C and E.

questions.q: Specializatons of the surface epithelial cells that permit passage of small molecular weight particles through cell membranes of contiguous cells are
o: Are not known to exist in humans
questions.e: Gap junctions are made of connexons — aqueous channels that let ions and small molecules (under about 1 kDa) pass straight from one cytoplasm to the next. Tight junctions do the opposite: they block passage.

questions.q: Tissue macrophages are
o: Highly phagocytic and rich in lysosomes
Not part of the the reticuloendothelial system
The producers of connective tissue fibres
questions.e: Macrophages come from blood monocytes, are packed with lysosomes for digesting what they engulf, and are the core of the mononuclear phagocyte (reticuloendothelial) system. Fibres are made by fibroblasts.

questions.q: The most generalized type of connective tissue with the greatest variety of connective tissue components is/are:
o: Reticular connective tissue and loose connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue and hyaline cartilage
questions.e: Loose (areolar) connective tissue is the all-purpose packing tissue — it contains every fibre type and nearly every connective tissue cell type, which is exactly why it is called the most generalised.

questions.q: Connective tissue fibres and glycosaminoglycans (acid mucopolysaccharides) are synthesized by:
o: Plasma cells, fibroblats and reticular cells
questions.e: The fibroblast is the single manufacturer of both the fibres and the ground substance of connective tissue proper. Macrophages digest, mast cells release mediators, plasma cells make antibodies.

questions.q: Elastic connective tissue:
o: Is present in adults and foetuses
Is present in the vocal ligaments of the larynx
Is typical of the umbilical cord and placenta
Contains stellate fibroblasts and a mucoid ground substance
Contains jelly-like intercellular substance with collagenous fibers
questions.e: The vocal ligaments and the ligamenta flava are the classic elastic ligaments. Options C, D and E all describe mucous connective tissue (Wharton's jelly), not elastic tissue.

questions.q: Which of the following statements about the perichondrium is FALSE?
o: Has two layers, an outer fibrous and inner chondrogenic layers
Is the source of nutrients and metabolites for cartilage
questions.e: False — the perichondrium is vascular. That is the whole point of it: cartilage itself has no vessels and depends on diffusion from the perichondrium's capillaries.

questions.q: The symphysis pubis:
o: It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
It contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
It contains a large amount of ground substance
It has numerous chondroblasts and few collagen fibers
questions.e: The symphysis pubis is fibrocartilage — alternating layers of dense type I collagen with rows of chondrocytes between them, and relatively little ground substance.

questions.q: Pieces of cartilage were examined by an Anatomy Prosector and classified as elastic cartilage. He concluded that the samples were obtained from the:
o: Symphsis pubis and cricoid cartilage of the larynx
Thyroid cartilage of the larynx and the pinna of ear
Intervertebral discs and the epiglottis only
Arytenoid cartilage of the larynx and corniculate cartilage of the larynx
Corniculate and cuneiform cartilages of the larynx and the pinna of ear
questions.e: Only E lists elastic sites throughout. Learn the laryngeal split: thyroid, cricoid and most of the arytenoid are hyaline; corniculate, cuneiform, the arytenoid apex and the epiglottis are elastic.

questions.q: Collagen type IV is abundant in the:
o: External laminae of muscle cells and haematopoietic tissues
questions.e: Type IV is the sheet-forming, non-fibrillar collagen unique to basal laminae — including the thick basal lamina of the lens capsule. (Type III makes the reticular fibres of spleen, nodes and marrow.)

questions.q: A specimen with a meshwork of irregular polygonal profiles of cells was described as adult white fat cells. These cells have:
o: Centrally located nuclei and many small lipid droplets within the cells
Flattened basal nuclei and single large droplets of lipid within the cells
Centrally placed nuclei with large amounts of cytoplasm
Numerous flattened basal nuclei per cell with small peripheral cytoplasm
questions.e: White (unilocular) fat: one enormous lipid droplet fills the cell and pushes the flattened nucleus and a thin rim of cytoplasm to the edge — the signet-ring appearance. Many small droplets with a central nucleus would be brown, multilocular fat.

questions.q: Adipose tissue:
o: Constitutes up to 5% or more of the total body weight in infants
Constitutes up to 60% or more of the total body weight in adults and is highly cellular
Provides thermal insulation, serves as metabolic fuel and is highly phagocytic
Acts as shock absorbers in the soles of the feet
questions.e: Insulation and metabolic fuel are adipose's headline functions. note'Highly phagocytic' is a stretch — adipocytes are not phagocytes, and option E (shock absorption in the soles) is also true of adipose tissue. The paper's key is C; know both facts.

questions.q: Examination of Brown adipose tissue shows that it:
o: Is unilocular and mainly found in adults
Is multilocular and mainly found in adults
Has an extremely rich supply of capillaries
Is found both in adults and infants.
questions.e: Brown fat's colour comes from its dense capillary network plus abundant mitochondrial cytochromes — that vascularity carries the heat away. It is multilocular and mainly a newborn tissue, so B is wrong.

questions.q: You are given an epithelium from an unknown location, the epithelium has microvilli and cilia. This epithelium
o: Was involved with secretion or absorption
Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses
Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required
Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually.
questions.e: Microvilli tell you absorption; cilia tell you motility. Both together = the ductuli efferentes pattern — absorb fluid and move contents along.

questions.q: On the border separating epithelial cells and connective tissue can be found:
o: Tight junctions, adhering junctions and hemidesmosomes
Zonula occludens and zonula adherens only
Zonula adherens and macula adherens only
questions.e: The basal border carries hemidesmosomes anchoring cells to the basal lamina, with desmosomes also present low on the lateral surfaces. Tight and adherens junctions are apical, not basal.

questions.q: Junctional complexes are located on the:
questions.e: The complex sits at the apical end of the lateral membranes — an apicolateral position, encircling the cell just below the free surface.

questions.q: The structure of bone tissue suits its functions. Which of the following bone tissues is adapted to support weight and withstand tension stress?
questions.e: Dense compact (cortical) bone with its concentric osteons is built to carry weight and resist tension and torsion. Spongy bone resists forces from many directions but is far weaker in pure tension.

questions.q: The cell responsible for secreting the matrix of bone is the:
questions.e: Osteoblasts lay down osteoid; once trapped, they become osteocytes, which continue to maintain and turn over a thin layer of matrix around themselves. noteMany textbooks answer 'osteoblast' alone — the paper credits both.

questions.q: What kind of tissue serves as a model for long bones in the embryo?
questions.e: Endochondral ossification starts with a hyaline cartilage model of the future bone, which is progressively replaced by bone from primary and secondary centres.

questions.q: The term diploë refers to the:
o: Double-layered nature of the connective tissue covering the bone
Fact that most bones are formed of two types of bone tissue
Internal layer of spongy bone in flat bones
Two types of marrow found within most bones
questions.e: Diploë is the spongy bone sandwiched between the inner and outer compact tables of a flat bone such as the parietal — light, but stiff, like a girder.

questions.q: The most abundant cartilage type is
questions.e: Hyaline is the commonest — all articular surfaces, costal cartilages, the nose, most of the larynx, trachea and bronchi, plus every epiphyseal plate.

questions.q: Osteocytes are housed in
questions.e: Osteocytes sit in lacunae and communicate through canaliculi. Haversian and Volkmann's canals carry vessels; Howship's lacunae are the pits excavated by osteoclasts.

questions.q: All the following are bilateral organs EXCEPT?
questions.e: The brain is a single midline organ (its two hemispheres are parts of one organ), unlike the paired lungs, kidneys and testes. noteThe spleen is also unpaired — it sits alone in the left hypochondrium — so B is defensible too. The paper marks A.

questions.q: A body in anatomical position has the following characteristics EXCEPT?
o: Arms adjacent to sides with palms facing backward
Lower limbs close together with feet parallel and toes directed forward
questions.e: In anatomical position the palms face forwards (supinated), which is why the radius is described as the lateral forearm bone.

questions.q: Which body plane cuts across the long axis of the body?
questions.e: A transverse (horizontal/axial) plane cuts perpendicular to the long axis, dividing the body into superior and inferior parts. correctedThe paper's tick sits on B, but midsagittal runs along the long axis — it cannot cut across it. Frontal, coronal and median are all longitudinal planes too.

questions.q: Which term refers to the region of the body between the elbow and the shoulder?
questions.e: Brachium = arm proper (shoulder to elbow). Antebrachium is the forearm, manus the hand, pedis the foot, lumbus the loin.

questions.q: All the following body cavities are components of the ventral body cavity EXCEPT?
questions.e: The vertebral (spinal) cavity belongs to the dorsal body cavity, with the cranial cavity. The ventral cavity is thoracic (pleural + pericardial) plus abdominopelvic.

questions.q: Which abdominopelvic region is located directly beneath the umbilical region?
questions.e: The nine-region grid runs, down the midline: epigastric → umbilical → hypogastric (suprapubic). The lumbar and iliac regions flank them.

questions.q: Smooth muscle, unlike cardiac muscle is UNSTRIATED because:
o: It lacks many of the filaments found in cardiac muscle
Its myofilaments are not regularly arranged
It has more sarcoplasm so the striations are not prominent
Myosin filaments are attached to the sarcolemma
questions.e: Smooth muscle has the same actin and myosin, but they run obliquely and anchor to dense bodies rather than lining up into sarcomeres — no register, so no visible bands.

questions.q: The functional unit of skeletal muscle is the
questions.e: The sarcomere — the segment between two Z-lines — is the smallest unit that can contract. Myofibrils are chains of sarcomeres; fascicles are bundles of fibres.

questions.q: In a pseudostratified columnar epithelium, which of the following is characteristic of all cells:
o: Location of nuclei at the same horizontal level
Direct contact with the basement membrane
Possession of highly folded basal membranes
questions.e: Every cell touches the basement membrane — that is what makes it pseudo-stratified. Not all of them reach the free surface (the short basal cells do not), and the nuclei sit at deliberately different levels.

questions.q: Which is the commonest site of ectopic implantation?
questions.e: Over 95% of ectopic pregnancies implant in the uterine (fallopian) tube, most often the ampulla.

questions.q: Which of the following is among recurrent problems with in vitro fertilization (IVF)?
o: Legal battles over ownership of embryos following divorce
questions.e: All of these are genuine, recurring problems associated with IVF programmes.

questions.q: What is the largest cause of female infertility that necessitates assisted reproductive technology (ART)?
questions.e: Tubal factor infertility (often from pelvic inflammatory disease) is the classic indication that bypasses natural conception entirely, making IVF/ART necessary.

questions.q: The placenta produces ALL of the following hormones EXCEPT:
questions.e: The placenta makes hCG, HCS (hPL), progesterone and oestrogens — but never LH, which is strictly a pituitary hormone.

questions.q: Which are the first cells that differentiate from the morula?
questions.e: As the morula compacts, the outer cells differentiate first into the trophoblast; the inner cell mass (which later gives epiblast/hypoblast) differentiates afterward.

questions.q: Which is the hormone directly responsible for ovulation?
questions.e: The mid-cycle LH surge directly triggers follicular rupture and ovulation.

questions.q: In Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART) a conceptus is introduced into the uterus of a hormonally stimulated female at which stage of development?
questions.e: Cleavage-stage embryo transfer is classically done around the eight-cell stage (day 3), though blastocyst transfer is also used clinically — the eight-cell stage is the standard teaching answer.

questions.q: Which is the stem cell in the spermatogenic lineage?
questions.e: Type A spermatogonia (specifically the dark type) are the self-renewing stem cells of the lineage.

questions.q: Which hormone is directly responsible for maintenance of the corpus luteum of pregnancy?
questions.e: Once pregnancy occurs, hCG (secreted by the syncytiotrophoblast) takes over LH's role and rescues/maintains the corpus luteum. LH maintains the corpus luteum of a normal, non-pregnant cycle (compare Q51) — hCG is specific to pregnancy.

questions.q: What is the reason for unlimited and continuous production of spermatozoa throughout the post pubertal life of a male?
o: The delay from birth to puberty enables the spermatogonia to multiply into millions before commencement of meiosis at puberty
Each meiotic division in spermatogenesis produces eight haploid cells
Mitotic division of each Type A dark spermatogonium produces one Type A dark and one Type A pale cell
There is no meiotic arrest during spermatogenesis
questions.e: Type A dark spermatogonia divide asymmetrically — one daughter stays as a Type A dark stem cell (self-renewal), the other becomes Type A pale and continues down the differentiation pathway. This is what makes sperm production continuous for life.

questions.q: What is the biological advantage of menopause?
o: It protects middle-aged women from physical and physiological stresses of pregnancy
By diminishing libido of adult women, it saves them from adolescent sexual adventures
By ablating menstruation, it protects adult women from anaemia
Cessation of menstruation saves adult females from premenstrual mood swings
Cessation of reproductive capacity affords adult females uninterrupted working hours
questions.e: The standard teaching point is that menopause spares an ageing woman's body from the physiological demands and risks of pregnancy and childbirth at an age when those risks are higher.

questions.q: What is the reason why a male with complete masculine features and all secondary sexual characteristics, can have spermatozoa-related infertility?
o: Spermatogenesis requires a lower than body temperature to be effective
Secondary sexual characteristics occur earlier than spermatogenesis
Conditions that adversely affect spermatogenesis do not affect testosterone producing cells
questions.e: Leydig cells (testosterone/virilisation) and the germinal epithelium (sperm production) can be affected independently — a man can have entirely normal masculinisation while his sperm production is impaired by heat, toxins, or germ-cell-specific disease.

questions.q: ALL the following are interventions possible for an infertile marital couple to have their own baby, EXCEPT
questions.e: Masturbation is simply a method of collecting a semen sample — it is not itself a fertility intervention/treatment; IVF, IUI, surrogacy and ICSI all are.

questions.q: Which of the following cells are responsible for the production of a single haploid cell when meiosis is completed in oogenesis?
questions.e: Unequal cytokinesis at each meiotic division extrudes a small polar body, keeping almost all the cytoplasm in one large functional cell — this is what leaves oogenesis with a single viable haploid ovum instead of four equal cells.

questions.q: Which of the following is produced when the second meiotic division is completed during oogenesis?
questions.e: Meiosis II only completes after a sperm penetrates the secondary oocyte. Completion yields the female pronucleus and the second polar body.

questions.q: What is the process called in which specific glycoproteins are removed from the outer membrane of the acrosomal cap to expose receptor sites for binding of the ligand which initiates acrosomal reaction?
questions.e: This surface 'unmasking' of the sperm membrane is exactly what capacitation does, in the female tract, priming the sperm to undergo the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Semen analysis of a man in an infertile marriage showed that he had adequate numbers of spermatozoa but they had very POOR MOTILITY. What is his condition called?
questions.e: Asthenozoospermia = normal/adequate sperm count with reduced motility.

questions.q: Which is the spermatogenic cell that negotiates the blood-testis barrier to move from ABLUMINAL TO THE ADLUMINAL COMPARTMENT of the seminiferous epithelium?
questions.e: Primary spermatocytes are the cells that cross the blood-testis barrier, moving from the basal (abluminal) to the adluminal compartment as new Sertoli-Sertoli junctions form behind them.

questions.q: ALL the following spermatogenic cells are nourished directly from the blood vessels in the interstitial connective tissue between seminiferous tubules, EXCEPT:
questions.e: Type A dark and Type A pale spermatogonia sit in the basal compartment, nourished directly by interstitial blood vessels. Type B spermatogonia, positioned closest to the blood-testis barrier just before dividing into primary spermatocytes, depend on Sertoli cell support rather than direct diffusion.

questions.q: How many days does it take daughter cells from the first meiotic division in spermatogenesis to complete second meiotic division and differentiate to become spermatozoa?
questions.e: Human spermatogenesis runs roughly 64–74 days end-to-end; from the secondary spermatocyte stage through meiosis II and full spermiogenesis to a mature spermatozoon takes close to the full duration.

questions.q: How many days does it take daughter cells of first meiotic division to escape from arrest and complete the process to be ovulated?
questions.e: This tracks the ~14-day follicular phase: the primary oocyte only resumes/completes meiosis I (forming the secondary oocyte) around the time of the LH surge, roughly 14 days into the cycle, just before ovulation.

questions.q: What is the maternal contribution to the placenta?
questions.e: Decidua basalis is the maternal endometrial tissue at the implantation site that forms the maternal part of the placenta.

questions.q: Which is the foetal component of the placenta?
questions.e: Chorion frondosum (the 'bushy' chorion with well-developed villi at the implantation site) is the foetal contribution to the placenta.

questions.q: The mesenchyme in the umbilical cord, called Wharton's jelly develops from which of the following?
questions.e: Wharton's jelly is mucous connective tissue derived from extraembryonic mesoderm.

questions.q: During embryonic development, the embryo undergoes lateral folding which results in the amniotic cavity becoming enlarged to encircle the embryo. Which cavity is directly obliterated by this process?
questions.e: As the amnion expands around the embryo during folding, it pinches off and obliterates the connection to the yolk sac (leaving only the narrow vitelline duct).

questions.q: In a late placenta, the barrier between maternal blood entering the intervillous space and the foetal (chorionic) capillary lumen includes ALL the following EXCEPT:
questions.e: The cytotrophoblast layer becomes discontinuous and largely disappears as pregnancy advances, thinning the placental barrier — it is not part of the mature (late) placental membrane.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a function of amniotic fluid?
o: Protection of foetus from external shocks.
Maintenance of foetus at an even temperature.
questions.e: Amniotic fluid mainly cushions, thermoregulates, and prevents desiccation/adhesion of foetal parts. Direct lubrication of foetal skin is more the role of vernix caseosa, not the fluid itself.

questions.q: Which of the following events is decisive for initiation of implantation?
o: Hatching of blastocyst from zona pellucida
questions.e: The blastocyst must first hatch out of the zona pellucida before its trophoblast can make direct contact with, and attach to, the endometrium.

questions.q: Binding of the sperm head to the ovum during fertilization is facilitated by which of the following?
questions.e: ZP3, a zona pellucida glycoprotein, is the primary sperm-binding receptor recognised by receptors on the sperm head.

questions.q: Which hormone is directly responsible for the maintenance of the corpus luteum on menstruation?
questions.e: In a normal (non-pregnant) cycle, LH sustains the corpus luteum during the luteal phase; without a rescuing pregnancy signal it regresses and menstruation follows.

questions.q: The chorion includes ALL of the following EXCEPT.
questions.e: The chorion = trophoblast (cyto- + syncytiotrophoblast) plus extraembryonic somatic mesoderm — not splanchnic mesoderm, which lines the yolk sac/gut region instead.

questions.q: Which terminology refers to the changes that the endometrium undergoes in response to implantation?
questions.e: Decidualization is specifically the endometrial stromal transformation that occurs in response to implantation.

questions.q: Which embryonic process involves morphogenetic movement of cells?
questions.e: Gastrulation is defined by large-scale, coordinated cell migrations that establish the three germ layers.

questions.q: Which of the following is the primary reason for the hormones contained in the female contraceptive pill?
o: Stimulation of zona reaction of ovum before sperms reach it
Suppression of hypothalamic secretion of gonadotrophin releasing hormone
Suppression of female orgasm during coitus
questions.e: The combined pill's primary contraceptive action is suppressing hypothalamic GnRH pulsatility, which prevents the LH surge and therefore ovulation.

questions.q: Which component of semen changes the direction of fluid current created by the "ciliary escalator" in the oviduct towards the ovary?
questions.e: Seminal prostaglandins act on the female tract's smooth muscle/ciliary activity, helping redirect flow toward the ovary to aid sperm transport.

questions.q: Which is the greatest cause of infertility in the male that necessitates recourse to ART?
questions.e: A large proportion of male infertility remains idiopathic — unexplained despite full work-up — making it the single biggest category driving ART.

questions.q: What is/are the most plausible reason(s) why spermatogenesis produces millions of spermatozoa with about 10% abnormality instead of a single perfect gamete as occurs in oogenesis?
o: Many spermatozoa die during storage in the duct of epididymis before they are released in an ejaculate.
Many spermatozoa must necessarily die to neutralize hostile environment within female genital tract.
Many spermatozoa die if they have to wait in the female genital tract before ovulation occurs to make an ovum available for fertilization.
All of the above are correct
Only B and C are correct
questions.e: All three attritional pressures are real — sperm are lost in storage, in overcoming the hostile vaginal/cervical environment, and while waiting for ovulation — which is why nature over-produces sperm rather than making one perfect gamete.

questions.q: Which of the following processes facilitates implantation?
questions.e: The decidual reaction (endometrial stromal transformation) prepares and facilitates the receptive environment for implantation.

questions.q: Which of the following is/are implicated in hydatidiform molar pregnancy?
o: Both A and B are correct
Both B and C are correct
questions.e: A complete hydatidiform mole classically arises when the female (maternal) pronucleus is lost/absent and the paternal genome duplicates alone, giving an androgenetic conceptus.

questions.q: Which hormone is routinely tested for in urine to confirm a pregnancy?
questions.e: Urine pregnancy tests detect hCG.

questions.q: Which is the cell that undergoes spermiogenesis?
questions.e: Spermiogenesis is the transformation of the round spermatid into a mature, streamlined spermatozoon.

questions.q: Completion of the first meiotic division entails separation of homologous (paternally and maternally inherited) chromosomes. In spermatogenesis, in which cell do homologous chromosomes separate?
questions.e: The primary spermatocyte is the cell undergoing meiosis I, where homologous chromosomes separate.

questions.q: Completion of the second meiotic division entails separation of sister chromatids held together at the centromere. In spermatogenesis which cell do sister chromatids separate?
questions.e: The secondary spermatocyte undergoes meiosis II, separating sister chromatids to form spermatids.

questions.q: Which is the gametogenic stem cell in the spermatogenic cell lineage?
questions.e: Type A dark spermatogonia are the reserve stem-cell population that self-renews throughout adult life.

questions.q: The "morning after" emergency contraceptive pill works by delivering a large dose of oestrogen within 72 hours of coitus. Which of the following explains how it works, EXCEPT:
o: If an ovulation has not recently occurred, it prevents the ovum from being released.
If an ovum has been released, its fertilization may be impaired.
If fertilization has already occurred, implantation is inhibited
Cleavage division and production of the blastocyst is adversely affected.
questions.e: All four listed mechanisms (blocking/delaying ovulation, impairing fertilization, inhibiting implantation, disrupting cleavage) are proposed ways the high-dose oestrogen morning-after pill can act — so none of A-D is excluded, meaning 'all of the above' (claiming every option is a valid explanation, with no exception) is itself the option that mismatches the EXCEPT framing.

questions.q: All of the following are reasons for permitting emergency contraceptive use within 72 hours of coitus, EXCEPT:
o: A couple who plan for a baby may change their mind.
Condoms being used for contraception may tear.
Women on contraceptive pills may forget to take them.
Coitus may be forced as in rape or incest.
questions.e: Emergency contraception exists for accidental/failed protection or non-consensual sex — not as a fallback for a couple who consented to trying for a baby and then changed their mind.

questions.q: The "abortion" emergency contraceptive pill RU486 works by blocking endometrial development necessary to support pregnancy, as well as causing uterine contraction promoting expulsion of an implanted conceptus. Which of the following hormones does RU486 directly antagonize?
questions.e: Mifepristone (RU486) is a progesterone receptor antagonist — it directly blocks progesterone's action, destabilising the decidua and promoting expulsion.

questions.q: Which of the following hormones is NOT produced by the placenta?
questions.e: As with Q25/Q45, LH is never a placental product — it is exclusively pituitary.

questions.q: The hormones released during acrosomal reaction include the following.
questions.e: The acrosome releases a cocktail of hydrolytic enzymes — acrosin, hyaluronidase and neuraminidase among them — that help the sperm penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida.

questions.q: Capacitation of spermatozoa involves which of the following?
o: Conversion of golgi apparatus into an acrosomal cap
Conversion of centriole into a flagellum
Shedding of excess cytoplasm to give a slimmer cell
Condensation of chromatin in sperm head
Removal of glycoproteins in acrosomal cap
questions.e: Options A–D describe events of spermiogenesis (sperm maturation in the testis). Capacitation itself is a female-tract event: the stripping of glycoproteins/decapacitation factors from the sperm surface, priming it for the acrosomal reaction.

questions.q: Acrosomal reaction of spermatozoa achieves ALL of the following purposes EXCEPT:
o: Exposure of membrane of sperm head
Release of enzymes that detach corona radiata cells
Release of enzymes that permit penetration of zona pellucida
questions.e: The acrosomal reaction removes/vesiculates the acrosomal cap and releases enzymes to clear the corona radiata and zona pellucida — but the sperm head never detaches from the rest of the sperm.

questions.q: Fast block to polyspermy during fertilization achieves which of the following?
o: Stimulates completion of second meiotic division of oocyte.
Facilitates penetration of oocyte plasma membrane by sperm head.
Resistance of corona radiata cells to spermatozoa
Molecular alteration of zona pellucida to become impenetrable to spermatozoa.
Fusion of male and female pronuclei
questions.e: This describes the zona reaction — hardening/alteration of the zona pellucida so it can no longer be penetrated by additional sperm, blocking polyspermy.

questions.q: In Assisted Reproductive Technology (ART), which of the following can be stored (frozen) for use at a later date?
questions.e: Sperm, oocytes and embryos can all be cryopreserved for later use in ART.

questions.q: What are the early cells that appear from cleavage of the zygote called?
questions.e: The individual cells produced by early cleavage divisions of the zygote are called blastomeres.

questions.q: Which method of contraception is NOT RECOMMENDABLE to young people who have not had any children?
questions.e: Surgical sterilisation is generally discouraged in people who haven't yet had children, mainly because of its irreversibility.

questions.q: What is the basis for not recommending a specific contraceptive method to a young person who does not have a child?
questions.e: It is the permanence/irreversibility of surgical methods that makes them unsuitable for someone who may still want children later.

questions.q: Which of the following methods of contraception is 100% effective?
questions.e: No contraceptive method (short of abstinence) offers a true 100% guarantee — all listed methods carry some failure rate.

questions.q: Which of the following sites of implantation will give rise to a placenta praevia?
questions.e: Placenta praevia is defined by implantation in the LOWER uterine segment/near the cervix. Implantation in the upper (fundal) part of the uterus is the normal site and does not give rise to praevia — it is the one that does NOT fit the pattern.

questions.q: Spermatogenesis is susceptible to ALL of the following EXCEPT?
questions.e: Spermatogenesis needs a temperature below core body temperature, and is impaired by radiation, anti-mitotic drugs and viral orchitis (e.g. mumps) — migraine headaches have no established effect on it.

questions.q: Which of the following cavities is also called the chorionic cavity?
questions.e: The extraembryonic coelom is another name for the chorionic cavity.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a usual component of semen?
questions.e: Sperm plus secretions from the prostate, bulbourethral glands, and seminal vesicles are all normal components of semen — none is the odd one out.

questions.q: A woman's physiological response to pregnancy including being nauseous and feeling "bloated". What is the name of the hormone responsible for these changes in a pregnant woman?
questions.e: Rising hCG in early pregnancy is classically linked to nausea/'morning sickness' and bloating.

questions.q: Which of the following is acrosomal reaction necessary for?
questions.e: The acrosomal reaction lets the sperm penetrate the corona radiata and zona pellucida — it's a prerequisite step of fertilization.

questions.q: With which of the listed parts is the spermatozoon self-propelled?
questions.e: The tail (flagellum) provides the whip-like motion that propels the sperm; the mid-piece supplies the ATP (via mitochondria) that powers it.

questions.q: What is contained in the head of a spermatozoon?
questions.e: The sperm head is essentially a nucleus (with condensed chromatin) capped by the acrosome; mitochondria are confined to the mid-piece.

questions.q: Which two structures are NOT among those that appear in the second week of human development?
o: Amniotic cavity and primary yolk sac
questions.e: The blastocyst cavity is a first-week structure (present from day 5) that has already been reorganised by week 2, whereas the chorionic cavity only forms during week 2 — pairing them together is the mismatched option.

questions.q: In which stage of cyclic development must the endometrium be to facilitate implantation?
questions.e: The 'window of implantation' falls in the mid-secretory phase (roughly cycle days 20–24).

questions.q: There is a report of a hormonal test for ovulation in the saliva of a woman. Which hormone would more directly indicate ovulation?
questions.e: Salivary 'ferning' ovulation predictor tests rely on the pre-ovulatory oestrogen surge, which changes salt/mucus content of saliva causing a characteristic fern pattern.

questions.q: Which gamete provides the cytoplasm of the zygote?
questions.e: The oocyte contributes essentially all of the zygote's cytoplasm (and organelles, including mitochondria); the sperm contributes almost exclusively its nuclear genome.

questions.q: For a surrogate mother to achieve successful implantation of an inseminated blastocyst, she must have hormonal treatment to prepare her endometrium. Which hormone would be used for such preparatory treatment?
questions.e: Progesterone drives the secretory transformation of the endometrium needed for a receptive, implantation-ready lining (often after oestrogen priming).

questions.q: How is the zygote nourished?
o: Via diffusible nutrients from ovarian follicular liquid
By diffusion from extravasated fluid from oviductal veins
By osmotic transfer of nutrients from mucosal folds in oviduct
Via diffusible nutrients from secretions of oviductal epithelial cells
questions.e: Before implantation, the zygote/early embryo is nourished by secretions from the oviductal (tubal) epithelium as it travels toward the uterus.

questions.q: What is the likely event that can result in the birth of identical triplets?
o: A highly fortuitous spermatogenic process that fertilized three identical ova released in a single ovulation.
Two cell-stage blastomeres from a single zygote separated into two separate blastomeres and one of them further split into new individuals.
A polyspermic zygote produced under ovarian stimulation in their fertilization in addition to the definitive ovum in oogenesis.
Failure of ejection of first and secondary polar bodies in addition to their fertilization by three separate identical spermatozoa.
Fortuitous production of three identical ova during oogenesis, which were fertilized by three separate identical spermatozoa.
questions.e: Identical (monozygotic) multiples arise from the splitting of blastomeres from a single zygote — not from multiple separately fertilized ova (that gives non-identical multiples) and not from polar bodies (which are not normally viable).

questions.q: Which of the following is a defect of an ovum, which increases in occurrence with increasing age of a woman older than 35 years?
questions.e: Chromosomal non-disjunction (aneuploidy risk) rises sharply with maternal age past 35, the well-known driver of age-related ovum defects.

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT a correct thing to do on a female partner when evaluating an infertile marriage?
o: Vaginal examination to determine adequate length (depth).
Pelvic examination to determine the disposition of the vulval structures.
Breast examination to determine the degree of development.
Urine test to check for infections.
Blood test to check for hormonal problems.
questions.e: Vulval structures are external genitalia — assessed by external/visual examination, not an internal pelvic examination. This mismatch makes B the incorrect description.

questions.q: A physical examination of a male partner of an infertile marriage will look for ALL of the following, EXCEPT:
questions.e: Urethral position, hair distribution, varicocoeles and testicular size are all relevant to a male fertility exam. The presence of an Adam's apple has no bearing on fertility assessment.

questions.q: In semen analysis to evaluate an infertile marriage which characteristic feature or attribute is NOT of clinical importance?
questions.e: Volume, pH, and WBC concentration (a marker of infection) are all clinically meaningful. Semen colour is not a diagnostically important parameter.

questions.q: Bilateral undescended testes causes infertility because it causes one of the following.
o: Inability to release sperms during ejaculation.
questions.e: Cryptorchidism impairs spermatogenesis because sperm production needs a cooler-than-core temperature; Leydig cell (testosterone) function is comparatively preserved, so the main problem is inadequate sperm output.

questions.q: What is the commonest cause of female infertility worldwide?
questions.e: Globally, tubal factor infertility (often secondary to untreated pelvic infection) is the single commonest cause of female infertility.

questions.q: Which of the following hormonal tests in a FEMALE PARTNER will NOT help in evaluating an infertile marriage?
questions.e: hCG is a pregnancy marker, not a diagnostic test used to investigate the cause of infertility. FSH, LH, thyroid hormone and prolactin are all standard parts of a female infertility work-up.

questions.q: Which of the following hormonal tests in a MALE PARTNER will NOT help in evaluating an infertile marriage?
questions.e: Oestrogen is not part of a standard male infertility hormonal panel; FSH, LH, AMH and testosterone all are.

questions.q: A man who has had BILATERAL VASECTOMY hid this from a female sexual partner who then accompanied him to see a specialist at a fertility clinic. When his semen is analyzed, which of the following diagnosis will be made?
questions.e: Vasectomy blocks sperm from reaching the ejaculate, but seminal fluid (from the accessory glands) is still produced — so the ejaculate exists but contains zero sperm: azoospermia, not aspermia.

questions.q: What will be the best diagnosis of a semen analysis in a man who has primary ciliary dyskinesia (PCD) or Kartagener' syndrome?
questions.e: PCD/Kartagener syndrome involves defective dynein arms affecting ciliary/flagellar motility — sperm are present but essentially immotile: asthenozoospermia.

questions.q: Two years ago a 65-year old widower underwent BILATERAL ORCHIDECTOMY as part of treatment for cancer of the prostate. Recently he has fallen in love with a 34-year old woman who desires to have a baby by her lover. If the man pretends to be ignorant about his sterility on account of orchidectomy and goes for a semen analysis, what will be the likely diagnosis?
questions.e: With both testes removed there is no sperm production at all, but accessory glands still contribute seminal fluid — so the diagnosis is azoospermia (ejaculate present, zero sperm), not aspermia.

questions.q: A 30 year old woman had HYSTERECTOMY at age 19 to save her from complications of a botched abortion. She has recently married a 32 year old business tycoon who accompanies her to a fertility clinic for evaluation of their infertile marriage. Which of the following tests will be most appropriate, economical, and non-invasive in diagnosing the woman's lack of uterus?
o: Endometrial biopsy to verify cyclical tandem with ovarian cycle.
Transvaginal ultrasound test to view the uterus, ovaries and cervix.
Hysterosalpingography to verify patency of oviducts.
Laparoscopy to view the outside of the uterus, ovaries, and fallopian tubes.
Pelvic ultrasound test to view the uterus, ovaries and fallopian tubes
questions.e: Transvaginal ultrasound is quick, non-invasive, and economical, and would readily confirm the absent uterus — the other options are either invasive, unnecessary, or less appropriate here.

questions.q: At which stage in oogenesis is the process suspended or arrested?
questions.e: Primary oocytes are arrested in prophase of meiosis I (specifically the diplotene/dictyate substage) from fetal life until just before ovulation.

questions.q: Which cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor responsible for meiotic arrest in oogenesis?
questions.e: Follicular (granulosa) cells secrete oocyte maturation inhibitor (OMI), which keeps the enclosed oocyte arrested until the LH surge overrides it.

questions.q: What types of follicles are present in pre-pubertal human ovaries?
questions.e: Before puberty, the ovary contains the resting pool of primordial follicles and ongoing background atresia, but lacks the further-developed (gonadotropin-dependent) follicle stages that require pubertal hormone levels.

questions.q: How long does it take an oocyte in a post-pubertal human ovary to mature and be released at ovulation?
questions.e: Follicular development from the antral stage through to ovulation spans roughly the ~14-day follicular phase of the cycle.

questions.q: Within the female genital tract, how long does the ovulated oocyte remain capable of being fertilized by a spermatozoon?
questions.e: The ovulated oocyte is classically viable for fertilization for about 24 hours (sperm, by contrast, can survive several days in the tract).

questions.q: At which stage of development does implantation occur?
questions.e: Implantation begins once the conceptus has reached and hatched from the blastocyst stage.

questions.q: Which cells of the spermatogenic lineage are directly dependent on testosterone for development?
questions.e: Testosterone (acting via Sertoli cell androgen receptors) is most critical for driving spermiogenesis — the maturation of round spermatids into elongated, mature spermatozoa.

questions.q: Which cells of the spermatogenic lineage complete the second meiotic division?
questions.e: Secondary spermatocytes are the cells that undergo (and complete) meiosis II, producing spermatids.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly indicates the direct role of luteinizing hormone (LH) in spermatogenesis? It stimulates:
questions.e: LH's direct target in the testis is the interstitial (Leydig) cells, which it stimulates to produce testosterone — everything else in spermatogenesis is downstream of that testosterone (and FSH) signal.

questions.q: Which of the following correctly indicates the direct role of luteinizing hormone (LH) in oogenesis? It stimulates:
o: Release of secondary oocyte in ovulation
Completion of first meiotic division by primary oocyte
Release of primary oocyte from effect of oocyte maturation inhibitor
Secretion of oestrogen by granulosa cells
Completion of second meiotic division by secondary oocyte
questions.e: The mid-cycle LH surge directly triggers the primary oocyte to resume and complete meiosis I, forming the secondary oocyte — this is LH's key direct cellular action in oogenesis.

questions.q: In reproductive biology which of the following is generally called the ovum or egg?
questions.e: The cell released at ovulation and commonly called 'the egg' is the secondary oocyte (arrested in metaphase II until fertilization).

questions.q: In which of the following types of ovarian follicles does the ovum reside?
questions.e: Just before ovulation the oocyte sits within a mature Graafian (tertiary) follicle.

questions.q: The ovum is an oocyte in which of the following states of development?
o: Daughter cell of Meiosis I containing very little cytoplasm
questions.e: At ovulation the oocyte (secondary oocyte) has completed meiosis I (extruding the first polar body) and is arrested in metaphase of meiosis II — meiosis II only finishes upon fertilization.

questions.q: The first polar body is NOT different from the second polar body in ALL of the following ways EXCEPT that it:
o: Results from completion of second meiotic division.
Does not contribute to the development of the embryo
questions.e: Both polar bodies are haploid, cytoplasm-poor and non-contributory to the embryo — but only the SECOND polar body results from meiosis II. The first comes from meiosis I, so this is where they actually differ.

questions.q: Which of the statements below is NOT CORRECT concerning the male pronucleus?
o: Produced only after fertilization of ovum
Fuses with daughter cell of meiosis II of ovum
It is the polar body of meiosis II of ovum
questions.e: The male pronucleus comes from the sperm's nuclear material — it has nothing to do with the ovum's polar bodies, which are byproducts of oocyte meiosis.

questions.q: Which of the following results from fusion of the male and female pronuclei?
questions.e: Fusion of the male and female pronuclei restores the diploid number and forms the zygote.

questions.q: Male-specific causes of infertility typically involve ALL of the following abnormalities of spermatozoa, EXCEPT:
questions.e: Chromosomal, structural (morphology), numerical (oligospermia) and motility (asthenospermia) defects are all recognised categories of sperm abnormality — 'physiological immaturity' isn't a standard classification.

questions.q: What is the commonest ovum-specific cause of infertility?
questions.e: Chromosomal abnormality (aneuploidy), especially with advancing maternal age, is the leading ovum-specific cause of infertility.

questions.q: What is the clinical terminology for male infertility arising from a molecular deficiency in the microtubules of spermatozoa?
questions.e: Primary ciliary dyskinesia is caused by defects in the microtubule/dynein arm machinery, which cripples flagellar (and ciliary) function.

questions.q: Which of the following IS NOT a cause of infertility in females?
questions.e: Cervical factors, tubal blockage, endometriosis, and ovulatory failure are all established anatomical/functional causes of female infertility. Low libido affects intercourse frequency but is not itself classified as an infertility cause.

questions.q: In general, couples in which of the following ages are MOST FERTILE?
questions.e: Female fertility peaks in the early-to-mid twenties and gradually declines thereafter.

questions.q: In which of the following ages are couples most likely to access assisted reproductive technology (ART) USING THEIR OWN GAMETES?
questions.e: Most people seeking ART with their own eggs/sperm are in their mid-to-late 30s — old enough to have run into age-related subfertility, but still young enough that their own gametes are usually viable.

questions.q: In which of the following ages are couples accessing assisted reproductive technology (ART) likely to USE DONOR GAMETES?
questions.e: Beyond the late 30s/early 40s, declining oocyte quality/quantity pushes more couples toward donor eggs (or donor sperm) for ART.

questions.q: For a couple whose coitus does not result in pregnancy to be classified as infertile, ALL of the following features must be present, EXCEPT that it must:
o: Result in mutually coincident orgasm of both male and female
Have appropriate timing with respect to the female's menstrual cycle
questions.e: Female orgasm has no bearing on the ability to conceive — the accepted clinical definition of infertility is regular, appropriately timed, unprotected intercourse (which does require male orgasm/ejaculation) for a year without pregnancy.

questions.q: Worrying issues about in vitro fertilization (IVF) include ALL of the following EXCEPT:
o: Prohibitive cost that makes it inaccessible to the poor
Doubtful fertility of children born by IVF
questions.e: Children conceived by IVF have normal fertility as adults — this is not a genuine concern, unlike cost, misuse, or the ethics of gamete donation.

questions.q: Which method of contraception depends on charting a female's menstrual cycle and predicting her fertile/infertile periods?
questions.e: This describes the rhythm/calendar (fertility awareness) method exactly.

questions.q: Injectable or implantable contraceptives fall under which broad method of contraception?
questions.e: Injectables and implants deliver progestin (± oestrogen) — they are hormonal methods.

questions.q: Which of the following are classified as permanent methods of contraception?
questions.e: Tubal ligation and vasectomy are surgical/permanent methods; implants are hormonal and fully reversible, so they don't belong in this group.

questions.q: What is the crucial role of zona reaction in the process of fertilization?
o: Stimulation of fusion of male and female pronuclei
Triggering completion of second meiotic division of ovum
questions.e: The zona reaction's defining role is hardening the zona pellucida so it can no longer be penetrated by additional sperm — i.e., preventing polyspermy.

questions.q: What is released during acrosomal reaction that facilitates fertilization?
questions.e: The acrosome releases hydrolytic enzymes (acrosin, hyaluronidase, etc.), not hormones.

questions.q: The placenta forms from which of the following?
questions.e: The placenta is built from the maternal decidua basalis and the foetal chorion frondosum — decidua capsularis has no placental role.

questions.q: At what stage of early development or how many days post fertilization, does implantation occur?
questions.e: Implantation begins around day 5–7 post-fertilization, once the blastocyst has hatched and attaches to the endometrium.

questions.q: Which hormone is directly responsible for achievement and maintenance of implantation?
questions.e: hCG rescues and sustains the corpus luteum, which secretes the progesterone needed to make and keep the endometrium receptive — together these two hormones achieve and maintain implantation.

questions.q: During development, which of the following cavities is the first to form or appear?
questions.e: The blastocyst cavity forms first (around day 5), well before the amniotic cavity, yolk sac, or chorionic cavity/extraembryonic coelom (all week 2 structures).

questions.q: Which of the structures classified as foetal membranes is formed in conjunction with the formation of the chorionic cavity?
questions.e: As the extraembryonic coelom (chorionic cavity) forms around day 12–13, the primary yolk sac pinches off and reforms as the (secondary/definitive) yolk sac at the same time.

questions.q: In cervix self-examination (CSE) when a woman learns to determine whether or not she is in the fertile phase of her menstrual cycle, ALL of the following features are positive indicators of fertility, EXCEPT that the cervix must be:
o: Soft to the touch like the lip as compared to the tip of the nose
Easy to reach through the vagina with a finger
questions.e: During the fertile phase the cervix actually rises higher in the vagina, making it HARDER (not easier) to reach — 'easy to reach' is a feature of the infertile phase, not the fertile one.

questions.q: Which of the features below characterize the cervix of a woman who is in the infertile stage of her menstrual cycle.
o: Its entrance is relatively narrow or 'closed'
It is difficult to reach with a finger through the vagina.
It feels soft to the touch like the lip compared to the tip of the nose.
questions.e: During the infertile phase the cervix is low, firm ('like the tip of the nose'), and closed — the standard mnemonic is Low/Firm/Closed/Dry.

questions.q: In natural conception, which of the following is NOT a requirement with respect to spermatozoa?
o: Resistance to normal acidity of vaginal fluid.
Unidirectional movement in a straight line.
questions.e: Fertile sperm need NORMAL morphology, resistance to vaginal acidity, straight-line motility, adequate numbers, and the ability to acrosome-react — 'morphological abnormality' is the opposite of a requirement.

questions.q: How many oocytes result from the completion of maturation of a single oocyte in a primordial follicle?
questions.e: Unequal cytokinesis at each meiotic division means only one functional ovum results per primordial follicle (the rest become non-functional polar bodies).

questions.q: The functions of the umbilical cord includes ALL of the following, EXCEPT:
o: Provides direct conduit for nutrients to pass from mother to foetus.
Forms a sheath that protects umbilical vessels.
Connects the foetus to the placenta.
questions.e: Nutrient/gas exchange actually happens across the placental villi, not the cord itself — the cord simply carries the vessels that connect the foetus to the placenta.

questions.q: The blood-testis barrier is formed between which of the following when they are adjacent?
o: Type A and Type B spermatogonia
Sertoli cell and another Sertoli cell
Seminiferous tubule and another seminiferous tubule
questions.e: The blood-testis barrier is built from tight junctions between adjacent Sertoli cells.

questions.q: The chorion of an embryo is composed of which of the following?
questions.e: The chorion is made up of both trophoblast layers plus the extraembryonic mesoderm lining them.

questions.q: What is the biological basis for menopause?
o: Females are born with all their oocytes in meiosis
Females are born with a finite number of oocytes
Meiotic division does not allow for production of additional cells.
All oocytes in a female neonate have been arrested in the 2nd prophase
questions.e: This item is really phrased as i-iv statements (see options): i) true — oocytes are arrested in meiosis I from before birth; ii) true — the ovarian reserve is fixed at birth, never replenished; iii) true — since no new oogonia form after birth, meiosis can't create additional oocytes; iv) false (arrest is in PROPHASE I, not a '2nd prophase'). The correct combination is i, ii and iii only — closest to option B, which captures the fixed-number-at-birth basis for menopause.

questions.q: Which of the following are functions of the testis? i. Secretion of testesterone ii. Manufacture of male germ cells iii. Secretion of luteinising hormone iv. Secretion of follicle stimulating hormone v. Secretion of testicular fluid
questions.e: The testis secretes testosterone, produces germ cells, and secretes testicular fluid (i, ii, v). LH and FSH are pituitary gonadotrophins, not testicular secretions.

questions.q: Which of the following are functions of Sertoli cells? i. Formation of the blood-testis barrier ii. They engineer the release of the late spermatids iii. Secretion of Androgen Binding Protein iv. Responsible for phagocytosis v. Secretion of testicular fluid
questions.e: Sertoli cells do all five: form the blood-testis barrier, mediate spermiation, secrete androgen-binding protein and testicular fluid, and phagocytose residual bodies/degenerating germ cells.

questions.q: Which of the following are functions of the ovaries? i. Secretion of oestrogen ii. Manufacture of female germ cells iii. Secretion of relaxin iv. Secretion of follicle stimulating hormone v. Secretion of testicular fluid
questions.e: Ovaries secrete oestrogen, house/produce female germ cells, and (via the corpus luteum) secrete relaxin. FSH is pituitary; 'testicular fluid' is a Sertoli cell secretion and doesn't apply to the ovary.

questions.q: Which of the following are functions of the uterine tube? i. Provides a site for fertilization ii. Transports both male and female germ cells iii.
