Provides a suitable environment for growth and development of the preimplantation embryo iv. Transports the fertilized ovum to the uterus v. Provides nutritive support for the preimplantation embryo
questions.e: The uterine tube does all five of these — it is fertilization site, dual-gamete transport route, supportive environment, conduit to the uterus, and nutrient source for the early embryo.

questions.q: In evaluating an infertile marriage which of the listed qualities of spermatozoa are relevant? i. Number or count ii. Motility or movement iii. Proportion with big or small heads. iv. Morphology or shape v. Coagulation time
questions.e: The core WHO semen-analysis parameters for sperm quality are count, motility, and morphology (i, ii, iv). Head-size proportion largely duplicates morphology, and coagulation time is a seminal-plasma property rather than a sperm-specific quality.

questions.q: Which of the following characterize an infertile marriage? i. Absence of pregnancy after one year. ii. Adoption of right position during coitus. iii. Appropriate timing of coitus. iv. Regular coitus without contraception. v. Absence of orgasm in female partner during coitus.
questions.e: The clinical definition centres on regular, appropriately timed, unprotected intercourse for a year without pregnancy (i, iii, iv). Coital position and female orgasm are not part of the definition.

questions.q: In humans, there are 23 chromosomes in a haploid cell. Which of the following spermatogenic cells are haploid? (i) Spermatozoon (ii) Spermatid (iii) Secondary spermatocyte (iv) Primary spermatocyte (v) Type B spermatogonium
questions.e: Everything from the secondary spermatocyte onward (secondary spermatocyte, spermatid, spermatozoon) is haploid, having already passed through meiosis I. Primary spermatocytes and spermatogonia are still diploid.

questions.q: Which of the following may account for an infertile marriage of two partners who are individually fertile? i. Regular vaginal douching immediately after coitus. ii. Regularly poor coital timing. iii. Excessive vaginal acidity. iv. Premature ejaculation of male partner. v. Immune reaction of female to partner's spermatozoa.
questions.e: Every one of these can create a 'combined' infertility even when each partner is individually fertile: douching flushes out sperm, poor timing misses the fertile window, excessive acidity kills sperm, premature ejaculation prevents proper deposition, and sperm-antibody reactions attack the partner's own sperm.

questions.q: Ethical issues associated with assisted reproductive technology (ART) include the following. i. Unnecessary manipulation of female reproductive system. ii. Anonymity or otherwise of gamete donors. iii. Post-menopausal (grandmother) pregnancies. iv. Harvesting of oocytes from poor women and underpaying them. v. Overuse of specific sperm donors leading to excessive numbers of children.
o: ii, iii, iv, and v only.
questions.e: All five are genuine, widely-discussed ethical concerns raised about ART.

questions.q: Why must an obstetrician be concerned when examination of a delivered placenta shows missing tissue, likely to have been retained in the uterus?
o: Retained tissue may interfere with myometrial contraction
Possibility of infection when retained tissue rots
Proliferation of retained tissue may give rise to choriocarcinoma.
questions.e: Retained placental tissue can impair uterine contraction (leading to PPH), cause infection, and rarely undergo malignant change — all are legitimate concerns.

questions.q: Which is the event that directly causes the placenta to detach and be expelled from the uterine wall during the third stage of labour?
o: Inability of the placenta to accommodate itself on a decreased surface area as the uterus shrinks in size.
Rupture of the hydrostatic wedge of amniotic membrane that dilates the cervix.
Ligation and cutting of the umbilical cord
Traction exerted on it whilst the baby is being expelled from the uterus.
Cessation of blood supply to the placental bed after the baby has been delivered.
questions.e: After delivery the uterus continues contracting and its wall shrinks, but the relatively non-elastic placenta cannot shrink to match — this mismatch is what shears it off the wall.

questions.q: Which layer of the endometrium is totally eroded by the placenta at its site of attachment?
questions.e: Trophoblast invasion at the implantation site completely erodes the compact layer directly overlying it.

questions.q: During delivery of the placenta, in which layer of the endometrium does it separate from the deciduas?
questions.e: Placental separation occurs along a cleavage plane through the spongy layer, leaving the basal layer intact to regenerate the endometrium.

questions.q: Which is the focal point in the caudal region of the embryo where ectoderm and endoderm remain in direct contact after gastrulation?
questions.e: The prochordal plate (cranial bilaminar area, becomes the oropharyngeal membrane) has its caudal counterpart in the cloacal membrane.

questions.q: Which of the following forms the floor of the amniotic cavity?
questions.e: The embryonic ectoderm (epiblast) forms the floor of the amniotic cavity; the amnion proper forms its roof/walls.

questions.q: Which of the following structures becomes partly enclosed within the body stalk (umbilical cord).
questions.e: As the umbilical cord forms, the vitelline duct/stalk (connecting to the yolk sac) becomes partly enclosed within it as a remnant structure.

questions.q: Which embryonic process involves morphogenetic movement of cells? (second appearance)
questions.e: As in Q54, gastrulation is the process defined by large-scale morphogenetic cell movement.

questions.q: Which decidua is NOT in direct contact with any trophoblast throughout embryonic development?
questions.e: Decidua parietalis lines the rest of the uterine cavity away from the implantation site and never touches trophoblast; capsularis and basalis both do.

questions.q: When extraembryonic mesoderm forms, which cavity does it directly obliterate?
questions.e: The proliferation of extraembryonic mesoderm (and the coelom that splits within it) displaces and obliterates the original blastocyst cavity.

questions.q: Capacitation of spermatozoa involves which of the following?
o: Removal of specific glycoproteins from membrane covering acrosomal cap.
Perforations in membrane covering acrosomal cap.
Release of proteases from acrosomal cap.
Detachment of acrosomal cap to expose membrane covering sperm head.
questions.e: Capacitation itself is the surface 'unmasking' step (glycoprotein removal). The perforation/protease release/cap detachment described in B–D are events of the later acrosomal reaction, not capacitation.

questions.q: The average duration of gestation measured from the first day of the last normal menstrual period (LNMP) is
o: Determined by adding nine months to the first day of the LNMP
questions.e: Average gestation counted from LNMP is 40 weeks (Naegele's rule — LNMP + 9 months + 7 days — is just the method used to estimate that same ~40-week duration).

questions.q: Syncytiotrophoblast
o: gives rise to the decidua basalis
begins to develop on the 4th day after fertilization
is derived from the zona pellucida
degenerates once cytotrophoblast takes over its function
questions.e: The syncytiotrophoblast is the hCG-secreting layer of the trophoblast. It is derived from the cytotrophoblast (not the zona pellucida), begins forming around day 6 (not day 4), and persists throughout pregnancy rather than degenerating — decidua basalis is maternal tissue, not derived from trophoblast at all.

questions.q: Concerning the first week of development
o: Implantation usually occurs 12-24 hours after the morula enters the uterus
The morula forms within the uterine tube and enters the uterine lumen on the 5th day after fertilization
At the time of implantation, the embryo has reached the blastocyst stage
The extraembryonic mesoderm makes contact with the zona pellucida on the 5th day after fertilization
questions.e: By the time implantation begins the conceptus has reached and hatched from the blastocyst stage — this is the one unambiguously correct statement here.

questions.q: Concerning the second week of development
o: The embryoblast splits into two layers within primary ectoderm and primary endoderm
The amniotic cavity develops within the epiblast as a layer of cells derived from the hypoblast
The extraembryonic mesoderm results from the formation of several mitotic divisions
Oogenesis is completed only after fertilization occurs
Spermatogenesis is completed only after fertilization occurs
questions.e: Week 2 is exactly when the embryoblast reorganises into the bilaminar germ disc (epiblast/primary ectoderm and hypoblast/primary endoderm).

questions.q: What is the major difference between spermatogenesis and oogenesis?
o: Spermatogenesis begins while the male foetus is in the uterus.
Oogenesis results in the formation of one viable ovum instead of four viable sperm
Oogenesis is the result of several mitotic divisions
Oogenesis is completed only before fertilization occurs
Spermatogenesis is completed only after fertilization occurs
questions.e: The classic distinguishing fact: unequal cytokinesis in oogenesis yields just one functional ovum (plus non-functional polar bodies) per primary oocyte, whereas each primary spermatocyte yields four equally functional spermatozoa. (Note: it's actually oogenesis, not spermatogenesis, that begins in fetal life — spermatogenesis only starts at puberty.)

questions.q: Which part of the uterus receives the embryo and provides nourishment until the placenta is formed?
questions.e: The endometrium (its secretory-phase lining) is what receives and nourishes the early conceptus before the placenta takes over.

questions.q: From a hormonal standpoint, why is the first day of a new cycle counted as the first day of bleeding rather than as the end of the previous cycle?
o: Hormone secretion from the pituitary peaks at day 1 and causes menstruation
Menstrual flow is a distinct, easily-identified marker of the point where falling progesterone/oestrogen withdraws negative feedback and a new follicular (FSH) drive begins
Without feedback, hormones are no longer under ovarian negative feedback
The cycle is overestimated with ovulation, so each time ovulation occurs the cycle resets
The first day of bleeding is the first day after the LH surge
questions.e: The fall in progesterone (and oestrogen) as the corpus luteum regresses removes negative feedback on the pituitary, letting FSH rise again to start the next follicular wave — bleeding is simply the clear, outwardly observable marker of that hormonal reset, unlike ovulation which isn't directly observable.

questions.q: Where in the male reproductive system would you expect to find the most numerous spermatozoa?
o: In the head of the epididymis
In the ductus deferens and ejaculatory duct
questions.e: The seminiferous tubules are where every sperm cell originates and where, cumulatively, cells at every stage of spermatogenesis are present at once — giving the greatest total number of spermatozoa-lineage cells of any single site (sperm are only concentrated for storage later, in the epididymal tail/vas deferens).

questions.q: Human egg and sperm are similar in that
o: About the same number of each is produced per month
They have the same degree of motility
They have the same number of chromosomes
They are about the same size
questions.e: Egg and sperm are wildly different in size, motility, and production numbers — but both are haploid, carrying 23 chromosomes each.

questions.q: Follicle with a zona pellucida and a simple cuboidal epithelium
questions.e: A single layer of cuboidal granulosa cells plus a visible zona pellucida marks the primary unilaminar follicle.

questions.q: Follicle with a simple squamous epithelium
questions.e: A flat, single squamous layer around the oocyte, with no zona pellucida yet, is the primordial follicle — the resting/earliest stage.

questions.q: Follicle with a stratified epithelium and theca folliculi
questions.e: Multiple granulosa layers plus a developing theca folliculi define the primary multilaminar follicle.

questions.q: Primary multilaminar follicle
questions.e: Named directly in the description.

questions.q: Follicle with an antrum
questions.e: Development of a fluid-filled antrum marks progression to the antral/Graafian (tertiary) stage.

questions.q: Structure with granulosa lutein cells
questions.e: Granulosa cells luteinize after ovulation to form the corpus luteum.

questions.q: Structure with cumulous oophorus
questions.e: The cumulus oophorus (the mound of granulosa cells surrounding the oocyte) is a feature of the mature Graafian follicle.

questions.q: Leads to the development of a morula and then a blastocyst.
questions.e: Repeated mitotic divisions of the zygote without growth — cleavage — produce the morula, then the blastocyst.

questions.q: Leads to the formation of trophoblast cells.
questions.e: Trophoblast first differentiates from the outer cells of the morula/early blastocyst, as part of cleavage-stage development.

questions.q: Involves apposition, adhesion and penetration.
questions.e: These are the three classic sequential stages of implantation.

questions.q: Embedding of the blastocyst in the uterine wall.
questions.e: This is the definition of implantation.

questions.q: Leads to the formation of the first cell of the new individual.
questions.e: Fertilization creates the zygote — the first cell of the new individual.

questions.q: Leads to the establishment of the three primary germ layers.
questions.e: Gastrulation establishes ectoderm, mesoderm and endoderm.

questions.q: Appositional growth of cartilage is:
o: The secretion of new matrix against the external face of existing cartilage
questions.e: Appositional growth adds new matrix/cells onto the existing outer surface of cartilage from the perichondrium.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best describes interstitial growth?
o: Growth occurs in the lining of the long bones
Fibroblasts give rise to chondrocytes that differentiate and form cartilage
Unspecialized cells from mesenchyme develop into chondrocytes, which divide and form cartilage
Chondrocytes in the lacunae divide and secrete matrix, allowing the cartilage to grow from within
questions.e: Interstitial growth = chondrocytes within lacunae divide, expanding cartilage from the inside.

questions.q: In the epiphyseal plate, cartilage grows:
o: By pulling the diaphysis towards the epiphysis
By pushing the epiphysis away from the diaphysis
From the osteoblasts of the diaphysis
questions.e: Interstitial growth at the plate pushes the epiphysis further from the diaphysis, lengthening the bone.

questions.q: Spongy bones are made up of a framework called
questions.e: Spongy (cancellous) bone consists of a lattice of trabeculae.

questions.q: Osteogenesis is the process of
o: Making a cartilage model of the fetal bone
Making collagen fibers for calcified cartilage
questions.e: Osteogenesis literally means bone formation.

questions.q: Lengthwise, long bone growth during infancy and youth is exclusively through
o: Interstitial growth of the epiphyseal plates
The secretion of bone matrix into the medullary cavity
questions.e: Longitudinal growth happens at the epiphyseal (growth) plate via interstitial cartilage growth.

questions.q: Growth of bones is controlled by a symphony of hormones. Which hormone is important for bone growth during infancy and childhood?
questions.e: Growth hormone (via somatomedins/IGF-1) drives childhood bone growth.

questions.q: In some cases the epiphyseal plate of the long bones of children closes too early. What might be the cause?
o: Too much vitamin D in the diet
questions.e: A surge in sex hormones (puberty) accelerates plate closure, ending longitudinal growth early.

questions.q: Normal bone formation and growth are dependent on the adequate intake of
o: Sodium, potassium, phosphate and vitamin E
questions.e: Calcium and phosphate are the mineral substrate; vitamin D enables their intestinal absorption.

questions.q: Ostealgia is
o: Defect in the formation of bone tissue
questions.e: '-algia' = pain; ostealgia = bone pain.

questions.q: Calcium's importance to the body is primarily
o: To function in numerous metabolic activities (muscle contraction, blood coagulation, etc.)
questions.e: While calcium does strengthen bone, its primary systemic importance is in metabolic signalling/function.

questions.q: In a patient whose parathyroid glands have been removed, you would expect his blood calcium levels to
questions.e: No PTH → less bone resorption/renal reabsorption of calcium → blood calcium falls (hypocalcemia).

questions.q: Which two hormones work in opposition to control homeostatic blood levels of calcium via bone remodeling?
questions.e: PTH raises blood calcium; calcitonin lowers it — a classic antagonistic pair.

questions.q: The primary metabolic signal that triggers bone deposition is
questions.e: Vitamin D (via calcitriol) is the key regulatory signal promoting calcium handling for bone deposition.

questions.q: Epithelial tissue
o: Contains a number of neuron types
questions.e: Epithelium is avascular but always sits on a basement membrane.

questions.q: Which of the following would be of most importance to goblet cells and other glandular epithelium?
questions.e: Golgi apparatus packages the mucus/secretory product these cells produce.

questions.q: Mammary glands exhibit a glandular arrangement called
questions.e: Mammary glands are compound alveolar (acinar) exocrine glands.

questions.q: What feature characterizes simple columnar epithelium of the digestive tract?
questions.e: The absorptive brush border of dense microvilli is characteristic of gut simple columnar epithelium.

questions.q: Pseudostratified columnar ciliated epithelium
o: Is exclusive to the male reproductive tract
questions.e: Classic respiratory epithelium — cilia + goblet cells, lining the airway.

questions.q: Which of the following is a single-celled layer of epithelium that forms the lining of serous membranes?
questions.e: Mesothelium (lining serous membranes) is simple squamous epithelium.

questions.q: Which tissue type arises from all three embryonic germ layers?
questions.e: Epithelium arises from ectoderm, mesoderm, and endoderm depending on location.

questions.q: How is hyaline cartilage different from elastic or fibrocartilage?
questions.e: Hyaline cartilage's collagen II fibrils are fine and not visible by light microscopy, unlike elastic/fibrocartilage.

questions.q: Which of the following statements best describes connective tissue?
o: Usually contains a large amount of matrix
Always arranged in a single layer of cells
questions.e: Connective tissue is defined by an abundant extracellular matrix relative to its cells.

questions.q: Extracellular Matrix is composed of
questions.e: ECM = fibers (collagen/elastic/reticular) + ground substance.

questions.q: The following cell types are likely to be seen in areolar connective tissue except
questions.e: Chondroblasts belong to cartilage, not loose areolar connective tissue.

questions.q: The fiber type that gives connective tissue great tensile strength is
questions.e: Collagen fibers resist tension/pulling forces.

questions.q: The shape of the external ear is maintained by
questions.e: The pinna's flexible, springy shape comes from elastic cartilage.

questions.q: Which of the following statements is true concerning muscle tissue?
o: Contains contractile units made of collagen
questions.e: Muscle tissue is densely cellular and richly supplied with blood vessels to meet metabolic demand.

questions.q: The first step in tissue repair involves
o: Replacement of destroyed tissue by the same kind of cells
questions.e: Repair begins with the inflammatory phase (vasodilation, permeability, immune cell influx).

questions.q: Select the correct statement (fiber properties):
o: Elastin fibers are sometimes called white fibers
When connective tissue is stretched, collagen gives it the ability to snap back
Collagen fibers provide high tensile strength
Reticular fibers form thick, rope-like structures
Ground substance is thick and semi-rigid
questions.e: Collagen = high tensile strength (elastin, not collagen, gives 'snap-back'; collagen is the 'white fiber').

questions.q: Select the correct statement regarding the cells of connective tissue.
o: Connective tissue does not contain cells
Chondroblasts are the main cell type of connective tissue proper
'Blast' cells are undifferentiated, actively dividing cells
questions.e: '-blast' suffix cells (fibroblasts, chondroblasts, osteoblasts) are the actively dividing, matrix-producing precursors.

questions.q: Select the correct statement regarding factors that affect the tissue repair process.
o: The type of tissue injured is not an important factor
Nutrition does not seem to influence tissue repair
The age of the person is a factor in the repair process
The health of an individual does not make any difference to speed of repair
Only connective tissue is important in the repair process
questions.e: Older age generally slows tissue repair.

questions.q: Goblet cells are found in each of the following organs except the
questions.e: Gastric surface mucous cells (not true goblet cells) line the stomach; goblet cells are absent there.

questions.q: Which organelle works closely with the endoplasmic reticulum in protein synthesis?
questions.e: Ribosomes (on rough ER) synthesize the proteins the ER processes.

questions.q: Acid phosphatase can be used as a chemical marker for the identification of centrifugal fractions of
questions.e: Acid phosphatase is a classic lysosomal enzyme marker.

questions.q: Elastic cartilage is found in each of the following except the
questions.e: Intervertebral discs are fibrocartilage, not elastic cartilage.

questions.q: The presence of microvilli and cilia on a cell usually indicates that it functions in
questions.e: Microvilli increase absorptive surface area; cilia provide motility of surface fluid/particles.

questions.q: Which of the following best describes the term sarcoplasmic reticulum?
o: Protein that accounts for elasticity of resting muscle
Storage and release site for calcium ions
questions.e: The SR is a specialized smooth ER that sequesters and releases Ca²⁺ for contraction.

questions.q: The function of a cell that has a basophilic cytoplasm, an eccentric nucleus and a postnuclear Golgi apparatus is
questions.e: This describes a plasma cell — an antibody-secreting factory.

questions.q: The correct sequential order of the components of a junctional complex is
o: A zonula occludens, a zonula adherens and a desmosome
A gap junction, a hemidesmosome and a tight junction
A tight junction, a hemidesmosome and a terminal web
A tight junction, a macula adherens and a terminal web
A zonula occludens, a macula adherens, a hemidesmosome and a gap junction
questions.e: Apex-to-base order: tight junction (zonula occludens) → zonula adherens → desmosome (macula adherens).

questions.q: Osteocytes of spongy bone are
o: Located within the organic bone matrix
questions.e: Spongy bone lacks Haversian systems; osteocytes are nourished via canaliculi from surface, not internal vessels.

questions.q: Specializations of surface epithelial cells that permit passage of small molecular-weight particles through the membranes of contiguous cells are
o: Are not known to exist in humans
questions.e: Gap junctions form channels (connexons) allowing small molecules/ions to pass directly between adjacent cells.

questions.q: Microscopically visible manifestations of the presence of desmosomes are best seen with the light microscope in tissue sections of the
questions.e: Desmosomes appear as 'intercellular bridges'/prickles between epidermal (skin) cells.

questions.q: Tissue macrophages are
o: Highly phagocytic and rich in lysosomes
questions.e: Macrophages are avid phagocytes, packed with lysosomes for digesting engulfed material.

questions.q: Regarding the sarcoplasmic reticulum, which of the following is true?
o: Is part of the neuromuscular junction
Is more abundant in cardiac than skeletal muscle
Releases calcium which allows actin to interact with myosin
questions.e: SR releases Ca²⁺, which binds troponin and permits actin–myosin cross-bridge formation.

questions.q: Long bones are the site of:
questions.e: Long bones store fat (yellow marrow), form blood cells (red marrow) and store minerals.

questions.q: The most generalized type of connective tissue with the greatest variety of connective tissue components is/are:
o: Reticular connective tissue and loose connective tissue
Dense regular connective tissue and hyaline cartilage
questions.e: Loose (areolar) connective tissue contains the widest variety of cell types and fibers.

questions.q: Connective tissue fibers and glycosaminoglycans (acid mucopolysaccharides) are synthesized by:
o: Plasma cells, fibroblasts and reticular cells
questions.e: Fibroblasts are the sole synthesizers of both fibers and ground substance in connective tissue proper.

questions.q: Appositional growth of cartilage:
o: Enhances the differentiation of chondroblasts to chondroclasts
Causes clones of chondrocytes to form within the core of the cartilage
Adds matrix to cartilage, but not cells
Occurs from the chondrogenic layer of the perichondrium as well as the interstitial chondrocytes
Is the differentiation of chondrocytes from mesenchyme
questions.e: Cartilage grows both appositionally (from the perichondrium's chondrogenic layer) and interstitially (existing chondrocytes).

questions.q: Aponeuroses:
o: Are filament sheets of dense connective tissue
Are composed to muscle fibers or shape
Are composed of collagenous bundles and fibroblasts
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Aponeuroses are broad, flat sheets of dense connective tissue continuous with muscle.

questions.q: Aponeuroses:
o: Are classified as regular dense connective tissue
Are similar to tendons in their structural organization
Are classified as irregular dense connective tissue
questions.e: Aponeuroses are dense regular connective tissue, structurally similar to tendons but sheet-shaped.

questions.q: You are given an epithelium from an unknown location; the epithelium has microvilli and cilia. This epithelium
o: Was involved with secretion or absorption
Was normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses
Is from a surface where both absorption and motility are required
Is from a chamber that changes its volume continually
questions.e: Co-existing microvilli (absorption) and cilia (motility) point to a surface needing both — e.g. the oviduct/efferent ductules.

questions.q: On the border separating epithelial cells from connective tissue can be found:
o: Tight junctions, adhering junctions and hemidesmosomes
Gap junctions and zonula adherens only
questions.e: Hemidesmosomes anchor epithelial cells to the basal lamina; desmosomes link adjacent epithelial cells.

questions.q: Striated (brush) borders of tightly packed microvilli are typically found lining the:
questions.e: The proximal convoluted tubule of the kidney has a prominent microvillous brush border for reabsorption.

questions.q: Which of the following statements regarding epithelial tissues is false?
o: Junctional complexes are found at numerous sites between adjacent epithelial cells
Stereocilia are extremely long forms of microvilli
The principal function of microvilli is to greatly increase the surface area of cells
Desmosomes are sites of strong intercellular adhesion and provide points of attachment for elements of the cytoskeleton
Cilia constitute the characteristic brush border of the small intestine
questions.e: The small intestine's brush border is made of microvilli, not cilia — this statement is false.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location showed 3 layers of cells that were taller than wide, with cells lacking surface specialization. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
o: Prostatic urethra, membranous urethra and ureter
Ureter, spongy urethra and prostatic urethra
Membranous urethra and fossa navicularis of the penis
questions.e: This describes stratified columnar epithelium, found in the spongy and membranous urethra.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium from an unknown location revealed cells that were taller than wide, appeared to be more than one cell layer thick, all cells attached to the basement membrane, some had cilia, and goblet cells were also present. This epithelium is most likely to be located in the:
o: Nasal cavity, larynx and secondary bronchi
Trachea, membranous urethra and vas deferens
Primary bronchi, terminal bronchioles and the epiglottis
Penile urethra, primary bronchi and respiratory bronchioles
questions.e: This describes pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium — classic respiratory tract lining.

questions.q: Examination of three specimens: A from a chamber that changes its volume continually, B from a surface where both absorption and secretion are required, C from an internal surface where friction may occur. Specimens A, B, C were obtained from:
o: Urinary bladder, ileum and vagina respectively
Vas deferens, small intestine and pharynx respectively
Ureter, ductuli efferentes and cornea respectively
Penile urethra, jejunum, laryngeal surface of epiglottis respectively
questions.e: Bladder = transitional (volume change); ileum = simple columnar (absorption/secretion); vagina = stratified squamous (friction).

questions.q: Examination of three specimens: A from a surface normally subjected to severe mechanical stresses, B from a surface where filtration or diffusion occurs, C from an internal chamber where absorption and motility are required. Specimens A, B, C were obtained from:
o: Filiform papillae of tongue, parietal layer of renal corpuscle and vagina respectively
Hard palate, respiratory bronchioles and oesophagus respectively
Skin, alveoli of lungs, efferent ductules respectively
Soles of feet, visceral layer of renal corpuscle and oesophagus respectively
Filiform papillae of tongue, endothelium of blood vessels and skin respectively
questions.e: Skin = stratified squamous (mechanical stress); alveoli = simple squamous (diffusion); efferent ductules = ciliated + absorptive.

questions.q: Transitional epithelium prevents urine from leaking out of the urinary bladder due to its:
questions.e: Tight junctions between the umbrella cells create a watertight barrier.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the lymphatic system
o: Body immunity and filtration of lymph
Absorption of fats and collection of cellular debris
Drainage of tissue fluid and production of lymphocytes
questions.e: The lymphatic system performs immunity/filtration, fat absorption, and fluid drainage/lymphocyte production — all three.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the skeletal system
o: Mineral storage and attachment of muscles
Protection, production of blood cells and filtration of blood
questions.e: The skeleton performs mineral storage, muscle attachment, haematopoiesis, protection and support — all listed.

questions.q: The following functions are performed by the female reproductive system
o: Production of ova and hormones and elimination of nitrogenous waste products
Provision of a site for fertilization and implantation
Nourishment and development of the preimplantation embryo
questions.e: Elimination of nitrogenous waste (option A's second half) is a urinary, not reproductive, function — so only B & C hold.

questions.q: The muscular system:
o: Is responsible for locomotion and facial expression
questions.e: All listed functions (manipulation, locomotion/expression, posture, heat production) belong to the muscular system.

questions.q: Excretory glands are classified as simple branched tubular and merocrine by the:
o: Types of secretory products and mechanism of secretion
Shape of secretory units and types of ducts only
Presence or absence of ducts and mechanism of secretion
Mechanism of secretion and shape of secretory units
Nature of the ducts, shape of secretory unit and mechanism of secretion
questions.e: Glands are classified by duct structure, secretory unit shape, and secretion mechanism together.

questions.q: Merocrine secretion from cells of exocrine glands:
o: Involves exocytosis via the apical membrane of cells
Involves secretion of part of the apical cytoplasm of cells
Involves secretion of whole cells and their contents
questions.e: Merocrine = eccrine secretion, achieved via exocytosis at the apical membrane — both A and B are correct.

questions.q: Regarding hyaline cartilage, which statement is accurate?
o: It has a smooth appearance and contains abundant ground substance and isogenous groups of chondrocytes
It contains more elastic fibres than collagen type II fibres, found in the thyroid, cricoid and corniculate cartilages of the larynx
It contains collagen type I fibres, few chondrocytes arranged in rows, and a fluid small ground substance
Its chondrocytes occur singly and it forms the epiglottis and cuneiform cartilage exclusively
It never contains isogenous groups of chondrocytes
questions.e: Hyaline cartilage: smooth matrix, abundant ground substance, chondrocytes typically in isogenous clusters (from interstitial growth).

questions.q: The functions of the nervous system include the following
o: Responds to internal and external changes
Regulates processes such as growth and reproduction
Transport of hormones and regulation of water content of the body
questions.e: Responding to internal/external stimuli is the defining nervous system function (B, D, E describe endocrine functions).

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium revealed cells taller than wide, more than one cell layer thick, all attached to the basement membrane, some with extensive apical microvilli. Goblets cells and cilia were absent, and the epithelium contained some bipolar neurons. This epithelium is most likely to be:
o: Located in the olfactory and respiratory segments
A modified type of respiratory epithelium with sensory neurons
A, B and C are correct
questions.e: Bipolar neurons + microvilli + pseudostratified structure without goblets/cilia = olfactory epithelium, a modified respiratory-type epithelium.

questions.q: Examination of an epithelium revealed several layers of cells; only the basal layer was attached to the basement membrane. Basal cells were taller than wide, intermediate layers had polyhedral cells, and superficial cell nuclei were flattened. Superficial cells were covered with an eosinophilic translucent, anucleated band; parts of the surface had fibrillar, anucleated, eosinophilic structures. Goblet cells, cilia, microvilli, and stereocilia were absent. This epithelium is most likely located in:
o: Tongue, soft palate, oral surface of lips and anal canal
In an internal environment subject to abrasion or the external environment
questions.e: This describes stratified squamous (keratinized in parts) epithelium — found wherever abrasion protection is needed, internally or externally.

questions.q: A specimen with a delicate meshwork of cells and fibres that are argyrophilic is:
o: Collagen type III in the spleen and lymph nodes
Reticular connective of the lymph nodes and thymus
Collagen type I in the red bone marrow and kidney
Collagen type II in the liver and lung
questions.e: Reticular fibers (collagen type III) are argyrophilic and form the stromal meshwork of the spleen and lymph nodes.

questions.q: You are given cartilage from an unknown location. You think it is from the pinna of the ear or the epiglottis because:
o: It contains alternating layers of collagen fibers and chondrocytes
It contains hyaline cartilage with chondrocytes that occur singly
Numerous chondroblasts are arranged into isogenous groups
questions.e: The pinna and epiglottis are made of elastic cartilage.

questions.q: Cartilage is different from bone in that
o: Cartilage contains about 80% water and is more resilient
Cartilage regenerates faster than bone when damaged in the adult skeleton
questions.e: Cartilage matrix is ~70-80% water, giving it resilience; unlike bone it is avascular.

questions.q: The osteon exhibits
o: A central canal containing blood vessels, nerves and osteocytes
Concentric lamellae of matrix and osteocytes in lacunae
Osteocytes in concentric lamellae and canaliculi with osteocyte processes and blood vessels
A central canal containing blood vessels and bony lamellae
A central canal containing osteocytes, canaliculi and nerves
questions.e: The osteon = concentric lamellae with osteocytes in lacunae, linked by canaliculi carrying osteocyte processes, around a central (Haversian) canal with vessels.

questions.q: The organic components of bone matrix are important in providing all but
o: Hardness and ability to resist twisting
Ability to resist twisting and rigidity
Tensile strength and the ability to resist twisting
questions.e: Hardness comes from the inorganic (mineral) component, not the organic (collagen) component.

questions.q: Which of the following relationships between a tissue and its general function is not correct?
questions.e: 'Digestion' is too specific/inaccurate as epithelium's general function (covering/lining/secretion is more accurate).

questions.q: Which of the following terms reflects the epithelial tissue found where all the cells are in contact with the basement membrane although it appears layered?
questions.e: Pseudostratified epithelium: every cell touches the basement membrane despite the false 'layered' appearance.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about epithelia?
o: Simple epithelia are commonly found in areas of high abrasion
Stratified epithelia are associated with filtration
Endothelium provides a slick surface lining all hollow cardiovascular organs
questions.e: Endothelium (simple squamous) lines the entire cardiovascular system, providing a smooth, low-friction surface.

questions.q: Which of the following is true about the mode of secretion of exocrine glands?
o: Merocrine glands are not altered by the secretory process
Apocrine cells are destroyed, then replaced, after secretion
Holocrine cells are slightly damaged by the secretory process but repair themselves
Apocrine cells retain their secretory products
questions.e: Merocrine (eccrine) secretion is via exocytosis only — the cell itself is unaltered.

questions.q: In adults, new surface epithelial cells and the epithelial cells lining the intestine are derived from
o: Mitotic division of existing epithelial cells
Stem cells only, never dividing epithelial cells
questions.e: Epithelium continually renews via mitosis of existing (basal/stem) epithelial cells.

questions.q: Select the correct statement regarding epithelia.
o: Stratified epithelia are tall, narrow cells
Stratified epithelia are present where protection from abrasion is important
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of at least two layers of cells stacked on top of one another
Pseudostratified epithelia consist of several layers of cuboidal cells
questions.e: Stratified epithelia's multiple layers give mechanical protection against abrasion.

questions.q: Select the correct statement regarding multicellular exocrine glands.
o: Compound glands are so called because they are constructed from more than one cell type
The secretory cells of holocrine glands release their product by rupturing
Merocrine glands release their secretion by pinching off part of the cell
Compound glands are always constructed from mucous cells
questions.e: Holocrine secretion (e.g. sebaceous glands) involves whole-cell disintegration to release product.

questions.q: Which of the following is not found in the matrix of cartilage but present in bone?
questions.e: Cartilage matrix is avascular; bone matrix, via Haversian canals, contains blood vessels.

questions.q: Which of the following tissues contains lacunae, calcium salts, and blood vessels?
questions.e: Bone (osseous tissue) uniquely combines lacunae, mineralized matrix, and vascular canals.

questions.q: Which of the following bone tissues is adapted to support weight and withstand tension stress?
questions.e: Dense compact bone forms the shafts of long bones, bearing weight and tension.

questions.q: Yellow bone marrow contains a large percentage of:
questions.e: Yellow marrow is largely fat (adipocytes), inactive in haematopoiesis.

questions.q: The cell responsible for secreting the matrix of bone is the:
questions.e: Osteoblasts actively secrete osteoid (bone matrix); once entrapped in matrix they become osteocytes and largely stop secreting.

questions.q: A deficiency of growth hormone during bone formation causes:
o: Decreased proliferation of the epiphyseal plate cartilage
Increased proliferation of the epiphyseal plate cartilage
questions.e: Without GH, chondrocyte proliferation at the epiphyseal plate slows, stunting growth.

questions.q: Factors in preventing osteoporosis include:
questions.e: Adequate vitamin C supports collagen synthesis, important for bone matrix integrity.

questions.q: Ossification of the ends of long bones:
o: Is a characteristic of intramembranous bone formation
Is produced by secondary ossification centers
Takes twice as long as the diaphysis
Continues throughout the life of an individual
questions.e: Epiphyseal ossification arises from secondary ossification centers within the cartilage model.

questions.q: What is the structural unit of compact bone?
questions.e: The osteon (Haversian system) is compact bone's structural/functional unit.

questions.q: The periosteum is secured to the underlying bone by dense connective tissue called
o: A bony matrix with hyaline cartilage
The struts of bone known as spicules
questions.e: Perforating (Sharpey's) fibers anchor the periosteum firmly into the underlying bone matrix.

questions.q: The canal that runs through the core of each osteon is the site of
questions.e: The central (Haversian) canal houses the blood supply and nerve fibers of the osteon.

questions.q: Osteocytes are housed in
questions.e: Osteocytes occupy small spaces called lacunae within the bone matrix.

questions.q: Cranial bones develop:
questions.e: Cranial bones form by intramembranous ossification, directly within fibrous connective tissue membranes.

questions.q: Which glands/organs produce hormones that tend to decrease blood calcium levels?
questions.e: The thyroid's parafollicular (C) cells secrete calcitonin, which lowers blood calcium.

questions.q: Osteomyelitis is:
o: Partially due to insufficient dietary calcium
Caused by altered vitamin D metabolism
questions.e: Osteomyelitis is a bone infection typically caused by pyogenic (pus-forming) bacteria.

questions.q: Bone is always being reformed to withstand changing stresses on it. Which of the following cells is responsible for the resorption of bone?
questions.e: Osteoclasts are the large, multinucleated cells that resorb bone.

questions.q: Which statement best describes transcytosis?
o: Combining an endosome with a lysosome and degrading or releasing the contents
Transporting an endosome from one side of a cell to the other and releasing the contents by exocytosis
Recycling the contents of the endosome back to the surface of the cell
Storing the contents of the endosome
questions.e: Transcytosis moves material across a cell, endosome-to-endosome, releasing it by exocytosis on the far side.

questions.q: In certain kinds of muscle cells, calcium ions are stored in
questions.e: The sarcoplasmic reticulum — a specialized smooth ER — stores and releases calcium in muscle cells.

questions.q: Which of the following describes the plasma membrane?
o: A single-layered membrane that surrounds the nucleus of the cell
A double layer of protein enclosing the plasma
The phospholipid bilayer surrounding the cell
A membrane composed of tiny shelves or cristae
questions.e: The plasma membrane is fundamentally a phospholipid bilayer enclosing the cell.

questions.q: Which of these is not a function of the plasma membrane?
o: It prevents potassium ions from leaking out and sodium ions from crossing into the cell absolutely
It acts as a site of cell-to-cell interaction and recognition
questions.e: Membranes are selectively permeable, not absolute barriers — ions do cross via channels/transporters.

questions.q: Which structures are fingerlike projections that greatly increase the absorbing surface of cells?
questions.e: Microvilli are the classic surface-area-increasing projections for absorption.

questions.q: Cell junctions that promote the coordinated activity of cells by physically binding them together into a cell community include all of the following except
questions.e: Peroxisomes are metabolic organelles, not intercellular junctions.

questions.q: Which of the following is not a subcellular structure?
questions.e: Intercellular material lies between cells (extracellular), not within a single cell.

questions.q: Once solid material is phagocytized and taken into a vacuole, which of the following statements best describes what happens?
o: A ribosome enters the vacuole and uses the amino acids in the 'invader' to form new protein
A lysosome combines with the vacuole and digests the enclosed solid material
The vacuole remains separated from the cytoplasm and the solid material persists unchanged
Nitrogen enters the vacuole and 'burns' the enclosed solid material
questions.e: Lysosomes fuse with phagosomes to digest the engulfed material via hydrolytic enzymes.

questions.q: Which of the following is a function of a plasma membrane protein?
questions.e: Membrane proteins (channels/carriers) mediate transport of molecules across the membrane.

questions.q: Which of the following would not be a constituent of a plasma membrane?
questions.e: mRNA is not a membrane component; membranes are built from lipids and proteins.

questions.q: Mitosis
o: Is the formation of sex cells
Always results in division of a cell
questions.e: Mitosis replicates the nucleus (and its genetic material) faithfully into two daughter nuclei.

questions.q: The electron microscope has revealed that one of the components within the cell consists of microtubules arranged to form a hollow tube. This structure is a
questions.e: Centrioles are cylindrical structures made of triplet microtubules arranged in a hollow tube.

questions.q: Which of these is an inclusion, not an organelle?
questions.e: Melanin is a pigment (inclusion), not a membrane-bound organelle.

questions.q: Mitochondria
o: Are single-membrane structures involved in the breakdown of ATP
Contain some of the DNA and RNA code necessary for their own function
Synthesize proteins for use outside the cell
questions.e: Mitochondria have their own mtDNA/RNA, a legacy of their endosymbiotic origin.

questions.q: Ribosomes, ER, and the Golgi apparatus functionally act in sequence to synthesize and modify proteins for secretory (export) use only, never for use by the cell. This statement is
o: False, proteins thus manufactured are for use inside the cell only
False, integral cell membrane proteins are also synthesized this way
False, lipids, not proteins, are synthesized this way
questions.e: Membrane proteins are also produced via the rough ER → Golgi pathway, not just secretory proteins.

questions.q: Peroxisomes
o: Are also called microbodies, and contain acid hydrolases
Are able to detoxify substances by enzymatic action
Function to digest particles ingested by endocytosis
questions.e: Peroxisomes contain oxidative enzymes (catalase etc.) that detoxify substances like alcohol and peroxide.

questions.q: DNA replication
o: Is spontaneous, not requiring enzyme action
Takes place during interphase of the cell cycle
Occurs only in translationally active areas
questions.e: DNA replication occurs during the S phase of interphase, before mitosis begins.

questions.q: Which of the following is a concept of the cell theory?
o: Simple cells can arise spontaneously from rotting vegetation
A cell is the basic structural and functional unit of living organisms
The subcellular organelle is the basic unit of life
Only higher organisms are composed of cells
questions.e: Cell theory: the cell is the fundamental unit of structure and function in all living things.

questions.q: Which of the following is a principle of the fluid mosaic model of cell membrane structure?
o: Phospholipids form a bilayer that is largely impermeable to water-soluble molecules
Phospholipids consist of a polar head and a nonpolar tail made of three fatty acid chains
The lipid bilayer is a solid at body temperature, thus protecting the cell
All proteins associated with the cell membrane are contained in a fluid layer on the outside of the cell
questions.e: The hydrophobic bilayer interior blocks water-soluble molecules from freely crossing.

questions.q: The main component of the cytosol is
questions.e: Water makes up the bulk of the cytosol, the fluid medium of the cytoplasm.

questions.q: Lysosomes
o: Are always used for the cell to 'commit suicide'
Contain acid hydrolases that are potentially dangerous to the cell
Maintain a highly alkaline internal environment
Are the major site of protein synthesis
questions.e: Lysosomal hydrolytic enzymes could digest the cell itself if released — hence they're membrane-contained.

questions.q: The endomembrane system is
o: A system by which cells are riveted together by desmosomes
An interactive system of organelles whose membranes are physically or functionally connected
The process by which bacteria took up residence in ancient cells
A system of hydrophilic lipid monolayers that surround many cell organelles
questions.e: The endomembrane system links the nuclear envelope, ER, Golgi, lysosomes and vesicles functionally/physically.

questions.q: The functions of centrioles include
o: Organizing the mitotic spindle in cell division
Providing a whiplike beating motion to move substances along cell surfaces
Serving as the site for ribosomal RNA synthesis
questions.e: Centrioles organize the microtubule spindle apparatus during mitosis.

questions.q: Endocrine glands empty their products into cells.
questions.e: They secrete into the blood/interstitial fluid, not directly into cells.

questions.q: Secretory units of exocrine glands are either tubular or spherical (acinar) in shape.
A gland formed by cells arranged in a blind pocket with a single unbranched duct is termed tubuloacinar.
questions.e: That describes a simple acinar gland, not tubuloacinar.

questions.q: Antiangiogenesis factor is a chemical produced by chondrocytes that blocks the growth of blood vessels.
Tight junctions are abundant in stratified epithelia tissues that are adapted to resist mechanical forces.
Mucous membranes line cavities that communicate with the exterior of the body.
Mucous membranes are responsible for the reduction of friction between the parietal and visceral surfaces of an internal cavity.
questions.e: That is the role of serous membranes, not mucous membranes.

questions.q: Chondroitin sulphate is abundant in the matrix of cartilage.
Cartilage is separated from surrounding tissues by a fibrous periosteum.
questions.e: Cartilage is covered by perichondrium, not periosteum.

questions.q: Dense irregular connective tissue forms the framework or stroma of the spleen, liver, and lymph nodes.
questions.e: Reticular connective tissue forms this stroma, not dense irregular CT.

questions.q: Epithelial tissues always exhibit polarity; that is, they have a free surface and a basal surface.
Simple cuboidal epithelia tissues are usually associated with secretion and absorption.
Stratified cuboidal epithelium is moderately rare in the body and found only in the pharynx, larynx, and anorectal junction.
questions.e: Stratified cuboidal is found mainly in sweat gland ducts, not those locations.

questions.q: Endothelium covers and lines internal cavities such as the pleural and peritoneal cavities.
questions.e: Mesothelium lines these cavities; endothelium lines blood/lymph vessels and the heart.

questions.q: Connective tissues have a high regenerative capacity.
Connective tissues function as binding, supportive, insulatory and protective materials.
Most epithelial tissues do not have the capacity to regenerate.
questions.e: Epithelium regenerates readily/rapidly.

questions.q: Adipocytes contain fat-filled vacuoles that can fill or empty, causing the cell to gain or lose volume.
Tendon tears or breaks are difficult to repair both physiologically and surgically.
Tendons are composed of densely packed parallel connective tissue fibres.
Tendons have relatively few cells and a poor vascular supply consequently, repair is slow in tendons.
Epithelial tissues are avascular sheets with closely packed cells.
All connective tissue has cells that are widely spaced and is highly vascular.
The cells of connective tissue vary greatly in shape and size.
Connective tissue has a large amount of ground substance but epithelial tissue does not contain ground substance.
Blood does not give mechanical support; its matrix is fluid, its cells are loose and the fibres are soluble.
Epithelial cells undergo metastases because they divide more, leading to more spread.
The mesoderm produces muscles and connective tissue.
The endoderm produces all internal organs.
The sweeping action of ciliated epithelium is essential to propel inhaled dust and other debris out of the respiratory tract.
The skin is made up of stratified squamous keratinized epithelium and connective tissue.
Chondroblasts located deep to the perichondrium divide and secrete new matrix on the internal portions of the cartilage.
Chondroblasts never lose their ability to divide.
Chondroblasts are mature cartilage cells located in spaces called lacunae.
questions.e: That describes chondrocytes, not chondroblasts.

questions.q: The secretory cells of holocrine glands release their product by rupturing.
Merocrine glands release their secretion by pinching off part of the cell.
questions.e: That describes apocrine secretion.

questions.q: 'Blast' cells are undifferentiated, actively dividing cells.
Chondroblasts are the main cell type of connective tissue proper.
Muscle tissues and connective tissues share a common embryological origin from mesoderm.
Ground substance is the highly proteinaceous material in which the cells and fibres of connective tissue are embedded.
Hyaluronic acid is the principal constituent of ground substance in soft connective tissues.
Fibroblasts are responsible for the synthesis of collagen and ground substance.
Ligaments connect bones to bones; aponeuroses connect muscles to bone.
Mucous connective tissue supports the surface epithelium of the mucous membranes in the respiratory and gastro-intestinal tracts.
Mesenchyme is the primitive form of connective tissue and the embryological precursor of the soft connective tissues and skeletal tissues.
Elastin fibres resist permanent deformation resulting from normal physiological movements.
Mast cells exhibit the property of metachromasia when stained with certain blue basic dyes.
Mast cells are responsible for the production of certain pharmacological agents in the body for allergic reactions.
Macrophages are capable of phagocytosis of a wide variety of non-specific particulate materials of endogenous and exogenous origin.
Adipose tissue is a specialised form of connective tissue constituting about 35 to 40 percent of body weight in normal human adults.
questions.e: Normal adipose tissue is closer to 15-20% of body weight, not 35-40%.

questions.q: Pseudostratified columnar epithelium is mainly confined to the respiratory and male reproductive tracts in humans.
Stereocilia is solely found in the male reproductive system.
Cilia and microvilli may co-habit in the same epithelial lining, providing motility and an increased surface area for absorption.
The oral cavity is lined by stratified squamous non-keratinised and keratinised epithelium.
Cilia are much longer in length than microvilli, much greater in diameter and far less numerous.
Wharton's jelly is a type of embryonic connective tissue.
Fibroblasts are responsible for the synthesis of the fibrous element of cartilage matrix.
questions.e: Chondroblasts/chondrocytes synthesize cartilage matrix, not fibroblasts.

questions.q: Blood vessels pass through the epiphyseal cartilage to reach the central zone of secondary ossification.
Fibrocartilage typically forms the articular cartilage of synovial joints.
questions.e: Hyaline cartilage typically forms articular cartilage.

questions.q: Calcium hydroxyapatite is the principal mineral component of bone matrix.
Newly calcified bone is termed osteoid.
questions.e: Osteoid is the unmineralized (not newly calcified) organic bone matrix.

questions.q: The medullary cavity of long bones is lined by periosteum and bone marrow.
questions.e: The medullary cavity is lined by endosteum, not periosteum.

questions.q: The expanded ends of long bones which articulate with other bones is termed the epiphysis.
Haversian canals contain blood vessels and cells of the osteogenic series.
Osteocytes usually lie in lacunae within concentric lamellae of compact bone.
Numerous canaliculi convey minute blood vessels to the lacunae within lamellar bone.
questions.e: Canaliculi convey osteocyte processes/tissue fluid, not actual blood vessels.

questions.q: Spongy or cancellous bone consists of many trabeculae of lamellar bone, each invested by endosteum.
The principal function of red bone marrow is to produce erythrocytes.
Yellow bone marrow produces leucocytes and platelets.
Yellow bone marrow is inactive in haematopoiesis and consists mainly of adipocytes.
Yellow bone marrow may be transformed into red marrow when there is a greatly increased demand for erythrocytes.
In human adults, samples of bone marrow could be obtained from the sternum and iliac crests.
Intramembranous ossification involves deposition of woven bone within primitive connective tissue and subsequent remodelling to form lamellar bone.
Endochondral ossification involves the deposition of calcium hydroxyapatite in cartilage matrix and transformation of chondrocytes into osteocytes.
questions.e: Chondrocytes degenerate and die; they do not transform directly into osteocytes.

questions.q: During endochondral ossification the diaphyseal perichondrium becomes transformed into periosteum.
The perichondrium investing articular cartilage protects the articular surfaces against excessive functional stress.
questions.e: Articular cartilage lacks a perichondrium entirely.

questions.q: Synovium lines the inner aspect of the synovial capsule and its surface epithelium is responsible for the production of synovial fluid.
The annulus fibrosus of the intervertebral disc consists of concentric lamellae of dense fibroelastic connective tissue.
Contains undifferentiated connective tissue cells.
Surrounds hyaline cartilage.
Lines articular cartilage.
questions.e: Articular cartilage has no perichondrium covering it.

questions.q: Covers elastic cartilage.
Contains blood vessels.
Found in the central nervous system.
Found in the peripheral nervous system.
Flattened sheets of dense connective tissue.
Connected to muscular sheets.
Composed of collagenous bundles and fibroblasts.
Hyaluronic acid.
Heparin.
Histamine.
Elastic fibers.
Reticular fibers.
Is found on the border separating the external environment from the internal environment of the body.
Is important in homeostasis of the body.
Receives its nutrition from blood capillaries between its cells.
questions.e: Epithelium is avascular — it receives nutrition by diffusion from underlying connective tissue.

questions.q: Participates in the exchange of all the materials that enter or leave the body.
In some sites contains sensory cells.
